AAA: An actively managed fund holding the safest, top-rated slices of CLOs, which are bundles of loans to US companies, and the loans pay interest that moves with short-term rates. It is spread over many CLOs, with each of the largest around 4% or 5%.
AAAA: An actively managed fund of funds that mixes stock ETFs, bond ETFs and downside-protection ETFs to give an aggressive, stock-heavy mix. About 80% is in stocks, led by iShares S&P 100 and Invesco QQQ, with the rest in bonds and protection.
AAAB: US dollar corporate bonds from companies rated A or higher, with less than ten years left to run, following a FTSE index. Higher-rated bonds mean lower default risk than the average corporate bond, and it is non-diversified.
AAAC: An actively managed fund of the top-rated slices, rated AAA, of collateralized loan obligations, which are pools of loans to companies packaged into bonds. It holds many different CLOs, with none above about 4%, so it is an income-focused alternative to ordinary bonds.
AAAD: Holds mostly the AAA rated slices of collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), which are bundles of loans to companies sold as bonds in layers. It aims for a bit more sensitivity to interest rates than a plain short-term CLO fund, and it does so by mainly holding another PGIM fund.
AAAP: Mostly collateralized loan obligations, or CLOs, which are bundles of loans to companies packaged into bonds that pay interest. It is actively managed and spread across many CLOs, none above about 4%, and it can use more flexible approaches than plain CLO funds.
AAAU: Physical gold bars stored in a vault, so you own gold itself rather than mining companies. It's used as a hedge against inflation and market scares, but gold pays no income, and its price can be volatile and stay flat for years.
AADR: US-traded shares of foreign companies, mostly American depositary receipts, picked by a trend-following ranking system called Dorsey Wright. It rotates among stocks it sees as having strong momentum, and holds names like BBVA, Mitsubishi UFJ and Barclays.
AAEQ: A broad mix of US companies, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and health care making up much of the rest. It's a core stock holding, and the managers tilt toward companies with strong financial quality and value traits, so it won't move exactly like the overall market.
AAPR: Gives exposure to the S&P 500 using options, aiming to protect against a set amount of losses over a two-year period ending April 2028. In return, gains are limited, and the protection only fully applies if you hold for the whole period.
AAPW: An actively managed fund that aims for about 1.2 times the weekly return of Apple stock, using swaps and some direct shares, and it pays out income weekly. The Treasury bills it holds are collateral, so this is a leveraged bet on a single stock.
AAPY: Aims for income by using options tied to Apple stock, while keeping some exposure to Apple's price moves. It limits how much gain it can capture, and the Treasury bills it holds mostly back those options rather than being the fund's focus.
AAUA: An actively managed fund of US stocks chosen by a quantitative, rules-based process that favors cheap and high-quality companies. It looks like a large-company fund, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft making up about 19% of it.
AAUB: US companies chosen by a rules-based formula, with technology about 45 percent and health care, financials and communication companies each around a tenth. It's a core stock holding that leans heavily toward tech, so it can swing more than the broad market.
AAUS: A broad mix of US companies of all sizes and styles, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and health care next. It's a core stock holding, and the managers lean toward companies with strong financial quality, so it can move a little differently from the overall market.
AAVM: A fund of funds that owns four other Alpha Architect ETFs, splitting money across US and international stocks picked for momentum or low prices. About half is in international funds, and the mix is tilted toward smaller companies.
AAXJ: Stocks from Asia's growth economies outside Japan, such as China, Taiwan, India and South Korea, with technology about half and financials under a fifth. It's a way to add emerging Asian growth to a portfolio, but it leaves out Japan and swings more than US stocks.
ABCS: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US stocks, built mostly by holding Vanguard small-cap and mid-cap ETFs. The managers shift the mix with market conditions, so it is not a fixed index fund, and financials and health care are the biggest sectors.
ABEQ: An actively managed fund buying mostly US stocks that its manager thinks trade well below their true worth. It is concentrated: Berkshire Hathaway is about 11% of it, and a chunk is also held in Treasuries, so it behaves differently from a typical value index fund.
ABFL: An actively managed group of US companies chosen for strong free cash flow, the cash left after paying business expenses. Technology is about a third and health care a fifth, so it's a growth-leaning core holding with a more concentrated mix than the broad market.
ABI: Bonds backed by pools of assets such as loans, leases and other receivables, with a cash portion, actively managed for income. It aims for higher yield than regular bonds, but it carries more credit risk and can fall when borrowers have trouble.
ABIG: An actively managed fund of large US companies that the manager sees as high quality, enduring businesses. It is concentrated: Amazon, Alphabet and NVIDIA are each about 10% of the fund.
ABLD: A fund of companies tied to real assets, such as oil and gas, pipelines, real estate, mining and farming. It is spread fairly evenly, with no single holding above roughly 4% of the fund.
ABLG: An actively managed fund of large companies outside the US, chosen with a focus on their free cash flow. Its biggest positions are around 5% or less each, led by Taiwan Semiconductor and ASML, with chip names and European firms prominent.
ABLS: A fund tracking a rules-based index of small US companies that generate strong free cash flow, meaning cash left after running the business. It is concentrated, with Argan the largest at about 12%, across health care, financial and technology companies.
ABND: An actively managed bond fund that spreads across Treasuries, mortgage-backed securities, corporate bonds and emerging market debt. It is a core-plus fund, meaning mostly investment-grade bonds with some riskier ones for extra income, and government debt is among its largest holdings.
ABOT: An actively managed fund of US companies picked for innovation and strong free cash flow, the cash left after running the business. Its top holdings, like Apple and NVIDIA, are each under 5%, so it is spread across many names and sectors.
ABUF: A fund made up of four buffer funds that reset in different quarters, each following SPY up to a cap while shielding against the first 15% of losses. Staggering the start dates smooths out when protection renews, but each piece still limits gains.
ABXB: An actively managed fund of bond ETFs rather than individual bonds, mixing short and medium US Treasuries with emerging market and high-yield bond funds. About half sits in Treasury funds, with the rest in riskier bonds that pay more.
ACBE: A fund that uses swaps to get exposure to autocallable notes, which pay income as long as a reference investment holds above a set level and can end early. It is built around enhanced income, with the risk of losses if markets fall sharply.
ACBH: A fund that uses swaps to get exposure to autocallable notes, which pay income as long as a reference investment stays above a set level and can end early. It aims for high income but carries the risk of heavy losses if markets fall sharply.
ACEI: An actively managed options fund that aims to pay regular income and offer some protection from a drop in the stock market. It is built around an autocallable approach, meaning a payoff that can end early if conditions are met, so outcomes are complex.
ACEP: An actively managed fund holding roughly 100% US stocks chosen by ARS Investment Partners rather than following an index. It is fairly concentrated, with Seagate, Lam Research and Broadcom each making up around 5% to 6%, and it leans toward technology, energy, financials and materials.
ACES: Follows an index of US and Canadian clean energy companies, covering solar, wind, hydrogen, geothermal and other renewables. It is a fairly concentrated theme fund, with Enphase, First Solar, Plug Power and NextPower each around 6%, and the stocks can swing a lot.
ACGO: An actively managed fund of large US growth stocks, run by Wellington Management. It is heavy in technology at over half the fund, and NVIDIA, Alphabet, Apple and Broadcom together make up roughly 36% of it.
ACGR: An actively managed fund of large US companies expected to grow faster than average. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Microsoft and Apple are about 33% of it, and the top eight holdings add up to roughly 57%.
ACHP: Semiconductor companies listed in Asia, held as local shares and American Depositary Receipts, which are US-traded versions of foreign stocks, tracking an index of those firms. It is focused on one industry and region, so chip cycles and a few big names matter a lot.
ACIG: An actively managed fund of growth-style companies outside the US, aiming to beat the MSCI EAFE Growth Index. It uses a rules-based approach called alpha capture, and it holds at least about two thirds of its assets in foreign stocks.
ACII: An actively managed fund that aims to pay income tied to the S&P 500, Russell 2000 and Nasdaq-100 indexes, using options-like contracts known as autocallables. It also carries downside exposure to those markets, so income is not guaranteed and losses are possible if they fall.
ACIO: Large US companies, with technology about 40 percent, protected by an options collar, which is a pair of options that limits both losses and gains. It's built for a smoother ride in stock markets, so it should fall less in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
ACIV: An actively managed fund of US and foreign companies, including emerging markets, that aim to address or benefit from climate change. It leans toward industrials and technology, and its largest holdings are only about 2% to 4% each, so it is quite spread out.
ACKY: Holds the top 20 US-listed stocks in Pershing Square's most recent public filing, the hedge fund run by Bill Ackman, and aims to pay out regular distributions. It is concentrated: Microsoft, Meta, Brookfield and Howard Hughes are about 44% of the fund.
ACLC: An actively managed fund of large US companies, with managers picking stocks they expect to do well rather than copying an index. It leans on big tech: NVIDIA, Alphabet and Microsoft are each about 7% to 9%, and the top five make up roughly 30%.
ACLO: The safest top-rated slices of loan bundles called CLOs, which are pools of loans to lower-rated companies. It's meant for steady income above cash with small price swings, and its interest adjusts with rates, but it can still dip in market panics.
ACMG: An actively managed fund of mid-sized US growth companies, using research-driven stock selection. It is tech-heavy: Monolithic Power, Cloudflare and Okta are each about 7% to 8%, and the top five stocks together are about a third of the fund.
ACOM: An actively managed fund that gains exposure to commodities such as energy, metals and farm goods, mainly through futures contracts. Much of the money sits in Treasury bills and cash as backing for those futures, and the manager picks the mix rather than following an index.
ACQQ: Follows an index built around autocallables tied to the Nasdaq-100, which are contracts that pay income but can end early if the index hits a target level. Most of the money sits in cash-like holdings, so the income comes from the contracts and carries risk if the index falls.
ACRT: Follows an index that mimics autocallable notes tied to the Russell 2000, which pay income at set intervals and can end early if the index is high enough. Most of the fund sits in a money market ETF, and the income comes with downside risk.
ACSG: An actively managed fund of small US companies expected to grow faster than average, picked by American Century using its own research and models. It leans toward health care, technology and industrials, and no single holding is much above 3% of the fund.
ACSI: US companies that score high on customer satisfaction surveys, chosen from over 400 companies by the American Customer Satisfaction Index. Dell is the biggest holding at about 10%, and the fund spreads across communication, consumer and financial companies.
ACSM: An actively managed fund of US small and mid-sized company stocks, with at least 80% in that group. The managers use a research-driven process to pick stocks they expect to beat the market, rather than following an index.
ACSP: Follows an index that mimics autocallable notes linked to the S&P 500, structured products that pay a coupon and can end early if the market is high enough. The fund pays out income, but the notes expose it to stock market losses.
ACSV: An actively managed fund of small US companies the managers think are priced cheaply compared with their fundamentals. It is well spread out, with no holding above about 2%, and leans toward banks and other financials, industrials and technology.
ACTS: An actively managed fund of stocks from the US and abroad, including emerging markets, picked by the manager rather than following an index. It is fairly concentrated, with Bloom Energy and Amkor Technology each around 6% and a tilt toward technology and industrials.
ACVF: A fund of large US companies chosen to fit conservative values, screening out companies that do not. It still looks like the broad market, with NVIDIA, Microsoft, Cisco and Broadcom among the top holdings and technology around 44% of it.
ACVT: Holds convertible bonds, which are bonds from companies that can be swapped for shares of that company's stock. They offer some income like a bond with some upside like a stock, and this fund is actively managed and spread across many issuers, with no holding above about 4%.
ACVU: An actively managed fund of large US value stocks, picked using a quantitative approach that scores companies. Big names lead it: Amazon at about 7% and Microsoft at about 7%, and ConocoPhillips and Chubb show it also holds energy and insurance.
ACWI: Stocks from around the world, from the US to developed and emerging markets, with technology the largest slice at about a third. It's a one-fund core holding for global stock exposure, though the US still makes up the biggest share.
ACWV: Stocks from developed and emerging countries picked to be less jumpy than the global market, led by technology, financials and health care. It's meant to give worldwide stock exposure with a smoother ride, though it usually trails when risky stocks surge higher.
ACWX: Stocks from developed and emerging countries around the world, everywhere except the US, with financials about a quarter and technology about a fifth. It's meant to round out a US-heavy portfolio with global exposure, and it moves with foreign economies and currencies rather than the American market.
ACYB: An income fund that uses swaps, contracts tied to the returns of an options-based structure, to pursue regular payouts. It uses laddered autocallable contracts with a built-in buffer against some losses, so the income and protection depend on how markets move over set periods.
ACYN: Notes that pay income and end early if a stock index holds above a set level, backed mostly by cash and bonds. It's meant for high monthly income, but gains are capped and it can lose money if the market falls too far.
ACYQ: A fund that uses swaps and options to mimic autocallable yield notes, which pay high income but can end early or lose value if the market falls past a set barrier. The Treasury holdings are collateral, and the strategy is complex and tied to market moves.
ACYS: A fund using swap contracts to deliver income tied to a laddered set of structured notes that pay out unless markets fall past a set level. It's built for high income, and the catch is that a sharp stock market drop can cut or wipe out those payments.
ADIV: Dividend-paying stocks of companies across the Asia Pacific region, in developed and emerging markets such as China, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore. Financials are about 37% of it, and the biggest holdings are each under 5%.
ADME: An actively managed fund of large US stocks that buys put options, contracts that gain value when markets fall, to limit big losses. The stocks are top-heavy in tech: NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet are about 20% of it, and the protection costs some upside.
ADPV: An actively managed fund of US stocks that moves its holdings based on market trend. It is invested in stocks during broad uptrends, and it is concentrated, with the top holdings like Intel and Arrowhead each about 5%.
ADVE: An actively managed fund of dividend-paying companies in Asia. Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung are about 22% of it, and technology and financials each make up about 30%, so it leans on a few big Asian companies.
AEMC: An actively managed fund of US mid-sized companies, using a computer driven approach to pick and weight them. It is spread widely, with no stock above about 4%, across technology, industrials, financials and health care.
AEMG: An actively managed fund of US mid-sized companies that are expected to grow faster, picked with a computer driven approach. Technology is about 40% of it, and no single stock is above about 5%.
AEMV: An actively managed fund of US mid-sized companies that look cheaply priced, picked with a computer driven approach. It is spread widely, with no stock above about 4%, and financials are the largest sector.
AESB: An actively managed fund of US small companies, using a computer driven approach to pick and weight them. It is spread widely, with no stock above about 3%, and financials and health care are the biggest sectors.
AESG: An actively managed fund of US small companies expected to grow faster, picked with a computer driven approach. It is spread widely, with no stock above about 3%, and health care and technology are the biggest sectors.
AESL: An actively managed fund of US small companies that look cheaply priced, picked with a computer driven approach. Financials are close to 30% of it, with real estate and industrials next, and no stock above about 3.5%.
AESR: An actively managed fund that rotates between US sector and theme ETFs instead of picking individual stocks. Its biggest holdings are an ARK innovation fund, a semiconductor fund and a SPDR sector fund, about 16% each, so it is a concentrated bet on tech.
AFDM: An actively managed fund of stocks from developed countries outside the US, picked with a quantitative model that scores factors like value and momentum. It is spread widely, with financials the largest group and names like HSBC, ASML and Shell near the top.
AFEM: An actively managed fund of emerging market stocks that uses factors like value, quality and momentum to pick them. It leans toward tech, with Taiwan Semiconductor at about 11% and MediaTek and Tencent also among the larger holdings.
AFGR: An actively managed fund of large US growth stocks, run by several managers who each pick their own. It is top-heavy in tech: NVIDIA, Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta are about 27% of the fund.
AFIF: An actively managed bond fund that can hold corporate bonds, government and agency securities and other income investments across the world. It uses a flexible approach, and US government bonds are about 8% of it.
AFIX: A broad fund of US investment-grade bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage-backed bonds from agencies like Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, and corporate debt. It is actively managed, so the managers choose bonds rather than copying an index, and it holds many individual bonds.
AFK: Follows an index of African companies, including firms listed in Africa and others earning at least half their revenue there. It leans toward mining and banks, with names like Attijariwafa Bank, Endeavour Mining, AngloGold Ashanti and Naspers among the largest holdings.
AFLG: Large US companies picked by a manager's rules that look for strong momentum, quality and good value, with technology the biggest slice at about two fifths. It's a core stock holding that tilts toward appealing stocks, so it can differ from the broad market.
AFMC: An actively managed fund of US mid-sized companies, chosen by a rules-based model that favors stocks with strong value, quality and momentum traits. It holds many stocks with none above about 2%, spread across industrials, technology, consumer and financial companies.
AFOS: An actively managed fund of stocks picked by ARS Investment Partners, focused on companies with solid finances and growth. It is currently top-heavy in tech hardware: Micron, Western Digital and Lam Research together are about 20% of it.
AFSC: An actively managed fund holding a limited number of US small-cap stocks that the manager has strong conviction in. The biggest holdings are each about 3%, and health care, financials and industrials lead.
AFSM: An actively managed fund of small US companies chosen with a rules-based scoring model that favors cheaper, higher quality stocks with positive price trends. It is spread widely, with the largest holdings only around 1% to 2% each.
AGEM: An actively managed fund of emerging-market companies that pay dividends, for the income. It is top-heavy in Asia: Samsung and Taiwan Semiconductor are about 25% of it, and technology makes up over 40%.
AGG: Nearly the whole US investment-grade bond market in one fund, including Treasuries, government-backed mortgage bonds and corporate bonds. It is meant for steady interest income and as a cushion for a stock portfolio, though its price falls when interest rates rise.
AGGA: An actively managed bond fund that gets its exposure by holding other bond ETFs rather than individual bonds. It mixes Treasuries, investment grade corporates, high yield and CLOs, adjusting the blend over time, so no single holding is more than about 15%.
AGGB: The broad US investment-grade bond market in one fund, including Treasuries, government-backed mortgage bonds and corporate bonds, following a FTSE index. It is a core bond holding, spread across thousands of bonds rather than a single type.
AGGH: Investment-grade US bonds held mainly through other bond funds, plus options and other tools meant to manage risk or boost income. It's meant as a core bond holding for income, and the extra strategies mean it can behave differently from a plain bond index.
AGGM: A broad mix of US investment grade bonds, including Treasuries, agency debt, corporate bonds and mortgage-backed securities, limited to those maturing in 1 to 10 years. Because it skips the longest bonds, it is more sensitive to rate changes than cash but less than a full-length bond index.
AGGS: An actively managed portfolio of mostly US dollar bonds, led by US Treasuries and also holding mortgage-backed and corporate bonds. It aims for steady income with moderate risk, using a rules-guided process to pick bonds rather than simply tracking an index.
AGGY: The broad US investment-grade bond market, meaning Treasuries, mortgage-backed bonds and corporate bonds, adjusted to lean toward bonds that pay a bit more income. It works as a core bond holding and cushion for stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
AGIQ: A fund of US-listed companies working on agentic AI, meaning software that can carry out tasks on its own. It tracks a rules-based index and is mostly technology, with Alphabet, Qualcomm, NVIDIA and Palo Alto Networks each at about 7%.
AGIX: Technology-focused companies riding the artificial intelligence boom, with technology about 70% and communication, consumer and financial companies adding the rest. It can include some private companies, and it's a concentrated growth bet that swings more than the broad market.
AGMI: A fund of silver mining companies around the world, following an index of firms with major exposure to silver. Newmont, Fresnillo and Penoles are about 29% of it, so it tends to rise and fall with the silver business.
AGNG: Tracks an index of developed-market companies that benefit from an aging population, mostly health care firms like Novo Nordisk, Eli Lilly and Roche. Health care is over 90% of the fund, so it is a narrow theme.
AGOX: An actively managed fund that holds other ETFs, mostly sector and broad stock funds such as technology and Nasdaq-100 funds, to chase growth. It shifts between stocks and cash depending on the manager's view, so a sizable part can sit in cash.
AGQI: An actively managed fund of income-producing stocks from around the world, with at least 40% typically outside the US. Holdings range from Microsoft and Chevron to Rio Tinto, and no single holding is above about 5% of the fund.
AGRW: An actively managed fund of large US growth companies, the size of S&P 500 members. It is quite top-heavy, with NVIDIA about 14% and Alphabet about 9%, and technology makes up over half of the fund.
AGZ: Short-to-medium term bonds issued by US government agencies, such as the mortgage-finance and farm-credit lenders. It's a low-risk place for steady income, and it moves little when stocks fall, but it pays less than corporate bonds.
AGZD: The broad US bond market, following the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index, but with short Treasury positions that reduce how much its price moves when interest rates change. It aims to keep the bond income while limiting damage from rising rates.
AHBM: Holds about ten Asian companies that make memory chips and related equipment, following an index of the sector. It is very concentrated, with SK hynix alone about a quarter of the fund, so it rides on one corner of the chip industry.
AHD: An income fund built around autocallables on Robinhood stock, which are contracts that pay a fixed coupon unless the stock falls below a set level. It can end early if the stock rises, and it carries the risk of a big drop in Robinhood.
AHIC: Short-term corporate bonds with lower credit ratings, often called junk bonds, paying higher interest because the issuers are riskier. It's meant for extra income with less rate sensitivity than longer high-yield funds, but it can still fall along with stocks in downturns.
AHLT: A trend-following fund that uses futures across over 20 global markets, including stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities, going long or short depending on the price trends its models see. The Treasury bills shown are mostly collateral for those positions.
AHYB: An actively managed fund of US junk bonds, meaning corporate bonds from lower-rated companies that pay higher interest for higher risk. It does not follow an index, and spreads its money across many bonds, none above about 1%.
AHYM: Municipal bonds issued by US states, cities and local projects, with interest generally free of federal income tax, focused on the lower-rated, higher-yielding part of the market. It is spread across many small positions, with no single bond above about 2%, and it carries more credit risk than top-rated munis.
AIA: Large companies across Asia outside Japan, with technology well over half, financials about a fifth, and the rest in consumer and communication firms. It's a way to add Asian growth to a portfolio, but it leans heavily on tech and swings more than the broad world market.
AIBF: US companies that Morningstar expects to benefit from artificial intelligence by using it, rather than building it, tracked with its AI Beneficiaries Select Index. That makes it unlike a typical AI fund: top holdings are Walmart, Costco, AbbVie and Eli Lilly, each about 4%.
AIBN: A fund holding corporate bonds from companies tied to building artificial intelligence infrastructure, such as data centers and power, following a specific index. It is non-diversified, meaning it can put larger amounts in fewer issuers than most bond funds.
AICH: Holds Chinese companies tied to artificial intelligence, mostly chip, optical and hardware makers. It is concentrated in technology, at about 80%, and its biggest holdings, including Hygon and Zhongji Innolight, are each around 6% of the fund.
AIED: An actively managed fund of large US companies that the managers pick using momentum and a theme around large language models and AI. It is mostly technology, spread over many names, with Cisco, Micron, AMD, Caterpillar and Palo Alto each around 4% to 5%.
AIEQ: An actively managed US stock fund that uses an artificial intelligence model built on IBM Watson to pick companies from the broad US market. Holdings are spread out, with the top five each around 5%, and technology is the biggest sector at about a third.
AIFD: An actively managed fund of companies the manager believes will benefit from artificial intelligence, mostly technology. NVIDIA, Palo Alto Networks, Arista and Broadcom are each about 6 to 7%, so it is fairly concentrated.
AIFR: A fund that follows an index of companies in the semiconductor foundry business, meaning firms that manufacture chips designed by others. Intel alone is about 21% of it, followed by GlobalFoundries and Tower Semiconductor, so it is a narrow, concentrated bet.
AIHY: An actively managed fund focused on US-listed companies building the huge data centers behind artificial intelligence. It is very concentrated: Microsoft and Meta are each over 20% of it, and a large chunk sits in a government money market fund.
AIMG: Tracks an index of ten companies across the artificial intelligence supply chain, from chips to software. It is very concentrated, and much of the holdings data here shows cash and derivatives rather than the stocks themselves.
AIMS: An actively managed fund of small US companies chosen by its managers, spread across industrials, tech, health care and financials. No single stock is above about 2% of it, so it is widely diversified.
AINF: A fund aimed at companies that make AI chips for inference, which means running trained AI models rather than training them. It holds a small number of companies in a narrow theme, so a few chipmakers drive most of its results.
AINP: An actively managed bond fund aiming for income from many kinds of debt, with a large share in mortgage-backed securities from government-backed agencies. It can also hold corporate and foreign bonds, so it is broader than a plain government bond fund.
AINT: An actively managed fund that uses artificial intelligence to pick US large company stocks to buy and others to bet against, keeping the two sides about equal in size. It aims to earn returns that do not depend on the market going up.
AIOO: A fund using options to follow US stock market returns over a one year period starting in September, aiming to protect against most losses. Gains are limited by a cap, and the protection only fully applies if held for the whole period.
AIPI: Artificial intelligence related companies, almost entirely technology, paired with an options strategy that trades away some upside for monthly income. It's for income from a focused tech theme, and it trails in strong rallies while still dropping when AI stocks fall.
AIPO: Companies that build the power and computing backbone for artificial intelligence: industrial firms making grid equipment and data center components make up over half, with chip and computing hardware, utilities and energy filling out the rest. It's a focused bet on one theme, so it swings more than the broad market.
AIQ: Companies building or using artificial intelligence and big data, with technology about 70% of the fund and the rest in communication, consumer and industrial firms. It's a focused growth bet on the AI theme, so it can swing more than the broad market when tech sentiment shifts.
AIQD: A note that aims to deliver the opposite of an artificial intelligence stock index, three times over, each day. Because it resets daily and uses leverage, results over longer periods can stray far from expectations, and as an ETN it also depends on its issuer's credit.
AIQU: An exchange-traded note, which is a loan to a bank rather than a fund, that aims for three times the daily move of an index of artificial intelligence companies. It is leveraged and resets daily, so losses can build up fast over time.
AIRR: Small and mid-sized US companies that make and build things, with industrials nearly 90%, including machinery, construction and engineering firms. It's a focused bet on the American industrial comeback, and because these firms are smaller, it swings more than the broad market.
AIS: Global companies at the heart of the artificial intelligence build-out, with technology over 90%, such as chip, software and hardware makers. It's a concentrated growth bet on one theme, so it swings far more than the broad market.
AIUP: An actively managed fund of US large companies, where an AI model decides what to buy and how much. It is very concentrated and tech-heavy: NVIDIA, Meta and Amazon are each about 15%, and technology is over 70% of the fund.
AIVC: Companies tied to artificial intelligence, chosen using a Bloomberg index and held in roughly equal amounts. It is mostly chips and hardware, with Micron, SK Hynix and MediaTek among the larger holdings at about 4% each, so it leans heavily on the semiconductor industry.
AIVI: Value-priced stocks from developed markets outside the US and Canada, with computer models using AI to help pick and weight them. It leans toward banks, with Financials about 38% of it, plus energy and tobacco names.
AIVL: An actively managed fund of US mid-sized value stocks, using an AI-assisted model to pick and weight stocks that look cheap but financially healthy. It is spread out, with Micron the largest at about 6%, and leans toward technology, financials and industrials.
AIX: A fund tracking the Indxx U.S. 100 index of companies expected to benefit from, or hold up well through, the growth of artificial intelligence. About 70% is in technology, with chipmakers like KLA, Intel, Micron and AMD among the largest holdings.
AIYY: Aims to pay high income by using options tied to the stock of C3.ai, a single company, rather than owning the shares directly. That options approach limits how much it can gain if the stock soars, while still being exposed to big losses if it falls.
AJAN: An options-based fund tied to the S&P 500 through a two-year outcome period ending in January 2028, designed to guard against a set amount of losses in return for a cap on gains. The protection only applies to those who hold for the full period.
AJUL: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to aim to cushion part of the losses from the US stock market over a two year period ending in July 2026. Gains are limited by a cap, and the protection only applies if held for the full period.
AKAF: An actively managed fund that holds a broad mix of large companies from around the world. Its top holdings are spread thinly, with FedEx, SLB, ConocoPhillips, Uber and Exxon each only about 2% of the fund, so no single stock dominates.
AKRE: A concentrated group of US stocks, with financials and technology each about 43%, chosen by an active manager looking for businesses that can grow for many years. Because it holds so few names, it can look very different from the market and swing both ways.
ALAI: Companies expected to benefit from artificial intelligence, with technology just under sixty percent, then communication, consumer and industrial firms. It's a growth bet on one theme, actively managed, and it swings more than the broad market.
ALDB: A fund made up of four other deep buffer funds, each starting in a different quarter, all tied to the S&P 500. Each aims to absorb a set amount of losses over a year, in exchange for capped gains, and the four are held in equal parts.
ALIL: An actively managed fund of small US companies that the manager sees as high quality, lasting businesses. It holds a concentrated group of stocks, with the top names such as Victory Capital and EnPro each at about 4%, so each holding has a real impact.
ALLW: A mix of bonds, stocks and other assets, with bonds the largest part, balanced to hold up across booming, slow, inflationary and falling price conditions. It's meant as a steadier, all-weather core holding, using borrowing that can magnify moves in the bond portion.
ALRG: An actively managed fund of large US companies, picked with a focus on quality businesses held for the long term. It is tilted to technology, and Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet together make up about 20% of the fund.
ALTL: A rules based fund of large US companies that rotates among sectors, aiming to hold the sectors that look strongest. Right now it leans toward utilities, financials and real estate, and it holds many stocks, each around 2% or less.
ALTY: A mix of income-focused funds that hold real estate, covered-call Nasdaq-100 stocks, preferred shares and emerging market bonds, plus infrastructure and pipeline companies. Four funds make up about 80% of it, so it is a simple way to blend several kinds of income.
AMAX: An actively managed fund of funds that holds other ETFs across stocks, bonds and other assets, with hedging to soften swings and aim for income. About a fifth of it is a long-term Treasury bond ETF.
AMDW: A leveraged single-stock fund aiming for about 1.2 times the weekly return of AMD shares, using swaps and the stock. It makes weekly payouts and resets each week, so it suits short-term use and can behave very differently from AMD over longer periods.
AMDY: An options strategy built around AMD, a single chip company, designed to pay out regular income instead of simply holding the stock. It earns monthly income from selling options, but it gives up much of AMD's upside and can still lose heavily if the stock falls.
AMEI: A fund of dividend-paying stocks, chosen to follow Islamic principles, which means avoiding things like interest-heavy businesses. Taiwan Semiconductor and Eli Lilly are each about 10% of it, and it leans toward technology, industrials and health care.
AMEM: A fund of stocks from developing countries, chosen to follow Islamic principles, which means avoiding things like interest-heavy businesses. Technology is almost half of the fund, with Samsung, Advantech, Delta Electronics and Taiwan Semiconductor among the largest holdings.
AMGR: Mostly large growth stocks from the US and abroad, picked by the manager and screened to follow Islamic principles, which rules out things like interest-based finance. It leans heavily on technology, with Apple, NVIDIA, Taiwan Semiconductor and Alphabet each around 7% of the fund.
AMHI: Municipal bonds, debt issued by state and local government agencies, that carry lower credit ratings and pay higher income. Its top holdings, such as Public Finance Authority bonds, are each about 3% to 4%, so it is spread across many issuers.
AMID: An actively managed fund of US mid-sized companies that the manager thinks are going through positive change, using the Russell Midcap Index as its size range. Holdings are fairly spread out, with Comfort Systems USA the largest at about 4%, and lean toward industrials and technology.
AMJB: Pipeline and energy storage partnerships in North America, packaged as a bank-issued note rather than a regular fund. It's for income from the energy infrastructure industry, and because it's a note, it also depends on the issuing bank's ability to pay, on top of swings in energy markets.
AMLP: Pipeline and energy infrastructure partnerships that move and store oil and gas, earning fees on volume rather than prices alone. It's built for high income, but it's structured as a corporation, so it pays tax itself and is a narrow bet on one industry.
AMMO: Holds companies in the defense supply chain around the world, such as makers of weapons, aerospace parts and defense software. Holdings include LIG Defense and Aerospace, Mildef, Rheinmetall and Palantir, each around 3% to 5%, and it holds a fairly small number of stocks.
AMYY: An options income fund built around AMD, using derivatives on an AMD ETF rather than owning the shares directly. It aims to pay high income by selling options, which limits how much it gains if AMD rises, and the Treasury bills it holds are mainly backing.
AMZA: Pipeline and energy infrastructure partnerships called MLPs, which move oil and gas and often pay large income. The fund borrows to boost its income, so it swings more than the broad market and is closely tied to energy demand and prices.
AMZP: An actively managed income fund tied to Amazon stock that uses options to pay out regularly. Selling options limits how much of Amazon's rise it can share in, and the Treasury bills listed are mostly collateral backing the strategy.
AMZW: An actively managed fund targeting about 1.2 times the weekly return of Amazon stock, using swaps and some shares, and it pays out distributions weekly. Because of the extra leverage it can move more than Amazon itself, and most of the fund is Treasury bills.
AMZY: An income fund tied to Amazon stock that uses options to collect payments, rather than owning the shares outright. The options cap how much it gains if Amazon rises, while it still takes much of the loss if the stock falls.
ANG: US dollar bonds from US and Canadian companies that used to be investment grade but were downgraded, known as fallen angels, following a FTSE index. They pay more interest than top-rated bonds, though the issuers have already shown some strain.
ANGL: Bonds from companies that once had investment-grade ratings but were later cut to junk, which often leaves them priced cheaply. It's built for higher income than safe bonds, though it tends to fall with stocks when the economy weakens.
ANGU: Large US companies chosen by a research based screen, with technology around 40% and communication, financials and health care each near a tenth. It's a core US stock holding with a tilt toward companies the model rates well, so it can differ from the plain market.
ANTW: A fund of companies tied to Anthropic, the AI lab, such as its cloud and chip partners and investors. It is concentrated, with Alphabet, TeraWulf, AMD, Amazon and Microsoft making up over a third of the fund.
ANV: A fund that uses derivatives tied to NVIDIA stock to pursue an autocallable payout, a contract that can end early and pay out if the stock hits certain levels. It does not simply own NVIDIA shares, and the outcome depends on how the stock moves over set dates.
AOA: A ready-made mix of about 80 percent stocks and 20 percent bonds, built from other funds that cover US and international companies. It's meant as a one-fund growth portfolio with a small bond cushion, and it still falls meaningfully in stock market declines.
AOCT: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to protect against part of the losses over a two-year period ending in October 2028. In exchange, gains are limited, and it only works if held for the whole period.
AOHY: An actively managed fund holding mostly high-yield corporate bonds, sometimes called junk bonds, which are bonds from companies with weaker credit that pay more interest. It is spread across many issuers, with the biggest, Venture Global LNG, only about 2% of the fund.
AOK: A ready-made mix of roughly two thirds bonds and one third stocks, spread across many countries. It's a conservative, all-in-one holding for people who want modest growth with a cushion, and it will fall less than an all-stock fund in a sell-off but also rise less.
AOM: A ready-made mix of about 60 percent bonds and 40 percent stocks, built from other index funds. It's meant as a one-fund, cautious portfolio, and the bond share means it should swing less than an all-stock fund but also grow more slowly in strong rallies.
AOR: A ready-made mix of about 60 percent stocks and 40 percent bonds, built from other funds. It's meant as a one-fund core holding with a moderate amount of risk, so it should fall less than an all-stock fund in a downturn and also rise less in a rally.
AOTG: An actively managed fund of US-listed growth stocks, mostly technology, picked for businesses expected to grow without much extra cost. It is concentrated in chips, with AMD, NVIDIA and Micron together making up about 35% of the fund.
APCB: A broad mix of US investment-grade bonds, mostly government and corporate, managed with a blend of active picks and index tracking. It's meant as a core bond holding for steady income that cushions a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
APDB: A defined outcome fund using options on an S&P 500 fund to absorb a large share of the losses over a set period starting in April. Gains are limited in exchange, and the result depends on when in the period you buy.
APIE: Large international companies, mostly foreign firms traded in the US as ADRs, spread across technology, financials, industrials and health care. It's a core way to own stocks outside the US, blending a hands-off index approach with some manager choices to try to beat its benchmark.
APLU: An actively managed bond fund holding US government, mortgage and corporate bonds, with room to add some lower-quality and foreign bonds. Treasuries and agency mortgage bonds make up a big chunk, so it works as a core bond holding with a little extra income.
APLY: Aims to earn income from Apple stock by using options on it, rather than holding the shares directly. The options pay out regular income but cap the gains if Apple rises, and the Treasury bills it holds are mainly backing for the strategy.
APMU: An actively managed fund of intermediate-term US municipal bonds, whose interest is generally free from federal income tax. It mixes active and passive approaches against its benchmark, and holds hundreds of bonds, with each one under 1% of the fund.
APOC: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on an S&P 500 ETF to cushion part of the losses over each six-month period, April to October. In exchange, gains are capped, so protection resets every period and depends on timing.
APRB: Uses options on an S&P 500 ETF to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts each April. In exchange, gains are limited by a cap, and the protection only applies if you hold for the whole period.
APRH: Holds Treasury bills and options on a broad US stock index to aim for income, in a one-year cycle starting in April. It is built to pay income and take part in some market gains, but a large market drop can cause losses.
APRJ: An actively managed fund that holds Treasury bills and options on the S&P 500 to pay regular income, with a barrier that decides how much of any stock market loss it takes over a set period starting in April. Results depend on how the market moves.
APRP: A fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in April. In return, gains are capped, so it behaves differently from a plain S&P 500 fund, and the outcome only applies when held for the full period.
APRT: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on an S&P 500 fund to cushion a set amount of losses over a roughly one-year period. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only applies to people who hold from the start of the period to the end.
APRW: Uses options on the S&P 500 fund SPY to cushion part of the losses over a one-year period that starts in April, as the name's Buffer20 suggests. In return, gains are capped at a set level, so it trades some upside for protection.
APRZ: An actively managed fund using options on the S&P 500 to follow the index's gains up to a limit while cushioning part of the losses over a set one year period starting in April. Most of the fund sits in US Treasuries backing the options.
APUE: A broad slice of the whole US stock market, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and consumer companies making up much of the rest. It's built as a core stock holding, and managers blend index-style holdings with active picks to try to edge past the market.
APXM: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on a US stock ETF to absorb most losses over a one-year period starting in April. In return, its gains are capped, and the protection only fully works if held from the start of the period to the end.
AQEC: High-quality US companies expected to grow over time, with technology about a third, followed by communication and health care. It's an actively managed core stock holding, and the manager's picks mean it can differ from the broad market.
AQLG: An actively managed fund of large US growth companies, meaning firms expected to grow faster than average, picked by HCM. The facts on its exact holdings are limited, so it is best read as a stock picker's large-cap growth fund.
AQLT: Stocks from developed and emerging markets worldwide that score well on quality: high return on equity, steady earnings growth and low debt. It leans toward big tech, with Taiwan Semiconductor, Apple and NVIDIA about 16% of it.
AQWA: Global stocks of companies tied to clean water, tracked by an index. Holdings mix water utilities and equipment makers, led by American Water Works, Ferguson and Xylem at roughly 8% each, with industrials about half and utilities about 40%.
ARB: Follows an index of merger arbitrage, a strategy of buying shares of companies being acquired and capturing the gap between the current price and the deal price. Its holdings change as deals close, and the results depend on deals being completed rather than on the overall stock market.
ARCM: An actively managed fund of very short term US dollar bonds, with an average maturity of two years or less, including a lot of US Treasuries. Because the bonds mature quickly, its price should move far less than a typical bond fund.
ARCP: An actively managed core bond fund holding mostly investment-grade debt such as corporate bonds, mortgage-related securities, asset-backed securities and US government bonds. It can also hold a smaller slice of lower-rated bonds to add income, with more credit risk.
ARGT: Argentine companies, led by consumer businesses at about 28%, then energy, financials and materials. It's a concentrated bet on one emerging country, so it swings widely with local politics, inflation and currency moves.
ARIA: A concentrated, actively managed fund holding only about 20 to 35 stocks from the US and abroad. Dell Technologies alone is roughly 27% of it, and technology is over half the fund, so a few companies drive most of the results.
ARKB: Holds actual bitcoin rather than company shares or bonds, so its price follows the price of bitcoin. It's a way to own bitcoin through a regular brokerage account, and it swings sharply, with no income and no cushion from other assets.
ARKD: A defined-outcome fund that holds options on ARK Innovation ETF, a fund of fast-growing, high-volatility companies, to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in the first quarter. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, and almost all of it is tied to that one fund.
ARKE: An actively managed defined outcome fund from ARK that aims to give a set risk and return profile over rolling 12 month periods running July to June. It mostly holds ARK Innovation ETF, so it is tied to a fund of high growth, disruptive companies.
ARKF: Companies reshaping money and payments, such as online payment, digital banking and crypto-related firms, split between technology and financials. It's a bet on financial technology, so it swings much more than the broad market, and a manager actively picks the stocks.
ARKG: Companies tied to genetics and biotech, such as gene editing, diagnostics and drug discovery, all in health care. It's a high risk bet on a single industry that is actively managed, so it swings far more than the broad market and can drop sharply.
ARKI: A fund that holds options on the ARK Innovation ETF to aim for a set amount of protection against losses, with a cap on gains, over a defined period starting in the second quarter. It effectively tracks one actively managed innovation fund with that downside cushion.
ARKK: Companies a manager believes are being reshaped by new technology, spread across health care, technology, financials and consumer firms. It's a high-risk growth bet on disruptive ideas, so it swings far more than the broad market, rising sharply in good times and falling hard in bad ones.
ARKQ: Companies working on self-driving vehicles, robots, drones and automation, mostly industrials and technology with some consumer companies. It's a focused growth bet on emerging technology, managed actively, so it swings much more than the broad market.
ARKT: Uses options on ARK Innovation ETF to cushion a set amount of losses over a set period starting in the fourth quarter. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if held for the whole period.
ARKW: Companies tied to the internet, cloud computing, digital payments and crypto, with technology about half and financials, consumer and communication firms making up most of the rest. It's an actively managed growth bet that swings far more than the broad market.
ARKX: Companies tied to space and defense, mostly industrials such as aerospace, with technology about a quarter. It's an actively managed bet on a narrow theme, so it swings more than the broad market and owns well-known stocks and small risky ones.
ARKY: An actively managed fund that aims to pay income by copying autocallable notes, which are contracts tied to the price of individual stocks. It uses derivatives and short-term bonds rather than owning many ordinary stocks, so its payouts depend on how those stocks perform.
ARLI: Tracks international developed-markets stocks through options on an EFA ETF, with a buffer meant to absorb the first 15% of losses over a set period ending in March 2027. Unlike capped versions, this one has no cap on gains.
ARLU: Uses options tied to an S&P 500 ETF to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period that starts in April, as the name says. Being uncapped means gains are not limited by a set cap, unlike many similar buffer funds.
ARMH: A fund holding almost entirely one stock, Arm Holdings, through its US-traded shares, with a currency swap that offsets moves between the US dollar and the British pound. That means it follows Arm's share price without the currency swings, and it is very concentrated.
ARMS: An actively managed bond fund mixing investment-grade and lower-rated debt such as corporate bonds, asset-backed securities and mortgage-related securities. It spreads across several parts of the bond market to pursue income, and the lower-rated portion adds more credit risk.
ARMW: Aims to return about 1.2 times the weekly return of ARM Holdings stock, using swaps and some shares, and pays out distributions every week. It is a bet on a single company, and most of the fund is held in Treasury bills as backing.
ARMY: An actively managed fund of defense and aerospace companies from outside the US, such as Rocket Lab, Elbit Systems, Kongsberg and Hensoldt. It is a concentrated bet on one industry, and the top holdings are each around 5% to 7%.
ARP: An actively managed fund that spreads money across stocks, bonds, commodities, gold and cash, mostly by holding other ETFs, and shifts the mix as market trends change. The biggest pieces are a commodity fund at about 34%, a Nasdaq 100 fund and a developed markets fund.
ARTY: Companies expected to benefit from artificial intelligence, such as chip designers, software and cloud firms, with technology about 85%. It's a focused growth bet on one theme, so it swings more than the broad market and can drop hard if AI enthusiasm fades.
ARVR: Companies supporting the metaverse, meaning virtual and augmented reality, such as chipmakers and tech platforms, tracked by the Indxx Metaverse Index. Micron, AMD, Intel and STMicroelectronics are all in the top holdings, and the fund is mostly technology and communication stocks.
ARWG: An actively managed fund of US growth companies picked for solid finances and strong growth potential, with at least 80% in stocks. It is spread out, with the largest holdings like Arista Networks and Semtech at only about 3% each.
ASCE: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US companies, which the managers pick by looking for stocks they consider reasonably priced and healthy. It is spread out, with no holding above about 3%, across technology, health care, financials and more.
ASCI: An actively managed fund of small companies outside the US, picked by abrdn's managers. It is widely spread, with the top names like Diploma, ASICS and Hill & Smith each at about 4%, and it leans toward industrials.
ASD: Global companies that make products, services or research for people with autism, such as therapy providers and drug developers, following a specialized index. About 87% is in health care, and no single holding is above roughly 5%.
ASEA: Tracks the 40 largest companies in five Southeast Asian countries: Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines. It leans heavily on banks, with Singapore's DBS, OCBC and UOB about 38% of it, so it is concentrated in a few firms.
ASEC: Mostly investment grade securitized debt, meaning loans packaged into bonds, focused on less common types like aircraft leases, equipment leases, consumer loans and cell towers. It is made up of many small positions, mostly around 1% each.
ASGM: An actively managed fund that tries to profit from big economic trends across global markets, using stock, bond and other positions. It aims to limit losses in rough markets, and a large part of it is held in broad index funds like the iShares Core S&P 500 ETF.
ASHR: Large mainland Chinese companies listed on China's domestic exchanges, with technology and financials leading and industrials and materials next. It's a focused bet on China's domestic market, which can swing more than global stocks and is heavily affected by Chinese policy.
ASHS: Tracks an index of about 500 small companies listed in mainland China, known as China A-shares. It is highly spread out, with no holding above about 1.5%, and technology, industrials and materials are the biggest areas.
ASIA: An actively managed fund investing in companies across Asia outside Japan, such as South Korea, Taiwan, China and India. Technology is about half the fund, and Samsung and Taiwan Semiconductor alone are around 24% of it.
ASLV: An actively managed fund of large US companies the manager sees as undervalued, with a small share allowed in foreign firms. It holds a focused group of stocks, with Amazon the largest at about 8% of the fund.
ASMF: An actively managed fund that uses futures and forward contracts to follow trends across stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities, and can profit from prices falling as well as rising. The Treasury bills it holds are mostly collateral for those contracts.
ASMH: A fund holding almost entirely one stock, ASML, the Dutch maker of the machines used to produce computer chips. It uses a currency swap to offset moves between the US dollar and the euro, so it follows the share price without the currency swings.
ASTM: Municipal bonds from state and local governments whose interest is free from regular federal income tax, mostly in the short term. It's meant for tax-friendly income, though a portion is in lower-rated bonds, which adds more risk than top-quality muni funds.
AT: Companies that make actuators, the motors and moving parts that let robots and machines do physical work. It holds about 90% industrials, spread worldwide, with SMC, Fanuc, RBC Bearings and Nidec each making up roughly 6% to 8% of the fund.
ATC: An actively managed income fund built on autocallables, contracts tied to Coinbase stock that pay a coupon and end early if the stock reaches a set level. It does not hold Coinbase shares directly, and its income depends on how that one stock behaves.
ATCL: An actively managed income fund that mimics autocallable notes, a type of contract that pays regular income and can end early if a market trigger is hit. Most of the fund sits in Treasury bills, which back the derivatives, and the payouts come from the notes.
ATFV: Around 35 companies of any size, with technology half of the fund and communication about a quarter. It's a concentrated growth bet on firms the managers think are changing for the better, so it swings far more than the broad market.
ATTR: A fund that uses options on large US stocks or the S&P 500 and can hold stocks and other ETFs, aiming to guard against severe market drops. It includes a tail risk ETF as a main holding, so its results depend heavily on how those hedges work.
AUAU: A fund tracking an index of gold mining companies around the world, so it owns the miners rather than gold itself. It is top-heavy, with Newmont, Agnico Eagle and Barrick together about 29% of the fund, and miners can swing more than gold prices.
AUGC: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cushion the first 10% of losses over a set one-year period starting in August. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, so it suits holding through the whole period rather than trading in and out.
AUGM: Uses options linked to the S&P 500 to absorb as much of a set amount of losses as possible over a one year period that starts in August. In return, the gains it can capture are capped, so it is designed to be held for the full period.
AUGP: A fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in August. In return, gains are capped, so it behaves differently from a plain S&P 500 fund, and the outcome only applies when held for the full period.
AUGT: Options on an S&P 500 fund, built to cushion the first 10% of losses over a one year period starting in August, as in its name. Gains are capped at a level reset each period, so results depend on when you buy.
AUGU: An S&P 500 fund using options to cushion part of the losses over a one-year period that starts in August, with no cap on gains from the index's price rise. It is built from options on the SPY fund, and the protection only applies if held for the full period.
AUGW: Uses options tied to the S&P 500, through the SPY fund, to aim for a defined outcome over a one-year period starting in August. It is built to absorb part of the losses in exchange for a cap on gains, so timing within the period matters.
AUGZ: An actively managed fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to aim for a set outcome over a one-year period starting in August, giving up some upside in exchange for some protection. Most of the money sits in Treasuries to support those options, and the results only apply if held for the whole period.
AUMI: Tracks an index of gold mining companies from around the world, such as Endeavour, Agnico Eagle and AngloGold. Their stocks tend to move with the gold price, often by more, and the top five holdings are each about 5% of the fund.
AUSF: US stocks spread across technology, financials, industrials and health care, with the mix shifting between value, quality and momentum styles as markets change. It's a core stock holding that tries to adapt on its own, so it may not move exactly in step with the broad market.
AV: An actively managed fund of aerospace and commercial aviation companies, from jet engine makers to defense contractors. GE Aerospace and RTX are about 20% of it, and everything held is in industrial companies.
AVDE: Companies of all sizes from developed countries outside the US, with financials the biggest slice, then industrials and materials. It's a core international holding that tilts toward cheaper, more profitable companies, and foreign currency swings affect it.
AVDS: Smaller companies outside the US that Avantis selects for value and profitability. It is very spread out across Japan, Europe and elsewhere, with no holding above about 0.5%, and leans toward industrials and materials.
AVDV: Small companies from developed countries outside the US that look cheap, spread across materials, industrials, consumer companies and financials. It's a way to add international small-company value stocks, and it swings more than large company funds, plus foreign currency moves affect it.
AVEE: Small companies in emerging markets, with extra weight on the ones that are cheaper and more profitable than their peers. It holds a very wide spread of stocks, with no single holding above about 2%, mostly from Taiwan, South Korea and other Asian markets.
AVEM: Companies from emerging countries like China, India and Taiwan, with technology about 39 percent and financials about a fifth. It's an actively managed way to add developing economies, tilting toward cheaper, more profitable firms, and it swings more than developed-market funds.
AVES: Emerging-market companies that look cheaper and more profitable, with financials at about a quarter and technology near a fifth. It's a value-leaning way to add developing-country stocks, and it swings more than developed-market funds.
AVGB: An actively managed fund of investment grade bonds from US and foreign companies, with the currency risk hedged back to US dollars. It is widely spread across many issuers, and each is only about 1% of it.
AVGE: A fund of funds that spreads money across stocks in the US, other developed countries and emerging markets. It tilts toward cheaper, more profitable companies, and works as a one-fund global stock portfolio, though it can trail when growth stocks lead.
AVGV: A basket of other funds holding value stocks around the world, large and small, with financials at a quarter and industrials, consumer companies and energy filling out much of the rest. It's a one fund global value tilt that can lag when growth stocks lead.
AVGW: A single-stock fund tied to Broadcom, using swaps and some direct shares to track the stock's moves, with payouts made weekly. Most of the rest is Treasury bills backing those swaps, so how it does depends mostly on one company.
AVIE: A fund of US companies the managers expect to hold up or gain when inflation rises, such as energy, health care and consumer staples firms. Berkshire Hathaway, ExxonMobil, Procter & Gamble and Eli Lilly are among the largest holdings, each around 4% to 5%.
AVIG: A broad mix of investment-grade bonds from US and foreign issuers, including government, corporate and mortgage debt. It's a core bond holding for steady income and a cushion for stocks, and managers tilt toward bonds that pay more for the risk, though prices drop when rates rise.
AVIV: Large companies outside the US that look cheaply priced, with financials about a third, then industrials, energy and materials. It's a value-focused holding for international stocks, so it leans away from tech and can trail in growth-led rallies.
AVLC: Large US companies across many industries, with technology about a third and financials, industrials and consumer companies filling out the rest. It leans toward more profitable, cheaper stocks and skips some weaker ones, so it works as a core holding with a value tilt.
AVLV: Large US companies that look cheap and profitable, with financials the biggest slice, then consumer companies, energy and technology. It's a core value holding that's actively screened for quality, and it can trail when fast-growing stocks lead the market.
AVMA: A fund of other Avantis ETFs that holds about two-thirds stocks and one-third bonds. It leans toward smaller and cheaper companies in stocks, so it is a ready-made mix in one fund.
AVMC: Mid-sized US companies across industrials, financials, technology and health care. It's a core mid-cap holding that tilts toward cheaper, more profitable and smaller firms, so it can behave differently from a plain mid-cap index, especially when value stocks fall out of favor.
AVMU: An actively managed fund of intermediate term US municipal bonds, loans to cities, states and public agencies whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It holds many bonds, none above about 2%, and uses Avantis's research-driven approach.
AVMV: Mid-sized US companies, led by financials, consumer companies, industrials and energy, picked because they look cheap and profitable. It's a value-tilted way to add mid-sized stocks to a portfolio, and it can trail growth-focused funds when tech-heavy markets lead.
AVNC: Holds stocks from companies outside the US, in both developed and emerging markets, with extra weight on smaller and cheaper companies and profitable ones. It is spread across thousands of holdings, with Taiwan Semiconductor and ASML among the larger ones, plus an emerging markets ETF at around 10%.
AVNM: Stocks from developed and emerging countries outside the US, led by financials, industrials, technology and materials. It's a one-fund way to add international stocks, and it leans toward cheaper, more profitable companies, so it can trail when growth stocks lead.
AVNV: A fund of funds that holds three Avantis ETFs, giving value-tilted exposure to large and small companies in developed markets plus emerging markets outside the US. Value means it favors cheaper-looking stocks, and financials are the biggest sector.
AVOS: An actively managed global stock fund that mostly buys other ETFs, with large pieces in Vanguard's developed-markets and emerging-markets funds. It is a one-fund mix of the world's stocks, including US names like Apple, at around 5%.
AVRE: Real estate companies around the world, mostly property owners that pass rental income to shareholders, spread across many kinds of buildings. It adds property exposure and income to a stock portfolio, and it can fall when interest rates rise because borrowing gets costlier for landlords.
AVRY: An actively managed fund that picks a small group of US stocks, mostly technology and internet companies. It is fairly concentrated, with Block, Zoom, Okta and Clear Secure each making up around 6% to 8% of it.
AVSC: Small US companies tilted toward cheaper, more profitable ones, spread over financials, consumer companies, industrials and health care. It's an actively managed small-company holding for growth over long periods, and it swings more than large company funds.
AVSD: Stocks of large and mid-sized companies outside the US that Avantis selects for value and profitability, while screening out firms that fail certain responsible-investing standards. It is broadly spread, with ASML, HSBC and Roche each around 1%.
AVSE: Emerging markets stocks, with a screen that leaves out companies that fail certain environmental and social standards. It leans toward value and profitable companies, and chipmakers SK Hynix, TSMC and Samsung are about 24% of the fund.
AVSF: Short-term, investment-grade bonds, largely US Treasuries plus some corporate bonds. It's meant for steady income and a cushion for a stock portfolio, with less rate risk than longer bonds, though its price still falls a bit when rates rise.
AVSU: Large and mid-sized US companies, with technology about 37 percent, then financials, consumer companies and health care. It's a core stock holding that screens out companies with poor environmental and social records and leans toward cheaper, more profitable firms.
AVTM: Stocks from companies worldwide, with technology about a third, then financials, industrials and consumer firms. It's an all-in-one global stock holding that leans toward cheaper, more profitable companies, and a manager adjusts the mix between the US and other countries.
AVUC: A broad fund of US companies of all sizes, tilted toward smaller and cheaper companies and those with higher profitability. The managers use rules based on academic research instead of a standard index, so it differs from a plain total market fund.
AVUQ: Large US companies that Avantis picks for high profitability and a growth tilt, using its own research rather than a standard index. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon are about 37% of the fund.
AVUS: US companies of all sizes across many industries, with technology about 30%, tilted toward cheaper and more profitable firms than a plain market-weighted fund. It's a core US stock holding aiming for a slight edge, though it still moves closely with the market.
AVUV: Small US companies that look cheap and are profitable, led by financials, consumer firms and energy. It's an actively managed bet on small value stocks, so it can swing more than the broad market, and it can lag when big tech leads.
AVXC: Emerging market companies outside China, with technology around 40% and financials about a fifth. It's a way to add developing economies without China exposure, tilting toward smaller and cheaper companies, so it swings more than a fund holding developed markets.
AWAY: Companies around the world that make technology for travel, such as booking sites, ride apps and airline reservation systems. It is spread out, with TravelSky, Sabre, Uber, Trainline and Expedia each around 5% of the fund.
AZTD: Small and mid-sized companies in developed markets outside the US, selected by a rules-based stock selection model. It holds many stocks with no single one above roughly 3%, spread over technology, consumer, industrials and health care.
AZYY: An income fund built around Amazon stock that uses options contracts to generate regular payouts, with Treasury bills held as backing. Selling those options limits how much it gains if Amazon jumps, and it does not simply hold Amazon shares.
BAB: Taxable bonds issued by US states, cities and other local governments to pay for projects like schools, roads and transit. It offers interest income from high quality borrowers, and unlike most municipal bonds the interest is taxable, but its price falls when interest rates rise.
BABO: An actively managed fund that aims for income by using options tied to Alibaba's stock, giving up some of the gains if the stock rises. It holds mostly Treasury bills to back the options, so it is a single-stock bet that pays income rather than owning Alibaba shares.
BABW: A fund giving exposure to Alibaba stock through swaps and shares, with a strategy built to pay income weekly. It tracks a single company, and the income approach means it will not capture all of Alibaba's gains.
BAFE: Large US companies picked by active managers, led by technology and financials, followed by communication and health care. It's a core growth holding that can include smaller companies, so it may differ from the broad market, and it can trail or lead it.
BAGX: An actively managed US stock fund that uses a quantitative, rules-driven process to pick companies of any size, and can put up to 10% in a single company. Big tech leads, with NVIDIA, Apple, Alphabet and Microsoft about 18% of the fund together.
BAGY: Gets exposure to Bitcoin's price and sells call options on it to produce high monthly income. The options limit how much of Bitcoin's gains it can capture, and Treasury bills in the portfolio mostly serve as backing.
BAI: Companies tied to artificial intelligence, chosen by managers, with nearly all in technology. It's a focused growth bet on one theme, so it swings more than the broad market, and managers can pick stocks across the US and abroad.
BAIV: An actively managed fund of stocks outside the US, in developed and emerging markets, that Brown Advisory thinks are priced below their worth. It is spread out, with no holding above about 5%, and leans toward financials, consumer and health care companies.
BALI: Large US companies, led by technology, paired with an options strategy that sells some upside in exchange for regular income. It aims to pay income and smooth the ride, so it usually holds up better when markets fall but trails in strong rallies.
BALQ: An actively managed fund of Nasdaq listed stocks that also uses options to earn extra income, with the aim of balancing that income and some growth. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 23% of it, and technology is over 60%.
BALT: Holds options tied to the S&P 500 that are designed to cushion the first part of any drop over a one-year period. In exchange, there is a cap on the gains, so it trails in strong rallies and is meant for a smoother ride.
BAMA: An actively managed fund of funds that spreads money across other ETFs holding US stocks, international and emerging market stocks, and bonds. Roughly two thirds is in stocks and the rest in bonds, with the manager adjusting the mix based on its outlook.
BAMB: An actively managed bond fund that mostly holds other ETFs of intermediate-term US Treasuries, including funds of 3 to 10 year Treasuries and bond funds that end in 2031 to 2033. It is a fund of funds, so it is built from six or so ETFs.
BAMD: An actively managed fund of US dividend-paying stocks, mostly mid-sized companies chosen for steady income. Paychex, JPMorgan Chase, ONEOK and Eversource are each around 5%, and the fund leans toward financials, energy and utilities.
BAMG: An actively managed fund of US stocks the manager expects to grow earnings strongly over the next several years. Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, NVIDIA and Amazon are each about 5%, so roughly a quarter of it sits in those big tech names.
BAMO: An actively managed fund of funds that holds ETFs, about two thirds in US stock index funds like the S&P 500 and the Dow, and the rest in short-term Treasury bill funds. The manager shifts the mix based on its market outlook.
BAMV: An actively managed fund where the manager picks US stocks that look like good value based on its own research. It leans toward financials and technology, and Microsoft is the biggest holding at about 9% of the fund.
BAMY: An actively managed fund of funds that spreads money across other ETFs holding high-yield bonds, preferred stocks and dividend payers. The top four holdings are each about 20% of the fund, so it is built around income from riskier, lower-rated bonds.
BAPR: A buffer fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to absorb a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in April. In exchange, gains are capped at a ceiling, and the protection works best if held for the full period.
BASG: Large US growth companies that meet the manager's sustainability criteria, with technology at half the portfolio and financials next. It's a growth-oriented core holding that screens by sustainability, and it swings more than the broad market.
BASV: An actively managed fund of large US companies that look cheap and also meet the manager's sustainability standards. It holds a fairly small group of stocks, with the top five, including Dell, Flex and Cardinal Health, making up about 21%.
BATT: Global companies tied to lithium batteries, including miners, battery makers and electric vehicle makers, tracked by an index. Materials companies are over half the fund, and Tesla, BHP and CATL are together roughly 20% of it.
BAUG: A US large-company fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion the first part of any losses over a one-year period that starts each August. In exchange, gains over that period are capped, so it works best if held for the full cycle.
BAVA: A fund that holds the Avalanche cryptocurrency, AVAX, directly and stakes part of it, meaning the coins help run the network in exchange for extra AVAX as rewards. Its value follows the price of Avalanche, which can swing a lot, and it holds no stocks or bonds.
