EMXF: Large and mid-sized emerging market stocks that score well on environmental, social and governance ratings, with fossil fuel companies removed. It leans on tech and financials: SK Hynix alone is over 11% of the fund.
ENDW: An actively managed fund that owns other Cambria funds to spread across stocks, bonds, real assets and alternatives in the US and abroad. It is modeled on the way big university endowments invest, so it is a mix in a single ticker.
ENFR: North American pipeline and storage companies that move oil and natural gas. It's a focused energy bet aimed at income, and it moves with energy volumes and interest rates, so it can swing more than the broad market.
ENHE: An actively managed fund of emerging market stocks, with the managers choosing holdings to try to beat the market. Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung are about 27% of it, and technology is around 42%.
ENHI: An actively managed fund of large company stocks from developed markets outside North America, aiming to stay close to the MSCI EAFE Index while trying to do a bit better. It is widely spread, with ASML the largest holding at only about 3%.
ENHU: An actively managed fund of large US companies that stays close to the Russell 1000 index but uses computer models to try to do a little better. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are together about 20% of the fund, much like the broad market.
ENOR: Large and mid-sized Norwegian companies, tracked with the MSCI Norway index and weighted by market value. Energy and banks dominate: Equinor and DNB are each roughly 12% of the fund, so it leans heavily on oil, gas and finance.
ENRG: An actively managed fund investing worldwide in companies that explore for, produce or distribute oil, gas, coal or uranium, including some in emerging markets. It is a bet on the energy industry, so its value tends to follow commodity prices.
ENZL: New Zealand stocks, tracking the MSCI New Zealand index, which covers the country's large and mid-sized companies. It is a small, concentrated market: Fisher & Paykel Healthcare is about 21% of the fund, and Infratil and Auckland Airport add roughly another 28%.
EOCT: Uses options on an emerging markets stock fund (the iShares MSCI Emerging Markets ETF) to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each October. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only works if held the full period.
EPAI: An actively managed fund of companies that the managers think will benefit from artificial intelligence, such as chip equipment makers. It is concentrated in technology, about 60% of the fund, with Applied Materials, Teradyne and Lam Research among the largest holdings.
EPEM: An actively managed fund of stocks in developing countries such as Taiwan, South Korea, India and others. It is top-heavy: Taiwan Semiconductor is about 14% and Samsung about 8%, so chip companies make up a big part of the fund.
EPHE: Philippine companies of all sizes, tracking the MSCI Philippines index. It is concentrated in one country and one name: International Container Terminal Services is about 24%, and banks, ports, property and utilities make up most of the rest.
EPI: Indian companies chosen by how much profit they earn, led by financials, with materials, industrials and energy also big. It's a way to invest in the Indian economy, so it swings more than a US fund and can be affected by currency changes.
EPIN: An actively managed fund of stocks from developed countries outside the US, such as Taiwan, the Netherlands, South Korea and the UK. It is spread broadly, with the largest holding, Taiwan Semiconductor, at only about 5% of the fund.
EPMB: An actively managed fund of US mid-sized companies, picked by the manager rather than an index, with a blend of growth and value stocks. It is widely spread, with the top holdings such as Keysight, Woodward and Cummins each around 3%.
EPMV: An actively managed fund of US mid-sized companies that the manager considers undervalued, using the Russell Midcap Index as its yardstick for company size. It is fairly spread out, with its largest positions, such as Flex and Cummins, each around 3% of the fund, and leans toward industrials, financials and technology.
EPOL: Polish companies, with banks and other financials close to half, then energy, consumer firms and materials. It's a focused bet on one emerging European economy, so it swings more than a broad international fund and leans heavily on the banking sector.
EPP: Companies in developed Asia Pacific countries outside Japan, mainly Australia, Hong Kong and Singapore, with financials making up nearly half and materials next. It's a way to add a specific region to a portfolio, and it's heavy in banks and miners rather than tech.
EPRF: Investment grade preferred stocks, which are shares that pay fixed dividends and rank ahead of regular shares, following an S&P index. All of them are financial companies, such as KKR, Ares, Voya and Northern Trust, and each is about 4% of the fund.
EPS: Large US companies chosen and weighted by their profits, with technology at over a third and financials, communication and health care behind. It's a core stock holding that leans toward earnings, so the biggest weights go to the most profitable firms rather than the biggest in price.
EPSB: An actively managed fund of US small and mid-sized companies, using the Russell 2500 Index as its guide for company size. It is widely spread, with the largest holdings such as Moog and Woodward each around 3%, and leans toward industrials and technology.
EPSV: An actively managed fund buying US small and mid-sized companies that the managers think are priced cheaply compared with what they are worth. It leans toward industrials, financials and technology, and no single stock is more than about 3% of the fund.
EPU: Companies tied to Peru, with materials (mostly miners) at roughly half and financials at nearly a third. It's a narrow bet on one small country's economy, so it swings widely with metal prices and local politics.
EQAL: About a thousand large US companies, each given roughly the same weight rather than being weighted by size. It spreads money across industries instead of leaning on a few giants, so it's a core holding that does better when smaller firms lead and trails when mega-caps rally.
EQIN: An actively managed fund of US companies that pay dividends, mostly large and established ones. Financials and energy stand out, with JPMorgan, Bank of America, ExxonMobil and Chevron each around 4% to 5% of the fund.
EQL: Large US stocks split evenly across the market's major sectors, such as technology, health care, energy and utilities, instead of letting big sectors dominate. It's a diversified core holding, and it gives smaller sectors more weight than the S&P 500, so it can trail when tech leads.
EQLT: A fund of emerging market stocks chosen for higher quality, such as strong profitability and stable earnings, than their peers. It is top-heavy in chips: SK Hynix and Samsung are together about 25% of it, with technology at around a third.
EQRR: Large US stocks that have tended to do better when interest rates are rising, picked by a Nasdaq index. It's spread across many companies, including Marvell, CrowdStrike and Lam Research, none above about 5%.
EQTY: A concentrated mix of US and foreign companies, with technology about a quarter, financials just under that, and health care and industrials next. Managers pick a limited number of stocks they like, so it's a core style holding that can differ a lot from the broad market.
EQWL: The 100 biggest US companies, each given the same weight instead of letting the giants dominate, with technology about a quarter, then health care, financials and industrials. It's a core holding with less reliance on a few mega-caps, so it can trail when those giants lead.
ERET: Real estate companies around the world chosen for their strong environmental practices, tracked using a FTSE EPRA Nareit green index. It holds property owners and REITs: Welltower, Prologis and Realty Income are the largest, each about 5% to 7%.
ERTH: Holds companies around the world picked by MSCI for products and services tied to sustainability, such as clean energy, green buildings and electric vehicles. Digital Realty, BYD, NVIDIA and Tesla are each about 4% to 5% of it.
ESBG: An actively managed fund mixing US Treasuries with futures that give exposure to stocks and gold. The futures add extra exposure on top of the bonds, so it aims to hold stocks, bonds and gold at once with a leveraged feel.
ESG: Large US and developed-market companies that score better on environmental, social and governance measures, chosen by a STOXX index. It still looks a lot like the broad market, with Microsoft, Apple, Broadcom and NVIDIA making up around 20% of it.
ESGD: Large and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside the US, led by financials, industrials and technology. It's meant as international exposure for a core portfolio, and it tilts toward companies with better environmental and social ratings while excluding some controversial businesses.
ESGE: Companies in emerging markets such as China, Taiwan, India and Brazil, with technology the biggest slice at over 40% and financials next, screened for better environmental and social records. It's a growth-oriented way to diversify abroad, and it swings more than developed market funds.
ESGG: Stocks from developed markets around the world that score better on environmental, social and governance measures than their peers in the STOXX Global 1800 Index. It is top-heavy in US names, with Microsoft, JPMorgan and Apple together about 16%, and about 39% in technology.
ESGU: Large US companies screened and weighted to favor better environmental, social and governance scores, with technology at about 40% and financials, health care and communication each around a tenth. It suits someone wanting a core US stock holding with a values tilt, though it will not match the broad market exactly.
ESGV: US companies of all sizes screened to favor better environmental, social and governance scores, with technology at over 40% and financials, communication and health care following. It suits a core US stock holding with a values tilt, though it's heavier in tech than the broad market.
ESIM: An actively managed fund of stocks from outside the US, chosen by the manager rather than by following an index. Its holdings are spread across many companies, with technology, industrials and financials the biggest areas, and no single stock above about 6%.
ESLG: An actively managed fund of large US companies the manager expects to grow faster than average over the long run. It is tilted to technology, and NVIDIA alone is about 10% of the fund, with Broadcom next at about 4%.
ESLV: An actively managed fund buying large US companies that look reasonably priced. It is spread out, led by ExxonMobil at about 5%, with Home Depot, Union Pacific and Medtronic each near 3%.
ESML: Small US companies across technology, industrials, health care and financials, tilted toward firms with better environmental and governance scores. It's a way to own small companies for long-term growth, and they swing more than large ones, though the tilt keeps it close to the broad small-cap market.
ESMV: Large and mid-sized US stocks chosen to be steadier than the market, using the MSCI USA ESG Optimized Minimum Volatility approach, which also screens for environmental and social factors. It is spread out, with no holding above about 2% of the fund.
ESN: An actively managed fund holding a basket of about 40 US stocks tied to the Essential 40 Stock Index, which focuses on businesses meant to be essential to the economy. It is fairly even, led by Intel at about 6%.
ESPO: Global video gaming and esports companies, including game makers, platforms and hardware firms, following the MarketVector Global Video Gaming & eSports index. Spread across names like NetEase, Tencent, Roblox and Take-Two at about 7% each, it is heavily communications stocks.
ESSC: An actively managed fund of US small companies, which it defines as worth less than $20 billion, chosen for quality. It is widely spread, with no stock above about 1%, across health care, technology, financials and industrials.
ESUM: An actively managed fund of US stocks that tries to beat the market by picking firms the managers think will do well for the long term. Technology is the largest area, and NVIDIA alone is about 7% of the fund.
ETCO: An income fund that sells options on an Ethereum ETF to collect premiums, so it earns cash payouts but gives up some gains if Ethereum jumps. It holds mostly Treasury bills as backing, and it still moves with Ethereum's ups and downs.
ETEC: Companies around the world working on breakthrough technologies that help address climate change, following a Morningstar index. It spreads across industrial, tech and auto-related firms, with the top holding, Kurita Water Industries, about 7% of the fund.
ETFT: An actively managed global stock fund run by Fundsmith, holding high-quality businesses it plans to keep for a long time, such as Waters, Amadeus and Mastercard. It holds relatively few companies, and about a tenth sits in a Treasury money fund.
ETH: Ether, the digital currency behind the Ethereum network, with the fund also earning staking rewards by helping run the network. It's a high-risk bet on a single digital asset, so its price can swing wildly, far more than stocks or bonds.
ETHA: A fund that holds ether, the digital currency behind the Ethereum network, so you get its price moves without setting up a crypto wallet. It's a high-risk bet on a single digital asset, and it can swing wildly in value and pays no income.
ETHB: Ethereum held by a trust, which also earns extra ether by helping run the network, known as staking. It's a bet on one digital currency, so the price can swing sharply in either direction and it behaves very differently from stocks and bonds.
ETHE: A fund that gives exposure to Ether, the digital currency of the Ethereum network, without having to buy it directly. It also earns staking rewards, which adds some income, but it's a high-risk bet on one crypto asset that can swing wildly.
ETHO: US stocks chosen and weighted by how well the companies handle their carbon footprint, with the fund tracking an index of climate leaders in their industries. It holds many small and mid-sized companies in roughly even amounts, so no stock is more than about 2%.
ETHV: A fund that holds actual Ether, the digital currency of the Ethereum network, and tracks its price using a MarketVector benchmark. It does nothing beyond following Ether's price, so it rises and falls with the crypto market, which can swing sharply.
ETHW: A trust that holds ether, the digital currency of the Ethereum network, directly, so its price follows the price of ether. It is passively managed, and because ether can swing sharply in price, the fund can move sharply too.
ETTY: A fund that follows the price of ether, the cryptocurrency on the Ethereum network, while selling options to collect extra income. Selling those options caps some of the gains, so it will not fully follow ether when the price jumps.
EUAD: European makers of airplanes, defense systems and related equipment, all in the industrials sector. It's a focused bet on one industry that depends heavily on government defense budgets, so it can swing a lot, and it gives exposure to Europe rather than the US.
EUDG: European companies with high quality finances and a record of growing their dividends, picked by a WisdomTree index. It leans toward big names like Novartis, Nestle and Roche, which are each around 4% to 5% of the fund, and mixes industrials, financials and health care.
EUDV: European companies in the MSCI Europe index that have a record of raising their dividends steadily over time. It holds many companies in small slices, with Logitech, ACS, Halma and London Stock Exchange each around 3%, across industrials, health care and financials.
EUFN: Banks, insurers and other financial companies from across Europe, with almost nothing outside finance. It's a focused bet on European financials, so it leans heavily on interest rates and the health of the region's banks, and it holds no tech or consumer names to balance it.
EUHY: Bonds issued by lower-rated European companies, paying higher interest because the issuers are riskier, with the euro exposure hedged back to US dollars. Holdings are spread thinly, with no single bond above about 1% of the fund, so no one company dominates.
EUIG: Investment grade corporate bonds issued in euros by European companies, following the Bloomberg Euro-Aggregate Corporates index, with the currency risk hedged back to US dollars. It is spread across many issuers, with none above about 1%.
EUM: A fund aiming to deliver the opposite of the daily return of the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, so it tends to rise when that index falls on a given day. It resets daily, so holding it for longer can produce results that differ a lot from simply betting against the index.
EUSA: About 600 large and mid-size US companies, each given roughly the same weight, spread across technology, industrials, financials and health care. It's a core holding that leans less on giant companies, so it can lag when the biggest stocks lead the market.
EUSB: A broad mix of US dollar bonds, mostly Treasuries and corporate bonds, with companies screened for environmental and social ratings. It's meant as a steady income core for the bond part of a portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise and the screens change what it holds.
EUV: An actively managed fund of companies that make or rely on chip-making and light-based technology, including extreme ultraviolet lithography, the process used to print advanced chips. It is concentrated in semiconductors: Taiwan Semiconductor and ASML are together about 21% of the fund.
EVHY: An actively managed fund of high yield bonds, which are corporate debt from companies with weaker credit that pay higher interest to make up for the risk. It is spread across hundreds of issuers, and no single bond is more than about 1% of the fund.
EVIM: Intermediate-term municipal bonds, loans to US state and local governments and public projects whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It holds many bonds, such as utility and power district revenue bonds, with each around 1% of the fund.
EVLN: Loans made to companies with weaker credit, whose interest rates reset as short-term rates change. It's meant for income that holds up when interest rates rise, but it can lose value in recessions when borrowers fail to repay.
EVLU: Emerging market stocks that look cheap compared with peers in the same sector, with a tilt toward higher quality, tracked by an MSCI index. Samsung is about 11% of the fund and technology about 43%, so it leans on Asian chipmakers.
EVMO: Mortgage-related bonds, including pass-through securities, commercial property loans and more specialized types. It aims for higher income than ordinary bonds, and since homeowners can repay early and the types are complex, its price can swing more than a plain bond fund.
EVMT: An actively managed fund that gets exposure to metals used in electric vehicle batteries, such as lithium, cobalt, nickel and copper, mainly through futures. Most of the money sits in a Treasury money fund as backing.
EVNT: An actively managed fund that buys and sells short shares and debt of companies facing announced events like mergers or buyouts, trying to profit from how the deals turn out. It mixes stocks, bonds and cash, and is meant to move less with the market.
EVPF: An actively managed fund of preferred securities and other income-producing securities, both US and foreign, aiming for steady payouts. Preferred stocks sit between bonds and regular stocks, paying fixed dividends, and many are issued by banks and insurers.
EVSD: Short-term US dollar bonds from governments, companies and other issuers, with a small cash cushion. It's meant for modest income with limited ups and downs, because short maturities mean its price is less affected when interest rates move.
EVSM: Short-term municipal bonds, loans to US states and local governments whose interest is generally exempt from regular federal income tax. It's meant for tax-friendly income with a calmer price, since short maturities mean it reacts less to interest rate moves than longer municipal bond funds.
EVTR: A broad mix of US dollar bonds, including government, corporate and mortgage-backed bonds, with some willingness to hold lower-rated ones for extra yield. It's meant as a core bond holding for income and a cushion against stock drops, and its price falls when interest rates rise.
EVUS: US large and mid-sized company stocks that look inexpensive relative to their size, filtered for environmental, social and governance (ESG) scores. It differs from a plain value index by tilting toward companies with better ESG profiles, and Alphabet is about 7% of it.
EVX: Follows an index of companies in environmental services, such as waste collection, water treatment, pollution control and recycling. It is fairly concentrated, with Ecolab, Waste Management, Waste Connections and Republic Services making up about 29% of the fund.
EVYM: An actively managed fund of high yield municipal bonds, issued by state and local governments and related agencies, with interest generally exempt from regular federal income tax. High yield means lower credit quality issuers, and holdings are spread thinly, with the biggest only about 2% to 3%.
EWA: Large and mid-sized Australian companies, with banks and financial firms making up about two fifths and miners and materials about a quarter. It's a focused bet on one country's economy, and it leans on banks and commodity prices, so it can swing more than a global fund.
EWC: Canadian companies, with financials about 40% of the fund, then energy, materials and technology. It's a way to add Canada to a portfolio, and its heavy tilt to banks, oil and mining means it moves with commodity prices.
EWD: Companies based in Sweden, with industrials the biggest slice at nearly half, then banks and other financials, and communication companies. It's a focused bet on one small developed country, so it moves differently from the US and swings with European markets and the Swedish krona.
EWG: German companies, with industrials the biggest slice at nearly a third, followed by financials, technology and health care. It's a focused bet on one European economy rather than a broad one, so it leans on exporters and can swing with global trade and the euro.
EWH: Large and mid-sized Hong Kong companies, with insurers, banks and exchanges at about 45%, plus property, utilities and industrial firms. It's a focused bet on one small market, so it swings more than a global fund and is sensitive to China's economy.
EWI: Large and mid-sized Italian companies, with banks and insurers making up more than half, plus utilities and industrial firms. It's a focused bet on one country's economy, so it swings more than a global fund and leans heavily on the financial sector.
EWJ: Large Japanese companies, spread across industrials, technology, financials and consumer businesses. It's a way to add a major developed economy to a portfolio, and because it's priced in yen, its value also moves with the Japanese currency against the dollar.
EWJV: Large and mid-sized Japanese companies that look cheap compared to their size, led by financials, industrials and consumer firms. It's a way to add Japan with a value tilt, and because it avoids pricier growth stocks, it can trail when expensive tech names lead.
EWK: Belgian stocks, following the MSCI Belgium index, which covers a small country's largest companies. It is very concentrated: Anheuser-Busch InBev is about 22% and argenx about 14%, so a few companies drive most of the results.
EWL: Large Swiss companies, with health care the biggest slice at nearly two fifths, followed by financials, consumer staples and industrials. It's a focused bet on one country with steady, defensive businesses, but with few companies and a strong currency, it can behave differently from the US market.
EWM: A fund that tracks the MSCI Malaysia index, giving exposure to large companies listed in Malaysia. Banks make up about half of it, and Public Bank, Maybank and CIMB alone are around 38%, so it is a concentrated bet on one country and its financial sector.
EWN: Dutch companies, led by technology at about a third, then financials, food and household brands, and industrials. It's a concentrated bet on one small European country, heavy in chip equipment makers, and it moves with the euro.
EWO: Austrian stocks, following the MSCI Austria index of the country's largest companies. It is concentrated: Erste Group, BAWAG and OMV are about 43% of the fund, and nearly half is in banks and other financials.
EWP: Spanish companies, with banks and other financials making up nearly half, utilities about a fifth and industrials most of the rest. It's a way to add a single European country to a portfolio, and with so much in banks and power companies it is less tech heavy than US funds.
EWQ: Large and mid-sized French companies, tracked through an MSCI index. It is a single-country fund, so it rises and falls with France, where TotalEnergies, Schneider Electric, LVMH, Safran and Airbus are together about 34% of it.
EWS: Singapore stocks, with financials a bit over half, mostly banks, followed by industrials and real estate. It's a focused bet on a small, trade driven economy, so it's heavy on banks and can swing with Asian and global markets.
EWT: Companies based in Taiwan, with technology about three quarters of the fund, mostly chip makers and electronics manufacturers. It's a concentrated bet on one country and one industry, so it swings a lot and carries political risk.
EWU: Large and mid-sized UK companies, with financials the biggest slice and consumer staples, industrials and health care close behind. It's a focused bet on one country's economy, with little tech, and its value also moves with the pound against the dollar.
EWUS: Small UK companies, tracked by an MSCI index, covering financials, industrials and consumer businesses. It is broadly spread, with the largest holdings, like Diploma, Beazley and IMI, each only about 2% or 3%, and it is priced in pounds.
EWW: Mexican stocks, with materials about a quarter, consumer staples another quarter, and financials and industrials making up much of the rest. It's a focused bet on one emerging market, so it swings more than a global fund and is sensitive to the peso and trade with the US.
EWX: Small companies in emerging markets, led by technology, industrials and consumer businesses, across many developing countries. It's a growth bet on small companies abroad, so it swings more than the broad market and than funds of big companies.
EWY: South Korean companies, with technology, mainly chip makers, making up over half, followed by industrials and financials. It's a focused bet on one country, so it swings more than a global fund and leans heavily on the health of the global chip industry.
EWZ: Brazilian companies, with financials about a third, then energy, mining and materials, and utilities. It's a focused bet on one emerging country, so it swings more than the broad market, and its returns also depend on the Brazilian real against the dollar.
EWZS: Small Brazilian companies, tracking the MSCI Brazil Small Cap Index. It is spread across utilities, retail and real estate, with no holding above about 5%, and its value also depends on the Brazilian real against the US dollar.
EXEQ: Tracks an index of the 50 top-ranked large US companies by ReturnOnLeadership, a score of how well firms treat employees, customers and other stakeholders. It is fairly concentrated: Delta Air Lines and United Airlines are together about 16% of the fund.
EXI: Industrial companies from around the world, such as aerospace and defense, machinery, transportation and construction. It's a focused bet on one sector, tied to economic growth, so it tends to do well in expansions and fall harder when the economy slows.
EXPN: An actively managed fund of large US companies the manager expects to expand, heavily in big tech. NVIDIA, Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon are about 30% of the fund together, and tech makes up about 44%.
EXUS: An actively managed fund of about 50 non-US stocks, in developed and emerging markets. It is concentrated, with Taiwan Semiconductor at about 8%, SK Hynix at 5% and ASML at 4.5%, and the manager picks companies by hand rather than following an index.
EYEG: A fund of investment-grade corporate bonds, meaning loans to companies seen as financially solid, from firms such as Amazon, Verizon and Sysco. It is very spread out: each of its top holdings is only about half a percent of the fund.
EYES: An actively managed fund holding companies in data analysis, monitoring and security, such as software and public safety firms. Palantir is about 16% of the fund and Datadog about 9%, so it is fairly concentrated in a few technology names.
EYLD: Emerging market stocks chosen for returning cash to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks, with financials the biggest group at about a quarter, followed by technology, industrials and energy. It aims for income plus growth abroad, and it can be volatile because emerging markets swing hard.
EZA: South African companies, with mining and materials around 40% and banks and other financials about a third. It's a focused bet on one emerging country, so it swings with commodity prices and the South African rand, and it's far less diversified than a global fund.
EZBC: Bitcoin itself, held directly by the fund, rather than stocks or bonds. It lets you own bitcoin in a regular brokerage account, but the price is very volatile and can swing sharply in either direction, so it's a high risk, speculative holding.
EZET: A fund that holds ether, the cryptocurrency behind Ethereum, so you can get its price moves in a regular stock account. Its value moves with ether, which can swing sharply, and it is not a proxy for owning ether directly.
EZM: Mid-sized US companies picked and weighted by their earnings rather than by their size, across financials, industrials, consumer businesses and technology. It's a value-leaning way to add mid-sized companies to a portfolio, and it can trail the market when large growth companies lead.
EZMO: A fund of funds that holds other ETFs, mostly one tracking the Nasdaq-100 and another tracking a broad market index, following an index built around momentum, meaning recent winners. About two thirds is in the Nasdaq-100 fund, so it leans heavily toward technology.
EZPZ: Holds bitcoin and ether directly, in roughly the same weights as an index that contains only those two coins. Prices can swing a lot, and it is crypto exposure rather than a stock or bond fund.
EZRO: A fund of funds that follows an index rotating among sector ETFs. Despite the word defensive, it is mostly in technology, with the Technology Select Sector fund at about 25% and others like Invesco QQQ and an AI fund making up the rest.
EZU: Companies from countries that use the euro, with financials about a quarter, industrials a fifth and technology and consumer firms behind. It's meant to add European exposure to a portfolio, and its returns depend on the euro's value against the dollar and on the eurozone's economy.
FAAA: Collateralized loan obligations (CLOs) rated AAA, the safest tier, which are bundles of corporate loans sold in slices. Holdings are widely spread, with none above about 2%, and the interest rate floats with market rates.
FAAR: An actively managed fund that goes long and short commodity futures, such as energy, metals and farm products, aiming to profit whether prices rise or fall. Its Treasury bill holdings are mostly collateral for those futures, not the main investment.
FAB: A fund of value-style US stocks across large, mid and small sizes, chosen by the AlphaDEX method, which ranks companies on growth and value measures rather than size. It is spread evenly, with no holding above about 1%.
FAD: US growth stocks of all sizes picked by a rules-based screen, with technology about 28% and industrials and health care next. It's for growth with a tilt toward smaller and mid-sized companies, so it usually swings more than the broad market.
FAI: Tracks a Bloomberg index of the 50 companies best positioned to benefit from artificial intelligence, chosen by their AI-related revenue and other measures. It is mostly technology, and chipmakers Micron, AMD and SK Hynix are each in the 7% to 9% range.
FALN: Bonds from companies that were once investment grade but were downgraded to high-yield, the so-called fallen angels. It's meant for higher income than safe bonds, and these issuers are often large and established, though prices can fall sharply in recessions.
FAN: Tracks an index of companies across the wind energy industry, such as turbine makers and wind power producers around the world. It is concentrated: Vestas, Nordex, Orsted and EDP Renewables are about 31% of the fund, and it is split between utilities and industrials.
FAPR: US large company stocks, with technology about 40 percent, wrapped in options that cushion some losses over a one year period that starts in April. The trade-off is a cap on gains, so it's for cautious investors, and the protection works best if held for that full period.
FARX: An actively managed mix of other funds spread across stocks, bonds, commodities and currencies, aiming for steady results whether markets rise or fall. Short-term bond, trend-following and commodity funds make up most of the top holdings, so it is a fund of funds.
FAUG: US large company stocks, mostly technology, reached through options on an S&P 500 fund. It's built to cushion some losses over a one year period starting in August, but it also caps your gains, and the protection only works fully if you hold from the start date to the end.
FB: Holds the S&P 500 and uses very short-term options to cushion part of the losses, in exchange for capping some of the upside. The buffer adjusts over time, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 16% of the underlying stocks.
FBCG: Well-established large US companies picked for growth, with technology more than half the fund and communication and consumer companies next. It's built for growth, and an active manager chooses the stocks, so it's heavily tied to tech and can swing more than the broad market.
FBCV: An actively managed fund of large and mid-sized, well-established US companies that Fidelity's managers think are priced below their worth. It holds some very big names, with Amazon, Microsoft and Apple together about 17% of the fund.
FBDC: Shares of business development companies and other specialty lenders, which make loans to mid sized businesses and often pay out most of their income as dividends. It is concentrated, with Main Street, Ares Capital and Hercules about 32% of the fund.
FBND: A broad mix of bonds that includes Treasuries, mortgage-backed bonds and corporate bonds, plus a smaller slice of riskier, higher-yielding debt. It's built as a one-fund core bond holding for income, and the manager can shift between bond types, so it won't match a plain bond index.
FBOT: Global companies the manager sees as benefiting from automation and robotics, such as chipmakers, equipment makers and industrial firms. Taiwan Semiconductor, Teradyne and NVIDIA are the top holdings at about 5% each, and half the fund is in industrials.
FBT: Thirty leading biotechnology companies held in roughly equal amounts, all in health care. It's a focused bet on drug research, so it swings more than the broad market, and because every company gets a similar share, smaller names matter as much as giants.
FBTC: Actual bitcoin held in storage by the fund, so there are no stocks or bonds inside. It's a way to own bitcoin through a regular brokerage account, and its price can swing wildly, with big moves up or down in a single day.
FBUF: Holds large US stocks picked by computer models that weigh value, growth and profitability, then uses options to soften a set amount of losses over a set period. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are together about 20% of it, and the options limit some upside.
FBY: A fund built around Meta Platforms stock that sells call options, contracts that give up some of Meta's upside in exchange for regular income. Most of its money sits in Treasury bills backing those options, and it holds a single company's exposure, so it is very concentrated.
FBYY: An income fund tied to Meta Platforms that uses options contracts on a Meta ETF instead of mainly owning the stock, with the rest sitting in Treasury bills. It aims to pay high income, and that options approach limits how much of Meta's gains it can capture.
FCA: About 90% or more of this fund is in Chinese stocks picked from the NASDAQ China Index using the AlphaDEX method, a rules-based screen that favors stocks with stronger growth and value traits. It is spread across financials, technology, industrials and health care, though one small holding is about 14%.
FCAL: California municipal bonds whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and often from California tax. It leans toward higher-yielding, longer bonds, and holds many issuers, none above about 1.5%.
FCBD: An actively managed fund of investment grade bonds, mostly built by holding other bond ETFs. The top holdings are funds from Vanguard, TCW and JPMorgan, so it works as a bond fund of funds with a small cash share.
FCEF: A fund of funds that owns closed-end funds and ETFs spread across stocks and bonds, chasing income. Closed-end funds can trade above or below their underlying value, and the fund is actively managed, with no single holding above about 4%.
FCFY: Companies from the S&P 500 with the highest free cash flow yield in each sector, meaning lots of spare cash generated compared with their stock price. Because it picks the best in every sector, it holds less well-known names, with technology the biggest group at about 40%.
FCG: Natural gas producers and related energy companies, nearly all of it in the energy sector, including some pipeline-style partnerships. It's a focused bet on gas prices and the energy industry, so it can swing sharply when energy prices jump or fall.
FCLD: Companies involved in cloud computing, from software to data storage hardware, following a Fidelity index. It is heavily technology, and the top four holdings, including Sandisk, Western Digital, Seagate and AppLovin, are each about 4 to 6% of it.
FCLO: An actively managed fund that holds collateralized loan obligations, which are bundles of corporate loans sliced into pieces that pay interest. Its returns follow interest rates and loan defaults, and no single holding is more than about 3% of it.
FCOM: US communication companies, such as social media, internet search, streaming, telecom and media firms. It's a focused bet on one sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and a few giant companies drive most of its moves.
FCOR: Mostly investment-grade corporate bonds, which are loans to companies, picked by Fidelity's managers. It is spread out, with no corporate issuer above about 1%, though a small slice is held in US government securities.
FCPI: A fund tracking the Fidelity Stocks for Inflation Factor Index, which picks large and mid-sized US companies seen as able to keep up with rising prices, such as those with pricing power or inflation-linked assets. It is still tech-heavy, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft about 16%.
FCSH: An actively managed fund of investment grade corporate bonds with short maturities, issued by companies like Bank of America, Citigroup and JPMorgan. Short maturities mean the price should move less when interest rates change, and no one bond is more than about 3% of it.
FCTE: An actively managed fund that holds roughly 20 US stocks from the S&P 500, picked by a model that looks for quality and attractive prices. With so few holdings, it is concentrated, with several stocks like Apple, Jabil and Meta at about 5% each.
FCTR: US stocks chosen from four factor based indexes, such as value, quality, momentum and low volatility, with the mix shifting over time by a rules based method. It spreads across many companies, with no single holding above about 3% of the fund.
FCUS: An actively managed, focused fund of US stocks, mostly technology. It is concentrated in memory and data storage companies: Micron, Sandisk, Western Digital and Seagate are about 22% of the fund.
FCVT: Holds convertible securities, which are bonds or preferred shares that can be swapped for a company's stock. It is actively managed and spread across companies like Nebius, Alphabet and Western Digital, and leans toward technology, so it moves partly like bonds and partly like stocks.
FDAT: An actively managed fund that holds other ETFs focused on US stocks or high yield bonds, switching between them over time. At the moment about two thirds is held in cash, so it behaves more like a cautious tactical mix than a stock fund.
FDCF: An actively managed fund of companies whose new technologies or business models could shake up how communications and media are delivered. It holds both communication and technology stocks, and the top holdings are Taiwan Semiconductor, Alphabet and Meta at about 26% combined.
FDD: Thirty high-dividend European companies, with financials such as banks and insurers over half, and the rest in consumer, industrials and energy. It's meant for dividend income from Europe, and the heavy bank tilt plus currency swings between the euro and the dollar make it bumpier than a broad fund.
FDEC: US large company stocks, with technology about 40 percent, wrapped in options that cushion some losses over a one year period that starts in December. The trade-off is a cap on gains, so it's for cautious investors, and the protection works best if bought at the start of that period.
FDEM: Large and mid-sized stocks from developing countries, tilted toward companies that look cheap, high quality or steady, with technology the biggest slice at nearly 40%. It adds emerging-market growth to a portfolio, but it swings more than US stocks.
FDEV: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed countries outside North America, tracking an index that favors companies scoring well on factors like value, quality, momentum and low volatility. It is widely spread, with Shell, Roche and Novartis each around 1 to 2% of the fund.
FDFF: An actively managed fund of financial companies that Fidelity believes are being changed by new technology, such as digital payments and online banking. Banks and asset managers like BlackRock, DBS and Capital One lead it, each at about 5% or 6%.
FDG: An actively managed fund holding only 30 to 45 large growth companies, mostly US technology, internet and consumer names. It is very concentrated: NVIDIA and Alphabet are together about a third of the fund, and Amazon is another 9%.
FDHY: Bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, the so-called junk bonds, with a little cash. It's for higher income than safer bonds, and it leans toward the better quality end of junk, but it can still fall when the economy weakens.
FDIF: A fund of five Fidelity stock funds, each focused on a theme of disruptive change, such as new technology and new health care approaches. Because it only holds those five funds, it is a way to own all five at once, each around 15% to 25%.
FDIG: Companies tied to cryptocurrency and digital payments, such as exchanges, Bitcoin miners and payment firms. It holds the stocks, not actual crypto, and its top holdings like Coinbase and miners are each only about 3% to 5%, but prices can swing a lot.
FDIQ: Follows an index of companies that supply financial data and analytics, such as ratings, indexes and market data. Names like MSCI, Cboe, Fair Isaac and Coinbase each make up about 5% of the fund, so it is a narrow bet on one corner of finance.
FDIS: US consumer companies that sell things people want rather than need, such as online retailers, carmakers, restaurants, hotels and home improvement. It's a focused bet on consumer spending, so it tends to do well when the economy is strong and fall when people cut back.
FDIV: An actively managed fund that buys US dividend paying stocks, mostly mid sized companies, chosen by the sub-adviser MarketDesk. It leans toward financials, technology, industrials and consumer staples, and its largest holdings are each only around 2% of the fund.
FDL: The 100 highest-yielding US stocks with a record of steady dividends, led by consumer staples, utilities, energy and financials. It's for dividend income, and it has little technology, so it can trail the broad market when growth stocks are leading.
FDLO: Large and mid-size US companies chosen for calmer share prices, with technology at roughly a third or more, then financials, health care and communication. It suits someone wanting a steadier core stock holding, though it usually lags in sharp rallies led by riskier stocks.
FDLS: Small US companies chosen using several factors, such as value and momentum, while following faith-based screening rules from Inspire. Holdings are spread thin, none above about 2%, and it spreads across technology, financials, health care and industrials.
FDM: Very small US companies, called micro-caps, taken from the Dow Jones Select MicroCap index and weighted fairly evenly. It holds many tiny stocks that trade less often, with no holding above about 2%, so it can swing sharply.
FDMO: Large and mid-sized US stocks that have been rising lately, with technology about 40 percent and financials and health care each around a tenth. It's a growth-leaning holding that rides winning trends, and it can fall behind or reverse quickly when the market's leadership changes.
FDN: Internet companies, including online retailers, search and social media firms, streaming services and internet software, spread across technology, communication and consumer sectors. It's a focused bet on the web economy, so it swings more than the broad market and holds many companies that other tech funds class elsewhere.
FDND: A fund of internet companies, based on a Dow Jones internet index, that also uses options to produce extra income. Amazon, Meta and Cisco are about 28% of it, and the options income comes in exchange for giving up some of the upside.
FDNI: Tracks an index of internet companies based outside the US, such as Shopify, Tencent, Alibaba and Spotify. Those four are about 35% of the fund, and it mixes online shopping, media and software businesses.
FDRR: Large and mid-sized US companies that pay dividends, led by technology, with financials, health care and communication next. It's built for dividend income, and it also screens for stocks that have historically held up better when interest rates rise.
FDRS: Fifty US companies where an original founder still holds a top executive role, tracked by an index. It is top-heavy: Meta, NVIDIA, Tesla and Palantir are about 35% of the fund, and technology is more than half of it.
FDRV: Global companies tied to electric vehicles and the future of transportation, such as automakers, battery makers and chip suppliers, tracked by an index. Tesla, Uber, CATL, Infineon and NXP are each about 5%, so it is spread over many names.
FDT: Companies from developed countries outside the US, with industrials the biggest slice at about a third, then financials, consumer goods and technology. It's for diversifying away from the US, picked by a scoring formula instead of by size, so its mix differs from standard international funds.
FDTS: Small companies from developed countries outside the US, picked by First Trust's AlphaDEX method, which ranks stocks on growth and value factors instead of simple size. It holds a very large number of stocks, none above about 1%.
FDTX: An actively managed fund of companies Fidelity thinks are building new or unconventional ways of doing business with technology. It is concentrated in chips: Micron, Marvell and Taiwan Semiconductor together make up about 24% of the fund.
FDV: Large US companies with a history of paying and growing dividends, spread across utilities, consumer staples, health care and financials. It's built for steady income and a calmer ride, so it usually holds up better in sell-offs but can trail when fast-growing technology companies lead the market.
FDVV: Large US companies that pay higher-than-average dividends, with technology about a third and financials, consumer and staples firms behind it. It aims for income plus growth in one stock fund, and it holds far more tech than most dividend funds, which often lean toward utilities and banks.
FEAC: An actively managed US stock fund of large, mid and small companies that uses research and models to try to beat the broad market. NVIDIA and Apple are about 13% of it, and technology is roughly 40%.
FEBM: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on a US stock fund to absorb a large share of losses over a one-year period starting in February. The trade-off is a cap on gains, and the protection works best if held for the full period.
FEBP: An actively managed fund that uses options on the S&P 500 over a set one-year period starting in February, aiming to protect against the first 12% of losses in exchange for a limit on gains. The buffer only works for those who hold the whole period.
FEBT: Uses options on the S&P 500 to follow it over a one-year period starting each February. Its name says buffer 10, so it absorbs a set first slice of losses, but the options cap the gains over the period.
FEBU: A fund using options to follow US stock market returns over a one year period starting in February, with a set amount of losses cushioned. Gains are not capped by a fixed limit, but the protection only fully applies if held for the whole period.
FEBW: Uses options on the S&P 500 fund SPY to cushion part of the losses over a one-year period that starts in February, as the name's Buffer20 suggests. In return, gains are capped, so it trades some upside for protection.
FEBZ: An actively managed fund using options on the S&P 500 to follow the index's gains up to a limit while cushioning part of the losses over a set one year period starting in February. Most of the fund sits in US Treasuries backing the options.
FECM: An actively managed fund of municipal bonds of medium maturities, whose interest is generally free of regular federal income tax, with at least 80% in those. It holds hundreds of issuers, so no single bond makes up much of the fund.
FEDM: Large and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside the US, picked to follow an index that favors better environmental, social and governance scores and lower climate risk. It is widely spread, with ASML the biggest holding at about 3%, and tilts toward financials and industrials.
FEGE: A manager-picked mix of companies from the US and abroad, with consumer staples, technology, health care and financials as the largest parts. It aims for steady growth with less risk, favoring sturdy businesses, so it tends to hold up better in downturns but may trail in booms.
FEIG: US dollar corporate bonds from companies with strong credit ratings, filtered to favor those scoring well on environmental, social and governance measures. It is widely spread, with big names like Morgan Stanley, HSBC and Ford Credit each only about 1% of the fund.
FELC: Mostly the large companies in the S&P 500, with technology over 40%, but a manager tilts the weights toward stocks that look promising. It's a core holding that aims to modestly beat the broad market, so it should move much like it with some differences.
FELG: Large US growth companies, with technology about 60% and communication, industrials and health care behind it. It's a growth fund that leans heavily on tech, so it tends to rise faster in rallies and fall harder in sell-offs, and the manager makes modest adjustments to try to beat its benchmark.
FELV: Large US companies that look cheaply priced, spread across technology, financials, health care and industrials. It's meant as a core value holding, and the managers tilt the picks using their own research, so it can differ from a plain value index in both good and bad stretches.
FEM: Stocks from emerging markets such as China, India and Brazil, with technology, industrials, energy and materials leading. It's a growth-oriented way to add developing economies, and it picks and weights stocks by a rules-based formula instead of size, so it swings more than the broad market.
FEMB: Government bonds from emerging countries such as Thailand, Malaysia, India and Indonesia, issued in their own local currencies rather than dollars. Its value moves with both bond prices and those currencies against the dollar, and it is spread across many countries.
FEMD: An actively managed fund of US mid-sized companies that the manager considers good value. It is widely spread, with the largest holdings such as Tenet Healthcare and GE HealthCare each around 2% to 3% of the fund.
FEMG: A fund of US mid-sized growth stocks, based on the Russell Midcap Growth Index, with the manager tilting the picks to try to beat the index. Technology is the biggest slice at about 37%, and no stock is more than about 3%.
FEMR: An actively managed emerging markets stock fund that starts from a broad index and tilts toward stocks its models like. Tech heavyweights dominate: Taiwan Semiconductor is about 12% and SK Hynix and Samsung are each over 6% of the fund.
FEMS: Small companies in emerging markets, selected and weighted from a NASDAQ index using First Trust's AlphaDEX method, which ranks stocks on growth and value traits instead of size. Holdings are spread across many countries, with no stock above about 2%.
FEMV: A fund of US mid-sized value stocks, based on the Russell Midcap Value Index, with the manager tilting the picks to try to beat the index. It is very spread out, with the largest holdings, such as Marathon Petroleum and Kinder Morgan, around 1% each.
FENI: Large companies in developed countries outside the US, led by financials and industrials, with technology and health care behind. It's an international core holding, and managers tilt the picks to try to beat a standard international index modestly.
FENY: US energy companies, such as oil and gas producers, refiners and equipment services firms. It's a focused bet on the energy sector, so it tends to rise and fall with oil and gas prices and swings more than the broad market.
FEOE: Companies outside the US, picked by managers who favor reasonably priced firms, spread across consumer staples, industrials, technology and financials. It's a way to own international stocks with a cautious style, so it may trail in strong rallies.
FEP: Stocks from developed European countries, with industrials the biggest slice at about a quarter, then energy, financials and materials. Stocks are picked and weighted by a rules-based screen for growth and value rather than size, so it's a way to add Europe and it can behave differently from a plain index.
FEPI: Big-name technology and internet companies, with tech about 70%, paired with an options strategy that trades some upside for monthly income. It's built for income, and it still swings with tech while giving up gains in strong rallies.
FESC: An actively managed fund of US small companies that the manager thinks are priced below their worth. It is widely spread, with no single stock above roughly 1% to 2%, and its biggest areas are industrials, technology and health care.
FESM: Small US companies from the Russell 2000, led by health care, technology, financials and industrials, picked by a manager using a computer-driven approach aiming to beat the index. It's a core small-company holding, and it swings more than large-company funds.
FETH: Ether, the digital currency that runs the Ethereum network, held directly rather than through companies or bonds. It's a high-risk bet on crypto, so it swings far more than stocks, and it pays no interest or dividends.
FEUS: Large US companies chosen to look like the broad market while favoring those with better environmental, social and governance and climate characteristics. It is top-heavy in tech, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together about 20% and technology around 41% of the fund.
FEUZ: Stocks from countries that use the euro, selected from a NASDAQ index using the AlphaDEX method, which ranks stocks on growth and value factors instead of just size. It is very evenly spread, with no holding above about 2%, and leans toward industrials, financials and energy.
FEX: Large US companies picked and weighted by a score for growth and value rather than by size, with technology near a fifth and industrials, financials and health care behind. It spreads money more evenly than the broad market, so it holds smaller weights in the giants.
FEZ: Fifty of the biggest companies in the eurozone, led by financials at about a quarter, then industrials and technology. It's a way to own big European firms in one fund, but it's concentrated in euro-area countries and tied to the euro's value against the dollar.
FFDI: An actively managed fund of large companies in developed countries outside the US, chosen by Fidelity's research on each business. It leans toward financials and industrials, and ASML, the Dutch chip equipment maker, is the biggest holding at roughly 5%.
FFEB: US large company stocks, with technology about 40 percent, wrapped in options that cushion some losses over a one year period that starts in February. The trade-off is a cap on gains, so it's for cautious investors, and the protection works best if bought at the start of that period.
FFEM: An actively managed fund of companies in emerging markets such as Taiwan, South Korea, China and India, chosen through in-depth company research. It is top-heavy in chips, as Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK Hynix are about a third of it.
FFF: An actively managed fund of US companies still led by their founders, such as Meta, NVIDIA, Dell and Palantir. It is non-diversified and tilted toward technology, with the top five holdings making up about 28% of the fund.
FFGX: An actively managed fund of stocks outside the US, including emerging markets, chosen through Fidelity's own company research. Taiwan Semiconductor is about 8% of it, and technology and financials are each about a quarter of the fund.
FFIU: An actively managed bond fund that can buy many kinds of fixed income, aiming for current income with an average duration of a few years. Much of it is in mortgage backed bonds and US Treasuries, such as Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac securities.
FFLC: An actively managed fund of large US companies picked by Fidelity's research into each business. Its top positions are NVIDIA at about 8% and Alphabet at about 7%, followed by Amazon and Apple.
FFLG: An actively managed fund of large US companies that Fidelity expects to grow faster than average. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA and Alphabet are about 29% of it, with Apple, Eli Lilly and Microsoft next.
FFLS: An actively managed long/short fund that buys stocks it likes and bets against others it expects to fall. Mostly mid and large US companies, with Amazon, NVIDIA and Alphabet among the top holdings, and a large cash balance that helps manage risk.
FFLV: An actively managed fund of large US companies that Fidelity's researchers think are priced below their worth. Amazon, Apple and Microsoft are among the top holdings, but each is under about 8%, so it is more spread out than the big tech focus suggests.
FFLX: An actively managed income fund holding a flexible mix of corporate bonds and bank loans, including lower-rated ones. The managers can shift between types and countries, so it differs from a fund that tracks one bond index.
FFND: An actively managed growth fund holding stocks from the US and abroad, with at least 30% in companies outside the US. It is topped by NVIDIA, Amazon and Apple, each around 4% to 5%, and about a third is technology.
FFOG: An actively managed fund holding a concentrated set of US companies the managers expect to grow fast. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Alphabet and Amazon are about 27% of it, and technology makes up well over half.
FFOX: An actively managed fund of mostly mid-sized US growth companies that the managers think are well placed to benefit from long-term trends. It is spread across technology, industrials and health care, with no single holding above about 3%.
FFSM: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US companies picked by Fidelity's research on each business. It is spread thinly, with no holding above about 2%, and it includes industrial, materials and services names.
FFTY: Holds about 50 fast-growing US stocks picked weekly from the IBD 50 index, a rules-based list built from growth and strength measures. The list changes often, and it leans toward health care and technology companies.
FFUT: An actively managed trend-following fund that takes bets in futures on stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities, going long or short depending on which way prices have been moving. Much of the fund sits in Treasury bills as collateral, so the futures drive the results.
FGD: High-dividend companies from around the world, led by financials at over a third, with industrials, energy and consumer companies behind. It's built for dividend income from global companies, and it holds little technology, so it can lag in tech-led rallies.
FGDL: Holds physical gold bars, sourced under responsible-sourcing standards, so its value follows the gold price. It owns only gold and a little cash, and unlike mining stocks it has no company risk, though gold itself pays no income.
FGM: Picks German stocks from the NASDAQ Germany Index using the AlphaDEX method, which ranks companies on growth and value measures instead of size. Holdings are fairly equal in weight, with industrials and consumer companies the biggest groups.
FGSI: Holds a spread of US growth stocks chosen for strength and sells call options on them to produce income. No stock is above about 2%, and the options limit how much it gains in strong rallies.
FGSM: Holds small companies from around the world by owning other small-cap ETFs, including US and international funds from Avantis and iShares. It is a fund of funds, so you get broad small-company exposure in one ticker, including some emerging markets.
FHDG: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 ETF to cushion part of the losses over each three-month period, in exchange for a limit on gains. The buffer is reset every quarter, so protection depends on when you hold it.
FHEQ: Large US companies, with technology the biggest slice at about 40%, combined with options that offset part of the market's drops. It's meant for stock growth with a smoother ride, so it usually falls less in sell-offs but gives up some gains in strong rallies.
FHIL: An actively managed fund buying large companies outside the US, such as AstraZeneca, ASML and Hitachi, aiming for long-term growth. It is spread across technology, industrials and financials, with no single holding above about 3%.
FHLC: Nearly all US health care companies: drugmakers, medical device makers, insurers and biotech firms, of all sizes. It's a focused bet on the health sector, which tends to hold up better than most in recessions but is exposed to drug pricing and regulation.
FHYS: US dollar junk bonds, meaning bonds from lower-rated companies, chosen to mature sooner than most. Shorter bonds usually swing less in price than longer ones, and the fund is spread across many issuers, none above about 1%.
FIAT: An actively managed fund that aims to pay income while moving opposite to Coinbase's share price, using options rather than owning the stock. Treasury bills mainly serve as collateral for those positions, and it can lose money when the stock rises.
FIAX: An actively managed fund that mostly holds US Treasury securities and also sells put options on stock indexes to earn extra income. The options can add income but also add risk if stocks fall sharply, so it behaves differently from a plain Treasury fund.
FICS: Holds about 100 companies in developed countries outside the US that look financially strong, using a First Trust index that screens for things like low debt and healthy cash flow. Banks, insurers and industrial firms lead, with no single holding above about 3%.
FID: High dividend paying companies from outside the US, picked from an S&P index of firms that have raised or maintained dividends for at least ten years. It is spread widely, with no stock above about 3%, and leans toward financials, utilities and industrials.
FIDI: Foreign companies in developed markets, picked by Fidelity's International High Dividend Index for paying above-average dividends. It leans toward financials, energy and consumer staples, and is spread out, with no holding above about 4%.
FIDU: US industrial companies, including aerospace and defense, machinery, airlines, railroads and construction firms, with small slices of technology. It's a focused bet on one sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and it tends to rise when the economy is growing and factories are busy.
FIFT: An actively managed fund that picks stocks from the S&P 500 using a proprietary model built with Ned Davis Research. The manager can shift its holdings as the model changes, so it may look quite different from the S&P 500 itself.
FIGB: Investment-grade bonds from companies and governments, spread across different types and maturities. It's a core bond holding for income and a cushion when stocks fall, and a manager adjusts the mix actively, but its price still drops when interest rates rise.
FIIG: Investment-grade bonds from US companies, with medium-length maturities. It's meant for steady income above Treasury bonds, and the mid-length maturity means its price swings moderately, dropping when interest rates rise or when company credit worsens.
FIMU: Intermediate-term bonds from state and local governments, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It suits investors in higher tax brackets who want steady, tax-friendly income, though prices dip when interest rates rise.
FINA: Big companies across the US and Canada, with technology about two fifths and financials, communication and health care behind it. It's a low-effort core holding for North American stocks, though it leans heavily on tech and so swings with that one sector.
FINT: A fund of funds that holds other ETFs covering stocks outside the US, including emerging markets and international quality companies. It is a ready-made international mix, with Avantis Emerging Markets and two iShares funds making up about half of it.
FINX: A fund of financial technology companies around the world, such as payments, online brokers and digital banking firms. Robinhood, Block, PayPal and Coinbase are each around 5% to 7% of it, so it is concentrated in a few well-known names.
FINY: A fund that aims to pay weekly income by selling put options on a leveraged ETF that gives three times the daily move of a financials index. The options and leverage make it risky and unlike a plain financials fund, and the Treasury bills are backing.
FISR: Bonds from governments, mortgage pools and companies, shifted among sectors by a model that follows market signals. It's a core bond holding for income and a cushion in stock drops, and the rotation means it can differ from a plain bond fund.
FITE: A fund of US-listed companies in security-related areas, such as cybersecurity, defense and surveillance, tracking the S&P Kensho Future Security index. It is spread evenly, with no holding above about 2%, and mostly technology and industrials.
FITZ: An actively managed fund of mostly US stocks chosen by a method called the Must Have Portfolio, aimed at companies that may gain from big long term shifts in the economy. It is fairly top-heavy and tech-focused, with JPMorgan, NVIDIA, AMD and Tesla each around 5%.
FIVA: Large and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside the US, picked because they look cheap, led by financials and industrials. It's for investors wanting overseas value stocks, and it tends to lag when fast-growing tech companies lead the market.
FIW: Companies that supply and clean drinking water and wastewater, mostly industrial firms like equipment and pipe makers, with health care, utilities and technology each around a tenth. It's a focused bet on the water theme, so it moves with industrial stocks more than with water utilities.
FIXD: A mix of mostly bonds, including government, mortgage-backed and corporate debt, plus a small slice of preferred stock. A manager picks the bonds, aiming for steady income as a core bond holding, and it can buy some lower-rated bonds, which adds more risk than a pure high-quality fund.
FIXP: An actively managed fund that owns other bond ETFs, such as short-term bonds, senior loans and mortgage real estate funds, with options layered on to boost income. It holds funds rather than individual bonds, so a handful of ETFs make up most of it.
FIXT: An actively managed bond fund that mostly buys investment-grade and other income-producing bonds, with the manager choosing which ones to hold. It is a flexible core bond fund rather than an index tracker, so what it owns can differ from a plain bond index.
FIYY: A fund that uses options on a leveraged ETF tied to 20 year US Treasury bonds to generate income. The leverage and options make it behave very differently from a plain Treasury fund, and the Treasury bills it holds are mostly backing for the contracts.
FIZY: An actively managed fund of US growth stocks, including Palantir, CrowdStrike, NVIDIA and Apple, which each make up around 5% to 7%. It also sells options on top of those holdings to earn extra income, which limits upside in strong markets.
FJAN: US large company stocks, mostly technology, reached through options on an S&P 500 fund. It's built to cushion some losses over a one year period starting in January, but it also caps your gains, and the protection only works fully if you hold from the start date to the end.
FJP: Japanese stocks picked by a rules-based screen that looks for companies with stronger growth and value traits, instead of weighting by company size. Because of that, it leans toward mid-sized firms and differs from a standard Japan index fund, with the top names each around 3%.
FJUL: US large company stocks, mostly technology, reached through options on an S&P 500 fund. It's built to cushion some losses over a one year period starting in July, but it also caps your gains, and the protection only works fully if you hold from the start date to the end.
FJUN: US large company stocks, mostly technology, reached through options on an S&P 500 fund. It's built to cushion some losses over a one year period starting in June, but it also caps your gains, and the protection only works fully if you hold from the start date to the end.
FKU: UK stocks picked from the NASDAQ United Kingdom Index using AlphaDEX scoring, which favors stocks with stronger growth and value traits. It is spread across many companies in financials, consumer discretionary and industrials, with no stock above about 4%.
FLAG: Follows an index of the top 50 US companies picked using a market leadership approach, rather than just the biggest by size. It holds them in fairly even slices of around 5% or less, spread across technology, health care and consumer stocks.
FLAO: Uses options on the S&P 500 to put a floor under losses over a six-month period that starts in April or October, in exchange for a limit on gains. It resets every six months, and the protection only works if held for the full period.
FLAU: Tracks the FTSE Australia Capped Index, a broad group of Australian companies. It leans heavily on banks and miners: BHP and Commonwealth Bank are each over 10% of the fund, and financials and materials together are more than 60%.
FLAX: Tracks the FTSE Asia ex Japan Capped Index, holding stocks from developed and emerging Asian markets outside Japan, such as Taiwan, China, South Korea and India. It is tech-heavy, with Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung together about 23% of it.
FLBL: Senior loans to companies with weaker credit ratings, where the interest rate floats up and down with market rates. It aims for income and holds up better than ordinary bonds when rates rise, but it can drop if borrowers have trouble repaying.
FLBR: Brazilian companies, led by banks and other financials, with energy, mining and utilities next. It's a focused bet on one emerging economy, and it swings with commodity prices and the Brazilian real, so it is more volatile than broad international funds.
FLCA: Large and mid-sized Canadian companies, with financials about two fifths, then energy, materials and industrials. It's a way to add Canada to a portfolio, and because it leans on banks, oil and mining, it tends to follow commodity prices more than the US market does.
FLCB: A broad mix of US government, corporate, mortgage-backed and asset-backed bonds, mostly investment grade. It's meant for steady income and as a cushion for a stock portfolio, and the managers can shift between bond types, though its price drops when rates rise.
FLCC: An actively managed fund of large US companies, chosen by a computer-driven model that looks for stocks with good value, quality and momentum traits. It holds big tech: Apple, NVIDIA and Alphabet make up about 20% of it.
FLCE: An actively managed fund of large US companies that mostly invests through other funds, such as a T Rowe Price research fund, iShares factor funds, and JPMorgan and Vanguard funds. It is a fund of funds, and only a few holdings are above 10%.
FLCG: Large US growth companies, with technology about 60 percent, then communication and consumer companies. It's built for growth and uses computer models to choose stocks, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
FLCH: Large and mid-sized Chinese companies, tracked through the FTSE China Index, which includes H-shares listed in Hong Kong and other share types. It is top-heavy: Tencent and Alibaba together are over 20% of the fund.
FLCO: Investment-grade bonds issued by US and foreign companies, across a range of maturities. It's meant for steady income with more yield than government bonds, though prices drop when interest rates rise and companies can have credit troubles.
FLCV: Large US companies that look cheaply priced, chosen by a quantitative model from the MDT team at Federated Hermes. It is actively managed and spread out, with no holding above about 5%, and leans toward technology, financials and health care.
FLDB: Investment-grade bonds with very short average lifespans, a duration of about a year or less, from the US government and companies. Because the bonds are short, the price moves little when interest rates change, and a big share is in Treasuries.
FLDR: Floating rate and short-term investment-grade bonds, whose payments adjust as interest rates change. It's meant as a place for cash-like money to earn a bit more than savings yields, and its price barely moves when rates rise because its payouts reset quickly.
FLDZ: An actively managed fund of mid and large US companies that the manager sees as tied to the US economy, with a stated focus on domestic strength. It is widely spread, with the largest holdings, such as Humana and Sterling Infrastructure, each under 1%.
FLEE: Large and mid-sized companies from developed European countries, tracking the FTSE Developed Europe Capped Index. It leans on financials, industrials and health care, and ASML is the biggest holding at about 5%.
FLEU: Large and mid-sized companies from the countries that use the euro, such as Germany, France, Spain and the Netherlands, tracking the FTSE Developed Eurozone Index. Dutch chipmaking equipment firm ASML is the largest holding at about 10%.
FLGB: Large and mid-sized UK companies, led by financials at about a quarter, then consumer staples, industrials and energy. It's a focused bet on one country, so it can swing more than a broad international fund, and the pound's moves against the dollar affect results.
FLGR: Large German companies, following the FTSE Germany Capped Index. It is concentrated in a few names: Siemens, Allianz, SAP and Siemens Energy are together about 37% of the fund, with industrials and financials the biggest sectors.
FLGV: Direct US government debt, including Treasury bonds, notes and bills plus inflation-protected ones, held across a range of maturities. It's a high-safety core bond holding for income and as a cushion for stocks, though prices fall when interest rates rise.
FLHY: Bonds from companies with weaker credit ratings, which pay more interest to make up for the higher chance of default, with a small share from outside the US. It's for extra income, and it tends to fall alongside stocks in downturns more than safer bonds do.
FLIA: Government and corporate bonds from countries outside the US, such as Germany, the UK, Japan and France. It hedges currency to cancel out swings in foreign currencies against the dollar, and the largest positions are government bonds at roughly 3% each.
FLIN: Large and mid-sized Indian companies, led by financials, with consumer, industrial and materials businesses behind them. It's a way to get exposure to a fast-growing emerging economy, and it can swing a lot with a single country's markets and currency.
FLJH: Large and mid-sized Japanese stocks, tracked with the FTSE Japan Capped Hedged Index, which offsets moves in the yen against the US dollar. Mitsubishi UFJ, Tokyo Electron and Toyota are among the biggest holdings, each about 3%.
FLJJ: Uses options on the S&P 500 to put a floor under losses over a six-month period that starts in January or July, in exchange for a limit on gains. It resets every six months, and the protection only works if held for the full period.
FLJP: Large Japanese companies spread across industrials, technology, financials and consumer firms. It's a single-country holding that adds Japan to a portfolio, and its results also depend on the yen's value against the dollar.
FLKR: Large and mid-size South Korean companies, with technology, mainly computer chips, over half the portfolio, followed by industrials and financials. It's a focused bet on one country, so it swings more than a global fund and depends heavily on chip demand.
FLLA: Large and mid-sized companies from Latin America, tracking the FTSE Latin America Index, with Brazil and Mexico the main markets. Banks lead the fund, followed by miners and energy, and Vale and Itau Unibanco are the biggest holdings.
FLMB: Tax-free municipal bonds whose proceeds fund environmentally friendly projects, known as green bonds, with interest generally exempt from federal income tax. It leans long term, and California issuers make up several of the top holdings.
FLMI: Municipal bonds issued by US states and cities whose interest is free from federal income tax, chosen by an active manager who can adjust to changing conditions. It's meant for tax-free income, and its price falls when interest rates rise.
FLMX: Large Mexican companies, following the FTSE Mexico Capped Index. It is concentrated, with Grupo Mexico, Grupo Financiero Banorte, Fomento Economico Mexicano and America Movil about 40% of the fund, and it leans toward consumer staples, materials and banks.
