IDX: Indonesian companies from a VanEck benchmark index, held in a broad mix of the country's largest businesses. It leans toward banks, with Bank Central Asia and Bank Rakyat Indonesia about 17% of it, and also holds materials and energy firms.
IDYN: An actively managed fund of stocks outside the US that shifts between investing styles, such as value, quality and momentum, depending on which the managers like. It is well spread out, with ASML the largest holding at around 4%.
IEF: US Treasury bonds that mature in seven to ten years, backed by the federal government. It's a middle-of-the-road cushion for a stock portfolio, with moderate price swings, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
IEFA: Companies in developed countries outside North America, such as in Europe, Japan and Australia, led by financials, industrials and technology. It is used to add international diversification to a US-heavy portfolio, and it leaves out Canada and emerging markets.
IEI: US Treasury bonds that mature in three to seven years, all backed by the US government. It's meant as a middle-of-the-road cushion for a stock portfolio, with less price swing than long-term Treasuries, though its price still drops when interest rates rise.
IEMG: Stocks from emerging markets such as China, India and Taiwan, with technology over 40 percent and financials next. It offers growth from developing economies, but it swings more than funds holding developed countries, and a few big tech and chip makers drive much of its movement.
IEO: Companies that find and pump oil and natural gas, with nearly the whole fund in energy. It's a focused bet on energy that rises and falls with oil prices, and it can offset inflation while swinging far more than the broad market.
IETC: US technology companies of all sizes, with tech about 85% and a bit in communication. It's a focused bet on the tech sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and its screen leaves out some familiar names.
IEUR: Large and mid-sized companies across developed European countries, with financials about a quarter, industrials a fifth and health care behind. It's a core way to add Europe to a portfolio, and its returns also depend on the euro and pound against the dollar.
IEUS: Small European companies from the MSCI Europe Small Cap Index, from countries like the UK, Sweden and Switzerland. It holds many names, with the biggest under 1% each, and leans toward industrials and financials.
IEV: Large European companies from across the continent, led by financials at about a quarter, with industrials, health care and technology behind. It's a way to add international diversification, and it moves with European economies and the euro and pound, not just US markets.
IEZ: US companies that provide equipment and services to the oil industry, tracked by a Dow Jones index. It is top-heavy: Baker Hughes and SLB alone are about 43% of the fund, so two companies drive much of the result.
IFEB: Uses options tied to the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, which holds large companies in developed markets outside the US and Canada, to absorb a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts in February. In return, gains over that period are capped.
IFED: An exchange traded note, which is a debt of the bank that issues it rather than a fund that owns stocks, tracking an index of companies expected to benefit from Federal Reserve policy. It carries the issuer's credit risk and does not hold the stocks itself.
IFGL: Real estate companies in developed countries outside the US, following the FTSE EPRA Nareit Developed ex US Index. It includes landlords and developers like Goodman Group, Mitsubishi Estate and Mitsui Fudosan, and is spread across many names.
IFLN: A fund holding corporate bonds that were once investment grade but have been downgraded to high-yield, called fallen angels, and tracks an enhanced version of the Bloomberg index. These bonds pay more interest than safer ones, but with higher risk, and the holdings are spread thinly, each under 5%.
IFLO: A fund of non-US stocks picked by an index that favors companies with strong free cash flow, which is the cash left after running and investing in the business. It holds many companies, each around 2%, across industrials, technology, energy and consumer sectors.
IFLR: An actively managed fund of stocks in developed countries outside the US, such as Europe and Japan, that uses options to limit how much it can lose over a set period. That managed floor comes at a cost, since part of the upside is given up.
IFRA: Companies that own and run the nuts and bolts of the US economy: utilities about two fifths, industrials a bit over a third, plus materials and energy. It's a focused bet on infrastructure spending, so it's heavy in slower, steady businesses and light on tech.
IFV: A fund of funds that holds five First Trust country ETFs outside the US, picked by Dorsey Wright's momentum rankings. Each pick is about 20% of the fund, so it is concentrated in five countries and the mix can change when the index is reshuffled.
IG: An actively managed fund buying investment-grade corporate bonds, meaning loans to companies seen as lower risk of default. Managers choose the bonds themselves instead of following an index, and big banks like Morgan Stanley and Bank of America are among the largest issuers it holds.
IGB: Investment-grade US dollar corporate bonds from US and foreign companies, following a FTSE index. Investment grade means the issuers have solid credit ratings, so the fund pays more interest than Treasuries with more risk, and it covers bonds of many lengths.
IGBH: A fund that holds long-term US corporate bonds but uses interest rate futures to cancel out most of the effect of rising or falling rates. It mainly owns an iShares long-term corporate bond fund, so it is mostly exposed to company credit rather than rate moves.
IGCB: An actively managed fund of US corporate bonds, mostly investment grade, with a range of maturities. The TCW team picks bonds themselves, so it can differ from a plain corporate bond index, and a small share sits in cash.
IGE: Oil and gas producers make up about 70% of this fund, with mining and materials companies close to a quarter, all based in North America. It's a focused bet on natural resources that can act as an inflation hedge, but it swings with commodity prices.
IGEB: Investment-grade US corporate bonds chosen with a rules based approach that favors qualities like value and momentum within the index. It aims for steady interest income as a core bond holding, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
IGF: Companies that run the essential systems of the economy worldwide: utilities and infrastructure-style industrial firms such as toll roads and airports each about 40%, plus energy pipelines at about a fifth. It's meant to add steady, income-oriented real-asset exposure, and it spreads across many countries rather than only the US.
IGGY: An actively managed fund of growth-oriented companies based outside the US, spread across at least three other countries. It leans on technology and industrials, and Taiwan Semiconductor, SK Hynix and ASML together are about 18% of the fund.
IGHG: US investment-grade corporate bonds, paired with interest rate hedges meant to offset losses when rates rise. That means it mostly earns the extra income from corporate bonds without taking as much interest rate risk as a normal bond fund.
IGIB: Bonds from financially sound companies that mature in five to ten years. It's meant for steady income with more yield than government bonds, but its price drops when interest rates rise, more than shorter corporate bonds.
IGLB: Investment-grade bonds from US companies that mature in ten years or more. It's meant for higher income than shorter bonds, but long maturities mean its price drops noticeably when interest rates rise, so it swings more than most bond funds.
IGLD: Short-term US Treasuries and cash paired with options that follow the price of gold. It's meant for gold-linked income without owning bars, and the options give up some of gold's gains in strong rallies while still losing when gold falls.
IGM: Technology companies plus internet, media and other tech-related businesses that standard tech funds leave out, with technology over 80 percent. It's a focused growth bet on the tech world, so it swings more than the broad market.
IGOV: Government bonds from developed countries outside the US, priced in local currencies instead of dollars. It's a way to diversify away from US bonds, but currency swings can add gains or losses, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
IGPT: Companies tied to artificial intelligence and next generation software, with technology about three quarters and communication companies about a fifth. It's a narrow growth bet on one theme, so it swings far more than the broad market.
IGRO: Large companies outside the US with a record of raising their dividends, led by financials at about a third, then industrials, health care and consumer staples. It's for steady, growing income with international diversification, and it tends to hold up better than flashier growth funds in sell-offs.
IGSB: Bonds from financially sound companies that mature in one to five years. It's meant for steady income with less price swing than longer corporate bonds, so it acts as a calmer cushion, though it still pays less than longer or riskier bonds.
IGV: Software companies, from business applications to cloud and security programs, with nearly all in technology. It's a focused bet on one industry within tech, so it swings more than the broad market, and it holds no chipmakers or hardware firms.
IHAK: Companies that sell cybersecurity software, hardware and services, almost entirely technology. It's a focused bet on digital security, so it swings more than the broad market and rises or falls with software company sentiment.
IHDG: Quality dividend-growing companies outside the US, spread across industrials, consumer, financial and tech firms. It's a way to own international stocks for steady growth, and it hedges the currency, so swings in the dollar versus foreign currencies mostly don't affect returns.
IHE: US drug makers that sell prescription and over-the-counter medicines and vaccines. It's a focused bet on the pharmaceutical industry, so it's tied to drug approvals, patents and pricing rules, and it moves differently from the broad health care sector.
IHF: Health insurers, hospital operators and other companies that deliver or pay for medical care, all within health care. It's a focused bet on one corner of the sector, so it swings more than the broad market and can react sharply to government policy changes.
IHI: US companies that make medical devices such as heart valves, surgical tools, diagnostic equipment and diabetes monitors, all within health care. It's a focused bet on medical technology, which grows steadily but swings more than the broad market and is sensitive to hospital spending.
IHY: High yield bonds, sometimes called junk bonds because the borrowers are riskier, issued by companies outside the US. It follows an index, and it holds a long list of bonds, with none above about 1% of the fund.
IIGD: Holds short-term US investment-grade bonds, choosing those with the highest quality scores from the index provider. It is extremely spread out, with each holding below 1%, aiming for a steadier ride than a regular bond fund.
IINC: A fund that holds a mix of large and mid-size US stocks and also sells options on them to generate extra income. The option premiums add income, but they also limit how much the fund can gain when stocks rise sharply, and a large part of it sits in cash.
IJAN: A fund that uses options on an international developed-markets stock fund to cover part of the losses over a one-year period starting each January, after a first stretch of losses is absorbed. In return, gains are capped, so protection only applies if you hold the full period.
IJH: Mid-sized US companies, led by industrials and technology with financials and health care next. It offers more growth potential than large companies with less risk than small ones, and it has far less tech than a large-company fund, so it behaves differently from the S&P 500.
IJJ: Mid-sized US companies that look inexpensive compared with their earnings and assets, led by financials, industrials and consumer firms. It's a value-leaning way to add mid-sized companies to a portfolio, and it can trail growth stocks when they lead the market.
IJK: Mid-sized US companies with growth traits, with industrials and technology each about a quarter, followed by health care. It's built for growth from companies bigger than small caps but nimbler than giants, and it tends to swing more than large-company funds.
IJR: Small US companies, spread across financials, technology, industrials and consumer companies, screened for profitability. It adds growth potential beyond large companies, but small firms are shakier, so it swings more than the broad market, though the profit screen filters out the weakest.
IJS: Small US companies that look cheap relative to their size, spread across financials, consumer companies, technology and industrials. It's a value tilt for the smaller end of the market, a way to diversify beyond large companies, and it can lag when growth stocks lead.
IJT: Small US companies expected to grow faster than average, spread across technology, industrials, health care and financials. It's a growth tilt for the smaller end of the market, so it swings more than large-company funds and can fall harder in downturns.
IJUL: A buffer fund using options on an iShares MSCI EAFE fund (developed markets outside the US and Canada) to absorb the first 15% of losses over a one-year period starting in July. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only holds if you stay the whole period.
IJUN: Uses options on the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, which covers developed markets outside the US and Canada, to cushion part of the losses over a one year period that starts in June. In return, the gains over that period are capped.
ILCG: Large and mid-sized US companies that are growing faster than average, with technology making up over half. It's built for growth in a stock portfolio, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market, and it has little exposure to slower-growing industries.
ILCV: Large and mid-size US companies that look cheaply priced, with technology about a quarter, then financials, health care and communication. It's a value tilt inside a core stock holding, with less tech than the broad market, so it can trail when growth stocks lead.
ILDR: An actively managed fund of US and foreign companies that may benefit from new technology, using a ranking method to pick them. It is top-heavy in tech: NVIDIA, Amazon, Alphabet and Broadcom together are about 23% of the fund.
ILF: Around 40 of the biggest companies in Latin America, mostly in Brazil and Mexico, led by financials with materials, energy and industrials behind. It's a focused bet on the region, so it moves with commodity prices and local currencies and swings more than US stocks.
ILIT: A fund holding lithium miners and producers around the world, picking the companies in a global lithium index. It is a narrow bet on one metal used in batteries, with Mineral Resources, Sociedad Quimica y Minera, Liontown and Albemarle each at about 7% to 8%.
ILOW: Stocks of companies outside the US that are picked to swing less than the market, with financials the biggest group, followed by industrials and technology. It's meant for a smoother international ride, though it may trail in strong rallies.
ILS: Mostly catastrophe bonds, which are bonds sold by insurers that pay investors interest but can lose value if a hurricane, earthquake or similar disaster hits. Their returns depend on weather and disaster events rather than the economy, and each single bond is a small slice of the fund.
ILTB: US dollar bonds from government, agencies and companies, all with more than ten years left until they mature. It aims for high income and a cushion for stocks, but its price swings hard, falling a lot when interest rates rise.
IMAR: Uses options tied to the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, which covers developed stock markets outside the US, to buffer part of the losses over a one-year period that starts in March. In return, the gains for that period are capped, and the buffer only applies if held for the full period.
IMAY: A fund using options on the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF to give returns from developed stock markets outside the US, up to a limit, over a one year period starting in May. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses, if held for the whole period.
IMCB: US mid-sized companies spread across industries, with technology near a fifth and industrials, financials and health care behind. It's a diversified core holding for the middle of the market, offering more growth potential than giant companies with more bumps than them too.
IMCG: Mid-sized US companies with above-average growth, led by technology and industrials at roughly a quarter each. It's a growth piece between large and small companies, so it can lag when value stocks lead and swings more than the broad market.
IMCV: Medium-sized US companies that look inexpensive, spread across financials, energy, health care and industrials. It's a value-style core holding for the middle of the market, and it tends to lag in growth-led rallies when expensive stocks do the winning.
IMF: An actively managed fund that takes both long and short positions in futures tied to over fifty global markets, including stocks, bonds, commodities and currencies. It tries to follow price trends in either direction, so it behaves differently from a plain stock or bond fund.
IMFL: Large companies in developed countries outside the US, led by industrials, technology, financials and health care, with weights that shift toward whichever investing styles suit the economic cycle. It's an international core holding with a tactical twist, and results depend on those calls being right.
IMOM: A fund of developed-market stocks outside the US that have shown strong recent price momentum, picked by a rules-based screen. It holds roughly 50 to 200 stocks and changes as the winners change, with financials, industrials and technology the largest groups.
IMTB: A broad bond fund covering US government, mortgage-backed and corporate bonds that mature in about five to ten years. It is meant as a core bond holding, with Treasuries as its largest holdings and moderate sensitivity to interest rate changes.
IMTG: An actively managed fund that mainly holds agency mortgage-backed securities, bonds backed by home loans guaranteed by government-linked agencies like Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. It aims for income, and its price can move when interest rates change or homeowners pay off loans early.
IMTM: Stocks outside the US that have been rising lately, with financials over a third and technology about a sixth. It's a momentum fund that chases recent winners, so its holdings turn over often and it can drop sharply when trends reverse.
IMVP: Follows an index of large and mid sized Indian companies chosen for momentum, value, steady prices and profitability. It holds companies like Bajaj Auto, Tata Consultancy, Infosys and Titan at around 4% each, so it is fairly evenly spread.
INCE: An actively managed fund holding mainly dividend paying US and international stocks, plus some preferred shares. Its holdings are spread over staples, banks, health care and utilities, with names like Chevron, Southern Company and Procter & Gamble each about 3%.
INCM: A flexible mix of bonds, preferred shares and dividend stocks from areas like consumer staples, energy and utilities. It's built for regular income, and the manager can shift between asset types, so it should be calmer than stocks but not as steady as plain bonds.
INCO: Indian consumer companies, such as food, retail and lifestyle brands, tracked with an index of that group. It is concentrated by theme: consumer discretionary is about 60% and staples about 33%, and its largest holdings are each about 5%.
IND: Roughly 500 of the largest companies listed on India's National Stock Exchange, following the Nifty 500 index and holding them mostly by company size. Banks are the biggest group, and HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank and Reliance Industries together make up about 15% of the fund.
INDA: Large Indian companies, with financials about 30% and consumer, industrial and materials businesses next. It's a focused bet on one fast-growing emerging economy, so it swings more than the US market and can be hit by currency moves and shifts in Indian policy.
INDE: An actively managed fund buying stocks of Indian companies, picked by managers rather than by following an index. It is fairly concentrated: HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank and Eternal are among the biggest holdings, and financials make up about a third of it.
INDH: A fund of Indian companies that also hedges the Indian rupee against the US dollar, so currency swings matter less to returns. Reliance Industries, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank are about 24% of it, with financials the biggest sector.
INDQ: An actively managed fund of Indian companies picked for quality using a rules-based method. It is spread over many stocks, with Titan, Eicher Motors, Hero MotoCorp and others each about 4% to 6%, and leans toward consumer companies and health care.
INDS: Tracks an index of developed-market real estate companies focused on industrial properties such as warehouses and self-storage. It is concentrated at the top: Public Storage, Extra Space and Prologis are each around 14% to 16%, which is about 45% combined.
INDY: The 50 largest Indian companies, with financials more than a third, then consumer companies, energy and industrials. It's a focused bet on one emerging country's economy, so it can swing more than a global fund and depends heavily on India's banks.
INDZ: An actively managed fund of companies tied to India, picked by the managers rather than following an index. Financials are about 30% of it, and Reliance Industries, HDFC Bank and Maruti Suzuki are among the biggest holdings at about 3% each.
INEQ: Holds dividend-paying stocks of large companies outside the US, picked by an active manager for income. It is spread across Europe, Asia and Australia, with names like DBS, UniCredit, Shell, BHP and TotalEnergies each around 4% to 5% of the fund, and financials the biggest sector.
INFL: Stocks of companies expected to benefit from rising prices, such as energy, financial and materials firms along with commodity producers. It's a hedge against inflation that's actively managed, so it can look very different from the broad market.
INFO: Large US companies chosen by a computer-driven model that scores them on traits like value and momentum, with technology about 40% of the fund. It's a core US stock holding with an active twist, so it can differ from the broad market in either direction.
INKM: A fund of funds holding other ETFs across bonds, stocks, real estate and other assets, aimed at producing income. It is actively managed, with mostly bond funds and some dividend and options-income stock funds.
INMU: Investment-grade municipal bonds with medium maturities, chosen by active managers, with interest generally free of federal income tax. It's meant for tax-aware income, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
INOV: Options on an iShares fund that holds developed markets outside the US and Canada, designed to absorb part of the first losses over a set one year period starting in November. The Power Buffer name signals this protection, and gains are capped in exchange.
INQQ: Publicly traded Indian internet and online companies, such as e-commerce, payments and online services, tracked through an index. It is fairly concentrated, with Reliance, Bajaj Finance and a few others each making up about 7% to 8% of the fund.
INRO: An actively managed fund of US stocks that shifts its weight between industries over time, using BlackRock's research models. For now it looks much like the big US market, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft making up about 21% of it and technology around 42%.
INTF: Stocks from developed countries outside the US, with financials the largest slice, then industrials, technology and consumer companies. It picks and weights stocks by traits like value, quality and momentum, so it's a way to add international diversification with a tilt toward those traits.
INTL: A fund of funds that holds other ETFs covering stocks outside the US, from developed markets and emerging markets. Its biggest pieces are iShares funds, about 38% and 19%, so it is a mix of existing international funds in one ticker.
INTM: An actively managed fund that buys intermediate term municipal bonds, which are debt from US states and cities whose interest is exempt from federal income tax. It works as a tax advantaged income holding, and it can also use derivatives that act like municipal bonds.
INVG: An actively managed fund of US investment-grade corporate bonds, meaning debt from companies seen as lower risk. It picks bonds with a computer-driven approach that weighs value, quality and momentum, and is spread over many issuers at roughly 1% each or less.
INVN: A fund following an index of US companies the manager sees as innovative but not yet fully recognized by the market, mostly mid-sized. It leans toward technology at about 57%, with health care next, and no single holding is above about 3%.
INYY: Aims to pay high income from Intel stock by using options on it, rather than owning the shares directly. That limits how much of a rise in Intel it can capture, and it holds mostly Treasury bills to back the options.
IOCT: Uses options on the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, a basket of stocks from developed markets outside the US and Canada, to follow its price over a set one-year period. It buffers part of the losses at the cost of capping gains, and the protection resets each October.
ION: A fund of companies that mine lithium, cobalt and nickel, the metals used in batteries, picked from a broad global stock index. It is almost entirely mining and materials stocks, with Australian lithium producers like Liontown and PLS among the largest holdings.
IOO: Just 100 of the world's biggest companies, with technology about half and communication, financials and health care behind. It's a concentrated core holding of global giants, and because so much sits in tech, it can swing more than a broader world fund.
IOPP: An actively managed fund of Indian companies, picked by the manager from across the country's market. It leans toward consumer-focused businesses like Eternal and Indian Hotels, and the top holdings are each around 5% to 6%.
IOYY: An income fund that sells options on a leveraged ETF tied to IonQ stock, aiming to turn the stock's big swings into payouts. That caps its gains on the upside while keeping most of the downside, and the fund mostly holds Treasury bills as backing.
IPAC: Companies from developed Asia-Pacific countries such as Japan and Australia, led by financials, then industrials and technology. It's a way to add diversification beyond the US and Europe, and it leaves out China and emerging markets, so it moves with the Japanese economy.
IPAV: A fund of companies outside the US that help build infrastructure, mostly materials and industrial businesses like steel makers and cable makers. It follows a Global X index, with Prysmian, ArcelorMittal and Shin-Etsu Chemical among the biggest holdings.
IPAY: Companies that run digital and mobile payment systems, tracking a specialized index. Visa, Mastercard, American Express and Capital One are each about 6%, so it is a blend of payment networks and card lenders spread across financials and technology.
IPB: A trust certificate tied to Merrill Lynch debt, paying a fixed 6.0518% rate, rather than a fund of many holdings. Its price depends on the credit of the company behind it and on interest rates, so it behaves like a single bond.
IPKW: Foreign companies that have been steadily shrinking their share counts by buying back their own stock. Financials, industrials and consumer companies lead the mix, and it suits investors who want international exposure with a tilt toward firms returning cash to shareholders.
IPO: Recently listed US companies, following the Renaissance IPO Index, which adds newly public firms and drops them after a couple of years. It is top-heavy: Astera Labs, CoreWeave and Arm are about 30% of the fund.
IPOS: Recently listed companies from outside the US, following an index of international IPOs. It is concentrated, with the top five holdings, like Kioxia, Galderma and CATL, making up about half of it, and tilts toward technology.
IQDF: Large companies outside the US that pay solid dividends and have strong financial quality, led by financials and technology with industrials and materials behind them. It's built for steady income from international stocks, and it carries currency swings and a heavy bank presence.
IQDG: Dividend-paying companies from developed countries outside the US, spread across industrials, consumer brands, financials and technology. It aims for steady, growing quality companies abroad, which makes it a way to add international stocks, and it picks firms for earnings quality rather than just size.
IQDY: Higher-quality companies outside the US that pay dividends, picked by a Northern Trust index that looks at the quality of earnings and dividend sustainability. It is spread out, with no holding above about 4%, and leans toward financials and tech.
IQGR: An actively managed fund of quality growth companies outside the US, chosen by its sub-adviser for strong, lasting growth. Samsung, Taiwan Semiconductor and SK hynix are among the biggest holdings, though none is more than about 4%.
IQHI: An actively managed fund of high-yield corporate bonds, from companies with lower credit ratings that pay more interest. It is highly diversified, with no single bond above about 1%, and the managers look for bonds with good yields compared with their risk.
IQLT: Large and mid-sized companies from developed countries outside the US with strong profits, steady earnings and low debt, led by financials at about a quarter. It's a core international holding that favors quality, so it may hold up better in rough markets but trail in speculative rallies.
IQM: An actively managed fund buying companies that build the technology behind intelligent machines, such as AI chips, robotics and automation. It leans on tech and industrials, with NVIDIA, Taiwan Semiconductor and SanDisk the biggest positions at roughly 6% each.
IQMM: Short-term government debt and cash-like holdings run as a government money market fund, built to meet rules for the reserves behind payment stablecoins. It's a safe place to park cash and earn interest, so it's meant to hold its value and not to grow.
IQQ: The 100 largest non-financial companies on the Nasdaq, with technology making up roughly 60% and communication, consumer and staples companies filling most of the rest. It's a growth tilt for a stock portfolio, and with no banks and so much tech it swings more than the broad market.
IQQQ: Holds Nasdaq-100 stocks and sells call options on the index to collect extra income, which it pays out often. The options limit gains when the market jumps, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together are about 18% of the fund.
IQSI: Large companies in developed countries outside North America, tracking an index that screens for environmental, social and governance standards. It holds a wide range of stocks, with ASML at about 5% and Roche, Novartis and Nestle each around 2%.
IQSM: US mid-sized companies that pass environmental, social and governance screens set by Candriam, weighted by company size like a regular index. It spreads money across many holdings, with none above about 1%, so no single stock drives results.
IQSU: Large US companies that pass environmental, social and governance screens set by Candriam, weighted by company size like a regular index. It is top-heavy in big tech, with Apple, Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon about 20% of it.
IQSZ: An actively managed fund of global stocks from companies that are helping the shift to lower carbon emissions, or plan to. It still looks like the broad market: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 14% of it.
IROC: An actively managed fund of high yield municipal bonds, issued by state and local bodies for things like hospitals, utilities and schools. Interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and it is spread over many issuers at about 1% each.
IRTR: A mix of about 40% stocks and 59% bonds, built from other iShares funds, aimed at people who are already retired. It is actively managed and adjusts the mix over time, so it is a ready-made portfolio in one fund.
ISCF: Small companies from developed countries outside the US, spread across industrials, consumer businesses, materials and financials. It's picked by factors like value and quality, so it adds international small caps, and it swings more than large-company funds.
ISCG: Smaller US companies with above-average growth, led by technology, industrials and health care. It's built for growth, with more small, fast-growing businesses than a typical fund, so it swings more than large-company funds.
ISCV: Small US companies that look cheap, led by financials, consumer businesses, health care and industrials. It's a value-leaning way to own small caps, so it swings more than large-company funds and can trail when growth leads.
ISEP: Uses options on a developed-markets stock fund outside North America (the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF) to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each September. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only works if held the full period.
ISHG: Short-term government bonds from developed countries outside the US, paid in their local currencies. It diversifies a bond portfolio abroad with little interest rate risk, but it doesn't hedge currencies, so a stronger dollar can erode its value.
ISHP: Companies around the world that make their money from online shopping, picked and weighted by the S-Network E-Commerce index. It is spread thinly: the biggest holdings, such as Allegro, Wayfair and Reddit, are each only about 2% of the fund.
ISMD: US small and mid sized companies, chosen by an index that screens for a company's values and impact. It spreads across thousands of tiny holdings, so no single one is above a few percent, and it tilts toward small, lesser known names.
ISMF: An actively managed managed-futures fund that trades futures on stock indexes, bonds, currencies and commodities, aiming to follow rising or falling trends. It can profit in falling markets as well as rising ones, so it behaves differently from a plain stock or bond fund.
ISPY: Large US stocks like the S&P 500, led by technology at about two fifths, with a cash cushion and options layered on top for a high income payout. The tradeoff is that it gives up some gains in strong rallies, so it suits income more than growth.
ISRA: A fund of Israeli companies tracking a VanEck index, so it is a bet on a single small country. Palo Alto Networks is about 13% of it, and technology and banks, such as Leumi and Hapoalim, make up most of the rest.
ISRL: The 120 largest companies in Israel, following a Defiance KSM index. It leans toward banks like Hapoalim and Leumi, plus Tower Semiconductor and defense firm Elbit Systems, so it tracks a single country's economy.
ISTB: US investment-grade bonds from government and corporate issuers that mature in one to five years. It's a steady, lower-risk holding for income and a cushion for a stock portfolio, and because the bonds are short, its price drops less than longer-term bond funds when interest rates rise.
ISTM: Tracks an index of futures contracts on metals used in industry and the energy transition, such as copper and aluminum. It holds futures instead of the metals themselves, so the small positions shown mostly reflect collateral and contracts.
ISVL: Small companies from developed countries outside the US and South Korea, tracking an FTSE index that favors cheaply priced stocks. It holds a wide spread of names, with none above about 1%, and leans toward industrials and financials.
ISWN: A mix of US Treasuries and long dated call options on an iShares fund of developed foreign stocks. Roughly 10% of the index goes to the options, which aim to gain in sharp market swings, while the Treasuries make up most of the fund.
ITA: US makers of airplanes, defense equipment, weapons and aerospace parts, all from the industrial sector. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it depends on government defense budgets and air travel and swings more than the broad market.
ITAN: An actively managed fund of US stocks picked using a method that tries to value hidden assets like brands, patents and software that regular accounting misses. It is fairly spread out, with Amazon the largest at about 5%, and leans toward technology and health care.
ITB: Homebuilders and the companies that supply them, such as building products and materials, with consumer discretionary names making up about three quarters. It's a focused bet on US housing, so it rises with home demand and falls when mortgage rates climb, swinging far more than the broad market.
ITDB: A fund that bundles other iShares funds in stocks and bonds, with the mix designed for people planning to retire around 2030. It is actively managed and gradually shifts toward bonds as 2030 approaches, so it is a ready-made portfolio in one fund.
ITDC: A target date fund aimed at people planning to retire around 2035, holding a mix of other iShares stock and bond ETFs. It is actively managed and leans toward stocks now at roughly two thirds, shifting more toward bonds as the date nears.
ITDD: A fund of funds that mixes stock and bond funds for people planning to retire around 2040. It holds mostly stocks, about three quarters, and gradually shifts toward bonds over time, a so-called glide path, as that date gets closer.
ITDE: A retirement-date fund for people planning to retire around 2045, built from other iShares funds. It is mostly stocks, about 87%, led by US large companies, with some bonds and real estate, and it shifts toward bonds automatically as 2045 gets closer.
ITDF: A target date fund aimed at around 2050, which holds a mix of other iShares funds covering US stocks, foreign stocks, bonds and real estate. It is mostly stocks now, around 93%, and it is designed to shift toward bonds as 2050 approaches.
ITDG: A retirement fund of funds aimed at people planning to retire around 2055. It is actively managed and mostly holds other iShares funds, with the bulk in US stocks, and the mix is meant to gradually shift toward safer investments as that date gets closer.
ITDH: A target-date fund that mixes other iShares funds, mostly US and international stocks with some bonds, aimed at people retiring around 2060. It is actively managed, and the mix is designed to shift toward safer holdings over time.
ITDI: A target-date fund aimed at someone retiring around 2065. It is actively managed and holds other iShares funds, mostly US and international stocks, and over time it is designed to shift gradually toward safer assets like bonds as that date approaches.
ITDJ: A target-date fund for people planning to retire around 2070, holding mostly stock index funds from iShares in US and international markets. It is nearly all stocks now, and the mix is designed to shift gradually toward bonds as the date gets closer.
ITEQ: Israeli technology companies, tracked by the BlueStar Israel Global Technology Index, covering software, chips and defense tech. Palo Alto Networks is the largest holding at about 12%, with Tower Semiconductor and Elbit Systems next.
ITM: Municipal bonds from US states and cities with medium-length maturities, which pay interest that is generally free of federal income tax. It's meant for tax-aware income and as a cushion for a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
ITOT: Nearly every publicly traded US company, from giants to small firms, with technology around a third and financials and health care next. It works as a one-fund core holding for US stocks, and its small-company slice makes it slightly broader than an S&P 500 fund.
ITWO: Holds the Russell 2000, an index of small US companies, and sells call options on it to earn extra income, which the fund pays out. The options cap how much it gains when small stocks rally, and it is spread over a large number of small positions.
IUS: Large US companies picked by measures like sales, cash flow and dividends instead of stock market size, spread across technology, health care, communication and consumer companies. It's a core US stock holding that leans value, so it holds fewer of the priciest stocks.
IUSB: A broad mix of US dollar bonds: Treasuries, government-backed mortgage bonds and corporate bonds, plus some other types beyond the usual core bond fund. It's meant for steady interest income and as a cushion for stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
IUSG: Large and mid-sized US growth companies, with technology a little over half and communication about a seventh. It's built for growth, but with so much in tech, it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
IUSV: Large and mid-sized US companies that look cheap compared with their earnings and assets, led by technology, financials, health care and industrials. It's a core value holding that can lag when fast-growing stocks lead the market and hold up better when they stumble.
IVAL: Cheap-looking companies outside the US, chosen by a rules-based quantitative screen for low prices compared with their business value. It is spread thinly, with no stock above about 2%, and tilts toward materials, energy and consumer companies.
IVE: The cheaper-looking half of the S&P 500, with technology at about a quarter, then financials, health care and industrials. It leans toward established, lower-priced companies, so it tends to hold up better than growth funds when tech stocks sell off but can lag in tech rallies.
IVEP: Companies that stand to benefit from the power and infrastructure needs of AI, chosen from a research report by Wedbush analyst Dan Ives. It holds about 30 stocks, such as Schneider Electric, Eaton and Bloom Energy, spread across industrials, utilities and energy.
IVES: Companies picked by one well-known tech analyst as winners of artificial intelligence, about three quarters technology, plus communication and consumer companies. It's a focused growth bet on a single theme, so it swings far more than the broad market.
IVLU: Developed-market companies outside the US that look cheap on measures like price versus earnings, led by financials at nearly a third, then industrials. It's a value tilt for foreign stocks, so it can lag when growth stocks lead, and it has less tech than the broad market.
IVOG: Mid-size US companies with strong growth, led by industrials and technology, followed by health care. It's a growth holding that sits between big and small companies, so it can swing more than the broad market in both directions.
IVOL: An actively managed fund that mostly holds inflation-protected US Treasuries (TIPS), plus options and swaps that gain when the gap between short and long interest rates changes. It aims to help against rising inflation and rate swings, so it behaves differently from a plain bond fund.
IVOO: Mid-sized US companies, with industrials the biggest group at about a fifth and technology, financials and health care behind it. It's a way to add companies that are bigger than small caps but nimbler than giants, and it swings somewhat more than the large-company market.
IVOV: Mid-size US companies that look cheaply priced, led by financials at about a fifth, then industrials, consumer companies and technology. It's a value tilt in the middle of the market, and it usually swings more than large company funds but less than small ones.
IVSI: A fund of large companies in developed markets outside North America, in places like Europe, Japan and Australia. ASML is the largest holding at about 7%, followed by Roche, BHP and Novartis.
IVSS: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US companies, picked with the manager's own research rather than tracking an index. It plans to hold at least 150 positions, so it is spread out, with no holding above about 3%.
IVSX: Small and mid-sized companies from developed countries outside North America, picked by a rules-based method from Applied Finance. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 2%, and it leans toward industrials, consumer and materials companies.
IVV: Hundreds of the largest US companies across every major industry, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and health care following. It serves as a core holding for US stock exposure, and because bigger companies count for more, a few tech giants drive much of its movement.
IVVB: A fund holding the S&P 500 through an iShares ETF plus options, with a layered set of quarterly periods that buffers a deeper amount of losses. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if held through each period.
IVVM: Holds a laddered set of options-based buffer positions on the S&P 500, staggered by start date so protection resets at different times. Each step cushions part of the losses on large US stocks in exchange for capping some of the gains.
IVVW: Holds the iShares Core S&P 500 ETF and sells one-month call options on the S&P 500 to bring in extra income. That income comes at a price: gains in strong months are capped, while most of the losses in falling markets remain.
IVW: The faster-growing half of the S&P 500, with technology over half and communication, financials and consumer companies next. It is built for growth, but it is concentrated in a few tech leaders, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
IWB: About a thousand of the biggest US companies, with technology at roughly 40 percent and financials, communication and health care at about a tenth each. It works as a core holding that moves with the overall US stock market.
IWC: Tiny US public companies, the smallest slice of the stock market, with health care about a quarter and financials another quarter. It's a high-growth, high-risk diversifier that swings far more than large company funds, and its shares can be harder to trade.
IWD: Large and mid-sized US value stocks, meaning companies priced cheaply relative to their size, led by financials, technology and health care. It leans toward established, steadier businesses, and it has far less tech than the broad market, so it often trails in growth-led rallies.
IWF: Large and mid-sized US growth companies, with technology close to 60 percent and communication, industrials and consumer companies next. It is built for growth and sits heavily in a few tech leaders, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
IWFG: An actively managed fund of about 30 large US growth companies chosen by Winslow. It is very top-heavy: NVIDIA and Alphabet are about 26% together, and technology makes up over half of it.
IWL: The 200 biggest US companies, with technology over 40 percent and communication, financials and health care next. It's a core holding focused on giants, so it behaves like the big end of the US market and leans more on tech than a fund covering all sizes.
IWLG: An actively managed fund holding large US companies that the manager thinks will grow quickly. Alphabet and NVIDIA are each about 12% of the fund, and with Broadcom, Microsoft and Apple the top five are about 40%.
IWM: Around two thousand small US companies, led by health care, financials, technology and industrials. It adds growth potential beyond large firms, but small companies are shakier, so it swings more than the broad market, and many of its health care holdings are unprofitable biotechs.
IWMI: Small US companies, with health care, financials and technology leading, paired with an options strategy that aims to pay high monthly income. The income comes at a price: gains are capped in strong rallies, and it still falls when small stocks drop.
IWMW: Holds the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, which covers US small companies, and sells one-month call options on the Russell 2000 to earn extra income. The options give up some of the gains if small companies rally strongly, in exchange for that income.
IWMY: An actively managed fund that seeks income by selling options tied to the Russell 2000 small company index, paying out distributions weekly. The options limit how much it gains when the index rises, and it still falls when the index falls.
IWN: Smaller US companies that look cheap, with financials at about 28% and industrials, health care and real estate each around an eighth. It's a value-focused bet on small companies, which can swing more than large ones and lag for long stretches.
IWO: Smaller US companies with strong growth traits, with health care at about 30% and technology around a fifth, then industrials and consumer companies. It's built for growth, but small growth stocks swing more than the broad market and can fall hard in downturns.
IWP: Mid-sized US companies with fast-growing sales and earnings, with technology the biggest slice, then industrials, health care and consumer companies. It's built for growth, so it swings more than the broad market and can drop sharply in downturns.
IWR: Mid-sized US companies, the ones just below the biggest names, spread across technology, industrials, financials and health care. It fills the middle gap in a portfolio, and these companies often grow faster than giants but can be bumpier.
IWS: Mid-sized US companies that look cheaper than the market, spread across financials, industrials, technology and health care at roughly an eighth to a sixth each. It's a value-tilted way to add the middle of the market to a portfolio, and it can lag when growth stocks lead.
IWV: Nearly the entire US stock market, from the largest companies to small ones, with technology the biggest slice at about 38 percent. It's a simple core holding that moves with the overall US market and economy.
IWX: The cheaper-looking half of America's 200 largest companies, picked for low prices compared with their assets and earnings. Technology, financials, health care and consumer firms lead, and it's a core value holding that tends to hold up better than growth funds when tech slumps.
IWY: The largest US growth-oriented companies, with technology at close to 60%, communication around a sixth, and consumer companies and industrials making up the rest. It's built for growth, so it leans heavily on tech and tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
IXC: Large oil and gas companies from around the world, all in the energy sector. It's a focused bet on energy, so it rises and falls with oil prices and swings more than the broad market, though it often pays solid dividends.
IXG: Banks, insurers, payment companies and other financial firms from around the world, almost all of it in the financial sector. It's a focused bet on global finance, so it swings with banking and the economy, and it has no technology or health care to balance it.
IXJ: Health care companies around the world, such as drug makers, medical device makers, insurers and biotech firms. It's a focused sector bet that is often steadier than the broad market in downturns, but it can be hit by drug pricing and regulation news.
IXN: Technology companies from around the world, including software, chip and hardware makers, spread across the US and other developed countries. It's a focused bet on global tech, so it swings more than the broad market, and it caps the biggest names so a few stocks don't dominate.
IXP: Global communication companies, nearly all in the communication sector, such as phone and cable providers, media, and social media and streaming companies. It's a focused bet on one sector worldwide, and it swings more than the broad market.
IXUS: Thousands of stocks from developed and emerging countries outside the US, led by financials and technology at roughly a fifth each, with industrials not far behind. It works as the non-US half of a stock portfolio, and it has no US companies at all.
IYC: US companies that sell things people want rather than need: online retail, cars, restaurants, home improvement, and some media and streaming. It's a focused bet on consumer spending, so it swings more than the broad market and falls when the economy weakens.
IYE: Almost entirely US energy companies, such as oil and gas producers, refiners and drilling service firms. It's a focused bet on the energy sector, so it rises and falls with oil and gas prices and swings more than the broad market.
IYF: Nearly all US financial companies: banks, insurers, asset managers and payment and exchange firms. It's a focused bet on the financial sector, so it does well when the economy and lending are healthy and tends to struggle in credit scares, and it holds almost no other industries.
IYG: US financial companies, including banks, insurers, asset managers and payment and credit firms. It's a focused bet on the financial sector, so it tends to move with interest rates and the economy and swings more than the broad market.
IYH: US health care companies such as drug makers, device makers, insurers and biotech firms. It's a focused sector bet that is often steadier than the broad market in downturns, but it can drop on drug pricing and regulation news.
IYJ: US industrial companies like aerospace, machinery and transportation, plus payment and business services firms, with industrials about two thirds and financials near a fifth. It's a focused bet on one part of the economy, so it swings more than the broad market.
IYK: Makers and sellers of everyday goods, with consumer staples at over four fifths, such as food, beverage, tobacco and household products, and health care around a tenth. It's a defensive holding that tends to fall less in downturns, though it trails in strong rallies.
IYLD: A fund of funds that holds other iShares ETFs covering floating rate bonds, short-term bonds, broad bonds, preferred stocks and income-focused stocks. It aims to produce income from a mix of bonds and stocks, with about four funds each making up around 15% of it.
IYM: Companies that make or dig up basic materials: mostly chemicals, gold and copper miners, and steel, with a small slice of industrials. It's a focused bet on one corner of the economy, so it tends to swing more than the broad market, especially when global growth shifts.
IYR: US real estate companies, nearly all real estate investment trusts that own things like cell towers, data centers, apartments and warehouses. It's for income and property exposure, and it tends to fall when interest rates rise.
IYRI: An actively managed fund of US real estate companies, mainly REITs, which also uses options strategies to boost income. It is led by Welltower, Prologis and Simon Property, together about a quarter of it, and the options cap some gains.
IYT: US transportation companies such as airlines, railroads, trucking and package delivery firms. It's a focused bet on one cyclical industry, so it tends to rise with the economy and fall hard when business slows or fuel costs jump.
IYW: US technology companies, with software, chip makers and hardware making up over 90 percent, plus a small slice of communication firms. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it swings more than the broad market, and a few giant companies carry a large share of it.
IYY: Nearly the whole US stock market in one fund, from large companies down to some small ones, with technology at about 40 percent. It's built to be a core holding, and its heavy tech weighting means it leans on that one sector.
IYZ: US telecommunications companies, including phone and cable providers and the network equipment makers that supply them, split between technology and communication businesses. It's a focused bet on one sector, often valued for dividends, and it can lag when growth stocks lead.
IZRL: Israeli companies, tracking an index of firms based or listed in Israel, with a focus on innovation. It spreads fairly evenly across stocks, with no holding above about 2%, and technology is about half of it, followed by health care and communications.
JA: Investment-grade collateralized loan obligations (CLOs) rated between AA and A, which are pools of corporate bank loans sliced into layers by risk. It is actively managed and holds many CLOs, each only about 3% of the fund.
JAAA: Top-rated loans bundled into securities called CLOs, which are pools of loans to companies. It aims for higher income than regular short-term bonds with little price movement, since the floating payments adjust with interest rates, though it's less liquid than Treasuries.
JABS: An actively managed fund of asset-backed securities, which are bonds backed by pools of loans such as auto loans and corporate loans. It holds many small positions, with the largest only about 2% of the fund.
JADB: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on a US stock market ETF to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in January. In exchange, it limits how much it can gain, and the protection only works if shares are held for the whole period.
JADE: An actively managed fund of stocks from emerging markets, the developing economies such as Taiwan, South Korea, China and India. It is tilted toward chip makers: Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung are about 20% of the fund, with Tencent also in the top few.
JAJL: A fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to protect against losses over a set six-month period starting in January or July. In return, it gives up some of the possible gains, and it works best if held for the full period.
JANB: Uses options on a broad US stock index fund to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in January. In exchange, the upside is capped, so a strong market year will not be fully captured.
JANH: An actively managed fund that holds Treasury bills plus options on the stock market to pay regular income, with a barrier that protects only as long as the market does not fall past a set level. Its gains are limited, and big drops can hurt.
JANI: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on an international developed-markets stock ETF (EFA) to absorb a set amount of losses over a one-year period ending in December 2026. Its upside is not capped, but the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
JANJ: An actively managed fund that uses Treasury bills and options tied to the S&P 500 to aim for income over a one-year period starting in January. It gives up some protection and upside: a drop in the index beyond a set barrier can mean real losses.
JANM: Uses customized options on US large stocks to aim for a defined outcome over a set period starting in January. It aims to protect against a large part of losses in exchange for a cap on gains, and works as intended only if held for the whole period.
JANP: A fund using options tied to the S&P 500 to give stock market gains up to a limit over a one year period starting in January. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses, and the stated outcomes only apply if held for the whole period.
JANT: Options contracts tied to the S&P 500 that aim to cushion the first 10% of losses over a set one-year period starting in January, in exchange for a limit on the gains. The cushion and cap only apply if you hold for the full period.
JANU: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 over a set period ending in December 2026, to absorb the first 15% of losses. Gains are not capped by a set limit, though the protection only works for someone holding for the full period.
JANW: A defined-outcome fund using options on the S&P 500 to absorb the first 20% of losses over a one-year period that starts each January. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold the whole period.
JANZ: An actively managed fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to aim for a set outcome over a one-year period starting in January. Most of the fund sits in Treasuries and option contracts, so its results depend on the options, not on owning stocks.
JAPN: An actively managed fund of Japanese companies run by owner operators, meaning leaders who hold a significant share of the business. It is concentrated, with Furuno Electric at about 9% of the fund, and many holdings are small and midsize companies.
JAVA: Large US companies that an active manager considers cheaply priced relative to their growth potential, across technology, financials, health care and consumer firms. It's a value-style core holding, and since the manager picks the stocks, it can differ from a standard value index.
JBBB: Lower-rated slices of collateralized loan obligations, which are bundles of company loans packaged and sold as bonds, mostly in the BBB and BB range. It's meant for higher income than ordinary bonds, with interest that floats with rates, but it can fall sharply in a credit scare.
JBND: A mix of US investment-grade bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate debt, chosen by a manager who tries to beat the broad bond market. It's meant for interest income and as a cushion for stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
JCAL: Mostly medium-term bonds issued by California cities and agencies, with a small cash cushion. It's meant for steady income that is generally free of federal and California income tax for state residents, and its price tends to dip when interest rates rise.
JCHI: An actively managed fund that buys stocks of companies tied to China, picked by the manager rather than following an index. It is concentrated at the top: Tencent is about 11% and Alibaba nearly 8%, with financials, consumer and communication companies making up most of it.
JCPB: A broad mix of US bonds, including Treasuries, corporate bonds and mortgage-backed bonds, with room for some lower-rated and foreign debt. It's meant as a core bond holding for income and stability, with managers aiming to beat a plain bond index, though its price drops when rates rise.
JCPI: Mostly bonds, including corporate, government and mortgage-related debt, managed to hold up when inflation rises. It aims to give steady income with some protection from rising prices, though its price can still fall when interest rates rise.
JDIV: An actively managed fund of dividend-paying large companies from around the world that the managers see as leaders in their industries. Technology and financials are the biggest sectors, and Microsoft and Taiwan Semiconductor together make up about 12% of it.
JDOC: Large health care companies that the managers believe are leaders, including drugmakers, biotech, medical device and health services firms. It is actively managed, and AbbVie, Eli Lilly, UnitedHealth, Merck and Johnson & Johnson together make up about 30% of the fund.
JDVI: Large and mid-sized companies outside the US that look cheap, led by financials, industrials, technology and materials. It's a value-focused way to add international stocks to a portfolio, and it can lag growth-heavy markets while still carrying currency swings.
JDVL: Large US companies that look cheap compared with their fundamentals, spread across technology (about a quarter), financials, health care and consumer businesses. It's a value-style core holding for stock investors, and it can lag growth-heavy markets when the most expensive companies are leading the rally.
JEDI: Stocks of companies tied to drones and modern defense, such as space, unmanned systems and military technology. It is concentrated in small companies: Redwire and Unusual Machines are over 20% of the fund between them, and it is non-diversified.
JELH: An actively managed fund that holds stocks and equity linked instruments, using options, futures and swaps with the goal of producing high income. Its returns depend on that derivatives strategy, so it will not behave like a plain stock fund.
JELM: An actively managed fund that aims to pay regular income, using stock-linked securities and options. Its holdings are mostly cash and short-term instruments, so its returns come from the income strategy more than from owning stocks.
JEMA: Stocks from developing countries, with technology the largest slice at over 40 percent, followed by financials and consumer companies. Managers actively pick the holdings, so it's a growth holding that can differ from the broad index and swings more than US funds.
JEMB: Government and company bonds from emerging market countries, all paid in US dollars or other major currencies rather than local ones. It's for higher income than US bonds, and it avoids local currency swings, but it can fall when investors get nervous about riskier countries.
JEPI: Large US companies picked for steadier, lower-swing stocks across many industries, paired with an options strategy that trades some of the market's upside for monthly income. The goal is income and a smoother ride: it usually falls less in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
JEPQ: Large growth companies, mostly technology at around 60 percent, paired with an options strategy that gives up some upside in exchange for monthly income. It's for income from a tech-heavy mix, and it usually trails in strong rallies while still swinging with tech.
JETS: Airlines, plane makers, airports and travel services from the US and abroad, with industrials making up about nine tenths. It's a focused bet on air travel, so it swings far more than the broad market, rising fast when travel booms and dropping hard when it stalls.
JFLI: An actively managed income fund that blends bond and stock exposure from around the world, mainly by owning other JPMorgan funds. About a third is a high-yield corporate bond fund and roughly 20% is an options-income fund on the Nasdaq.
JFLX: A flexible mix of mostly bonds, loans and a few convertible securities across the credit spectrum, with a small cash cushion. It's meant for income with some adaptability, since the manager can shift between bond types, though it still loses value when interest rates rise.
JGLO: Stocks from companies around the world, mostly in developed countries, with technology about a third and financials, consumer and communication companies filling out much of the rest. It's a one-fund global core holding, and since the manager picks a concentrated set of stocks, it can differ noticeably from the world market.
JGRO: Large US growth companies chosen by a manager, with technology about half and communication, health care and industrials behind it. It's built for long-term growth, and because it's concentrated in fast-growing tech, it tends to fall harder than the broad market in sell-offs.
JGRW: An actively managed fund of large US companies with long records of steady profits and growth. It is fairly top-heavy, with Alphabet, Apple, Microsoft and NVIDIA together around a third of the fund.
JHAC: An actively managed fund of US companies of any size, picked by the manager based on a company's fundamentals. It is top-heavy in big tech: Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft together are about 21% of the fund.
JHAI: An actively managed fund of companies around the world tied to artificial intelligence, mostly chip makers and other technology firms. It is concentrated: Taiwan Semiconductor and NVIDIA are about 29% of it, and technology is roughly three quarters of the whole fund.
JHCB: Holds US corporate bonds, which are loans to companies, mostly investment grade, with a small amount of bank loans allowed. It is actively managed and spread out, with no single issuer above about 2%, from names like Bank of America, Microsoft and Amazon.
JHCP: An actively managed fund of bonds, mixing corporate, mortgage-backed, Treasury and other types, with room to add riskier bonds beyond a plain core bond fund. US Treasuries are the largest holdings, though each one is small.
JHCR: Investment-grade bonds, meaning issuers rated as fairly safe borrowers, spread across government, corporate and mortgage-backed debt. It's meant as a steady income core for the bond part of a portfolio, though it is actively managed and its price falls when interest rates rise.
JHDG: An actively managed fund of about 100 large US stocks chosen by research, paired with a hedge that is meant to soften market drops. Technology is about a third of it, and Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon together make up roughly 19%.
JHDV: Dividend-paying large and mid-sized US companies chosen by a rules-based approach. Despite the income focus, it holds a lot of technology, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together about 16% of the fund.
JHEM: Companies in emerging markets such as China, India and Brazil, with technology about 30% and financials over a fifth. It's meant for growth from developing economies, with a tilt toward traits like value and smaller size, so it swings more than US or developed-market funds.
JHHY: Holds US dollar corporate bonds from companies with lower credit ratings (called high yield or junk bonds), which pay higher interest because the borrowers are riskier. It is very spread out, with no single bond above about 1% of the fund.
JHID: Dividend-paying large and mid-sized companies from developed countries outside the US, selected by a rules-based approach. Financial companies are about a third of the fund, and no single stock is more than roughly 2%.
JHLN: Floating-rate loans to lower-rated companies from around the world, plus a small cash cushion. It's meant for higher income than regular bonds, and because the interest adjusts with rates, its price holds up when rates rise, though it can drop if borrowers default.
JHMB: Mortgage-backed securities, which are bundles of home and commercial property loans that pay out interest and principal. It is actively managed, mixing agency-backed bonds from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac with private mortgage trusts, and it is spread across a large number of small holdings.
JHMD: Large and mid-sized companies in developed markets outside the US, with financials about a quarter and industrials just under a fifth. It's meant to add international diversification, with a tilt toward traits like value and smaller size instead of weighting only by company size.
JHML: Large US companies with a lean toward cheaper, higher-quality and smaller names within the large-company group, with technology at about a third. It's a core stock holding with a slight tilt, so it can behave a little differently from a plain index fund.
JHMM: US mid-sized companies spread across technology, industrials, financials and health care, picked with a tilt toward cheaper, higher-quality and smaller stocks. It's a core mid-size holding that sits between big and small companies, and the factor tilts mean it can differ from a plain mid-cap fund.
JHMU: An actively managed fund of municipal bonds, loans to US states and cities whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. It can hold bonds of any length, and the manager adjusts the mix, so no single bond is more than about 1% of it.
JHPI: Preferred stocks and other preferred securities, which pay fixed income but rank above common shares, plus some bonds, picked by an active manager. Holdings are widely spread, with no single position above about 1%, and utilities and energy-related issuers show up often.
JHSC: US small companies spread across financials, industrials, technology and consumer businesses, tilted toward cheaper, higher quality and smaller stocks. It's a way to own small caps in a diversified mix, and it swings more than large-company funds.
JIDE: An actively managed fund of stocks from developed markets outside the US, such as Europe and Japan, picked by a mix of research and quantitative models. It is spread widely, with the top holding ASML at about 4%.
JIG: Growth-oriented companies outside the US, including emerging markets, with technology about a third, then industrials, financials and consumer companies. It aims for capital growth and adds international exposure, but it tends to swing more than value-oriented foreign funds.
JIII: An actively managed fund that mixes many types of bonds, including corporate bonds, mortgage-backed securities and loans, from the US and abroad, aiming for high income. Because the manager can shift between sectors, it is more flexible than a plain bond index fund.
JINT: An actively managed fund of stocks from developed countries outside the US, picked using the manager's own models of company fundamentals. It is spread out, with the largest holdings like Novartis, Shell and BHP each under 3%, and about a third of it is in financials.
JIRE: Large companies in developed countries outside the US, led by financials, industrials and technology. It's an international core holding, and researchers tilt the picks to try to beat a standard international index while keeping similar risk.
JIVE: Developed and emerging-market companies outside the US that look cheap, with financials about 40% and energy, industrials and technology around a tenth each. It's a value tilt for foreign stocks, so it may lag when growth stocks lead, and it leans heavily on banks.
JLCO: An actively managed fund of large US companies that holds a mix of stocks the managers think have good potential. It leans toward big tech, with Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon together about 21% of the fund.
JLQD: An actively managed fund of US dollar corporate bonds, mainly investment grade, meaning borrowers rated as lower risk. It is spread thinly, with no single bond above about 2%, and the managers pick bonds rather than following an index.
JLVP: An actively managed fund of large US companies its managers consider undervalued, using both long positions (bets a stock rises) and short positions (bets it falls). Despite the value label, Amazon, Microsoft and Apple are its biggest holdings.
JMBS: Mostly mortgage-backed bonds, which are pools of home loans packaged into bonds, with a small slice of cash. It's meant for steady interest income and diversification from stocks, and because homeowners can repay loans early when rates fall, its income and price can shift in less predictable ways than ordinary bonds.
JMEE: Small and mid-sized US companies spread across industrials, technology, financials and consumer businesses. It's an actively tuned version of a small and mid-cap index, meant to be a core holding that tries to beat the index, and smaller firms swing more than large ones.
JMHI: A mix of municipal bonds, mostly lower-rated or higher-yield ones, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It is actively managed and spread across many issuers, with Puerto Rico sales tax bonds among the larger positions at about 1% each.
JMID: An actively managed fund of mid-size US companies chosen for growth potential using a computer-driven strategy. It is well spread out, with no holding above about 3%, and leans toward technology, industrials and consumer companies.
JMMF: A money market fund that holds only US Treasury obligations, with some cash kept on hand for redemptions. It works as a place to park cash that earns short-term interest, and the price stays very steady.
JMOM: Large US companies whose share prices have recently been rising, with technology the largest slice at over two fifths. It's a growth-leaning core holding that rides winners, and momentum can fade fast, so it may fall sharply when market leadership changes.
JMSI: A national mix of intermediate-term municipal bonds, issued by cities, states and agencies, with a focus on sustainability. The interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and holdings include water systems and local authorities, each around 1%.
JMTG: Investment-grade mortgage-backed bonds, which pool home loans and pass along homeowners' payments, picked by an active manager. It's meant for steady income and diversification from stocks, though its price falls when rates rise and borrowers' refinancing changes the payments.
JMUB: Intermediate-term bonds issued by US states and local governments, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It's meant for tax-free income, mostly for people in higher tax brackets, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
JNEU: An options-based fund that tracks the S&P 500 through a one-year outcome period starting in June, with a built-in 15% buffer against losses and no cap on gains up to the period's end. The buffer only applies to those holding for the full period.
JNK: Bonds from US companies with lower credit ratings, which pay higher interest because they are riskier. It's for extra income, and it tends to fall along with stocks in downturns when borrowers struggle to repay, unlike safer bonds.
JOET: US large companies chosen for being profitable and well run (quality) and having strong recent price gains (momentum). The index spreads money almost evenly, so each holding is about 1% of the fund and no single giant dominates.
JOJO: An actively managed fund that moves between credit-related investments, and it currently holds mostly two high-yield bond funds: about 70% in one iShares fund and 30% in an Xtrackers fund. It is a fund of funds, so it adds a manager's timing on top of junk bonds.
JOUL: An actively managed fund of companies that make or build high-voltage power grid equipment. Eaton and GE Vernova alone are more than a quarter of the fund, and almost all of it is industrials.
JOYT: An actively managed fund of large US stocks that also sells call options to earn extra income. Its income comes from dividends and option premiums, though the options can limit gains in strong markets, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 21% of it.
JPAN: An actively managed fund that puts at least 80% of its money in Japanese company stocks, chosen by the managers rather than an index. Tokyo Electron, Mitsubishi UFJ and Advantest are among the biggest holdings, and technology, industrials and financials make up most of it.
JPEF: A concentrated set of large US stocks picked by managers, with technology about a third of it. It's an actively managed core stock holding, and since it holds fewer companies than a broad index fund, it can differ a lot from the overall market.
JPEM: Stocks of large and mid-sized companies in emerging markets, selected and weighted by an index that favors lower-risk, value-priced and higher-quality names. It is very spread out: Taiwan Semiconductor is the largest at about 2%, and financials are the biggest group.
JPFP: An actively managed fund that combines two strategies: a managed futures approach that takes long or short positions across markets, and a portfolio of US large company stocks. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are among its biggest stock holdings, at about 3% to 4% each.
JPHY: Bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, which pay more interest to make up for a higher chance of default, plus a little cash. It's meant for higher income, but it acts more like stocks than safe bonds and tends to fall when the economy weakens.
JPIB: Bonds from borrowers outside the US across many industries, including companies and governments, with currency risk hedged back to US dollars. It's meant for income and diversification beyond the US, and hedging means exchange rates matter less, though prices still fall when rates rise.
