JPIE: A mix of bonds across several markets, including corporate bonds, mortgage-backed bonds and government debt, picked by managers. It's built for income above plain Treasuries, and managers can shift between areas, so it's less predictable than an index bond fund.
JPIN: Stocks of large and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside North America, picked and weighted by an index that favors lower-risk, value-priced and higher-quality names. It is very spread out, with no single holding above about 1%.
JPLD: Short-term bonds, mostly mortgage-backed and asset-backed securities. It's built for steady income with small price swings, a step up from cash that is less sensitive to interest rate changes than regular bond funds.
JPMB: Follows an index of US dollar bonds issued by emerging market governments and government related groups, such as Brazil, Turkey, Nigeria and Saudi Arabia. It is spread over many countries, and no single bond is more than about 2% of it.
JPME: US mid-sized companies chosen to balance several traits like value and quality, spread fairly evenly across health care, real estate, consumer staples and industrials. It's a diversified middle ground between large and small companies, with far less technology than most US stock funds.
JPO: A fund that tries to earn high income from JPMorgan stock by selling options on it, rather than owning the shares directly. It holds mostly Treasury bills as backing, and the options mean it gives up much of the gains if the stock rises a lot.
JPRE: Real estate investment trusts, companies that own properties like apartments, offices, warehouses and cell towers. It's for dividend income and a way to add real estate to a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
JPRF: Preferred stocks and bonds that pay steady income, with at least a quarter in financial companies such as banks. It's meant for income, mixing hybrid securities that sit between stocks and bonds, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
JPSE: Small US companies chosen to balance value, quality and momentum rather than by size, with real estate, technology, industrials and health care all roughly similar. It's a diversified small-company holding, and small stocks usually swing more than large ones.
JPSV: An actively managed fund of US small company stocks that look cheap compared with their worth, drawn from the same size range as the Russell 2000 Value Index. It is spread across many holdings, none above about 2%, and leans toward financial companies.
JPUS: US large and mid-size stocks chosen by a rules-based index that spreads its bets across several factors, such as value and quality, rather than weighting by company size. It is very spread out, with no holding above roughly 0.5%, so no single stock matters much.
JPXN: About 400 Japanese companies chosen for profitability and good governance, following the JPX-Nikkei 400 Index. It spans many industries, with the top holdings, like Tokyo Electron and Murata, each about 3% of the fund.
JPY: An actively managed fund of Japanese companies, bought for their quality and growth rather than by tracking an index. Big banks such as Mitsubishi UFJ, Sumitomo Mitsui and Mizuho, plus Tokyo Electron, are among the largest positions at about 4% to 5% each.
JQTY: US large companies picked for high quality, meaning strong profits and financial health, following the Jensen Quality Index of US stocks. It is a passive index fund, with NVIDIA, Microsoft and Apple each about 5% and technology around 37% of it.
JQUA: High-quality large US companies, meaning those with strong profits, steady earnings and low debt, with technology over 40%. It's meant as a core holding that aims for a smoother ride, though it can still trail in rallies led by riskier stocks.
JSCP: Mostly short-term investment-grade bonds from companies and governments, including mortgage-backed securities, with a small portion in riskier bonds. It's meant for steady income with a calm ride, and short maturities mean its price moves little when rates change.
JSI: Securitized debt, meaning bundles of loans like mortgages, car loans and company loans packaged into bonds, with a small cash cushion. It's meant for higher income than ordinary bonds, though it can lose value when borrowers struggle to repay.
JSMD: Small and mid-sized US companies expected to grow, with health care and technology each about a quarter, then industrials and consumer companies. It's built for growth beyond the biggest names, and chosen by active managers, so it swings more than the broad market.
JSML: Small US companies that Janus Henderson's quantitative models rank as likely to grow, held in an actively managed portfolio. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 2%, and it includes industrial, financial and real estate names.
JSTC: An actively managed global stock fund that picks companies whose business practices fit a social justice screen, such as how they treat workers and communities. It holds companies from at least three countries, with the biggest, Lam Research, at about 4%.
JTEK: US technology and tech-enabled companies picked by managers who think their growth is underappreciated, with technology about three quarters and communication, consumer and health care filling the rest. It's a growth bet on tech, so it swings more than the broad market.
JTNY: Investment-grade municipal bonds from New York issuers, with interest generally exempt from federal, New York State and New York City income tax. It is actively managed with an average maturity between three and twelve years, and a small cash holding.
JUCY: An actively managed fund that holds mostly US government bonds and pairs them with options to boost income. The options give up some gains in exchange for a higher payout, so it is not a plain bond fund.
JUDB: A defined-outcome fund that uses options to protect against a set amount of losses in the US stock market over a one-year period starting in July. In return it gives up some of the gains, so it only works as designed if held through the full period.
JUDO: An actively managed fund of large US companies that also uses options to earn extra income. It is tech-heavy, with NVIDIA, Alphabet and Microsoft making up about 21% of the fund, and the options can limit gains in strong markets.
JULB: A buffer fund that uses options on a broad US stock ETF to absorb a set amount of losses over a one-year period beginning in July. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection works as intended only if you hold for the whole period.
JULC: A defined outcome fund that uses options tied to the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cushion a set amount of losses, with a stated 10% buffer, over a set period starting in July. In return, gains over that period are limited, and results depend on timing.
JULH: An actively managed income fund that combines Treasury bills with options on the S&P 500, aiming for regular payouts over a one-year period starting in July. It carries a barrier: if the market falls past a set level, losses can pass through, and gains are limited.
JULI: A defined outcome fund using options on a developed markets international stock ETF to absorb a set amount of losses over a one year period ending in July. It has no cap on gains, but protection and results depend on when you buy during the period.
JULJ: An actively managed fund that uses Treasury bills and options tied to the S&P 500 to aim for income over a one-year period starting in July. It gives up some protection and upside: a drop in the index beyond a set barrier can mean real losses.
JULM: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to cushion a set amount of losses over a one year period starting in July. In return, upside is capped, so it only fully works if held for the whole period, and the options make up nearly the entire fund.
JULP: An actively managed fund using customized options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to aim for a defined outcome over a set period starting in July. It aims to absorb the first 12% of losses in exchange for a cap on gains, and works best held for the full period.
JULT: Uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion part of the losses over a one-year period starting each July, with 10 in the name for the buffer size. Gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold the whole period.
JULU: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 over a set period ending in mid 2027, to absorb the first 15% of losses. Gains are not capped by a set limit, though the protection only works for someone holding for the full period.
JULV: A defined-outcome fund that uses options tied to the US stock market to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in July. In exchange, gains are capped, and the outcome only applies if you hold the full period.
JULW: A buffer fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to absorb the first 20% of losses over a set one-year period starting in July. In exchange, it caps how much of the market's gain you can get, and the buffer only applies over the full period.
JULZ: An actively managed fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to aim for a defined outcome over a set one-year period starting in July. Most of the money sits in short-term Treasury bills, with options doing the work of tracking part of the market's gains while limiting some losses.
JUNC: A defined-outcome fund using options on a fund tracking the S&P 500 to aim for a set amount of protection against losses, with a cap on gains, over a one-year period starting in June. The name points to a 10% buffer, which applies only if held the full period.
JUNM: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to cushion a larger set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each June. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold from the start to the end.
JUNP: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion part of the losses over about a year starting each June, with a 12% buffer. In exchange, gains are limited by a cap, and the protection only applies if held for the full period.
JUNT: A defined outcome fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cover a set amount of losses over a one year period starting each June, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is meant to be held for the whole period to get that result.
JUNW: Uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion the first 20% of losses over a one-year period that starts each June. In exchange, gains are capped at a set level, and the protection only applies if shares are held for the full period.
JUNZ: An actively managed fund that uses options on the S&P 500, buying calls and selling puts, to follow a one-year outcome starting in June with limits on both losses and gains. Most of the fund sits in Treasuries as backing for those options.
JUSA: Large US companies, led by technology at about 40%, chosen by a research-driven manager who leans toward stocks with better outlooks. It's a core stock holding that stays close to the broad market while trying to edge past it.
JUST: Large US companies chosen for how they treat workers, customers, communities and the environment, with technology at around 40%. It's a core stock holding with a values screen, so it looks much like the broad market but overweights companies with strong social records.
JVAL: Large US companies that look cheap compared to their earnings and assets, though technology still makes up about 40%. It's a value-style core holding, and it can trail growth funds in rallies led by fast-growing companies.
JXI: Global utility companies, such as electric, gas and water providers, tracking the S&P Global 1200 Utilities Capped Index. NextEra Energy and Iberdrola are the largest, and the top five holdings are about 28% of the fund.
JXX: An actively managed fund holding only about 20 to 30 large companies that the managers expect to grow quickly. It is very concentrated: Taiwan Semiconductor, Amazon, Broadcom and Oracle together make up roughly 36% of it.
KAIT: A fund of Asian technology companies linked to artificial intelligence, mostly chip makers and electronics suppliers. Taiwan Semiconductor, SK hynix and Samsung are about 18% of it, and nearly all of the fund is in technology.
KAMO: An actively managed bond fund that mostly holds other bond ETFs, including short-term Treasury, AAA-rated CLO and ultra-short bond funds. It can also use derivatives to bet on bonds rising or falling, so it is more flexible than a plain bond index fund.
KAPR: A defined-outcome fund using options on a small-cap Russell 2000 ETF over a set one-year period starting in April. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses in return for a limit on gains, and results depend on buying at the start of the period.
KARS: Global companies tied to electric vehicles and future mobility, including carmakers, battery makers and the miners of materials used in them. Panasonic, STMicroelectronics, Tesla and CATL are each about 4 to 6% of it.
KAT: A concentrated mix of US companies a manager thinks can grow with limited downside, led by financials, health care and technology. It's an actively managed core stock holding, and because the picks are few and chosen by judgment, results can differ a lot from the broad market.
KAUG: Uses options on a small company stock fund, the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, to protect against part of the losses over a one year period that starts in August. In return, the gains over that period are capped, so it works best when held for the full period.
KBA: Holds 50 of the largest and most liquid mainland China companies that trade as A-shares, accessed through the Stock Connect program linking Chinese and Hong Kong markets. It leans toward technology, financials and materials, and the top holdings are each around 5% to 8% of the fund.
KBE: US banks and nothing else, from large national lenders to smaller regional ones. It's a focused bet on the banking industry, so it swings more than the broad market and is sensitive to interest rates and credit worries.
KBFR: An actively managed fund using options tied to small US companies over a one-year period, aiming to cushion a set amount of losses in exchange for limits on gains. The actual stocks are small and spread out, with none above about 1% of the fund.
KBUF: A defined outcome fund tied to a Chinese internet stocks ETF, using options to cushion part of the losses over a set period ending January 2027. In return, its gains are capped, and it is concentrated in Chinese internet and tech companies.
KBWB: US banks only, from the biggest national names to smaller regional lenders, all in the financial sector. It's a focused bet on banking, so it moves with interest rates and the lending economy, and it typically swings more than the broad market, especially when worries about bank health arise.
KBWD: Financial and real estate companies with high dividend yields, tracking a KBW index weighted by yield. It holds many business development companies and mortgage real estate trusts, which lend money and pass on income, and each top holding is about 4%.
KBWP: US property and casualty insurers, such as companies that cover homes, cars and businesses, picked and weighted by the KBW index. It is a narrow bet on one industry, with Travelers, Aon, Chubb and Progressive each around 8% of the fund.
KBWY: Small and mid-sized US real estate companies, mostly REITs, weighted by how much dividend they pay. It tilts toward higher yields and holds a mix of property types, and the largest holdings are only about 4% to 6% each.
KCAI: Chinese stocks picked by an index that looks for companies with strong expected growth, rather than just the biggest names. It is spread across financials, industrials and technology, and the largest holdings are each only about 3 to 5% of the fund.
KCCA: A fund that gets exposure to the price of California carbon allowances, permits that companies need to cover their greenhouse gas emissions, mainly through futures contracts. Most of the money in the holdings list is backing for the futures, and it follows one narrow market.
KCE: US capital markets companies such as brokers, asset managers and custody banks, nearly all financials. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it swings more than the broad market and rises and falls with trading activity.
KCHP: Follows an index of South Korean semiconductor companies. It is concentrated, with Samsung Electronics and SK hynix together making up about 35% of the fund, and nearly all of it is in chip related stocks.
KCOP: Aims for copper exposure through copper-linked funds, futures and copper mining company stocks, and adds income by selling options. Much of the money sits in Treasury bills as backing, and selling options can cap how much it gains when copper rises.
KDEC: Holds options on a fund of small US companies, the Russell 2000, aiming to cushion part of the losses over a one-year period starting each December. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
KDEF: South Korean defense and aerospace companies, tracking an index of firms with strong ties to defense. It is very concentrated: Hanwha Aerospace and Hyundai Rotem alone are about 35% of the fund.
KDRN: An actively managed bond fund that holds other bond ETFs rather than individual bonds, mixing Treasuries, mortgage-backed bonds and high-yield (lower-rated) corporate bonds. The manager shifts the mix as conditions change, so it is a blend of safer and riskier bonds.
KDVD: An actively managed fund of US mid-sized companies that pay and grow dividends, chosen by the manager rather than an index. Its biggest positions are each only a few percent of the fund, so it is fairly spread out across financials, consumer and industrial companies.
KEAT: An actively managed mix of US-listed stocks, including foreign companies traded as ADRs, plus a large inflation-protected bond fund. Energy, consumer staples and materials companies stand out, and the bond ETF alone is about 30% of the fund.
KEMQ: Emerging-market internet and technology companies, from e-commerce and online platforms to chipmakers, including some privately offered stakes. It is spread across many names, with the largest, such as United Microelectronics, Sea and SK Hynix, each only about 4% of the fund.
KEMX: Mid and large-sized stocks from emerging markets excluding China, tracking an MSCI index. It is heavy in Asian chipmakers: Taiwan Semiconductor is about 15%, and Samsung and SK Hynix add around 15% more, so technology is close to half of it.
KEO: A fund of other Kurv income funds, which in turn use options on stocks to produce regular payouts. Only five funds make up most of it, including one tied to SpaceX, so it is concentrated and options limit gains.
KFEB: A fund using options on the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, which holds US small companies, to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in February. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection applies only if held for the whole period.
KGLD: A fund tied to the price of gold that also writes options to earn extra income. Much of the portfolio sits in Treasury bills as collateral, and the options can limit the gains if the gold price jumps.
KGRN: Tracks an index of Chinese companies tied to cleaner technology, mostly utilities, industrials and electric vehicle makers. It is fairly concentrated: BYD, NIO, XPeng and CATL are the biggest names, with the top eight holdings making up about half of the fund.
KHPI: Holds the S&P 500 through a Vanguard fund, then sells call options to earn extra income and buys put options to cushion big drops. The call options cap how much it gains in a rising market, and the put protection is limited, not complete.
KHYB: Dollar-denominated bonds from companies and governments in the Asia-Pacific region, focused on high-yield bonds that pay more income but carry more credit risk. The bonds are spread widely, with no single one above about 3%.
KIE: US insurance companies, including property and casualty, life and health insurers. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it can behave differently from the broad market, and it spreads weight more evenly across companies than a typical large-company fund.
KIQQ: Tracks an index that holds Nasdaq-100 stocks and uses options to pay high income while cushioning a set amount of losses. NVIDIA, Apple and Micron are about 21% of it, and the buffer comes at the cost of limiting the gains.
KJAN: A buffer fund using options on a small company stock ETF, the iShares Russell 2000. It absorbs a set amount of losses over a one year period starting each January, in exchange for a cap on how much it can gain.
KJUL: A fund that uses options on the iShares Russell 2000 fund, which covers US small companies, to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each July. In return, gains are capped, so protection only applies if held for the full period.
KJUN: Uses options on the iShares Russell 2000 ETF to follow small US companies while cushioning part of the losses over a one-year period starting each June. Gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold the whole period.
KLIP: Holds the KraneShares KWEB fund, which owns Chinese internet companies, and sells call options on it to earn extra income. Those options cap some of the upside when prices rise, so it trades growth for income.
KLMN: Large North American companies, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and health care filling most of the rest. It's a core stock holding with a climate tilt, favoring companies with lower carbon emissions and better climate plans over the heaviest polluters.
KLMT: Large global companies, with technology at about a third and financials near a sixth, chosen to favor lower carbon emissions and climate-friendly practices. It's a core world stock holding with a climate tilt, so it leans away from heavy polluters like oil and coal producers.
KMAR: A fund that uses options on a small-company stock fund, the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, to absorb a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in March. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only applies when shares are held for the full period.
KMAY: A buffer fund that uses options on the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, a basket of small US companies, to absorb a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in May. In return, gains are capped, so upside is limited.
KMCA: A fund tracking an index of South Korean manufacturers, mostly makers of electronic parts and chips. It is very concentrated, with Samsung Electro-Mechanics, SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics making up about 35% of the fund.
KMEM: An actively managed fund focused on memory chip companies, the makers of the chips that store data in computers and phones. It is very concentrated: SK hynix and Samsung are about 28% of it, and it also uses derivatives and cash-like holdings.
KMID: An actively managed fund of mid sized US companies that the manager sees as high quality, aiming for less market risk than the Russell Midcap index. It leans heavily toward industrials, about half the fund, and holds companies like Ametek and Teledyne.
KMLM: Futures contracts on commodities, currencies and global bonds, following a rules-based trend approach that goes long or short depending on recent price direction. It's meant as a diversifier that can profit when markets fall, but it can lag badly when trends reverse quickly or stay choppy.
KNCT: Companies tied to next generation connectivity such as 5G, cloud and the internet of things, tracking an Invesco index. It is mostly technology, and Apple, Taiwan Semiconductor and Broadcom are each about 9% of the fund.
KNG: Established US companies that have raised dividends for many years, led by consumer staples, industrials and financials, paired with an options strategy that sells some upside for extra income. It aims for steadier payouts, but it trails in strong rallies.
KNGZ: Large US companies from the S&P 500 that have steadily kept paying dividends, picked by a First Trust index with limits to keep any one stock from dominating. It leans toward technology, with Qualcomm, HP and Texas Instruments each around 4% of it.
KNO: An actively managed global fund of mid and large companies the manager thinks are innovative leaders, spread across industrials, technology and health care. It is lopsided: Micron makes up about a fifth of the fund, far more than any other holding.
KNOV: An options-based fund tied to the Russell 2000 small-company index through a one-year outcome period starting in November, built to absorb part of the losses in exchange for a cap on gains. The protection only applies to those who hold for the full period.
KNOW: An actively managed mix of stocks and some bonds, using a buy-and-hold approach and picking companies based on fundamentals. It holds a lot of industrials and energy as well as technology, and it can invest globally rather than only in the US.
KNRG: An actively managed fund that buys bonds, preferred shares and convertibles issued by energy and infrastructure companies, looking for the best value among their debt. It is a credit fund, not a stock fund, so it leans on interest income from companies tied to energy and pipelines.
KOCT: Uses options tied to small US companies, as measured by the Russell 2000 index, to aim for a defined outcome over a one-year period starting in October. It is designed to absorb a set amount of losses in exchange for a cap on gains, so timing within the period matters.
KOID: An equal-weighted basket of companies tied to humanoid robots and physical AI, such as chip makers and component suppliers around the world. Equal weighting means no stock dominates, with the largest at only about 4%.
KOKU: Large companies from developed countries other than Japan, mostly the US, with technology about a third, then financials, industrials and health care. It works as a core global stock holding for someone who already owns Japanese stocks separately.
KOMP: Companies tied to new technologies like artificial intelligence, robotics, genomics and 3D printing, spread across technology, industrials and health care. It's a bet on innovation and growth, with equal-sized stakes in many firms, so it swings more than the broad market.
KONG: An actively managed fund of about 20 to 30 large and mid-size US companies, which the managers pick for financial strength and a record of returning cash to shareholders. It is fairly concentrated, with Fastenal, ServiceNow, Microsoft, Meta and F5 each around 4% to 5%.
KOOL: An actively managed fund that moves among US and foreign stocks, sector ETFs and stock market groups depending on where the manager sees opportunity. It spreads money widely, with no holding above about 6%, and the mix changes with views.
KORP: A broad mix of corporate bonds, mostly investment grade, with a small amount of preferred stock. It's meant for steady interest income above Treasuries as part of a core bond holding, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
KPHO: Vietnamese stocks listed on the Ho Chi Minh City exchange, following a Vietnam index. It leans heavily on banks, which are about three quarters of the fund, and a Vietnam ETF alone is roughly a quarter of it.
KPO: An actively managed options fund that builds synthetic exposure to the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100, taking part in some of their gains. Most of the fund sits in bonds and cash as backing, so returns come from the options rather than owning the stocks.
KPRO: A fund that holds the KraneShares China Internet ETF plus options to shape its results over a set period ending in January 2027. The options limit some upside in return for cushioning part of the losses, so it behaves differently from the plain China internet fund.
KQQQ: An actively managed fund holding about a dozen large technology stocks and using options on them to generate income. Alphabet, Amazon, Broadcom, AMD and Intel are the biggest positions, and the options strategy tends to limit gains when those stocks jump.
KRBN: A fund that tracks futures contracts on carbon credits, the permits companies need to emit greenhouse gases under cap-and-trade programs in places like Europe and California. It holds no stocks, so its price follows carbon credit prices, and the rest of its assets sit in short-term bonds and cash.
KRE: Regional US banks, from small community lenders to mid-sized ones, with almost nothing outside banking. It's a focused bet on the banking sector, so it swings more than big-bank funds and can drop sharply when there are worries about loans or deposits.
KROP: Companies involved in agriculture technology and food production, such as tractor makers, seed and fertilizer firms and food innovators, following an index. Kubota, Corteva, Nutrien and Deere are each about 13%, so it leans on a few farm industry giants.
KRYP: Tracks the CoinDesk 20 index of major cryptocurrencies, but through futures and other financial contracts rather than owning coins directly. That makes it a spread across big coins, though it behaves like a volatile crypto bet.
KSA: Saudi Arabian stocks, with banks and financials making up over 40%, followed by energy, materials and communication companies. It's a focused bet on a single country and a market tied to oil, so it can swing far more than a broad global fund.
KSEP: Uses customized options on the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, a small company index, to aim for a defined outcome over a set period starting in September. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses in exchange for a cap on gains, and is meant to be held for the full period.
KSLV: A fund that gets exposure to the price of silver through silver ETPs and derivatives and tries to add income with an options strategy. Most of its assets are Treasury bills used as backing, and because it follows one metal it can swing a lot.
KSMH: Invests in South Korean semiconductor companies, directly or through swaps and other ETFs, and focuses on chip makers and equipment suppliers. It is very concentrated: SK hynix and Samsung Electronics are each about 18% of it, so it rides one country's chip industry.
KSPY: Holds S&P 500 stocks through an SPDR fund and adds a hedging overlay of options, following a Hedgeye index, which aims to reduce the impact of market drops. In exchange, it may not fully capture gains when the market rises.
KSTR: Chinese companies listed on Shanghai's STAR Market, focused on technology and semiconductors, tracking the KraneShares China Technology and Semiconductor STAR 50 Index. It is concentrated: about 90% is technology, and its top four holdings make up roughly a third of the fund.
KTEC: Tracks the Hang Seng TECH Index, the 30 largest technology and internet companies listed in Hong Kong, covering areas like e-commerce, cloud and fintech. It is fairly concentrated: NetEase, Tencent and Meituan together make up about 28% of the fund.
KURE: Chinese health care companies, such as drug developers and medical suppliers, tracked by an MSCI index. It is almost all health care, and BeOne Medicines and Innovent Biologics are each about 9%, so a handful of names matter a lot.
KVLE: US dividend-paying stocks picked using Value Line's ranking system, which scores companies on their safety and expected value. The top names are big tech and growth companies, with NVIDIA at about 7% and Microsoft near 5%.
KWEB: Chinese internet companies such as online retailers, social media and gaming firms, with communication and consumer companies about 70% and technology about a sixth. It's a focused bet on one industry in one country, so it swings far more than the broad market and reacts to Chinese regulation.
KWH: Stocks of companies tied to power infrastructure, like electrical equipment makers and utilities, expected to gain from rising electricity demand from things like data centers. Industrials and utilities are about 78% of it, with Schneider Electric and Siemens the largest holdings at around 5% each.
KWIN: An index fund of US stocks, in this case technology based, chosen to meet Islamic investing rules and designed to pay income. It is very concentrated: Sandisk alone is about 22%, and AMD, Fortinet and CrowdStrike add roughly another 26%.
KWT: Companies listed in Kuwait, following the MSCI All Kuwait Select Size Liquidity Capped Index, which limits how much any one stock can take up. It is concentrated in banks: National Bank of Kuwait and Kuwait Finance House are each over 20% of it, and financials are about two thirds.
KXI: Global makers and sellers of everyday goods, such as food, drinks, household products and grocery chains, almost entirely consumer staples. It's a defensive holding that tends to fall less in downturns, though it usually lags when the market is racing ahead.
KYC: An actively managed fund of companies building digital banking and fintech technology, such as payments networks, online brokerages and mobile-first lenders. Visa and Mastercard are together about 18% of it, and roughly 46% sits in financials with about 40% in technology.
KYLD: An actively managed income fund that mixes stocks and other ETFs, including gold and commodity funds, and uses options to try to generate regular payouts. Much of the portfolio sits in Treasury bills and other funds, so it is a blend rather than a pure stock fund.
LADM: A fund of funds that spreads money across up to twelve Pacer Swan SOS Moderate funds, one for each starting month. Each uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion part of the losses, and staggering them smooths out the timing, with each holding about 8%.
LALT: An actively managed fund of other First Trust funds, spreading money across alternative strategies such as hedged stocks, managed futures and income. Because it holds funds rather than individual securities, it aims to behave differently from a plain stock and bond mix.
LAPR: Holds Treasury bills and options on an S&P 500 fund to produce monthly income while cushioning part of the losses over a one-year period that starts each April. The trade-off is that the options limit how much of the market's gains it can capture.
LATR: An actively managed fund of companies behind buy now, pay later lending and the payment systems and platforms that support it. Visa and Mastercard are each about 11% of the fund, and most of it sits in financial companies.
LAZR: An actively managed fund of companies in photonics and optics, the technology that uses light for things like data centers, lasers and chips. It is very concentrated, with Lumentum and AXT together making up about a quarter of it.
LBAY: An actively managed long and short fund that buys income-producing investments as an alternative to bonds, including stocks and preferreds. It can bet against some stocks as well, so it may behave differently from a plain stock or bond fund.
LBO: An actively managed fund of US listed private equity and private lending firms, companies that invest in or lend to private businesses. It is concentrated, with Ares Capital, Apollo, KKR and Blackstone Secured Lending making up about 35% of it.
LBOX: An actively managed fund that uses box spreads, combinations of options that lock in a fixed payoff, to work like a short-term loan that earns a rate of return. It is not a stock fund, and its value depends on how those option positions are priced.
LCAP: Mostly large US companies picked by active managers, with technology the biggest slice at nearly 40 percent, then financials and health care. It's a core growth-leaning holding, though the manager's picks can make it behave differently from the broad market.
LCDS: Large US companies picked by computer models that crunch lots of company data to find stocks likely to do well. It is top-heavy in big tech, with NVIDIA, Apple, Alphabet and Microsoft about 25% of the fund.
LCF: An actively managed fund holding a focused group of large US companies, picked by the managers rather than by an index. It leans heavily on tech and communication, with Alphabet, Apple, NVIDIA and Microsoft together around 30% of the fund.
LCIV: Large companies outside the US, mostly held through American Depositary Receipts, which are shares of foreign firms that trade on US exchanges. It leans toward value-style companies in financials, health care and consumer staples, and no single holding is more than about 3%.
LCLG: An actively managed fund of large US companies that managers expect to grow over the long term. It is fairly spread out, with Amphenol, Broadcom, Apple and Micron each around 5%, and technology is about 40% of it.
LCO: An actively managed fund of about 30 to 50 holdings chosen with a contrarian approach, buying ideas that are out of favor. It mixes stocks and other funds like a silver trust, leans toward technology, energy and materials, and no holding is above about 3%.
LCOW: Holds S&P 500 companies that have produced positive free cash flow (cash left after expenses and investment) for at least ten years. It is top-heavy with big names: Microsoft, Apple, Visa and Alphabet are each about 5%, and technology is nearly half.
LCR: An actively managed fund of funds that spreads money across other ETFs covering US stocks, sectors and inflation protected bonds. The managers shift the mix over time based on their view of the market, so it is not a fixed index.
LCTD: An actively managed fund of large and mid sized stocks from developed countries outside the US, aiming to beat the MSCI World ex USA index. It favors companies better prepared for the move to lower carbon, while spreading widely across banks, industrials and tech.
LCTO: A fund aiming to hold large US stocks with a tax conscious approach, using an S&P 500 ETF for about 40% of it. More than half is in municipal bonds, so it mixes stocks with bonds that can pay income free of federal tax.
LCTU: Large US companies chosen by a manager to beat the broad market while tilting toward firms better prepared for a lower-carbon economy. Technology is about two fifths, so it's a core stock holding that is heavier in tech than the average fund.
LDDR: A bucket of US Treasury bonds and Treasury-only money market funds built to pay out income and wind down around 2035. It is made to be one piece of a retirement income plan, and its value moves with interest rates until it matures.
LDEM: Tracks an index of large and mid sized stocks in emerging markets, chosen for strong environmental, social and governance ratings. Taiwan Semiconductor, Tencent and Alibaba are the biggest holdings, and financials and technology make up about half of it.
LDRC: A bundle of iShares iBonds corporate bond funds that each mature in a different year, from the next one to about five years out. About 20% sits in each, so it works like a ladder of short-term investment-grade bonds.
LDRH: A fund of funds holding five iShares iBonds high-yield ETFs, each maturing in a different year from 2027 to 2031. Each holds risky corporate bonds that mature in its target year, so the mix steps down as each one ends, at about 20% apiece.
LDRI: A ladder of inflation-protected bond funds, holding five iShares iBonds TIPS ETFs in roughly equal parts that mature one each year from 2027 onward. TIPS are Treasury bonds whose value adjusts with inflation, and as each fund ends, the ladder rolls forward.
LDRT: A ladder of US Treasury bond funds that mature in one to five years, held in roughly equal parts, with each rung maturing in a different December. As each rung matures, the money moves into a new one, keeping the fund short-term and low-risk.
LDRX: An actively managed fund that holds large US leaders, tilted toward tech, and uses options to try to earn extra income. NVIDIA, Apple, Alphabet and Microsoft together are about 35% of it, so it is concentrated in a few giants.
LDSF: An actively managed fund of bond ETFs that focuses on short to intermediate maturities, so it carries less interest rate risk than long bond funds. It is a fund of funds, with three First Trust bond ETFs making up most of it.
LDUR: Mostly bonds that mature soon, managed actively by PIMCO, with some flexibility to add other bond types for extra income. It aims for steady income with small price swings, so it's a cushion that is calmer than regular bond funds, but it earns less than longer bonds.
LEGR: Holds companies around the world involved in blockchain and other transaction technology, picked by an Indxx index. The list is a mix of chipmakers like Intel, AMD and Micron plus financial firms, and no single holding is above about 4%.
LEMB: Government bonds from emerging countries, issued in each country's own currency instead of dollars. It's built for high income and diversification, but its value swings with exchange rates, and a strong dollar tends to hurt it.
LEND: A mix of lower-rated corporate bonds and loans from alternative lenders, with real estate and communication companies among the borrowers. It's meant for high income, but the borrowers are riskier, so it can lose value when the economy weakens.
LENS: An actively managed global stock fund that picks companies and assets tied to themes the manager thinks are poised for growth. Right now it leans heavily on gold, silver and energy: gold funds, miners and Chevron and Exxon make up much of the top holdings.
LEXI: An actively managed fund that moves between stocks, bonds and other assets using other ETFs, depending on what the managers think suits the market. Right now it is mostly stock funds, with bond and short-term funds in smaller slices of about 5% each.
LFAI: A fund holding US Treasury bonds and government money market funds, set up to match a 2050 target date for a longevity-style income plan. Because it holds only US government debt, credit risk is very low, though prices can still move with interest rates.
LFAO: A fund holding US Treasury bonds timed to wind down around 2055, designed to turn savings into steady income for life. It works like a bond with an end date, and its payouts come from interest and returned principal, not stock market gains.
LFAW: Holds US Treasury bonds and money market funds in a plan meant to pay out income over a long retirement, up to the year 2060. It is mostly about steady payments rather than growth, and its value moves with interest rates.
LFBE: A set of US Treasury bonds and money market funds meant to provide income that lasts for life, with the bonds timed to a very long stretch ending in 2065. It is aimed at later in life payouts rather than growth.
LFDR: US Treasury bonds and money market funds that hold government debt, managed with a goal of steady, lasting income. It holds almost entirely government bonds, so credit risk is low, but longer bond prices still move when interest rates change.
LFEQ: Normally holds a Vanguard S&P 500 fund, but follows a trend-based model that can cut stock exposure, all the way to cash, when markets turn weak. The idea is to limit big drops, though it can miss out when markets rebound.
LFGY: Holds stocks of companies tied to crypto and tech, such as Block, PayPal, bitcoin miners and NVIDIA, and also sells options to generate income. The options bring in extra cash payouts but limit how much the fund can gain when those stocks rally.
LFSC: An actively managed fund of small life science companies, mostly biotech and medical device makers. It is concentrated and in unproven companies, with Travere, Cogent Biosciences and LivaNova each around 7% to 8% of the fund.
LGDS: Large US growth companies chosen by a data-driven model that looks at company fundamentals, with technology at more than half and communication near a fifth. It's built for growth, so it swings harder than the broad market and is heavy in tech.
LGDX: A fund of large US stocks that uses Intech's math-based method to reweight S&P 500 companies, aiming to beat the index through diversification. It still leans on big tech, with NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet around 23% of it.
LGH: Mostly large US companies in the style of the S&P 500, led by technology at over 40%, with some money held in other assets that adjust its risk. It's a core stock holding that adds a defensive twist, so it may behave differently from a plain market fund in sharp drops.
LGHT: Holds health care technology companies around the world, such as makers of medical devices, software and biotech tools. Intuitive Surgical, ResMed, Moderna and Veeva are the largest, together about 32% of the fund, so it is fairly concentrated.
LGLV: Large US companies picked because their shares have swung less than most, with industrials, real estate, financials and utilities leading. It's built for a smoother ride and tends to fall less in sell-offs, but it often trails in strong rallies led by technology.
LGOV: Long-term US government and government-backed bonds. It's a bet on safety from default and a cushion when stocks fall, but with such long maturities its price swings a lot, dropping sharply when interest rates rise and gaining when they fall.
LGRO: An actively managed fund of high-quality large US growth companies chosen by Level Four Capital Management. It is concentrated in big tech, with Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon making up about 24% of it.
LIAE: A fund holding US Treasury inflation-protected bonds (TIPS) timed to wind down around 2050, so it behaves like a bond with an end date. It is designed to turn savings into monthly payments that rise with inflation, not just to follow the market.
LIAM: US Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS), bonds whose value rises with inflation, held to fund income that is designed to run through 2055. It is built to provide inflation-adjusted income over a long retirement window, rather than to trade like an ordinary bond fund.
LIAU: Holds US Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS) and government money market funds, built around a 2060 target date to provide inflation-adjusted income for retirement. It is a bond fund, so its price still moves with interest rates, especially given the long timeline.
LIBD: A fund holding US Treasury bonds, mostly inflation-protected ones, set to wind down around 2065. It is designed to pay out income over a retiree's lifetime, with payments that adjust for inflation, rather than hold on indefinitely.
LIFT: A set of US Treasury bonds and money market funds meant to pay out steady income over a fixed stretch ending in 2028. Because it holds government debt to the end of that period, it works like a planned income stream.
LIGB: Investment-grade US dollar corporate bonds with at least ten years left until they mature, following a FTSE index. Longer bonds usually pay more interest but their prices swing more when rates change, and the fund is non-diversified so it may hold fewer issuers.
LIT: Companies across the lithium and battery chain, from miners and chemical makers to battery and electric vehicle parts makers. Materials are nearly half, with industrials and technology next, so it's a focused bet on one theme that swings far more than the broad market.
LITL: A fund of US small company stocks that also uses options to try to bring in extra income on top of any stock gains. It spreads money thinly across many companies, with none above about 1%, though the options can limit how much it gains when markets rise.
LITP: Tracks an index of companies that earn at least half their revenue from lithium mining or production, used in batteries. It is very concentrated, with the top four holdings, SQM, Albemarle, Ganfeng and PLS, making up about 38% of the fund.
LJAN: An actively managed fund that holds Treasury bills plus options on the S&P 500 to produce regular income while absorbing part of the market's losses over a set one-year period. Its gains are limited, so it will not fully follow a strong market rally.
LJUL: Uses US Treasury bills and options tied to the S&P 500 to aim for income and a cushion against part of the market's losses over a one-year period starting in July. Gains are limited, and the cushion only applies if you hold for the full period.
LKOR: Long-term US corporate bonds with investment-grade ratings, selected by an index that scores companies on credit quality, value and other signals. The bonds mature in many years, so prices swing more with interest rates, and it is spread out with no holding above about 1%.
LLDR: A ladder of US Treasury bonds maturing in 10 to 30 years, with roughly equal amounts spread across those maturities. Because the bonds are long, its price moves a lot when interest rates change, though the US government backs the debt.
LLMA: An actively managed fund of companies that build and train their own large language models, the AI behind chatbots, plus products built directly on them. It can also use derivatives to gain that exposure, and it is a focused bet on AI developers.
LMBS: Mortgage-backed bonds and similar debt chosen to keep a short average life, with some cash. It's for income with less sensitivity to interest rates than regular mortgage bonds, though an active manager's choices mean it can differ from a standard index.
LMUB: Long-term municipal bonds from US state and local governments, nearly all investment grade, with interest that is exempt from federal income tax. It suits higher earners wanting tax-free income, but the long maturities mean its price falls noticeably when interest rates rise.
LNGX: Companies involved in US natural gas, such as producers who drill for it, tracking a Global X index. It is very concentrated and tied to energy prices, with Devon Energy alone about 13% and the top four making up roughly 30%.
LOCT: Holds Treasury bills and options on an S&P 500 fund to produce monthly income while cushioning part of the losses over a one-year period that starts each October. The options also limit how much of the market's gains it can capture.
LODI: An actively managed fund of short-term US dollar bonds, including Treasuries, corporate bonds and auto loan bundles. Because the bonds mature fairly soon, the price tends to move less than longer bond funds, and the main goal is income.
LOEV: An actively managed fund of stocks from developed countries outside the US, chosen by Harding Loevner for high-quality growing businesses. It is spread across many companies with no holding above about 5%, such as BBVA, Shell and Recruit.
LOGO: An actively managed fund of global companies with strong consumer brands, chosen by the sub-adviser. Despite the theme, it holds a lot of tech, including Taiwan Semiconductor, NVIDIA and Broadcom, along with Eli Lilly, each about 4%.
LOHA: Holds a broad basket of US large companies with real assets and hard-to-replace businesses, such as energy, mining, shipping and industrials, following the Roundhill HALO index. It spreads money thinly, with no holding above roughly 1.3%, and leans toward energy and industrial names.
LONZ: Loans made to lower-rated companies, where the lender gets repaid before other creditors, with interest that adjusts as rates change. It aims for higher income than regular bonds, and its price holds up better when rates rise, but it can suffer when borrowers struggle to repay.
LOPP: US stocks, mostly mid-sized companies, chosen because they meet the manager's sustainability guidelines. It leans heavily toward industrials, around half the fund, with utilities next, and no single holding is more than about 4%.
LOTI: An actively managed mix of stocks and bond funds that aims for income, generally keeping between 35% and 65% in each. About half of it sits in bond ETFs such as JPMorgan Income and PIMCO Multisector Bond, with the rest in individual dividend stocks.
LOUP: An actively managed fund of companies the manager sees as being on the frontier of new technology, such as cloud software, chips and networking. It holds many mid-sized names, none above about 5%, and technology makes up about two thirds of it.
LOWV: An actively managed fund of US stocks chosen to be less jumpy than the overall market. Even so, it is concentrated in big tech: Alphabet, Apple, Microsoft and NVIDIA together are about 25% of the fund.
LPRE: An actively managed fund of companies tied to the real estate economy, mostly landlords and property owners such as apartment and healthcare real estate trusts. It holds a fairly small group of stocks, with the top four making up about 30% of the fund.
LPSV: An actively managed fund of small and mid sized US companies that look cheap compared with their value. It is spread across industrials, financials, technology and consumer companies, with no holding above about 6%.
LQ: An actively managed fund that invests in alternatives, meaning things other than plain stocks and bonds, with an eye on keeping taxes low. It mixes several strategies, so it does not follow a simple index and can behave differently from the stock market.
LQAI: An actively managed fund of large US companies, with an artificial intelligence model helping pick and weight the stocks. It leans heavily on technology, and Micron, NVIDIA and Microsoft are each roughly 5% of the fund.
LQD: Bonds issued by large, financially sound US companies, spread across many industries. It's meant for steady interest income with more yield than government bonds, but it carries some risk of company defaults, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
LQDB: Holds US dollar corporate bonds rated BBB, the lowest tier of investment grade, following a Bloomberg index of them. It spreads across hundreds of issuers, none above about 1%, and pays a bit more interest than higher-rated bonds with more credit risk.
LQDH: A basket of investment-grade US corporate bonds paired with interest rate swaps that cancel out most of the damage from rising rates. It's for people who want corporate bond income without as much interest-rate risk, though it gives up the gains when rates fall.
LQDI: Investment grade US corporate bonds, held mainly through another iShares bond fund, combined with contracts that offset the effect of rising inflation on bond prices. It aims to give the return of corporate bonds with less sensitivity to inflation and interest rates.
LQDM: A fund that holds a big US investment-grade corporate bond ETF (LQD) and sells options on it to generate extra income, aiming for a 12% target payout. Selling those options limits how much it gains if bond prices rise.
LQDW: Holds shares of the iShares LQD corporate bond ETF and sells call options on them to generate extra income. That income comes at a price: the options cap gains in strong months, while most losses in falling markets remain.
LQID: An actively managed fund that puts money into very short-term bonds and Treasury bills and also sells options to earn extra income. Many holdings are other short-maturity bond funds from iShares, so it is a fund of funds aiming for income with low price swings.
LQTI: Short-term US Treasuries paired with an options strategy that aims to produce extra income and a targeted payout over a set period. The options trade on a stock index and add risk beyond a plain bond fund.
LRGC: Large US companies chosen by active managers, with technology about a third, then financials, communication and industrials. It aims to be a core stock holding that beats the broad market, but since managers choose the holdings, results can differ from the market.
LRGE: An actively managed, concentrated fund of large US growth companies. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple, Amazon and Meta are about 37% of it, and technology is around half the fund.
LRGF: Large US companies chosen for traits like value, quality, momentum and low size, with technology about two fifths and financials, health care and consumer companies behind. It's a core stock holding with a tilt toward those traits, and it can trail the broad market when they fall out of favor.
LRGG: An actively managed fund holding a small group of large US companies expected to grow faster than the market. It is very concentrated in tech: NVIDIA, Microsoft and Apple together make up about 34% of the fund, so it behaves differently from a broad index fund.
LRND: Large US companies that spend heavily on research and development, led by technology at about 60% and communication around a fifth. It's built for growth, with few companies from slow moving industries, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
LRNZ: An actively managed fund of companies tied to technology, artificial intelligence and deep learning, including some smaller and mid-sized firms. Software and security names like Cloudflare and CrowdStrike sit alongside health care tech, and the top five holdings make up about a quarter of it.
LSAF: About 100 mid sized US companies picked by a model that scores stocks on several factors, such as value and quality, from a LeaderShares index. It spreads money evenly, so no stock is above about 2%, and it holds a mix of sectors.
LSAT: An actively managed fund of mid-sized US companies, picked using a rules-based model that scores stocks on several factors. It is spread across financials, consumer and tech companies, with no single holding above about 5% of the fund.
LSCP: An actively managed bond fund that can hold debt of any maturity, aiming to stay within about a year and a half of the interest-rate sensitivity of the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index. It is a broad, flexible core bond fund rather than a plain index tracker.
LSEQ: An actively managed fund that buys stocks it likes and bets against others it expects to do worse. That mix can soften market swings, and the portfolio is very spread out, with no single holding above about 3%.
LSGR: A concentrated mix of large US growth companies, with technology about a third, communication companies about a quarter, and consumer and health care firms filling out most of the rest. It's built for long-term growth, and because it holds relatively few stocks, it can swing more than the broad market.
LST: An actively managed US stock fund that picks stocks in industries its managers rate most attractive, rotating between them over time. It holds around 100 stocks with no holding above about 2%, tilted toward technology, health care and financials.
LSTB: An actively managed bond fund run by Loomis Sayles that aims for total return, meaning both income and price gains, from a broad mix of fixed income. It can hold many types of bonds, so what it owns depends on the manager's choices.
LSVD: Large US value stocks chosen by a computer model, with technology the biggest slice at about 40 percent, then communication, consumer and financial companies. It aims for cheap-looking companies, so it can trail when growth stocks lead.
LTAX: An actively managed fund of long-term US municipal bonds, which are loans to state and local governments and agencies. The income is exempt from federal income tax, and it holds bonds from many issuers, including some Puerto Rico debt.
LTB: US Treasury bonds with at least twenty years left until they mature, following a FTSE index. Long bonds swing more in price when interest rates change than short ones do, and the fund is non-diversified.
LTCC: A fund that holds actual Litecoin, a cryptocurrency, and tracks its price using the CoinDesk Litecoin Price Index. It does not hold stocks or bonds, so its value rises and falls with Litecoin alone, which can be very volatile.
LTPZ: US government bonds that adjust with inflation, all with long lives of 15 years or more. It's a hedge against rising prices, but the long length means the price swings a lot, and it drops sharply when interest rates rise.
LTTI: A fund that holds long-term US Treasury bonds and layers an options strategy on top, selling call options to bring in extra income. The tradeoff is that the options can limit gains if long Treasury prices rise, while the bonds themselves still move with interest rates.
LUMA: A fund of companies working in photonics and optics, the technology that uses light for things like data transfer and sensors. Holdings include Soitec, Lumentum and Marvell, with the top few each around 6% to 7%, and nearly all of it is technology.
LUNC: An actively managed global stock fund that hunts for companies the manager believes the market has misjudged as ordinary, then holds a small number of them. It is very concentrated and heavy in shipping, gold and oil: Scorpio Tankers, Newmont and ExxonMobil are about a third of it.
LVDS: Large, established US companies that look cheap compared with their value, picked by JPMorgan using data-driven stock screening rather than a standard index. It is fairly spread out, with Amazon, Apple and Microsoft together making up about 15% of the fund.
LVHD: US stocks picked for steady prices and high dividends, so utilities, consumer staples and real estate dominate while technology is scarce. It's built for income and a smoother ride, which means it usually falls less in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
LVHI: Stocks from developed countries outside the US that pay high dividends and have steadier prices, led by financials, energy, industrials and consumer staples. It's built for income and a smoother ride abroad, and it hedges currency, so moves in the dollar matter less to returns.
LVIG: An actively managed fund of funds that puts most of its money into other bond funds, mainly an Avantis core bond fund at about 80% plus a smaller BondBloxx fund. Together they give a broad mix of US investment grade bonds.
LYLD: About 100 large US companies chosen by Cambria's model for returning cash to shareholders through dividends, share buybacks and paying down debt. It is actively managed with no company above about 3%, and it leans toward financials, energy and health care.
LYTE: A fund of companies that make the lasers, optical parts and networking gear that move data with light, a key piece of AI data centers. It is concentrated: Lumentum, Coherent and Ciena together are about 40% of the fund.
MAAY: An actively managed income fund that uses options contracts tied to a leveraged fund on MARA Holdings stock, a bitcoin mining company, rather than owning shares directly. It aims to pay option income, but that strategy limits gains and still carries large losses.
MADE: Holds US companies involved in manufacturing, from machinery and electrical equipment to components, following an index of those businesses. It is mostly industrials, about three quarters, with Caterpillar, Amphenol, Eaton and Deere each around 4%.
MAGA: Follows an index of US companies whose employees and political action committees mostly give to Republican candidates. It holds many stocks, with no single one above about 1%, spread across industrials, financials, energy and consumer companies.
MAGC: An actively managed fund giving exposure to leading Chinese tech and consumer companies, such as PDD, BYD, NetEase and Xiaomi, mostly through swaps, contracts that pay the stocks' returns, backed by Treasury bills. It is a concentrated bet on a few Chinese companies.
MAGG: An actively managed fund of US investment grade bonds, similar in scope to the broad US bond market. A large part is in US Treasuries, with the rest mainly in corporate and mortgage bonds, and the managers choose bonds rather than following an index.
MAGS: Roughly equal bets on the seven mega tech companies: Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia, Meta and Tesla. It's a concentrated growth bet on a tiny group, so it swings more than the broad market, and it can't spread risk the way a diversified fund does.
MAGY: Holds the Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF and sells weekly call options on it to bring in income. The income helps cash flow, but the options cap how much it can gain when those seven big tech stocks rise a lot, while it still takes their losses.
MAMB: Tracks an index of income-producing bonds of mixed credit quality, and gets that exposure mostly by holding other bond ETFs rather than individual bonds. Most of the fund sits in a handful of iShares bond funds, so it works as a fund of funds focused on income.
MANI: An actively managed bond fund that spreads money across several types of credit, such as high yield and investment grade bonds, and can use derivatives to get exposure. The manager shifts the mix over time, so it differs from a fund that simply follows an index.
MARM: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund over a one-year period starting each March to protect against most losses, up to a set limit. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only works if you hold for the full period.
MARO: An actively managed fund that uses options on MARA Holdings, a bitcoin mining company, to produce income instead of simply owning the stock. This can limit gains if MARA surges while still taking on much of its losses, so income and price can swing a lot.
MARS: An actively managed fund investing in companies tied to space and related technology, such as rockets, satellites and space communications. It is concentrated: SpaceX is about a quarter of the fund and Rocket Lab is another 10% or so.
MART: A defined outcome fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 over a set one-year period starting in March, aiming to absorb the first 10% of losses in exchange for a cap on gains. The buffer applies only to people who hold for the full period.
MARU: Options on an S&P 500 fund that cushion the first 15% of losses over a one year period starting in March, as the name says. It has no cap on gains, though a fee-like cost to the strategy reduces returns versus the index.
MARW: Uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion a set amount of losses over a one year period starting in March, in exchange for capping how much it can gain. The protection only works if shares are held for the full period.
MARZ: An actively managed fund using options on the S&P 500 to follow the index's gains up to a limit while cushioning part of the losses over a set one year period starting in March. Most of the fund sits in Treasury bills that back the options.
MATE: A mix of two strategies: a stock holding that tracks the S&P 500, and a trend-following approach that takes positions in futures across global markets. About 56% sits in the S&P 500 fund, while the trend side is run by a computer model.
MATR: An actively managed mix of other ETFs spread across US stocks, international stocks and bonds, with the mix shifted based on the manager's view of the economy. About 70% sits in stocks, with the S&P 500 as the biggest piece.
MAUG: An actively managed defined outcome fund that uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cushion part of the losses over a one year period starting in August. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if held for the full period.
MAVF: An actively managed fund of US value stocks chosen by Matrix Asset Advisors, which looks for companies it considers priced below their worth. It is concentrated: Alphabet, Microsoft and Apple are about 20% of the fund.
MAXI: An actively managed fund aiming for bitcoin exposure plus income. It holds bitcoin through an ETF and futures, backs that with Treasury securities, and sells options for extra income, so its price moves with bitcoin but not always one for one.
MAXJ: Holds options on the S&P 500 to follow it over a one-year period starting each June. It aims to buffer a large amount of losses in return for a cap on gains, and the protection only applies if you hold across the whole period.
MAYC: A defined outcome fund that uses options tied to the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cushion a set amount of losses, with a stated 10% buffer, over a set period starting in May. In return, gains over that period are limited, and results depend on when you hold it.
MAYM: A fund using options on an S&P 500 ETF to cushion most of the losses over a one-year period starting in May. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection applies only if held for the whole period.
MAYP: A fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in May. In return, gains are capped, so it behaves differently from a plain S&P 500 fund, and the outcome only applies when held for the full period.
MAYT: A fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each May. In return, gains are capped, so it only makes sense to hold for the full period to get the intended outcome.
MAYU: An options-based fund that tracks the S&P 500 through a one-year outcome period starting in May, with a built-in 15% buffer against losses and no cap on gains up to the period's end. The buffer only applies to someone holding for the full period.
MAYW: A set of options tied to large US companies, with technology around 40%. It's built to take the first 20% of losses over a one year period starting in May, but it caps how much you can gain, so it's meant to be held for the full period.
MAYZ: An actively managed fund using options on the S&P 500 to follow the index's gains up to a limit while cushioning part of the losses over a set one year period starting in May. Most of the fund sits in US Treasuries backing the options.
MBB: Bonds made of pooled home loans that are guaranteed by the US government or its agencies. It's meant for steady income with high credit quality, though its price drops when rates rise and homeowners refinancing can change its payments.
MBBA: Home mortgage bonds, mostly backed by government-linked agencies, chosen by an active manager. It's meant for steady income with high credit quality, though its price drops when interest rates rise and homeowners' refinancing patterns can shorten payouts.
MBBB: US dollar corporate bonds rated BBB, the lowest tier of investment grade, picked by a Moody's Analytics index. It is spread over many issuers like AT&T, Capital One and Verizon, each under 2%, with more credit risk than higher-rated corporate bonds.
MBCE: A fund tracking an index of well-known large US companies selected by Monarch, with an unusually concentrated top end. Advanced Micro Devices is about 10% of it, and with Texas Instruments, Broadcom and NVIDIA the leading chip stocks make up a big share.
MBND: Holds investment-grade municipal bonds, loans to US state and local governments and agencies whose interest is generally exempt from regular federal income tax. It spreads money across many issuers, with none above about 3% of the fund, and targets medium-term maturities.
MBOX: An actively managed fund of US dividend-paying stocks chosen by the sub-adviser, Freedom Day Solutions. It is spread across financials, technology, energy and health care, with the biggest holdings, like KLA and JPMorgan, each about 3%.
MBS: Mortgage-backed securities, which are bundles of home loans that pay out interest and principal. It is actively managed and mixes agency bonds from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac with private mortgage trusts, including some bought for future delivery.
MBSD: US government agency mortgage backed bonds, where homeowners' mortgage payments are pooled and passed on to bondholders, tracking an index of such securities. Holdings are spread over many pools, each only about 2% to 3% of the fund.
MBSF: An actively managed fund of floating rate mortgage-backed securities, which are bonds backed by home loans whose rates reset with market rates. Many are issued by government-backed Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae, so its price moves less when interest rates change.
MBSX: An actively managed fund of fixed rate mortgage-backed securities, which are pools of home loans backed mostly by US government agencies such as Ginnie Mae and Freddie Mac. Payments come from homeowners' mortgage payments, so income depends partly on how quickly people repay their loans.
MCDS: About 96% in mid-sized US companies, chosen by JPMorgan with data science models that rank stocks on value, quality and momentum. Holdings are very spread out, with no company much above 1% of the fund, across technology, industrials, financials and health care.
MCH: An actively managed fund of companies based in China, including Hong Kong and Macau, picked for their potential for sustainable growth. Tencent is the largest holding at about 12%, and financial, consumer and tech companies make up most of the rest.
MCHI: Large Chinese companies, with consumer businesses, financials, internet and communication firms and technology as the main groups. It's a focused bet on the Chinese economy, so it swings more than the US market and is sensitive to Chinese government policy and tensions with the West.
MCHS: An actively managed fund of Chinese and Greater China companies that the managers see as innovative, mostly smaller businesses in industrials and technology. It is a bet on one region, and the top five holdings together are only about a quarter of it.
MCOW: Mid-sized US companies from the S&P MidCap 400 that have produced positive free cash flow (cash left after running and investing in the business) for at least seven years in a row. It has no single big holding, but technology is the largest sector at around 38%.
MCVT: Holds convertible bonds, which are company bonds that can be swapped for stock, aiming for growth with some bond cushioning. It is actively managed, picking issuers the manager considers to have strong growth characteristics.
MDAA: A mix that is mostly stocks right now, led by technology at about 40% and financials around 16%, with a manager free to shift between assets. It aims to be a flexible all in one holding, but its mix can change and may not match the market.
MDCR: An actively managed defined outcome fund that uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cushion part of the losses over a one year period starting in December. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if held for the full period.
MDEV: Companies around the world that make medical devices and related tools, tracked by an Indxx index. It is spread out, with no holding above about 3%, so it does not depend on any one company.
MDIV: A mix of high-yield stocks, REITs, preferred shares and energy partnerships, selected for the income they pay rather than growth. It leans heavily toward energy and real estate, and spreads across many holdings with none above about 2%.
MDLV: An actively managed fund of large US dividend-paying companies that the manager thinks are priced attractively. It is spread across sectors like financials, industrials and energy, with Citigroup, Cisco, Entergy and ExxonMobil among the top holdings.
MDPL: Holds 30 equally weighted US stocks from the Russell 1000 chosen for dividends, following the Monarch Dividend Plus Index. Because each stock gets the same weight, about 3 to 4% each, no single company dominates.
MDST: An actively managed fund of North American midstream energy companies, which run the pipelines and facilities that move and store oil and gas, along with an options strategy to boost income. Energy Transfer, Williams, Enbridge and Enterprise Products are about 33% of it.
MDY: Mid-sized US companies, larger than small caps but smaller than the giants, with industrials, technology, financials and health care leading. It's a core holding for the middle of the market, and it usually swings more than large company funds but less than small ones.
MDYG: Mid-sized US companies with faster growth, led by industrials and technology, followed by health care. It aims for growth beyond large companies without the full risk of tiny ones, and because growth stocks are priced for the future, it can drop hard when markets turn.
MDYV: Mid-sized US companies that look cheaply priced, led by financials and industrials, with consumer businesses and technology behind them. It's meant as a value-tilted core holding, and it often lags growth-driven rallies, since little of it is in high-flying technology.
MEAR: Short-term municipal bonds from US state and local governments, mostly investment grade, plus a bit of cash. It's meant as a stable place to park money with income that is exempt from federal income tax, and its short maturities keep price swings small.
MEDI: An actively managed fund of health care companies of any size, mostly drug and biotech makers. It is concentrated: Eli Lilly is about a fifth of the fund and Ascendis Pharma another 14% or so.
MEDX: An actively managed fund of health care companies, mostly drug makers. It is concentrated: Eli Lilly is about 18% of it, and AbbVie, Novartis and Johnson & Johnson add roughly another 20%.
MEIB: Gives exposure to Meta Platforms stock while aiming to pay out extra income, using swaps and options on the stock. It follows a single company, and the income strategy can limit gains if Meta rises sharply.
MEM: An actively managed fund of stocks in emerging markets, looking for companies capable of sustainable growth. It leans heavily on Asia: Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung are over a fifth of it, and technology is more than 40%.
MEMA: An actively managed fund holding stocks of companies in emerging markets such as Taiwan, South Korea and India, with some alternative strategy features. Chip makers dominate: Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK hynix together are about 30% of it.
MEME: An actively managed fund of meme stocks, shares that draw heavy trading and attention from online communities. Holdings change often and sit in speculative areas like space and fuel cells, so it is concentrated and can swing sharply.
MEMS: An actively managed fund of small companies in emerging markets, mostly in Asia. It leans toward technology, industrials and financials, and is spread over many names, with the largest, like Bandhan Bank, Eugene Technology and Elite Material, each around 4%.
MEMX: An actively managed fund of stocks in emerging markets outside China, such as Taiwan, South Korea and India. It is tech-heavy, with Samsung and Taiwan Semiconductor together about 21% of it.
MEMY: An actively managed fund that aims to pay income from "meme stocks", companies that became popular with everyday traders through social media. Most of the money sits in Treasury bills, with options and a small stock slice used to generate the income.
METL: An actively managed fund of mining and metals companies, covering miners of copper and other industrial metals plus related firms such as drillers and steelmakers. The manager picks the stocks, and the holdings are fairly evenly spread, with no single company above about 5%.
METV: An actively managed fund of stocks tied to the metaverse, meaning virtual worlds, gaming and immersive tech. Roblox and Apple are the biggest stocks at about 10% and 7%, and it also holds ETFs that own staked Solana and Ether.
METW: Aims to deliver about 1.2 times the weekly return of Meta Platforms stock, using swaps (contracts that pay the stock's returns) alongside some shares, and pays distributions weekly. It is a single-stock bet that is leveraged, so gains and losses are both magnified.
MFDX: Companies from developed countries outside the US, spread across industrials, financials, materials and technology. It picks stocks using several traits like value and size rather than just company size, so it's a way to add international stocks that differs from plain index funds.
MFEB: An actively managed defined outcome fund that uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cushion part of the losses over a one year period starting in February. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if held for the full period.
MFEM: A fund of emerging market stocks chosen by the RAFI Dynamic Multi-Factor index, which weights companies by business size rather than market value and shifts among factors like value and momentum. Technology is about a third of it, with firms from Taiwan and Korea.
