RYLD: Small US companies, with health care, financials and technology leading, paired with an options strategy that trades some of the upside for regular monthly income. The goal is income, but gains are capped in strong rallies and it still falls when small stocks drop.
RYLG: Holds a Russell 2000 small-company stock ETF and sells call options on part of it to generate income, while keeping some of the upside. The options bring in extra payouts but cap some gains, and small-company stocks can swing a lot.
RZG: Small US companies with the strongest growth traits, taken from the S&P SmallCap 600 Index and held in a pure growth subset of it. It is spread thin, with no holding above about 2%, and leans toward health care, industrials, financials and technology.
RZV: Small US companies from the S&P SmallCap 600 that look cheapest on measures like price compared with earnings and sales, weighted toward the strongest value scores. It spreads across hundreds of holdings, with no single stock above about 2%, and leans toward consumer and industrial businesses.
SAGP: An actively managed fund of US and international stocks of companies that are active in influencing public policy, such as through lobbying. It is spread widely, with health care and industrials the biggest sectors.
SALI: A fund that gets its returns from swaps, contracts that track an index of autocallable notes, structured products that pay income and can end early. It aims for a steady income stream, but it carries stock market risk and complexity.
SAMM: An actively managed fund that picks US stocks and other assets based on a macro and momentum approach, shifting toward areas the managers see gaining strength. It can hold a mix of company shares, REITs and other funds, so it is not a plain index fund.
SAMT: US stocks chosen by a manager to fit big economic trends, with technology about a quarter, then health care, consumer staples and industrials, plus some cash. It's a flexible, actively managed stock holding, so results can differ a lot from the broad market.
SAPH: A way to own SAP, the German software company, through its US traded shares while hedging out changes in the euro versus the dollar. It holds one company, so it rises and falls with SAP alone, minus the currency swings.
SASS: An actively managed fund holding a small group of US companies the manager thinks are undervalued. It is concentrated, with top names like Henry Schein, Primo Brands, AMETEK and Williams each about 6 or 7%.
SATO: Companies in the crypto economy, such as bitcoin miners and firms holding crypto, tracked by an Alerian Galaxy index, plus some direct bitcoin exposure through a bitcoin ETF. About 10% is in the iShares Bitcoin Trust, and it can swing sharply with crypto prices.
SAUG: Uses options tied to small US companies, through the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, to aim for a defined outcome over a one-year period starting in August. It is built to absorb a set amount of losses in exchange for a cap on gains.
SAWG: An actively managed fund buying large US companies the manager sees as high quality with solid growth. It is top-heavy in big tech: NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet together are about 20% of the fund.
SAWS: An actively managed fund of small US growth companies that the manager considers high quality. It spreads across health care, industrials and technology, with no holding above about 4% of the fund.
SBAR: An income fund that mostly sits in a government money market fund for interest, then adds option spreads that pay extra income as long as the market stays above a set level. The options can lose money in a sharp drop, so the income is not guaranteed.
SBB: A bet against small US companies, aiming to move opposite to the S&P SmallCap 600 Index each day. It uses derivatives and resets daily, so over longer periods the results can drift away from simply the opposite of the index.
SBIL: Short-term US government debt and cash-like holdings run under the rules of a government money market fund. It's meant for parking cash and earning short-term interest, so its price barely moves, but its income falls when interest rates fall.
SBIO: Small and mid-sized biotech companies with drugs in later stages of testing, tracked with a Poseidon index of such firms. It holds many stocks, none above about 5%, and results depend heavily on trial outcomes and approvals.
SBND: A bond fund holding short-term US investment-grade bonds, with a large share in mortgage-backed securities, which are pools of home loans. Shorter maturities usually mean smaller price swings than longer-term bond funds, and the fund is spread across many positions.
SCA: Uses derivatives called autocallables tied to Super Micro Computer stock, which pay out and end early if the stock reaches a set level. It is built around one company's shares and is a complex income strategy.
SCAP: An actively managed fund of small US companies chosen for value and income, with some preferred stock mixed in. No single stock is above about 4%, and it spreads across industrials, technology, consumer and financial companies.
SCAU: A defined-outcome fund using options on the iShares Russell 2000 ETF (small US companies) to aim for a set amount of protection against losses, with a cap on gains, over a one-year period starting in August. The name points to a 15% buffer, which applies only if held the full period.
SCCR: Investment-grade US bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage-backed securities and corporate bonds, with medium-length maturities. It's meant for steady interest income and as a cushion for a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
SCDS: About 95% in small US companies, picked by JPMorgan using data science models that score each company on measures of value, quality and momentum. It is spread thin: no holding is much more than 1% of the fund, across health care, financials and technology.
SCDV: Small US companies that pay and grow dividends, picked by the manager for steady earnings. It tilts toward industrials and health care, and the largest holding, Ensign Group, is only around 7%.
SCEC: A diversified mix of US government bonds, corporate bonds and other debt such as mortgage-backed securities, with a manager allowed to lean into higher-yielding corners. It aims for steady income as a core bond holding, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
SCEP: An actively managed fund of large and mid-sized US stocks that sells options to collect extra income and also buys protection against market drops. Apple, NVIDIA and Alphabet are each about 6%, and the options limit some upside in return.
SCHA: Small US companies spread fairly evenly across health care, financials, technology and industrials. It's a broad way to own the small-company slice of the market, and it swings more than large company funds, especially in a weak economy.
SCHB: Roughly the 2,500 largest US companies in one fund, with technology at about 38 percent and financials, health care and communication behind it. It's built to be a core holding that moves with the whole US stock market.
SCHC: Small companies from developed countries outside the US, with industrials the biggest group and materials, financials and technology behind it. It's a way to diversify into smaller overseas businesses, and it swings more than large-company funds because small stocks and foreign currencies both move around.
SCHD: Quality US companies with strong records of paying dividends, led by consumer staples, health care, technology and energy. It is built for dividend income and steady growth, and with little in the tech giants, it often trails in strong growth-led rallies.
SCHE: Large and mid-sized companies in developing countries such as China, India and Taiwan, with technology about a third and financials about a fifth. It's meant for growth and global variety, but it swings more than US funds and carries political and currency risk.
SCHF: Large and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside the US, such as in Europe and Japan, led by financials, technology and industrials. It adds international diversification to a US-heavy portfolio, and it leaves out emerging markets and small companies.
SCHG: Large US growth companies, with technology over half and communication, consumer companies and industrials next. It is built for growth, but it is concentrated in a few tech leaders, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
SCHH: US real estate investment trusts that own buildings like apartments, offices, warehouses, cell towers and shopping centers, leaving out those that lend money. It's for income and property exposure, and its price tends to drop when interest rates rise.
SCHI: Investment-grade US corporate bonds that mature in about five to ten years. It's meant for steady income above Treasuries, though its price drops when interest rates rise and can slide if companies' credit quality weakens.
SCHJ: Investment-grade corporate bonds from US companies that mature in one to five years. It's meant for steady interest income with less price swing than long-term bonds, though it pays a little less than longer maturities and can still lose value when interest rates rise.
SCHK: Essentially the 1,000 largest US companies, with technology near 40% and financials, health care and communication next. It's a core holding that covers the large and mid-sized US stock market in one fund, so it moves with the overall economy and leans heavily on tech.
SCHM: Mid-sized US companies, ranked roughly 501st to 1,000th in size, spread across industrials, technology, financials and health care. It's a way to add the middle of the market, which sits between the stability of large companies and the swings of small ones.
SCHO: US Treasury bonds that mature in one to three years, all backed by the government. It's a place to park money safely while earning interest, and because the bonds are so short, its price barely moves when interest rates change.
SCHP: US Treasury bonds whose principal rises with inflation, covering a range of maturities beyond one year. It's meant to protect buying power and diversify a stock and bond mix, though its price still drops when interest rates rise faster than inflation.
SCHQ: US Treasury bonds that mature in ten years or more, backed by the federal government. It's used as a cushion when stocks fall and for steady interest income, but because the maturities are so long, its price drops sharply when interest rates rise.
SCHR: US Treasury bonds that mature in roughly three to ten years, backed by the federal government. It's a middle-of-the-road choice for steady interest income and a cushion when stocks fall, though its price slips when interest rates rise.
SCHV: Large US companies that look cheaper than the market, with financials at about a fifth, then technology, health care and industrials. It's a value-tilted core holding, and it usually has less tech than the broad market, so it can trail when growth stocks lead.
SCHX: Large US companies across every major industry, with technology about 40 percent and financials, health care and communication next. It is a core holding for big-company US stocks, and a few tech leaders drive much of its movement.
SCHY: High-dividend companies outside the US, in developed and emerging countries, spread among consumer staples, financials, communication and industrials. It's built for income and international diversification, and it leans toward mature, slow-growing businesses, so it often trails in growth-driven rallies.
SCHZ: Nearly the whole US investment-grade bond market in one fund, including Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate bonds. It's meant for steady interest income and as a cushion for a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
SCIN: A broad fund of investment-grade bonds issued outside the US, tracking an international bond index from Schwab. It spreads money across many governments and companies in other countries, which adds currency effects on top of interest rate moves.
SCIO: Bonds backed by pools of loans and mortgages, such as asset-backed and mortgage securities, rather than by a single company. It aims for higher income than ordinary bonds, with the tradeoff that it carries more credit risk and can drop sharply when borrowers struggle.
SCJ: Small Japanese companies, following the MSCI Japan Small Cap Index, which covers roughly the smallest 14% of the Japanese stock market. It spreads across industrials, consumer companies, financials and technology, and no single holding is above about 2%.
SCJL: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, which tracks small US companies to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period starting in July. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, so it suits holding through the whole period rather than trading in and out.
SCJN: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, which tracks small US companies to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period starting in June. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, so it suits holding through the whole period rather than trading in and out.
SCLZ: An actively managed fund of dividend-paying large and mid sized US stocks that also uses options to try to boost income. Micron, Apple and NVIDIA make up about 20% of it, and the options can limit gains when stocks rally.
SCMB: Investment-grade municipal bonds issued by US states, cities and other local governments, paying interest free of regular federal income tax. It's meant for steady, tax-friendly income in a bond mix, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
SCMC: An actively managed fund that invests in a mix of bonds across sectors, such as corporate, government and securitized debt, aiming for income. The manager decides where to invest, so it is more flexible than a fund that follows a bond index.
SCMY: A defined outcome fund that uses options tied to a US small-cap stock ETF to cushion a set amount of losses, with a stated 15% buffer, over a set period starting in May. In return, gains over that period are limited, and results depend on timing.
SCNM: An actively managed fund buying US municipal bonds of medium length, whose interest is generally free from federal income tax. The manager chooses bonds from many states and issuers, so it is a flexible approach rather than a fixed index.
SCOP: A trust that holds physical copper, so its price follows the price of copper itself rather than copper mining companies. It owns the metal directly and pays no income, so what happens to it depends on swings in the copper market.
SCOW: Holds small US companies from the S&P SmallCap 600 that have produced positive free cash flow, meaning real cash left over after expenses, for at least seven years in a row. It also favors high cash margins and returns, and is spread across technology, financials and more.
SCSB: An actively managed fund of investment-grade bonds with short maturities, which can include municipal bonds, convertible bonds and preferred stocks. Because the bonds mature soon, it is less sensitive to interest rate changes than a typical bond fund, and it is meant to supply income.
SCSE: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, which tracks small US companies to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period starting in September. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, so it suits holding through the whole period rather than trading in and out.
SCYB: Corporate bonds from US companies with lower credit ratings, often called junk bonds, which pay higher interest because the issuers are riskier. It's meant for extra income, but it can fall alongside stocks in downturns, so it isn't as steady as high-quality bonds.
SCZ: Small companies in developed countries outside the US, such as Europe and Japan, led by industrials, with financials, consumer companies and materials next. It adds smaller-company growth potential to a global portfolio, but it swings more than large-company funds.
SDCI: A diversified basket of commodities such as energy, metals and farm products, held through futures contracts with the rest in cash and short-term bonds. It can hedge against inflation and moves differently from stocks, and it picks commodities by a rules-based method and avoids tax form K-1.
SDCP: An actively managed fund of mostly investment-grade US bonds, with an average maturity of about one to three years, so prices move little when rates change. It holds Treasuries, mortgage and auto-loan bonds, and aims for income with low volatility.
SDEM: Tracks 50 emerging market stocks that pay some of the highest dividends, each held in equal amounts. It leans toward financials and spreads across many countries, so no one company is above about 3%, and its high yield is the main focus.
SDFI: An actively managed fund of income-producing bonds with short maturities, so its price should move less when interest rates change than longer bond funds. It holds a mix of corporate, government and securitized debt chosen by the managers.
SDG: Global companies whose products and services help meet UN Sustainable Development Goals, like clean energy, health and nutrition, tracking an MSCI index. It is spread over many countries and sectors, with Marvell Technology at about 10% the biggest holding.
SDIV: About 100 of the highest dividend-paying companies around the world, weighted equally, with real estate at about a third and financials and energy next. It's for high income, but the payout can be cut, and prices may swing more than the broad market.
SDMF: A fund that follows an index mimicking managed futures, or trend-following strategies that bet on rising or falling prices in commodities, currencies, bonds and stock indexes. It gets this through futures contracts, with Treasury bills held as backing, so it tends to move differently from stocks.
SDOG: Fifty large US companies, five from each of ten sectors, that pay the highest dividends, spread across consumer goods, technology, health care and more. It's an income-focused fund, and since the highest payers are often out-of-favor stocks, it can trail in strong rallies.
SDSI: An actively managed fund of short-term bonds, mixing safer investment-grade and riskier high-yield debt, plus government, mortgage-backed and asset-backed securities. Because the bonds mature fairly soon, it is less sensitive to rate changes, and US Treasuries are about a fifth of it.
SDTY: An actively managed fund that uses a synthetic covered call strategy on the S&P 500, with options expiring the same day, to pay income weekly. Its gains are capped, and it holds mostly option contracts and Treasury bills rather than the stocks themselves.
SDUR: An actively managed fund of short-term, investment grade bonds, such as corporate debt, mortgage-related and asset-backed securities and US government bonds. Short maturities are meant to keep the price steadier than a bond fund of longer-term bonds.
SDVD: Small and mid-sized US companies with a record of raising dividends, led by financials and industrials, plus an options strategy that adds extra monthly income. It's built for income, but selling options limits gains, so it can trail in strong rallies.
SDVY: Small and mid-sized US companies with long records of growing their dividends, led by financials and industrials. It's built for dividend income plus growth, and because the companies are smaller, it swings more than funds of large dividend payers.
SDY: US companies that have raised their dividends for at least 20 years in a row, with industrials, consumer staples, utilities and financials leading. It's aimed at steady, growing income, and it holds little technology, so it can trail in tech-led rallies.
SEA: Global shipping and freight companies: ocean tankers and container lines, air cargo and ports, following an index of them. Holdings are fairly even at around 5% each, and it moves with world trade and shipping rates.
SECA: An actively managed fund that rotates between market sectors, mostly by holding other sector ETFs plus some individual stocks. The manager shifts the mix over time, and it currently leans heavily on technology, with about 44% in tech companies.
SECR: An actively managed fund that invests mainly in securitized debt, which means pools of loans like mortgages bundled into bonds. Holdings are spread widely, with Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac issues among the larger ones, each only about 2% of the fund.
SECT: A fund that holds other sector funds and shifts between them, with technology about half, then financials, industrials and health care. Its purpose is to chase whichever sectors look strongest, so results depend on the manager's calls and it can lag a plain index.
SECU: Bonds backed by pools of loans, such as home mortgages, car loans and commercial property, picked by an active manager. It's meant for income higher than plain government bonds, and it carries more risk if borrowers fall behind on payments.
SEEM: Companies in emerging markets such as Taiwan, Korea and China, with technology about 40 percent and financials next. It's for growth from developing economies, run by managers who pick stocks, so it swings more than US funds.
SEF: A fund that aims to deliver the opposite of the daily return of US financial stocks in the S&P 500, so it tends to rise when they fall. It resets daily, so over longer periods the results can drift well away from the simple reverse.
SEIE: Stocks from companies in many countries outside the US, led by financials and industrials, then consumer and health care firms. It's actively managed and meant as a core international holding, so a manager's picks, not an index, decide what it owns.
SEIM: Large US stocks that have recently been rising fastest, with technology at over two fifths and industrials, financials and consumer companies behind. It's a momentum bet, so it can surge in trending markets but may fall hard when leadership suddenly changes.
SEIQ: Large US companies chosen for strong profits and sound finances, with technology the biggest slice at about 40%. It's a core stock holding with a quality tilt, so it may hold up better when markets are shaky but lag in junk-driven rallies.
SEIS: Small US companies chosen by active managers, spread across technology, health care, financials and industrials at roughly a fifth each. It's a growth-oriented slice of the market for a portfolio's smaller-company exposure, and small companies usually swing more than large ones.
SEIV: Large US value stocks selected for cheapness and other quality traits, with technology at a third and financials and health care behind. It's a core stock holding with a value tilt, so it can trail growth-heavy funds when expensive stocks lead.
SEIX: Senior loans, which are loans to companies with below-investment-grade credit that are paid back before other debts and carry floating interest rates that move with market rates. It holds many loans, with each one around 1%.
SELV: US large company stocks screened to be less jumpy than the market, using a model that favors steadier shares. Holdings are spread out, with Cardinal Health and Johnson & Johnson each around 3%, and it leans toward tech, health care and consumer staples.
SEMG: An actively managed fund of high quality US growth companies. It is top-heavy: Alphabet, NVIDIA and Microsoft together make up about 30% of the fund, and technology is the largest sector at around 45%.
SEMI: An actively managed fund that puts at least 80% of its money in chip makers, chip equipment makers and related technology companies. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Broadcom and Apple are about 30% of the fund.
SEMY: An income fund that sells options on a leveraged semiconductor ETF to produce high payouts, with Treasury bills backing the contracts. Because it sits on a leveraged fund and options cap the gains, results can swing a lot and depend on semiconductors.
SEPC: A defined-outcome fund using options on a fund tracking the S&P 500 to aim for a set amount of protection against losses, with a cap on gains, over a one-year period starting in September. The name points to a 10% buffer, which applies only if held the full period.
SEPI: An actively managed fund of large US stocks that also sells call options to earn extra income, which tends to cap how much it gains when stocks surge. Technology is about 38% of it, and the top holdings are AMD, Caterpillar and Micron at roughly 7% each.
SEPM: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to cushion a set amount of losses over a one year period starting in September. In return, upside is capped, so it works best when held for the full period, and the options are nearly the whole fund.
SEPP: A fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in September. In return, gains are capped, so it behaves differently from a plain S&P 500 fund, and the outcome only applies when held for the full period.
SEPQ: An actively managed fund holding large Nasdaq stocks while using options to lower risk and earn some income. NVIDIA, Apple and Micron are about 20% of the fund, and nearly 60% is technology.
SEPT: A defined-outcome fund using options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF over a set period starting in September. It aims to cushion the first 10% of losses, in exchange for a cap on gains, and works as intended only if held for the whole period.
SEPU: Uses options on the S&P 500 to follow it over a one-year period starting each September, with a set amount of losses absorbed first. Its name says buffer 15 and uncapped, so gains are not limited by a cap, though a fee reduces the upside.
SEPW: A fund that uses customized options on an S&P 500 ETF to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each September. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold through the whole period.
SEPZ: An actively managed fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to aim for a defined outcome over a one-year period starting in September. It is meant to give part of the market's gains while cushioning some losses, so results depend on when you buy within that period.
SEQ: An actively managed portfolio of a small number of global companies picked for long-term growth, spread over industrials, health care, communication and technology. It's a concentrated bet on the manager's picks, so it can look very different from the market and swing more.
SETH: An inverse fund that aims to move opposite to the price of ether, the second largest cryptocurrency, on a daily basis. It rises when ether falls and falls when ether rises, and because it resets each day, it is a short-term trading tool rather than a long-term hold.
SETM: Miners and processors of materials used in the energy transition, such as lithium, copper and uranium, with materials near three quarters and energy about a quarter. It's a narrow bet on one theme, so it swings far more than the broad market.
SEUS: US companies of all sizes, with technology about a third and health care, financials and consumer companies each making up roughly a tenth. A manager tilts toward traits like value, quality and momentum, so it's a core stock holding that may behave a little differently from a plain market fund.
SFEB: Uses options tied to small US companies, through the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, to aim for a defined outcome over a one-year period starting in February. It is built to absorb a set amount of losses in exchange for a cap on gains.
SFGV: Global stocks that look cheap compared with their earnings and assets, spread across industrials, financials, technology and consumer companies. It's a value-focused core holding for world stock exposure, and it can lag when fast-growing companies lead the market.
SFLO: Small US companies that generate a lot of spare cash after their expenses, with technology, energy, consumer firms and health care leading. It's a value-minded way to add smaller companies to a portfolio, and it swings more than large company funds.
SFLR: Large US companies, with technology about 40 percent, paired with options that aim to limit how much it can lose over a set period. It's built for a cushion against big drops, so it should fall less than the market in sell-offs but gives up some gains in strong rallies.
SFTX: Stocks from developed and emerging countries outside the US, led by technology, financials, industrials and energy, paired with a strategy that cuts exposure when markets turn shaky. It aims for a smoother ride, but that protection can lag in quick rebounds.
SFTY: US stocks, with technology about 40 percent, paired with a risk-control strategy that cuts stock exposure when markets turn shaky. It aims for a smoother ride than the broad market, but that protection can lag in quick rebounds, and it follows an actively managed plan.
SFY: Five hundred of the largest US companies, with technology about half, weighted by both size and company fundamentals instead of size alone. It's a core growth-leaning holding that looks like the S&P 500 but leans harder into tech.
SFYF: Fifty US stocks that are the most widely held in self-directed brokerage accounts at SoFi, a snapshot of what individual investors own. It is concentrated: Tesla and NVIDIA are about 17% of the fund, and technology is roughly 40% of it.
SFYI: Holds stocks popular with retail investors, chosen from social media and trading activity, and sells options on them to produce income. Tesla, Amazon and NVIDIA are about 25% of it, and the options limit how much it gains in strong rallies.
SGDJ: Smaller, "junior" gold mining companies, mostly in the US, Canada and Australia, tracked through an index of their shares. It is a narrow, volatile corner of the market, with no single miner above roughly 6% and every holding in the materials sector.
SGDM: Gold mining companies in the US and Canada, all in the materials sector, from large producers to smaller ones. It's a focused bet on gold, so it swings far more than gold itself and than the broad market.
SGLC: An actively managed fund of large US companies chosen by a quantitative model, so it can differ from the S&P 500. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together are about 20% of the fund, and technology is about 40%.
SGOL: Physical gold bars held in vaults, so the fund simply follows the price of gold. It's a hedge against inflation and market stress that can diversify a stock and bond mix, but it pays no income and the price can swing a lot.
SGOV: US Treasury bills that mature in three months or less. It's a place to park cash that earns interest close to short-term rates, and its price barely moves, but its income falls when interest rates are cut.
SGRT: An actively managed fund of large US companies picked for strong earnings growth. It is concentrated and tilted to tech hardware: Vertiv, Western Digital and Micron are roughly 31% of it, with Energy and health care names making up the rest.
SGRW: An actively managed fund of US small companies that its manager thinks can grow faster than average, mostly in technology, health care and industrials. It is spread widely: no single holding is more than about 4% of it.
SGVT: Short-term US government debt such as Treasury bills, held much like a money market account. It's a place to park cash that pays interest with very little price movement, but it won't grow much and may not keep up with inflation.
SHAG: Short-term US bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage-backed bonds and corporate debt, following an index of those bonds with a tilt to boost yield. Because the bonds mature soon, the fund's price tends to move less than longer-term bond funds.
SHDG: A fund that mostly holds a big S&P 500 index fund and adds an options overlay meant to soften market drops. That hedge means it may fall less in a downturn, but it can also lag when stocks rise.
SHE: US large company stocks that the index picks for having more women in leadership and on their boards. It is tech heavy, with Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Intel and NVIDIA making up about 18% of the fund.
SHEH: A fund tied to a single stock, Shell, the big energy company, with currency moves hedged so the US dollar value follows the share price more closely. Almost all of it, about 96%, is that one company, so it moves with one oil and gas giant.
SHLD: Companies building defense technology, such as aerospace, cybersecurity, drones and military electronics, mostly industrials with some technology. It's a focused bet on rising defense spending, so it moves with government budgets and global tensions more than the broad market.
SHM: Short-term municipal bonds from state and local governments across the US, paying income that is generally free of federal tax. It's a low-risk tax-friendly place to hold money, and because maturities are short, its price barely moves when interest rates change.
SHOC: US semiconductor companies, such as chip designers, memory makers and equipment suppliers, following a Strive index of the sector. It is concentrated: NVIDIA, Micron and Broadcom make up about 40% of the fund.
SHPP: Tracks an index of global industrial and logistics companies, including railroads, engineering firms and software. SAP, ABB and Union Pacific are about 28% of the fund, and it holds both US and foreign stocks.
SHRD: A bond fund tracking an index of US investment-grade bonds screened to follow Catholic values, so some issuers are excluded. Treasuries make up a big share of the top holdings, so it behaves much like a core bond fund focused on steady income.
SHRT: An actively managed fund that both buys stocks it likes and bets against stocks it expects to fall, a strategy called long/short. It is built to hold up better than the market when stocks drop, and no single position is more than a small slice.
SHRY: Follows a Bloomberg index of large and mid-sized US companies that return cash to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks. It is spread out, with no holding above about 5%, and leans toward value-style companies like MetLife and Fox.
SHUS: Holds large US stocks weighted by a method that tries to avoid piling too much into any one business area, then uses index options to hedge against market losses. The options can limit gains in strong markets.
SHV: US Treasury bills and notes that mature in under a year, about half of them held as cash-like short-term debt. It's a place to park cash with almost no risk, earning interest that follows short-term rates, and its price barely moves.
SHY: US Treasury bonds that come due in one to three years, so they're backed by the government. It's a low-risk place to park money for income and stability, and because the bonds are short, its price moves very little when interest rates change.
SHYD: Short-term municipal bonds from US state and local governments that carry lower credit ratings, so they pay higher interest. It's meant for income that is generally free of federal income tax, and the short maturities soften rate swings but credit risk remains.
SHYG: Short-term bonds from US companies with weaker credit ratings, maturing within about five years. It aims for higher interest income than safe bonds, with less sensitivity to interest rate moves than longer high-yield bonds, but it can still fall when the economy sours and defaults rise.
SHYL: Short-term, lower-rated corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, that mature within a few years. Shorter maturities mean less sensitivity to interest rates than a regular high-yield fund, though the bonds still carry real credit risk, and no issuer is above about 1%.
SHYM: An actively managed fund of high yield municipal bonds with short maturities. These are bonds from state and local governments that pay higher interest because they are riskier, and the short length helps limit swings from interest rates.
SIFI: An actively managed fund of bonds from many sectors, mainly corporate debt, including higher-risk issuers, selected with a rules-based computer approach. It uses derivatives such as credit default swaps and Treasury futures to manage risk, and is spread across lots of small positions.
SIHY: An actively managed fund of high yield corporate bonds, sometimes called junk bonds, which pay more interest because the companies carry more risk. A systematic, rules-based approach picks them, and no single bond is more than about 1% of the fund.
SIL: Companies that mine silver, all classified as materials. It's a focused bet on silver prices, so it often swings more than silver itself and can behave very differently from ordinary stocks.
SILJ: Smaller companies that mine silver and other precious metals, all in the materials sector. It's a high-risk bet on silver prices, and because the miners are small and borrow to operate, it swings much harder than silver itself or the stock market.
SIMS: About 100 US-listed companies worldwide that build and run smart infrastructure, such as clean power, smart grids, water systems and automation, following the S&P Kensho Intelligent Structures Index. It is spread thinly, with no holding above roughly 3% of the fund, and leans toward industrial and tech names.
SIO: An actively managed bond fund that mixes many types of income-producing debt, including US Treasuries, corporate bonds and other higher-yielding bonds, to aim for steady income. It spreads across several kinds of bonds instead of following one index, so its risk depends on the manager's choices.
SIOO: An actively managed fund holding large US stocks from the S&P 100 and selling options on them to earn extra income, with a target of paying out about 15% a year. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 25% of it, and the options can limit gains when stocks surge.
SIVR: Physical silver bars held in a vault, so it holds no stocks or bonds. It's a way to own silver without storing metal, used as a hedge against inflation or market stress, but silver pays no income and its price swings a lot.
SIXA: The very largest US companies, spread across consumer staples, technology, health care and communications. It aims to be a core holding focused on stable giants, with a tilt toward food and household names that makes it look different from a standard large-company fund.
SIXD: Uses stock-index options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion the first 10% of losses over a six-month period that resets each June and December. In exchange, gains over that period are capped, and the protection only works if shares are held for the full period.
SIXF: A fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to follow large US companies over a six month period starting in February and August. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses in exchange for limiting gains, and the protection only fully applies if held for the whole period.
SIXH: US stocks, led by consumer staples, technology and health care, paired with index options that cushion some losses. It's meant for a smoother ride than the market, and the hedge limits gains, so it trails in strong rallies.
SIXJ: A defined outcome fund using S&P 500 options over a set six-month period starting in January or July. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses, and in return gains are capped.
SIXL: Mid-sized US stocks picked for being less jumpy than the overall market, meaning a low beta, so it favors steadier areas like financials, consumer staples, utilities and health care. It is spread thinly, with no holding above about 1% of the fund.
SIXO: A defined outcome fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to give a set amount of protection against losses over a six month period, in exchange for a cap on gains. It resets twice a year, April and October, and the protection applies only over the full period.
SIXP: A fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to follow large US companies over a six month period starting in March and September. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses in exchange for limiting gains, and the protection only fully applies if held for the whole period.
SIXS: An actively managed fund of small US companies, similar in size to those in the S&P SmallCap 600. It tilts toward lower-priced value stocks, spread across real estate, health care, energy and financials, with no holding above about 2%.
SIXZ: Uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion a set amount of losses over six months, from November to May and May to November. In return, the gains it can capture are capped, so it is designed to be held for the full period.
SIZE: US stocks from the MSCI USA index weighted to tilt toward smaller companies, so it holds a broad mix of large and mid-sized firms with more weight on the smaller ones. No single stock is more than a sliver of the fund, so it is very spread out.
SJB: Aims to go up when US high yield corporate bonds fall, delivering roughly the opposite of their daily return. It resets every day, so over longer periods results can drift away from the opposite of the bond market.
SJCP: An actively managed bond fund holding mostly investment-grade US corporate and government bonds, plus some preferred stocks, which pay fixed dividends. US Treasuries are about a third of the fund, so it is aimed at steady income.
SJLD: An actively managed fund of short-term, high-quality debt, aiming to keep its average sensitivity to interest rates low. It mixes Treasury bills with corporate debt and preferred shares, so it is a bit riskier than a plain Treasury fund.
SJNK: Short-term bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, which pay higher interest than safer bonds. It's for extra income with less sensitivity to interest rates than longer junk bonds, but these companies are more likely to default, so it can drop in recessions.
SKOR: US corporate bonds from companies with solid credit ratings, medium in length, screened for better value and financial strength. It's meant for steady interest income above Treasuries, though its price drops when interest rates rise and it can slip when the economy weakens.
SKYY: Companies that sell cloud computing, meaning software and services delivered over the internet, almost all in technology. It's a focused bet on one fast-growing corner of tech, so it tends to swing more than the broad market, especially when growth stocks fall out of favor.
SLDR: A ladder of US Treasury bonds with short maturities, tracking an index that spreads money evenly across different end dates. As each bond matures, the money is reinvested, so the fund stays short-term and is less sensitive to interest rate changes.
SLJY: Holds shares of junior silver mining companies, mostly through another Amplify silver miners ETF, and sells call options on them to earn extra income. The options cap gains when silver miners surge, while the miners can still fall sharply.
SLNZ: An actively managed fund buying senior secured loans, which are floating-rate loans to companies that get paid back first if a borrower runs into trouble. The interest rates reset as short-term rates move, so income changes with interest rates.
SLQD: Short-term bonds from financially solid US companies, all coming due within five years, plus a little cash. It's meant for modest, steady income with a gentler ride than longer bonds, so it rises less than the broad bond market when rates fall but also loses less when they rise.
SLV: Physical silver held in a vault, rather than companies or bonds. It's used as a hedge and a bet on metal prices, but it pays no income and swings more than gold because industry demand also moves it.
SLVI: A fund tied to the price of silver that also aims to pay high monthly income, using options on silver investments to earn extra cash. Selling those options gives up some of silver's gains in strong rallies, so it trades some upside for income.
SLVO: An exchange-traded note that follows a covered call strategy on the iShares Silver Trust, meaning it tracks silver while collecting option income. That income is paid out regularly, but it caps gains if silver rises sharply, and as a note it also carries the issuer's credit risk.
SLVP: Mining companies focused on silver and other metals, all classed in the materials sector. It's a focused bet on the miners rather than on metal itself, so it swings more than the broad market, and its price tends to follow silver and metals prices up and down.
SLVR: Silver mining companies, plus some physical silver bars, with the stock part nearly all in materials. It's a focused bet on silver prices that can work as an inflation hedge, but it swings far more than the broad market.
SLVX: Silver mining companies, a silver trust, and options on silver stocks, aimed at producing income. About 15% of the fund is a physical silver fund and the rest is miners like First Majestic, SSR Mining and Silvercorp, and selling options caps some of the upside.
SLVY: Aims to follow the price of silver while also paying income, using options on silver-related investments. Selling options for income caps how much of silver's rise it can capture, and it holds no physical silver bars itself.
SLWS: An actively managed fund of short-term bonds from many sectors and countries, including corporate debt and securities backed by loans. Because the bonds are short, prices move less than in a typical bond fund, and it is spread across many small holdings.
SLX: Companies in the steel industry worldwide, from iron ore miners to steel producers, tracking a VanEck index. It is concentrated in a few names, with BHP, Vale and Rio Tinto about 23% together, so it follows a cyclical corner of materials.
SLYG: Small US companies with faster growth, spread across technology, industrials, health care and financials, each roughly a fifth or less. It's for long-term growth, and small companies tend to swing more than large ones and can lag in downturns.
SLYV: Small US companies that look cheap relative to their size, led by financials at about a fifth, then consumer, technology and industrial companies. It's a value-oriented piece for a portfolio, and small companies tend to swing more than large ones and can struggle in downturns.
SMAX: Holds an iShares S&P 500 fund and options to cushion a larger amount of losses over a one-year period starting in September. The tradeoff is a cap on gains, so a strong market will not be fully captured.
SMAY: Uses options on a small-company stock fund (the iShares Russell 2000 ETF) to cushion part of the losses over a one-year period that starts each May. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
SMB: Short term, tax exempt municipal bonds issued by US states, cities and agencies, tracked through a VanEck index. Interest is generally free of federal income tax, and the shorter maturities mean the price moves less than longer muni funds.
SMBS: Nearly all bonds backed by pools of home mortgages that are issued or guaranteed by US government agencies. It's meant for steady interest income with high credit quality, but its price falls when interest rates rise, and homeowners paying off loans early can change how long the income lasts.
SMCO: An actively managed fund of 50 to 75 small and mid-sized US companies that the manager sees as solid and fairly priced. It spreads across industrials, tech, health care and financials, with no holding above about 3%.
SMCP: An actively managed fund of mid-sized companies listed on US exchanges, including some based abroad. It is a concentrated mix of miners, energy and drug companies, with the largest few holdings each around 6% to 8% of the fund.
SMCY: Aims to pay high income from Super Micro Computer stock by selling call options on it, rather than holding the shares. That caps the gains if the stock climbs but leaves much of the downside, and the Treasury bills are collateral.
SMDV: Small US companies that have raised their dividends every year for at least ten years, led by financials and industrials. It's a steadier small-cap fund for dividend growth, so it trails in strong rallies led by risky stocks.
SMDX: Holds small and mid sized US companies drawn from the S&P Small-Mid Cap index, with the weights adjusted by a math-based method meant to beat the index a little. It is very spread out, with the largest holdings only around 1% each.
SMH: Companies that design and make semiconductors, the chips that power computers, phones and AI, with all of it in technology. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it swings far more than the broad market, and a few big chip makers dominate it.
SMHC: Tracks an index of the largest and most traded Chinese semiconductor companies, around 25 stocks. It is concentrated and all technology: Cambricon, Hygon and Eoptolink are each roughly 7% to 9% of the fund.
SMHX: Fabless semiconductor companies, meaning chip designers that have others manufacture their chips, tracked by the VanEck Fabless Semiconductor index. It is concentrated: NVIDIA and Broadcom make up about a third of it.
SMIG: Small and mid-sized US companies that pay and grow dividends, spread across financials, industrials, consumer companies and energy. Managers pick the stocks themselves, so it's meant for steady growth with some income, and tends to hold up better in downturns than rallies.
SMIN: Small Indian companies spread across industrials, consumer companies, financials and health care. It's a high-growth bet on one emerging market, so it swings more than large-company funds and is affected by currency moves.
SMIZ: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US companies picked with Zacks research that ranks stocks by earnings outlook. It holds many companies in small slices, with none above about 2%, and tilts toward technology, industrials and financials.
SMLF: Small US companies picked for four traits: momentum, quality, value and low volatility, spread across technology, industrials, health care and financials. It's a diversified small-company holding with a built-in tilt, so it can swing more than large-company funds.
SMLL: An actively managed fund of smaller US companies chosen by the managers rather than an index. Holdings are fairly spread out, with Pool Corp, Morningstar, WillScot and Wintrust each around 4% to 5%, and industrials and financials are the largest sectors.
SMLV: Small US companies with lower price swings, picked from the Russell 2000 for being less volatile than the group as a whole. It holds many small positions of about 0.6% each and leans toward financials, industrials, technology and real estate.
SMMD: Small and mid-sized US companies spread evenly across industrials, technology, health care and financials. It adds the part of the market the biggest companies miss, so it tends to swing more than a large-company fund.
SMMU: Short-term municipal bonds from state and local governments, mostly high quality, with a bit of cash. It's a low-risk place to park money for income that is generally free of federal income tax, and because maturities are short, prices move less when interest rates change.
SMMV: Small US companies chosen and weighted to have lower price swings than the overall small-company market. It leans toward steadier areas like real estate, utilities, health care and insurance, with no holding above about 2%.
SMNG: A fund holding stocks of companies in the Samsung group, the large South Korean conglomerate, which spans electronics, finance, shipbuilding and more. It is concentrated in one corporate family and one country, so it depends on a small group of related businesses.
SMOG: Holds companies tied to low carbon energy, such as clean power producers, electric vehicle makers and fuel cell firms, from around the world. Tesla, Iberdrola and Bloom Energy are each about 8% of it, so a few names have a big influence.
SMOM: An actively managed fund of funds that holds sector ETFs from the S&P 500, shifting toward the sectors with the strongest recent momentum. This means it can be heavily tilted, with technology and energy funds being about half now.
SMOT: Small and mid-sized US companies that Morningstar judges to have lasting competitive advantages, sometimes called moats, and that look reasonably priced. Holdings are spread out, with the largest, like Acuity and Bio-Techne, only about 2% each.
SMOX: An actively managed fund of small and mid-size US companies, which also can include real estate trusts. It is very spread out, with the largest holdings, like Twilio, TD Synnex and Okta, each only about 1 to 2%.
SMRF: Holds companies tied to nuclear energy, including uranium miners and nuclear power producers around the world, plus small modular reactor developers. It is a narrow theme, with uranium names like NexGen and Uranium Energy among the top holdings.
SMRI: Mid-sized US value stocks, led by technology and health care, with energy and consumer companies behind them. It's a manager-picked stock fund for growth beyond the largest companies, and it swings more than the broad market.
SMRZ: A fund holding companies involved in small modular reactors, compact nuclear power plants built in factories, including those that build them, supply fuel or provide parts. It is narrow and non-diversified, so a few companies can drive its results.
SMTH: An actively managed mix of high-quality bonds, mainly mortgage-backed and other government-related debt along with some corporate bonds. It's a core bond holding aimed at steady income, and the manager has room to depart from the broad bond market, so results can differ.
SMTJ: An actively managed fund of Japanese stocks, chosen to benefit from long-term shifts in society and industry. It is fairly concentrated: big banks like Mitsubishi UFJ, plus Hitachi and Sony, lead the list, and industrials and financials are about half the fund.
SMYY: An income fund tied to Super Micro Computer stock that uses options and swaps instead of owning the shares directly, aiming to pay large distributions. Most of the money sits in Treasury bills as backing, and the strategy limits how much it can gain if the stock rises.
SNAV: An actively managed fund of funds that spreads money across other ETFs, mainly an equal weight S&P 500 fund and sector funds such as technology and health care. The manager shifts between them, so it is a US stock mix that can change over time.
SNOV: Uses options on a small-company stock fund (the iShares Russell 2000 ETF) to cushion part of the losses over a one-year period that starts each November. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
SNOY: A fund that gives income and partial exposure to Snowflake's stock price using options, rather than owning the shares. Its option strategy caps how much it gains if Snowflake rises, while losses can still be large, and most assets are held in Treasury bills.
SNPD: US companies from the S&P High Yield Dividend Aristocrats, which have raised their dividends for decades, screened for certain environmental and other concerns. It leans toward consumer staples, industrials and utilities, with each holding only about 2 to 3%.
SNPE: Large US companies in roughly the same industry mix as the S&P 500, with technology about two fifths, after screening out firms that score poorly on environmental and social measures. It's a core stock holding with a values filter, so it behaves much like the broad market.
SNPG: US large companies from the S&P 500 that show strong growth, screened and scored on environmental, social and governance measures and weighted by company size. It is top-heavy: Micron, Microsoft and NVIDIA are each about 8% of it, and technology is nearly half the fund.
SNSR: Companies tied to the Internet of Things, meaning everyday devices connected to the web, including chip makers and sensor and medical device firms. Technology is about 80% of it, with STMicroelectronics the largest holding at roughly 9%.
SNTH: An actively managed fund that uses options and Treasury bonds to mimic stock market returns without holding stocks directly. Most of the fund sits in US Treasuries, with options supplying the stock exposure, so it behaves like a stock fund built from different parts.
SNTQ: An actively managed fund that mixes options with Treasuries to get Nasdaq-100 type returns in a different way than owning the stocks. It is a defined outcome style fund, so its results can differ noticeably from the index in both directions.
SOCL: Social media and online networking companies from around the world, tracked by a Global X index. It is concentrated in a few big names: Tencent, Naver and Meta are each about 9% to 10% of the fund, and nearly all of it is communication companies.
SOEZ: A fund that aims to follow the price of Solana, a cryptocurrency, by holding it directly rather than owning company shares. Its value can swing sharply, and it behaves like a single crypto asset rather than a diversified basket.
SOFR: Short term cash style investments that aim to earn the overnight SOFR rate, a key benchmark for short term US borrowing. It's a place to park money with very little price movement, and its income rises and falls with short term interest rates.
SOLC: Holds actual Solana (SOL), a cryptocurrency, in a trust, so its price follows the price of the coin. A portion of the coins may be staked through Marinade to earn extra rewards, and the value can swing sharply, as with other crypto.
SOLM: Aims to follow Solana's price while selling monthly options on Solana funds to bring in extra income. It holds a Solana staking fund and cash like holdings, and the options limit gains if Solana jumps.
SOLZ: A fund giving exposure to Solana (SOL), a digital currency that runs on its own computer network. It invests in SOL-linked instruments rather than only holding the coin, so its price follows Solana, which can swing sharply, and part of the fund sits in cash.
SOVF: An actively managed fund of US companies, mostly small and mid sized, picked by its adviser. It leans toward tech and financials, and no single stock is much above 4%, with names like Molina, Paycom and Repay at the top.
SOXQ: The 30 largest chip companies listed in the US, all in semiconductors. It's a focused bet on the engines behind computers, phones and artificial intelligence, so it swings far more than the broad market and rises and falls with the chip industry's cycles.
SOXX: Computer chip designers and makers, including companies that build the equipment used to produce chips. It's a focused bet on one fast-moving industry, so it swings far more than the broad market and does best when chip demand is booming.
SOXY: Holds semiconductor stocks such as NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom and ASML, and sells options on them to generate income. Those options cap how much it can gain when chip stocks rise, so it trades some upside for monthly payouts.
SOYB: Gets exposure to soybean prices by holding futures contracts on soybeans, rather than the beans themselves. Its value follows soybean futures, which can move sharply with weather and crop news, and the fund also holds cash to back its contracts.
SPAB: Nearly the whole US investment-grade bond market in one fund, mostly Treasuries, government-backed mortgage bonds and corporate bonds. It's meant for steady interest income and as a cushion for a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
SPAM: Companies in the cybersecurity industry, such as Palo Alto Networks, Okta and CrowdStrike, following a Themes index. It is concentrated in tech, and each of the top holdings is around 6% of the fund.
SPAQ: An actively managed fund of SPACs, shell companies that raise money in a stock market listing so they can buy a business later. It aims to beat what bank CDs pay, and holds many SPACs, each around 4% to 5% of the fund.
SPBC: Mostly a fund tracking the S&P 500, about 90% of it, plus a smaller slice, around 8%, in a Bitcoin ETF. It is actively managed, so it gives large US stocks with a modest dose of Bitcoin exposure added on top.
SPBO: Bonds issued by US and international companies, mostly investment grade, meaning borrowers rated fairly safe. It's meant for steady income and to diversify a stock portfolio, and it pays more than Treasuries but its price drops when interest rates rise.
SPBU: A fund of twelve other buffer funds that stagger their one-year periods across the calendar, each aimed at cushioning part of the losses on the S&P 500. It has no cap on gains, so each period's upside is not limited, though the protection costs a fee.
SPBW: A mix of one-year buffered funds that follow the S&P 500, each cushioning a set amount of losses while capping gains. The funds start at different times of year, so protection is staggered rather than all resetting at once.
SPBX: A mix of six-month buffered funds that follow the S&P 500 and cushion a set amount of losses at the end of each period. In exchange, each caps how much of the market's gain you can capture, and the funds are staggered across the year.
SPCI: A fund giving exposure to space industry companies using stocks, call options and synthetic positions, and earning extra income with a put spread, a paired options trade. The options strategy trades away some upside in exchange for that income.
SPCK: Special purpose acquisition companies (SPACs), empty shell companies that raise money to buy a business later, plus companies that recently went public. Because SPACs are mostly cash waiting for a deal, its holdings are small, with none above about 5%.
SPCT: Large US companies with a strong record of raising their dividends, picked by the managers rather than an index. It is spread widely, with the top names such as Apple, Amazon, Caterpillar and Eli Lilly each around 3% of the fund.
SPD: Holds the S&P 500 through an iShares ETF, about 95% of the fund, and adds put options that pay off if the market drops sharply. The options cost money to carry, which can drag on gains in calmer markets.
SPDF: An actively managed fund that holds US large company stocks, mostly through a single S&P 500 index fund. A rules based risk overlay can move the fund toward cash when markets look weak, so it differs from simply owning the index.
SPDG: US dividend-paying large companies, weighted so that no sector gets far bigger than the others, tracking an S&P index. Even so, tech is the largest sector at about 40%, with Cisco, Verizon, IBM and Texas Instruments among the biggest holdings.
SPDV: Tracks an index of S&P 500 companies with high dividend yields and dividends that look sustainable, weighted equally instead of by size. It spreads across many sectors, with the largest holdings at only about 2% to 3% each.
SPDW: Large companies from developed countries outside the US, such as Europe, Japan and Canada, led by financials, industrials and technology. It works as the international portion of a stock portfolio, and it has no US companies or emerging markets.
SPEM: Stocks from emerging markets such as China, India and Taiwan, with technology about a third and financials a fifth. It's a way to add faster-growing but riskier economies to a portfolio, and it can swing more than developed-market funds because of politics and currency moves.
SPEU: Companies across developed Europe, led by financials and industrials, then health care and technology. It's a way to add European stocks to a portfolio, with much less tech than US funds, and it's affected by the euro and pound.
SPFF: Preferred shares, which are stock-like securities that pay a fixed dividend, selected to follow a Global X preferred stock index. It is built for income, and the holdings are a mix of companies from many industries instead of just banks.
SPGM: Companies from around the world, both developed and emerging countries, with technology the largest slice at about a third and financials next. It's a one-fund core holding for global stock exposure, with a large share in US companies.
SPGP: Large US companies chosen for steady growth at reasonable prices, with financials about a third and technology about a fifth. It's a blend of growth and value for a stock portfolio, and it holds far less tech than the broad market.
SPHB: The 100 stocks in the S&P 500 that have swung the most compared to the market, with technology over half and industrials about a seventh. It's a bet on rallies, built to rise faster in good times, but it also falls harder in sell-offs.
SPHD: The 50 S&P 500 stocks with high dividends and low price swings, led by real estate, consumer staples, utilities and financials. It's built for income and a calmer ride, but it holds little technology, so it tends to lag when growth stocks lead.
SPHQ: The 100 S&P 500 companies with the strongest profits, steady earnings and low debt, led by technology, industrials and financials. It's a core holding built around company quality, and it can lag when riskier stocks lead a rally.
SPHY: Bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, often called junk bonds, that pay higher interest because they are riskier. It's built for extra income, but it tends to fall alongside stocks in a downturn, so it's a weaker cushion than safer bonds.
SPIB: Investment-grade bonds from US companies that mature in roughly three to ten years. It's built for steady income that pays more than Treasuries, though it falls when interest rates rise or when company credit worries grow.
SPIN: Holds large US companies, then adds a strategy to earn extra income from selling options on them. NVIDIA, Alphabet, Microsoft and Apple are about 27% of it, and the option income can limit how much it gains in strong markets.
SPIP: US government bonds whose payments rise with inflation, across a range of lengths. It's meant to protect buying power and diversify a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise faster than inflation.
SPIT: An actively managed fund buying US companies in special situations, such as ones going through restructurings or other major changes. It leans toward mid and small sized companies, spread across technology, health care and industrials, with no one holding above about 5%.
SPLB: Long-term US corporate bonds, all maturing in ten years or more. It pays higher interest than shorter bonds, but its price swings widely when interest rates change, falling sharply when they rise, so it's for income seekers who can ride out the swings.
SPLS: A fund that holds S&P 500 stock exposure and adds an actively managed bond portfolio on top, using funds, futures and swaps to do both at once. It gives stock market returns plus a bond manager's attempt to earn extra, so it differs from a plain S&P 500 fund.
SPLV: The 100 S&P 500 stocks that have swung the least over the past year, heavy in utilities, financials, real estate and industrials. It's built for a smoother ride and falls less in sell-offs, but it trails in strong rallies.
SPMB: Mortgage-backed bonds, which pool home loans backed by government-sponsored agencies and pay out homeowners' monthly payments. It's meant for steady income with high credit quality, though it falls when rates rise and homeowners' refinancing can change the payments.
SPMD: Mid-sized US companies, larger than small caps but smaller than the giants, with industrials, technology, financials and health care leading. It's a core holding for the middle of the market, and it usually swings more than large company funds but less than small ones.
SPMO: About 100 stocks in the S&P 500 that have been rising fastest lately, with technology making up over half the fund. It's a bet that winners keep winning, and since it reshuffles as trends change, it can drop sharply when market leadership turns.
SPPP: A trust that holds physical platinum and palladium bars in storage, so its price follows those two metals. They are used heavily in car exhaust systems, and the fund owns the metal itself and pays no income.
SPRE: Holds real estate investment trusts (REITs) from around the world that pass a Sharia (Islamic law) screen, tracking an S&P index. It is concentrated, with Goodman Group, Prologis, Equinix and Welltower each around 12% of the fund.
SPRX: An actively managed fund of technology companies that the manager thinks benefit from big shifts like AI, cloud and chips, with nearly 90% in tech. It is concentrated: Astera Labs, KLA, Coherent and Arm are about 35% of the fund.
SPSB: Investment-grade US corporate bonds that mature in one to three years. It's a low-risk choice for income that pays more than Treasuries, and because the bonds mature soon, its price moves very little when interest rates change.
SPSK: Investment grade sukuk, which are bond like certificates structured to follow Islamic law, issued in US dollars around the world. It's for steady income that fits Sharia principles, and its price drops when interest rates rise like ordinary bonds.
SPSM: About 600 small US companies that meet profitability screens, spread across financials, technology, industrials and consumer companies at roughly an eighth to a sixth each. It's a way to add smaller-company growth to a portfolio, but it swings more than large-company funds.
SPTB: US Treasury bonds across short and medium lengths, backed by the government. It's meant for safe, steady interest income and as a cushion when stocks drop, though its price slips when interest rates rise.
SPTE: Large global technology companies that pass Shariah screens, which exclude businesses and finances that conflict with Islamic investing rules. It is very concentrated: NVIDIA, Apple and Taiwan Semiconductor are each about 11%, and Microsoft adds about 9%.
SPTI: US Treasury bonds that mature in roughly three to ten years, backed by the federal government. It's a middle-of-the-road choice for steady income and a cushion when stocks fall, though its price slips when interest rates rise.
SPTL: US Treasury bonds that mature in over ten years, backed by the federal government. It's a cushion that often rises when stocks fall, but with such long maturities its price swings sharply when interest rates change.
SPTM: The whole US stock market in one fund, from large to small companies, with technology around 40% and financials, health care and communication following. It's a core holding that moves with the overall US economy, with a bit of small company exposure.
SPTS: US Treasury bonds that mature in one to three years. It's a very safe place for money that wants some income, with small price changes when interest rates move, though it pays less than longer bonds.
SPUC: Holds an S&P 500 index fund and adds an options strategy that aims to give more of the market's gains on strong rises while also paying income. Nearly all of it is the underlying S&P 500 fund, so tech giants drive most of its movement.
SPUS: Large US companies screened to follow Islamic investing rules, with technology making up over half and health care a distant second. It fits investors who want a stock fund that avoids things like banks and alcohol, and its heavy tech weighting makes it swing more.
SPUT: An actively managed income fund that sells put options on a broad US stock index to collect payments, alongside holding stocks. It aims for steady income while still keeping some growth, though selling puts means it can lose money in sharp market drops.
SPVM: 100 stocks from the S&P 500 that rank high on both value (looking cheap) and momentum (recently rising). It leans toward financials, energy and utilities, with Allstate, General Motors and United Airlines each about 2%.
SPWO: Companies outside the US, in developed and emerging markets, that pass screens for following Islamic (Shariah) rules, following the S&P Shariah World ex-US index. It is top-heavy with Taiwan Semiconductor at about 20%, and technology makes up over half of it.
SPXD: The S&P 500 reweighted so sectors are more balanced and no single giant dominates. Compared with a plain S&P 500 fund, it holds less of the biggest tech names and more of areas like health care and consumer staples.
SPXE: The S&P 500 with every energy company removed, so it holds the other US large companies in similar proportions to the index. It is top heavy, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft making up about 20% of the fund.
SPXN: The S&P 500 without its financial companies such as banks and insurers, held in index proportions. Technology dominates: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 23% of the fund, so it works as a US large-company fund that skips the financial sector.
SPXP: A fund that follows an index which pairs exposure to the S&P 500 with extra investments in other assets, hence the "plus" in its name. It can use derivatives, and it is non-diversified, so it can behave differently from a plain S&P 500 fund.
SPXT: The S&P 500 without its information technology companies, so it holds the other large US companies in the index in the same proportions. With tech removed, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Tesla become the biggest holdings, and financials, communication and health care carry more weight.
SPXV: The S&P 500 with the health care companies taken out, so it holds the other large US companies in similar proportions to the index. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together make up about 22% of the fund.
SPY: America's largest companies in one fund, covering every major industry. Technology is the biggest slice at about 40%, followed by financials, health care and consumer companies, so it's built to be a core holding that moves with the overall US economy.
SPYA: A fund in the equity hedged category, meaning it generally holds stocks alongside a hedge meant to soften market drops. It is a careful middle ground between owning the stock market outright and staying out of it.
SPYC: Mostly an S&P 500 index fund, with a small side of options bought to try to gain more when stocks fall sharply. The options are meant to add a cushion in bad markets, but they cost money, so in calm or rising markets it can trail a plain S&P 500 fund.
SPYD: The 80 highest-dividend-paying stocks in the S&P 500, with real estate the biggest slice, followed by consumer staples, financials and utilities. It's for dividend income, and it has little technology, so it can trail the broad market in growth-led rallies.
SPYG: The faster-growing half of the S&P 500, where technology is more than half the fund and communication companies add about a seventh. It's meant for growth, but it's concentrated in a few industries, so it tends to fall harder than the broad market in downturns.
SPYH: S&P 500 stocks combined with an options collar: sold call options bring in income, while bought put options protect against drops. This limits both big losses and big gains, and the top holdings NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 18% of it.
SPYI: Large US companies in the S&P 500, led by technology at about 40 percent, paired with an options strategy that sells some upside in exchange for monthly income. It's aimed at income, so it trails in strong rallies and still falls when stocks drop.
SPYM: Hundreds of the largest US companies, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and health care making up much of the rest. It is a core holding for US stock exposure, and since bigger companies count for more, a few tech leaders drive much of its movement.
SPYT: Holds an S&P 500 index fund and sells daily call spreads on the index, an options strategy that earns extra income. That income is paid out as distributions, but the options limit how much the fund gains when the market jumps.
SPYV: The cheaper-looking half of the S&P 500, with technology at about a quarter, then financials, health care and industrials. It leans toward established, lower-priced companies, so it tends to hold up better than growth funds when tech stocks sell off but can lag in tech rallies.
SPYX: America's 500 largest companies with the fossil fuel producers removed, so technology is the biggest slice at about two fifths. It's a core US stock holding for people who want to skip coal, oil and gas reserve owners, so it differs slightly from the plain index.
SQBA: A fund using options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cushion a set amount of losses over a three-month period, in exchange for a cap on gains. The protection resets every quarter, and the 15 in the name refers to the buffer level.
SQBR: A fund using options on US stocks to protect against losses over a set quarterly period, as long as the market does not fall past a barrier level. In return, gains are capped, and the protection can end if the barrier is breached.
SQLT: A fund tracking US small company stocks screened for quality, meaning high profitability, steady earnings and low debt. It is spread across technology, industrials, health care and financials, with no stock above about 1%, so no single company dominates.
SQLV: Small US companies that an actively run quantitative model rates as both high quality and reasonably priced. It spreads money across many tiny positions, each around 1% or less, and trades often, so the mix changes frequently.
SQMX: Uses customized options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to follow large US stocks while protecting against a larger part of losses over a set period that resets each quarter. In return, gains are capped, and protection only fully applies if you hold the whole period.
SQS: Companies the managers see as high quality and growing, with technology the biggest slice at over two fifths, plus communication, consumer and financial companies. It's a growth leaning stock fund held in a limited number of names, so it can swing more than the broad market.
SRET: Real estate investment trusts, or REITs, that pay high dividends, picked from around the world by a Global X index. Holdings are equally spread across many names, none above about 5%, and it focuses on yield.
SRHQ: A fund of US companies with steady, moderate revenue growth that are not priced too richly, following an index built on that growth-at-a-reasonable-price idea. It spreads across many mid-sized stocks, with no holding above about 2% and the most weight in technology, health care and industrials.
SRHR: Real estate investment trusts (REITs) listed in the US, with the fund selling covered call options on them to earn extra income. That income comes at the cost of capping some of the upside, and Lamar Advertising is the largest holding at about 10%.
SRLN: Senior bank loans, which are floating-rate loans to companies with weaker credit ratings that get repaid before other debts. It's meant for income that adjusts upward when interest rates rise, so its price is steadier than regular bonds, but it can fall when the economy weakens and borrowers default.
SROI: An actively managed global stock fund that picks companies using sustainability criteria rather than following an index. It still ends up top-heavy in big tech: Alphabet, Apple, NVIDIA and Microsoft are about 18% of it.
SRVR: Real estate companies tied to data and infrastructure, such as data centers, cell towers and storage. Digital Realty, Equinix and American Tower alone are about 48% of the fund, so a few companies drive most of the result.
SSCP: An actively managed fund of small companies listed on US exchanges, including some based abroad. Its top holdings are a mix of aerospace, aluminum, food and firearms makers, each about 5% to 7%, so a few names matter a lot.
SSFI: A fund of funds that holds other bond ETFs, moving among bond types like emerging market, high yield and Treasury bonds depending on the manager's view. Its top four holdings are each about 19% of it, so it is made of only a few funds.
SSK: A fund giving exposure to the Solana cryptocurrency, held partly directly and partly through other crypto products, with staking, where coins are locked up to earn rewards. Solana is about half of it, so it moves with the price of one crypto asset.
