SSMG: An actively managed fund buying small and mid-sized US growth companies, mostly in technology, industrials and health care. It is well spread out, with the biggest holdings, such as Sterling Infrastructure and TechnipFMC, each only around 3%.
SSPY: Tracks an index of large US companies that are weighted by a mix of company fundamentals rather than by size alone, created by Syntax. It is spread very evenly, with no holding above about 1%, so it looks quite different from a standard S&P 500 fund.
SSS: About three quarters of this fund is in the S&P 500, the 500 largest US companies, and about a quarter is in Solana, a cryptocurrency, held directly and through another fund. It mixes a broad stock index with a risky crypto bet.
SSUS: A fund of sector ETFs for the S&P 500, with technology the largest at over two fifths and financials next. It's meant to be a core US stock holding that shifts toward the stronger industries, and the manager's moves can cause it to lag the market.
SSXU: An actively managed fund of funds that holds international stock ETFs, aiming to beat the MSCI ACWI ex USA Index by owning more or less of certain countries. Japan, the UK, China and South Korea ETFs are the biggest holdings.
STAX: Short-term US municipal bonds, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It is actively managed and spread across many issuers, such as cities, states and hospitals, with no single bond above about 2.5%.
STBF: An actively managed fund of short term bonds that can include both investment grade and lower rated ones. Because the bonds mature soon, it is less sensitive to interest rate changes, and it is spread widely with no holding above about 3%.
STBQ: Holds companies involved in the technology behind stablecoins, which are digital coins pegged to the dollar, tracked by a rules-based index. It also holds some crypto funds such as Chainlink, Solana and Ethereum, so it is a niche and volatile mix.
STCE: Stocks of companies tied to crypto, such as bitcoin miners and digital asset firms, tracking a Schwab index that uses language analysis of company filings to find them. It holds no cryptocurrency itself, and the top holdings like Bitdeer, Hive and Core Scientific are about 6% to 8% each.
STEN: A defined-outcome fund that holds options tied to the iShares Core S&P 500 ETF over a set period starting in September. It aims to cushion the first 10% of S&P 500 losses, in exchange for a cap on gains, and works best when held for the full period.
STHH: A single stock fund holding American depositary receipts of STMicroelectronics, the European chip maker, with a currency swap meant to hedge the euro against the dollar. It is a bet on one company's shares.
STIP: Treasury bonds whose payments rise with inflation, limited to those maturing within five years. It's meant to protect purchasing power with little price swing, and because the bonds are short, it's far less sensitive to interest rate moves than longer inflation-protected funds.
STLR: Gives exposure to XLM, the digital coin of the Stellar network, through futures contracts traded on a regulated US exchange rather than holding the coin directly. It is actively managed and tied to a single, volatile crypto asset.
STNC: An actively managed fund of US stocks selected for strong finances and sustainable business practices. It is spread widely, with no holding above about 4%, and has a mix of technology, health care and consumer companies.
STOT: Short-term bonds from the US government, mortgage-backed issuers and corporations, actively managed with room to pick any credit quality. It aims for steady income with less sensitivity to interest rates than longer bond funds, so its price moves less.
STOX: An actively managed fund that mostly holds big US stocks, plus some other ETFs, and blends in some exposure to the biggest tech names. NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet are each about 6%, and a Roundhill Magnificent Seven fund is another big slice.
STPZ: Treasury bonds with maturities of one to five years whose principal rises with inflation. It's meant to protect purchasing power with relatively modest price swings, though it still loses some value when real interest rates rise.
STRN: An actively managed fund of large US companies chosen using a trend-following approach, which favors stocks that have been rising. It holds only a small number of stocks, with Eli Lilly, Vertiv, Welltower and Howmet each near 7%, so it is fairly concentrated.
STXD: Large and mid-sized US growth companies that also have a record of paying and growing dividends, tracking a Strive index. It holds a mix of tech, financials, industrials and health care, with Eli Lilly, Broadcom, JPMorgan and Microsoft each around 4% to 6%.
STXE: Large and mid-size companies from 24 emerging markets, leaving out China. It is concentrated in technology and in Asia: Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK hynix together are about 40% of the fund.
STXF: The 500 largest US companies in one fund, covering every major industry, with technology the biggest slice at about two fifths. It's built to be a core holding that moves with the overall US economy.
STXG: A fund of large US growth stocks from the Strive 1000 index, which covers the biggest 1,000 US companies. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 23% of it, and technology is nearly half.
STXK: US small-company stocks, following a Strive index of small caps. It is very widely spread, with every top holding around 0.5%, and technology, financials and industrials are the biggest areas.
STXT: An actively managed bond fund holding bonds of varying maturities, including mortgage bonds from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, Treasuries and some Strategy Inc preferred shares. It is aimed at a mix of income and price gains, and the top holdings are each only a few percent.
STXV: About 1,000 large US companies that look cheap compared with their size, such as banks, health care and energy firms, following a Strive value index. It is spread widely, with no single stock above about 3% of the fund.
STYL: An actively managed fund of consumer lifestyle brands, covering apparel, footwear, accessories, outdoor gear and specialty retail. Ferrari and Nike are each about 8% of it, and nearly all of the fund is in consumer discretionary companies.
SUB: Short-term bonds from state and local governments, with interest generally exempt from federal income tax. It's a low-risk home for cash you want to earn tax-friendly income on, and because the bonds mature soon, the price barely moves when rates change.
SUIS: A trust that holds SUI, the digital token of the Sui blockchain, and tracks its price. It also stakes the coins, meaning they are used to help run the network, which may earn extra rewards, and it carries the large price swings of crypto.
SUPP: An actively managed fund of companies that help move and make goods around the world, such as chip makers and industrial firms, in the US and abroad. Taiwan Semiconductor, NVIDIA, Carpenter Technology and Eaton are each about 6% to 8%.
SURE: An actively managed fund that picks from the 3,000 largest US companies, with a focus on company insider activity, as the name suggests. It leans toward technology at about a quarter of the fund, and positions are small, with the biggest around 2% each.
SURI: An actively managed fund that puts its money into a small number of biotech, pharmaceutical and healthcare companies, plus some energy holdings. It is concentrated in a few names, and it also uses Treasury bills and other instruments alongside the stocks.
SUSA: Large US companies tilted toward stronger environmental, social and governance scores, with technology about 43%. It's a core holding for investors who care about ESG, built to stay close to the broad US market while leaving out or underweighting some companies.
SUSB: Investment-grade corporate bonds from US companies, maturing in one to five years, with a tilt toward firms that score better on environmental and social measures. It's meant for steady income with smaller price swings than longer bonds, though prices still drop when rates rise.
SUSC: Investment-grade corporate bonds from US companies, screened to favor those with better environmental, social and governance records. It's meant for steady interest income with less risk than stocks, though its price falls when interest rates rise and it can slip when the economy weakens.
SUSL: Large US companies chosen for stronger environmental, social and governance records, with technology at about two fifths of the fund. It's meant as a core stock holding for people who want to screen out some laggards, and it is heavier in tech than a typical broad fund.
SVAL: A fund tracking the Russell 2000 Focused Value Select Index, which picks cheaper small US companies and weights them equally. Because of equal weighting, no holding is above about 1%, so it is spread evenly across many small firms.
SVOL: Mostly short-term Treasuries as collateral, combined with a strategy that sells insurance against stock market volatility to earn income. It pays well when markets are calm but can lose heavily, and fast, when markets drop sharply.
SVTN: US Treasury bonds with between seven and ten years left until they mature, following a FTSE index. It sits in the middle of the bond maturity range, so its price moves moderately when interest rates change.
SWAN: A fund that mostly holds US Treasury securities, with a smaller part in long-dated call options on the S&P 500 for stock market gains. The Treasuries aim to protect the money while the options give some upside.
SWP: An actively managed fund of US income-paying stocks that also show strong growth traits, picked by the adviser. It tilts toward technology, with Microsoft, Broadcom, Apple and Oracle each about 4 to 6%.
SXQG: An actively managed fund of large US companies that the manager sees as high quality and growing. It leans toward tech and health care: Alphabet, Apple, NVIDIA and Microsoft are about 23% of the fund.
SYFI: Mostly bonds from companies with weaker credit ratings (often called junk bonds), limited to shorter maturities. It aims to pay higher income than safer bonds, and the short maturities mean it should react less to interest rate moves, though it can still fall when the economy sours and defaults rise.
SYLD: US mid-sized companies that return cash to shareholders through dividends and buybacks, spread across financials, consumer companies, energy and industrials. It's a value-style holding meant for steady returns, and it holds more cyclical businesses than the broad market.
SYSB: A rules-based mix of Treasuries, mortgage bonds, and investment-grade and high-yield corporate bonds, shifted among them as conditions change. It's meant as a core bond holding with a bit more income, though the riskier corporate bonds can fall when the economy weakens.
SYZ: An actively managed fund of small US companies chosen by Lazard using a systematic, rules-based process. It is very spread out, with no holding above 1%, which is much less top-heavy than most funds.
TABD: An actively managed fund of US investment-grade and some lower-rated bonds, including mortgage-backed securities, aiming for income plus some price growth. A manager picks the bonds rather than following an index, and no single holding is more than about 3% of it.
TACK: An actively managed fund that holds sector ETFs, such as energy, health care, materials and consumer staples, and shifts between them based on a model of which sectors are doing best. It can also move into bonds when markets look weak, so its mix changes over time.
TACN: An actively managed fund of large companies from developed countries outside the US, such as ASML, HSBC, AstraZeneca and Roche. It is widely spread, with no holding above about 3%, and the manager picks stocks rather than copying an index.
TACU: An actively managed fund of US stocks that mixes research with computer models, aiming to beat the broad US market. It resembles the market, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft about 17% of it and technology near 40%.
TAFI: Mostly short-term municipal bonds, which are loans to local governments, with a small amount of taxable bonds and cash. It aims for tax-friendly income with little price movement, though short bonds usually pay less than longer ones, and it's actively managed.
TAFL: A national mix of long-term municipal bonds from US states, cities and public agencies, with interest that is mostly exempt from federal income tax. It is actively managed with an eye on taxes, and holds many bonds, none above about 3%.
TAFM: Mostly municipal bonds issued by US states and cities, with interest that's generally exempt from federal income tax, plus some taxable bonds. It's for tax-aware income from medium-term bonds, mainly useful for people in higher tax brackets, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
TAGG: A mix of US government, mortgage-backed and corporate bonds that are mostly investment grade. A manager tries to beat the standard bond market using research on the bonds, and it works as a core income holding and cushion for stocks, though prices drop when rates rise.
TAGS: Holds four Teucrium funds, each tracking futures contracts on one crop: soybeans, sugar, wheat and corn, in roughly equal amounts. It follows farm commodity prices rather than company stocks, and futures can behave differently from the day to day price of the crops themselves.
TAIL: A hedging fund that holds mostly US Treasuries and buys put options on the S&P 500, which pay off when the stock market falls sharply. Over time it tends to lose a little in calm markets, since the puts cost money to hold.
TALV: An actively managed fund of large US companies the managers think are undervalued. It is broadly spread across financials, tech and health care, with Amazon, JPMorgan and Apple the largest holdings at about 4% to 5% each.
TAN: Companies in the solar power business, with technology firms making solar panels and equipment about 60 percent and utilities and power producers about a third. It's a focused bet on one clean energy industry, so it swings far more than the broad market and can drop hard when interest rates rise.
TAOZ: US companies the managers think are priced below their worth, led by technology and financials, then communication and consumer companies. It's a core stock holding with a value tilt, and the managers pick stocks themselves, so results can differ from a plain index.
TAPR: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to protect against a set amount of losses over a two-year period ending in April 2027. In exchange, it gives up some gains, and the protection only applies if you hold through the whole period.
TAX: An actively managed fund of US mid and large companies that picks value stocks with lower dividends, to keep taxable income down. It is spread across many holdings, none above about 2%, and leans toward health care, technology and industrials.
TAXE: An actively managed fund of investment-grade municipal bonds, issued by US states, cities and agencies, with income that is generally free from federal income tax. It holds many bonds with intermediate maturities, and each is roughly 2% or less of the fund.
TAXF: A varied mix of US municipal bonds, mostly investment-grade, with interest generally free of federal income tax. It's meant for tax-aware income with medium maturities, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
TAXI: Investment-grade municipal bonds from across the US with maturities under 15 years, following an ICE index. The interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and the fund is very spread out, with each bond only about 0.2% of the total.
TAXM: A fund of investment-grade bonds chosen to give Massachusetts residents income that is generally free of federal and state income tax. It is actively managed, so it picks bonds rather than following an index, and almost all of it is in bonds.
TAXS: Short-term bonds issued by US states and local governments, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It follows an ICE index of investment-grade municipal bonds maturing in under five years, spread across hundreds of issuers.
TAXT: Investment-grade municipal bonds, issued by US states and local governments, following an ICE index. The interest is generally free of federal income tax, and the fund is very spread out, with no single bond above about 1%.
TAXX: An actively managed fund of short-term municipal and taxable bonds, aiming to produce income that is mostly tax-aware while keeping interest rate sensitivity low. It holds many bonds from different issuers, each around 1% or 2%, such as transit, gas and housing authorities.
TBFC: An actively managed fund of other ETFs, mixing stocks and bonds across the world. It shifts the blend using two in-house strategies and leans toward bonds, with top holdings being Vanguard, Xtrackers and iShares bond funds, which fits its conservative label.
TBFG: An actively managed fund of funds that spreads money across other ETFs holding US and global stocks and some bonds. It adjusts the mix over time, and the largest holdings are broad S&P 500 and growth funds, each under about 12% of the total.
TBG: An actively managed fund of US companies that its manager thinks can raise their dividends over time, across small, mid and large sizes. It is fairly spread out, with Blackstone, Merck, Verizon and Chevron each around 4%, and leans toward value stocks.
TBIL: Ultra-short US Treasury bills that mature in about three months, which makes it essentially a cash parking spot. It's meant for safety and income that follows short-term interest rates, with almost no price swings, though its income falls if rates drop.
TBJL: Uses options on a long-term US Treasury bond ETF to cushion part of its losses over a one-year period starting in July, while capping gains. The protection works only if the fund is held for the full period, and long-term bonds can swing a lot.
TBLL: Very short-term US Treasury bills that mature within a year, split between bonds and cash-like holdings. It's a place to park money safely while still earning interest, and since the bills mature so quickly, its price barely moves when interest rates change.
TBLU: Stocks of water companies in developed countries, including utilities, pipe and equipment makers and water treatment firms, following a rules-based index. Veolia, Ferguson, Ecolab and American Water Works are each about 7% to 8% of the fund.
TBX: A fund that aims to move opposite to 7 to 10 year US Treasury bonds each day, so it tends to gain when those bonds fall in price. It resets daily, which means over longer periods its results can drift away from simply the reverse of the bonds.
TCAF: Large US companies picked by a manager who looks for steady growth at reasonable prices, with technology over a third and health care about a sixth. It's a core growth holding, and because it's actively managed, it can behave quite differently from the broad market.
TCAI: An actively managed fund of companies building the equipment behind artificial intelligence, such as servers, memory, storage, networking and power. Dell, Micron, Seagate and Western Digital are about 27% combined, so it is concentrated in hardware names.
TCAL: An actively managed fund of stocks that sells covered call options, contracts that give up some upside in exchange for cash payments, to produce regular income on top of dividends. The stocks are spread out, with the biggest each near 2%.
TCAN: A fund built to hold Canton Coin, the token of the Canton Network, a blockchain used by financial institutions. Roughly half of the fund is the coin itself, and the rest is mostly cash-like holdings, so it is a concentrated bet on one crypto asset.
TCHI: Chinese technology companies across several areas, such as internet, hardware, software and e-commerce, tracked by an MSCI index. Holdings are fairly even, with Lenovo, JD.com, NetEase and Baidu each at roughly 4% to 5% of the fund.
TCHP: Large, well-established US companies with strong growth, with technology over half and communication and consumer companies next. It's built for growth, so it leans much more on tech than the broad market and tends to rise and fall harder, with managers picking the stocks.
TCPB: A broad mix of mostly investment-grade US bonds, including government, corporate and mortgage-backed bonds, with room for riskier bonds. It's meant as a core bond holding for steady income, and its price tends to fall when interest rates rise.
TCV: An actively managed fund of smaller US companies that its manager thinks are priced below their worth. It holds a spread of roughly equal-sized positions, with no stock above about 4% of the fund, across technology, consumer, industrial and health care businesses.
TDAQ: Holds a Nasdaq-100 ETF and sells call options on it to earn extra income, paid out regularly. The options cap the gains when tech stocks surge, and since it follows the Nasdaq-100, it leans heavily toward technology.
TDAX: A leveraged fund aiming for roughly 120% to 140% of the daily performance of an index tied to Nasdaq-listed stocks. It uses derivatives to get that extra exposure, so gains and losses are magnified and the results can drift over longer periods.
TDEC: A defined outcome fund that holds options on an emerging markets stock ETF over a one-year period starting each December. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses in exchange for capping gains, so it works best held for the full period.
TDEM: Bonds issued by governments and companies in emerging markets across Latin America, Asia, Europe, Africa and the Middle East, a mix of government and corporate debt. These bonds tend to pay more interest than developed market bonds but carry more risk.
TDI: Stocks from companies outside the US, led by financials and technology, followed by industrials and energy. It's a way to add international stocks to a portfolio, and the managers adjust holdings actively, so it can differ noticeably from a standard international index.
TDIV: Technology and telecom companies that pay dividends, with technology about 85% and communication about an eighth. It's for income plus tech exposure, and it leans toward established, cash-rich firms, so it can trail pure growth tech funds in strong rallies.
TDNA: An actively managed fund of biotechnology companies, the ones developing new treatments for disease. It is spread thinly across many names, with the biggest, argenx, only about 5% of the fund, and it is entirely health care.
TDOG: A trust that holds Dogecoin, the meme-born cryptocurrency, so its price follows Dogecoin directly. It is a single-coin crypto holding, so it can swing sharply and it does not produce income.
TDOT: A fund that holds Polkadot (DOT), a cryptocurrency, directly and stakes it to earn extra rewards. Its price follows the price of DOT, so it is a bet on one cryptocurrency and can swing sharply.
TDSB: An actively managed fund of funds that spreads money across stocks, bonds, real estate, currencies and commodities, aiming for limited ups and downs. Its holdings are other ETFs, such as an Nasdaq 100 fund, a gold fund and sector funds, each around 10%.
TDSC: An actively managed fund that mixes other ETFs across stocks, bonds, gold and other assets, aiming to keep losses from peak to trough near 10%, though that is only a goal. About 79% is stocks, led by Nasdaq-100, health care and energy funds.
TDTF: US government bonds whose payments rise with inflation, kept to a medium length of about five years. It's meant to protect buying power while limiting how much the price moves, though it still drops when interest rates rise faster than inflation.
TDTT: US Treasury bonds whose principal rises with inflation, kept to about three years of average sensitivity to rates. It's meant to protect buying power while keeping price swings small, though it can still lose a bit when interest rates rise.
TDV: US technology companies with long records of raising their dividends every year, tracked by the S&P Technology Dividend Aristocrats index. It is spread fairly evenly, with Qualcomm, Cisco, Texas Instruments and Skyworks each about 3 to 5%, so it avoids the usual mega-cap tech giants.
TDVG: Large US companies with a record of paying and growing dividends, with technology the biggest slice and financials, health care and industrials next. It aims for steady growth plus rising income, so it's a core holding that may lag when fast growing stocks lead.
TDVI: Dividend-paying technology companies, mostly software and chip makers, with some communication firms, plus an options strategy that gives up some gains for extra income. It's meant for income from tech, and it trails in strong rallies while still falling when tech falls.
TEC: An actively managed fund of companies the manager thinks can grow from new technologies, mostly in the tech sector but across others too. It is top-heavy: Apple, NVIDIA, Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft together make up about a third of the fund.
TECB: US technology companies working on areas like robotics, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, cloud and fintech, plus some genomics firms. Tech is about 60% and health care about an eighth, so it's a growth theme bet that swings more than the broad market.
TECY: An actively managed fund that aims to pay weekly income by selling put options on a leveraged technology ETF, which moves at three times the daily move of its index. Treasury bills back the options, and it gives up upside while carrying real downside risk.
TEK: An actively managed fund of technology companies in the US and abroad, with at least 80% of its money in that area. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Microsoft, Broadcom and Apple are about 28% of the fund, and the manager picks holdings rather than following an index.
TEKX: An actively managed fund of companies that supply the technology and power behind areas like AI and digital assets, in the US and abroad. It is concentrated in bitcoin miners and data-center companies such as Riot Platforms and CleanSpark, which swing widely in price.
TEKY: An actively managed fund of technology companies around the world that the manager sees as the next wave, such as chips and AI. It is tech heavy at about 79%, with SK Hynix, Alphabet and NVIDIA the biggest holdings.
TEMD: An actively managed fund of bonds issued by governments and companies in emerging markets, the developing economies of the world. Because these countries can be riskier borrowers, such bonds usually pay more interest than those from richer countries.
TEMR: An actively managed fund of stocks from emerging markets such as Taiwan, South Korea and China, picked using the manager's in-house research. It leans toward technology, and Taiwan Semiconductor is about 13% of it, with more through its US-listed shares.
TEMX: An actively managed fund buying growth stocks in emerging markets, but leaving out China and Hong Kong. It is concentrated in Asian chip makers: Samsung Electronics is about 14%, Taiwan Semiconductor about 10%, and SK Hynix about 8%.
TEND: Holds the iShares Core S&P 500 ETF and uses options to try to cushion a set amount of losses over a 12-month period, in exchange for limiting gains. The name points to a 10% buffer, and the protection only applies to people who hold through the full period.
TENJ: A buffer fund that tracks the S&P 500 through options and is built to absorb a set amount of losses over a 12-month period starting in June. The trade-off is a cap on gains, and the outcomes only apply to those who hold from the start of that period.
TENM: Holds options tied to the iShares Core S&P 500 ETF to cushion the first 10% of losses over a 12-month period, as the name says. The trade-off is a cap on gains, and the protection only works if you hold for the full period.
TEQI: Large US companies with a record of paying dividends that look underpriced, spread across technology, financials, health care and industrials. It's meant as a core value holding that earns income, and it tends to trail growth funds when tech-heavy stocks lead the market.
TESL: A fund built around Tesla, mixing Tesla stock with options on it and Treasury bills held as backing. Tesla is about a quarter of the fund, and the options are meant to shape its income and risk, so it is a bet on one company.
TEST: An actively managed income fund that uses options and swaps tied to Tesla stock, aiming for a targeted yearly payout of about 25%. The options limit gains when Tesla rises, and the fund keeps a lot of its money in Treasury bills as backing.
TETH: A fund that holds Ethereum directly, so its price follows the price of ether, the coin that powers the Ethereum network. It owns the coin itself rather than companies, and it pays no income.
TEXN: Companies based in Texas, following the Russell Texas Equity Index. It is heavy in energy, with Tesla, ExxonMobil and Caterpillar being the biggest holdings at about 10% each, so it is a regional bet that looks different from the broad US market.
TEXX: An actively managed fund buying stocks of companies tied to Texas, mostly in energy. Its biggest holdings are Landbridge, Permian Basin Royalty Trust and Texas Pacific Land, each around 5% to 7%, so it leans heavily on oil and gas land and royalties.
TFFI: An actively managed fund that follows price trends in bond and interest rate markets using futures, contracts on future prices that can rise or fall with the trend. It holds other bond ETFs and cash as backup, and it can go long or short.
TFGZ: An actively managed fund holding a small number of large US growth companies that the managers expect to grow fast. It is concentrated: Microsoft, Alphabet, Broadcom and Credo are together about 27% of the fund, and tech is about 40% of it.
TFI: Long-term bonds from US state and local governments, whose interest is generally free from federal income tax. It suits investors in higher tax brackets who want steady tax-friendly income, though prices fall when interest rates rise, especially for long maturities.
TFJL: A fund that uses options tied to a long-term US Treasury bond ETF to build in a floor on losses over a set one-year period. In exchange, gains are limited, and the protection only applies if held for the full period.
TFLO: Short-term US Treasury notes whose interest payments reset as rates change. It's a safe place to park cash, and since its income follows short-term rates up, its price barely drops when rates rise, though income falls when rates are cut.
TFLR: Mostly loans to companies with weaker credit ratings, where the interest rate resets as market rates change. It aims for higher income, and its price holds up better than ordinary bonds when rates rise, but it can fall if borrowers struggle to repay.
TFNS: An actively managed fund of financial companies such as banks, payments firms and insurers. Berkshire Hathaway is about 10% of it, and Visa, Mastercard, Bank of America and JPMorgan are each around 5% to 7%, so a handful of big names drive it.
TFPN: An actively managed fund that follows price trends across stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities using the Chesapeake trend-following program. It goes where prices are moving rather than holding a fixed mix, so what it owns can change a lot over time.
TGLB: An actively managed fund of stocks from developed markets around the world, with the US as its biggest part. Technology is about a third, and NVIDIA, Alphabet and Advanced Micro Devices are among the biggest holdings at roughly 4% to 5%.
TGLR: Large US companies the managers think have strong earnings and dividend growth plus an above-average dividend yield. It is actively managed with holdings like Lam Research, Goldman Sachs, American Express and Walmart each making up about 5%.
TGRT: Large US companies a manager picks for strong growth, with technology at well over half and communication companies next. It's a growth fund and an actively managed one, so it's built to rise faster in good markets and fall harder in bad ones than the broad market.
TGRW: Large US companies with fast-growing sales and profits, with technology over half and communication companies next. It's built for long-term growth, and with so much in tech it tends to swing more than the broad market.
TGRZ: An actively managed fund investing in Chinese companies that build large AI language models and related AI technology, using both stocks and derivatives. It is a narrow bet on a handful of China-based AI developers, so it can swing a lot.
THD: Thai stocks, covering large, mid-size and small companies in Thailand's stock market, following an MSCI index. It is a single-country fund with a concentrated top: Delta Electronics Thailand alone is about 20%, and energy, industrials and financials are significant.
THEQ: A mix of US stocks, picked by the manager's own research, combined with options-based hedging meant to soften losses when markets fall. Most of the money sits in a stock research fund, so the hedging may also limit some gains.
THIR: Moves between large US stock ETFs following a rules-based index, aiming to capture US large company returns while trying to avoid some losses. Right now it is essentially two holdings: an Invesco QQQ fund and an S&P 500 fund, each about half.
THLV: A fund of US sector ETFs held in roughly equal amounts, aiming for large US stock exposure with smaller swings by avoiding sectors that are trending down. When it steps away from sectors it holds cash instead, which was about 40% of the fund recently.
THMR: An actively managed fund of funds that shifts money among stocks, other ETFs, gold, bonds and cryptocurrency strategies, including some leveraged ETFs, as its sub-adviser sees fit. Its mix can change a lot over time, so it is not tied to any one index or asset type.
THMZ: An actively managed fund of established large companies around the world, picked to benefit from long-term themes such as technology change. Technology is about a third of it, and Taiwan Semiconductor and Applied Materials are the biggest holdings at roughly 6% each.
THNQ: Companies that earn a big share of revenue from artificial intelligence, with technology about three quarters of the fund. It's a focused growth bet on the AI theme, so it swings more than the broad market and can drop sharply if tech stocks fall.
THNR: A fund of global companies expected to benefit from weight loss drugs, including drug makers and related health care businesses. It is fairly concentrated: Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk together are about 18% of the fund, and everything in it is health care.
THOR: A global fund of dividend paying stocks that also sells options to earn extra income, which can limit gains. It is actively managed and spread across financials, communication, technology and health care, with no single stock above about 4%.
THRO: US stocks chosen by an active manager who rotates among themes expected to grow faster than average, with technology close to half. It's a growth holding, and the themes change over time, so it can swing more than the broad market.
THRU: An actively managed fund of companies tied to the infrastructure behind commodities, such as pipelines, storage, ports and transport. Its results lean on the energy and materials economy, so it differs from a broad stock fund.
THRV: An actively managed fund that spreads money across other bond ETFs, closed-end funds and similar holdings to produce income. About 60% is in bonds, with a good share in short-term and high yield funds, so it is more a mix of funds than individual securities.
THTA: Short-term US Treasury bills with a set of options spreads layered on top to try to earn extra income. The bills are the core holding, while the options add income but also add risk compared with a plain Treasury fund.
THY: An actively managed income fund that shifts between high yield bonds, investment grade bonds, municipal bonds, Treasuries and cash depending on the market. It may use futures or other ETFs to hedge, so its mix can change a lot over time.
THYF: Bonds from US companies with lower credit ratings, spread across financials, materials, health care and consumer firms. It pays higher interest than safer bonds, but those companies are more likely to miss payments, so it tends to fall alongside stocks in downturns.
THYM: An actively managed fund of higher-yielding municipal bonds, including lower-rated ones, whose income is exempt from federal income tax. It reaches for more income by taking more credit risk, and its largest holdings are each only about 2% of it.
THYP: Holds Hyperliquid's HYPE token directly, a cryptocurrency, and stakes it to earn additional rewards. Its price follows HYPE, which can swing sharply, and the fund holds no stocks or bonds.
TIER: An actively managed fund of stocks from outside the US, spread across developed and emerging countries, where managers pick companies one by one using their own research. Taiwan Semiconductor (shares and ADRs together), Samsung and ASML are the biggest names, and tech and financials make up about half of it.
TIH: A manager's picks of large US growth companies, with technology the biggest slice at over a third, then communication, health care and consumer businesses. It's a growth fund with only a modest number of holdings, so it can swing more than the broad market.
TIIV: An actively managed fund of stocks from outside the US, including American Depositary Receipts, shares of foreign companies that trade on US exchanges. It leans toward banks and industrial firms, and no single holding is more than about 3%, so it is spread out.
TILC: Large companies from developed countries outside the US, led by financials at about 30 percent, then industrials, technology and health care. It's a way to diversify beyond US stocks for long-term growth, and currency moves can add to its ups and downs.
TILL: An actively managed fund that holds futures contracts on farm commodities such as corn, wheat and soybeans, and is set up so investors don't get a K-1 tax form. Its price follows crop futures, not agricultural company stocks.
TILT: A broad mix of US companies of all sizes, with technology about a third and financials about a sixth. It's a core holding that leans toward smaller and cheaper companies than the broad market, so it can lag when big growth stocks lead.
TIME: An actively managed fund of large US companies, with at least 80% in US stocks and a heavy tilt toward technology. It is concentrated: Apple, Alphabet, NVIDIA and Microsoft together make up about 34% of the fund.
TINS: An actively managed fund buying large companies from developed markets outside the US. The managers choose stocks themselves rather than following an index, so its mix of countries and industries can differ from a plain international index fund.
TINY: Companies working in nanotechnology, such as tools and materials that operate at atomic scale, tracked by a rules-based index. It is global and spread across smaller holdings: no single stock is more than about 7%, and technology makes up around 70% of it.
TIP: US Treasury bonds whose principal rises with inflation, with maturities longer than one year. It's meant to protect buying power and diversify a portfolio, but its price still drops when interest rates rise faster than inflation.
TIPA: A ladder of US Treasury inflation-protected bonds that mature through 2030, so the amount they pay grows with inflation. It pays out income regularly and the bonds mostly run off by 2030, which keeps its sensitivity to interest rate changes fairly modest.
TIPB: A fund of US Treasury inflation-protected bonds, whose payments rise with inflation, laddered to mature around 2035. It pays out income regularly, and nearly all of it is US government debt.
TIPC: A ladder of US Treasury inflation-linked bonds, whose value adjusts with inflation, maturing around 2045. It is made up almost entirely of US government debt and pays out income regularly, so it is a low credit risk way to hold inflation-protected bonds.
TIPD: A ladder of US inflation-linked Treasury bonds (TIPS) that mature around 2055, so the bonds' value adjusts with inflation. It pays out income regularly, and because the maturity is so far off, its price can swing a lot when interest rates move.
TIPE: A ladder of US inflation-linked Treasury bonds (TIPS) set to mature around 2031. Their value adjusts with inflation, and the fund pays out income on a regular schedule rather than reinvesting it.
TIPF: A ladder of US inflation-linked Treasury bonds (TIPS) set to mature around 2036. Their value adjusts with inflation, and the fund pays out income on a regular schedule rather than reinvesting it.
TIPG: A ladder of inflation-protected US Treasury bonds, TIPS, timed to mature around 2046, which pay out income along the way. Because TIPS adjust with inflation, it aims to keep buying power, though prices still move with interest rates.
TIPH: A ladder of US inflation-linked Treasury bonds (TIPS) set to mature around 2056. Their value adjusts with inflation, and the fund pays out income on a regular schedule rather than reinvesting it.
TIPX: Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, US government bonds whose value rises with inflation, with maturities from one to ten years. It's meant to protect buying power and cushion a stock portfolio, though its price can still drop when real interest rates rise.
TIPZ: US Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, or TIPS, following an ICE BofA index of them. Their principal rises with inflation, so the fund is a way to hold government bonds that adjust for rising prices, with holdings spread across many Treasury issues.
TISC: An actively managed fund of small companies outside the US, mostly in developed countries such as Japan and the UK. It is spread very thinly across many stocks, with no holding above about 1%, and leans toward industrials and financials.
TIZE: An actively managed fund of securitized debt, which are bonds backed by pools of loans such as mortgages. Some are guaranteed by the US government or its agencies, and the fund aims to pay regular income.
TJAN: A two-year defined-outcome fund that uses options tied to the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to protect against a set amount of losses on the US large-company index. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, and the protection only applies if shares are held for the full period ending January 2027.
TJUL: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to cover part of the losses over a two year period ending in July 2027, in exchange for limited gains. It is designed to be held for the whole period to get that result.
TJUN: Uses options tied to an emerging markets stock fund to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts each June. In return, gains over that period are capped, and the protection only works if you hold for the full period.
TKNQ: Companies and crypto products involved in tokenization, which means putting real-world assets like stocks and bonds on blockchains. It mixes stocks with crypto funds such as Chainlink and Solana products, with financials about 80% of the stock part.
TKNS: An actively managed fund that spreads money across crypto assets, mostly by holding other crypto ETFs rather than coins directly. Bitcoin is about 41% of it, with Solana, Ethereum and Hyperliquid making up most of the rest, so it moves with the crypto market.
TKNZ: An actively managed fund that invests in a basket of crypto assets, chosen by the manager rather than by copying an index. It measures itself against a crypto index but tries to beat it, and crypto prices can move a lot in short periods.
TLA: An actively managed fund that uses contracts tied to an autocallable note on Tesla stock instead of owning the shares. An autocallable pays out income if Tesla stays above a set level, but it can end early or lose money if the stock falls sharply.
TLCE: An actively managed fund of large US companies chosen by Thrivent's managers. Instead of copying an index, the managers pick stocks they like, so it can differ quite a bit from a plain large-company index fund.
TLCI: A concentrated fund of 25 to 40 large non-US companies, selected by managers rather than an index. Taiwan Semiconductor, Safran, InterContinental Hotels and ASML are each around 4% to 6%, and it spreads across industrials, consumer staples and tech.
TLDR: A ladder of short-term US Treasury bills with staggered maturities, aiming to earn income while keeping the money safe and easy to get out. Since the bills are so short, the price barely moves and income follows short-term interest rates.
TLG: An actively managed fund of large US growth stocks, run by Touchstone. It is heavy in technology, with NVIDIA, Alphabet, Broadcom and Amazon together making up about 39% of the fund.
TLH: US Treasury bonds that mature in 10 to 20 years, backed by the federal government. It's a safe-credit cushion for stock portfolios in downturns, but its price drops noticeably when interest rates rise.
TLIE: An actively managed fund of US dividend-paying large companies, chosen for income. It is spread across technology, financials, industrials and health care, with Apple the largest holding at about 6% and most others around 4% to 5%.
TLT: US Treasury bonds that won't be repaid for more than twenty years. It can jump when stocks fall and is used as a cushion, but it drops sharply when interest rates rise because the bonds are so long.
TLTD: Stocks from developed countries outside the US, led by financials and industrials, tilted toward smaller and cheaper companies. It's a way to add international diversification, and the value tilt means it can trail when growth stocks lead.
TLTE: Stocks from emerging markets, such as Taiwan, South Korea, China and India, tilted toward smaller and cheaper companies than a standard index would favor. Chip makers lead: Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK Hynix are about 17% of it.
TLTI: Holds US Treasury bonds maturing in 20 years or more and sells S&P 500 put options to earn extra income. That extra income comes with added risk, and long-term bonds can swing a lot in price when interest rates change.
TLTP: Owns long-term US Treasury bonds, mainly through the iShares 20+ Year Treasury fund, and sells call options on it each week to generate extra income. Those options cap some of the gains if bond prices rise.
TLTW: Long-term US Treasury bonds, with a call options strategy layered on top that gives up some price gains in exchange for extra monthly income. It's meant for income from long bonds, but it still drops when interest rates rise and trails if bond prices jump.
TLTX: An actively managed Treasury fund that holds long-term government bonds and sells options on them to boost income. Those options cap some of the gains if bond prices rise, and long bonds can fall in value when interest rates climb.
TMAR: A defined outcome fund that holds options on an emerging markets stock ETF over a one-year period starting each March. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses in exchange for capping gains, so it works best held for the full period.
TMAT: An actively managed fund of global small and mid-sized companies tied to themes like cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and other new technology. The manager rotates between themes over time, and the top holdings include Palo Alto Networks, Micron and CrowdStrike at about 3 to 5% each.
TMB: An actively managed bond fund that can buy almost any kind of debt, at any quality and maturity, including Treasuries, corporate and mortgage-backed bonds. The manager has wide freedom, and the fund pays out income regularly, with Treasuries among its largest holdings.
TMDV: About 100 US companies from the Russell 3000 that have raised their dividends every year for at least 35 years, tilted toward mid-sized firms. It is spread out, with no holding above roughly 2% of the fund, and leans toward consumer staples, industrials, financials and utilities.
TMED: An actively managed fund of health care companies such as drugmakers, insurers and medical tool makers. Eli Lilly alone is about 17% of it, and with UnitedHealth the top two holdings are over a fifth of the fund.
TMFC: About 100 large US growth companies picked by the Motley Fool using its own rules, with technology nearly half and communication and financials next. It's built for growth, so it leans heavily on tech and tends to swing more than the broad market.
TMFE: About 100 large US companies picked by a Motley Fool index that scores how well each uses its money, and that the Motley Fool has recommended. Alphabet, Lam Research, Amazon and Apple are each around 5 or 6% of it.
TMFG: An actively managed fund holding a focused group of high quality growth companies from the US and around the world, with at least 30% to 40% kept outside the US. Alphabet and Amazon are the two biggest holdings, at roughly 8% and 7% of the fund.
TMFM: An actively managed fund of a few dozen US mid-sized companies that the managers consider high quality and still growing. It is fairly concentrated: StoneX, DexCom and HealthEquity are the largest holdings, and technology and health care together are over half of it.
TMFS: An actively managed fund of US small company stocks that the Motley Fool team picks as high quality businesses with room to grow. It holds a focused list, with its top four holdings making up about 19% of the fund.
TMFX: An index of US mid and small sized companies recommended by Motley Fool analysts and newsletters, held in a rules based mix. It is spread widely, with no single stock above about 3%, and leans toward technology, health care and industrials.
TMGN: An actively managed fund tracking ten big growth stocks like Palantir, AMD and Meta, and it sells covered call options to pay daily income. Those options cap some of the upside, and a few holdings are each around 16% of the fund, so it is very concentrated.
TMH: Holds Toyota Motor shares through its US-listed ADRs and uses a currency contract to offset swings between the US dollar and the Japanese yen. That makes it a single-stock bet on Toyota, with the yen's moves largely hedged away.
TMID: An actively managed fund of mid-sized US companies chosen using the manager's in-house research. It is widely spread across technology, industrials, health care and financials, with no holding above about 1.5%.
TMLP: Companies organized as master limited partnerships, which run energy pipelines and storage, tracked through total return swaps (contracts that pay the index's return) rather than owning shares directly. It is a narrow bet on energy infrastructure.
TMNL: Long term municipal bonds, which are loans to US state and local governments whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It is spread across many issuers such as New York City water and tax revenue agencies, toll roads and universities, with none above about 5%.
TMNS: Short-term municipal bonds, which are loans to US state and local governments, airports and housing agencies, with income generally exempt from federal income tax. It is actively managed and widely spread, with no bond above about 3%.
TMSF: An actively managed bond fund spreading across several sectors, such as corporate bonds, floating-rate loans, mortgage-backed securities and government debt, to pursue income. Mixing sectors is meant to diversify, and no single holding is more than about 4%.
TMSL: Small and mid-sized US companies spread fairly evenly across technology, health care, industrials and financials. It's an actively managed growth holding for the middle of the market, and it swings more than large company funds.
TMVE: An actively managed fund of mid-sized US companies that look undervalued. It spreads across industrials, financials, technology and consumer companies, including regional banks like M&T and US Bancorp, with no holding above about 3%.
TMYY: A fund that uses options on a leveraged ETF tied to the total US stock market to produce income. Because of the leverage and options, its results can differ a lot from the market itself, and most of what it holds is Treasury bills used as backing.
TNGY: Nearly all energy companies, mostly oil, gas and pipeline businesses, with a small slice of utilities. It's a focused bet on the energy sector, so it swings more than the broad market and moves closely with oil and gas prices.
TNTW: US Treasury bonds with between ten and twenty years left until they mature, following a FTSE index. They pay more than short bonds but move more when interest rates change, and the government stands behind them.
TNUK: Companies tied to the nuclear industry, such as uranium miners, reactor parts makers and plant builders, including Cameco, BWX Technologies and Doosan Enerbility. About half is in industrials, and the top five holdings are roughly 8% each or less.
TNXT: An actively managed fund of companies that lead in innovation, with large holdings in technology and health care. NVIDIA is about 7% and Apple about 5%, and it is spread across many names, so no single stock dominates.
TOAK: An actively managed fund that uses stock options, mainly bought calls, puts and spreads, to aim for steady returns while keeping a short time horizon of under a year. The options are structured so each one can lose no more than what was paid for it.
TOAO: An actively managed mix of stocks and other funds, with a heavy tilt toward large technology and growth companies. Its top eight holdings, including Amazon, CrowdStrike, Broadcom and NVIDIA, are about half of the fund, so it is fairly concentrated.
TOCT: An actively managed fund using options tied to the S&P 500 over a two year period ending in October 2027. It aims to protect against a set amount of losses in exchange for a cap on gains, and the protection only fully applies if held for the full period.
TOGA: An actively managed fund of growth companies from around the world, picked by Tremblant Capital. It is global but fairly spread out, with no holding above about 6%, and it leans toward technology, consumer and communication companies.
TOK: Large and mid-sized companies from developed countries outside Canada, tracking the MSCI Kokusai Index, which is mostly US stocks. It is top-heavy in tech: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft make up about 15% of the fund.
TOLL: US and foreign stocks of companies in markets dominated by just a few players, picked by how concentrated their industry is. It leans toward technology, financials and industrials, with names like Lam Research, General Electric and Visa among its biggest holdings.
TOLZ: A fund of infrastructure companies around the world, such as pipelines, power grids and toll roads, tracking the Dow Jones Brookfield Global Infrastructure index. Utilities and energy firms are about 80% of it, with Enbridge and National Grid among the top holdings.
TOPC: Tracks the S&P 500 3% Capped Index, which holds the same companies as the S&P 500 but limits any one stock to about 3%. That keeps NVIDIA, Apple, Amazon and Broadcom near 3% each instead of letting them grow larger.
TOPT: Only the 20 largest US companies, with technology over half, so the fund is far more concentrated than the full S&P 500. It's a core-style holding that gives big-company exposure, but when a few giants stumble, it falls harder.
TOPW: A fund that owns single-stock WeeklyPay ETFs from Roundhill, each tied to a big US company such as NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon. Those underlying funds aim to pay income weekly, so this is a payout-focused way to hold a basket of the largest US stocks.
TORK: Holds companies that make actuators, the motors and parts that make robots and machines move. It is concentrated in Asia: Harmonic Drive Systems in China and Japan, plus Hyundai Mobis, together make up about 30% of the fund.
TOS: An actively managed fund mixing US and foreign stocks with other funds, aiming for total return. It is very concentrated: ASML, Coherent and NVIDIA are each about 10% of it, and technology makes up more than half.
TOT: An actively managed fund that mostly holds a broad US stock market ETF, so it behaves much like the overall US market. It is run to cut down on taxable payouts, and nearly all of it sits in that single underlying fund.
TOTL: An actively managed mix of bonds of all kinds, including government, mortgage-backed and corporate debt, with no limit on credit quality. It's a core bond holding that aims to beat the broad bond market, but the manager's choices mean it can differ a lot from it.
TOTR: A manager-picked mix of US government bonds, corporate bonds, mortgage-backed securities and other debt. It aims for steady income and total return as a core bond holding, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
TOUS: Companies from developed countries outside the US, led by financials at about a quarter, with industrials, technology and health care behind. It's an actively managed way to add international diversification, so a manager's picks, not just the index, decide how it differs from the market.
TOV: A fund tracking the 500 largest US companies, but adjusted to line up with Jewish values, as defined by its issuer, JLens. Top holdings are NVIDIA, Apple, Alphabet and Microsoft, about 25% together, so it looks a lot like a regular large-company index fund.
TOXR: A fund that holds XRP, a cryptocurrency, directly and tracks its price, valued each day as of 4 p.m. Eastern; it has no stocks or bonds inside, so it moves with the price of XRP, which can swing widely.
TPAY: A fund built around the S&P 500 that aims to pay out a steady set distribution, drawn from a target of about 10% a year. Payouts can include a return of your own money, and the fund's value can still rise and fall with the stock market.
TPFC: Large US companies picked for strong free cash flow, which is the cash left after running and investing in the business, using a rules-based index. It holds a mix of sectors, and no single stock is above about 5%.
TPFG: US growth companies picked by a rules-based index that favors firms producing strong free cash flow, meaning cash left after running and investing in the business. It is led by technology and industrials, with holdings like Newmont, Palo Alto Networks and ServiceNow at about 4% to 5% each.
TPFI: An actively managed bond fund that can hold government bonds, company bonds and other debt, aiming for medium-term bonds with some extra yield. The manager picks the mix, so it differs from a fund that simply follows a bond index.
TPHD: Large US companies with high dividends, picked and weighted by a volatility-based index from Victory Capital so calmer stocks count more. It leans toward utilities such as Alliant Energy, Evergy and WEC, each about 2% of it.
TPIF: International stocks from developed markets, picked and weighted by a volatility-based index so that steadier companies get more weight. It also screens out companies that conflict with Christian values, and no single holding is above about 1%.
TPLC: US large and mid-sized stocks picked and weighted by a rules-based index that tries to dampen volatility, the size of price swings. It is screened to follow Timothy Plan's faith-based values, and holdings are spread thin, with the top ones such as utilities near 1%.
TPLS: An actively managed bond fund that mainly holds US investment-grade bonds such as Treasuries, mortgage-backed and corporate debt, with room for some riskier bonds too. It aims for steady income plus a little extra return than a plain core bond fund, and can use lower-quality bonds to get it.
TPRY: An actively managed fund holding about 25 to 30 large US and global stocks, mostly in technology, and using derivatives to pay out a steady, targeted distribution. It is top-heavy: Micron and Amazon alone are about 25% of the fund.
TPSC: About a few hundred small US companies chosen and weighted using a volatility-based index from Victory Capital, so calmer stocks get bigger positions. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 1% and a mix of utilities, financials and industrials.
TPUT: An actively managed fund that uses options to try to profit from market swings, while holding Treasury securities and cash as collateral. The Treasury bills are there as backing, not the main goal, and the options strategy is what shapes how the fund behaves.
TPYP: Companies that own pipelines carrying oil and natural gas across North America, nearly all energy with a small slice of utilities. It's meant for income from steady fee-based businesses, and it's a focused bet on one industry, so it moves with energy markets and interest rates.
TPZ: Companies that build and run the power systems behind electrification, mainly pipeline and energy operators plus electric utilities. It is actively managed and concentrated, with the top four holdings, Energy Transfer, Entergy, Targa and Clearway, making up about a quarter of it.
TQQY: An actively managed fund that earns income by selling options linked to a leveraged Nasdaq 100 ETF, backed mostly by Treasury bills. The options generate high income but limit gains if the underlying ETF rises, and it can lose a lot if that ETF falls.
TRBF: An actively managed bond fund focused on mortgage-related debt, including home loans and commercial mortgage bonds, plus bonds backed by loans. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac securities are among its top holdings, and no single holding is more than about 3%.
TRFK: Companies behind data and digital infrastructure, almost all technology, with chip makers, networking and security firms leading. It's a focused bet on the tech build-out, so it swings more than the broad market and does best when tech spending is strong.
TRFM: A fund that tracks an index of companies seen as using transformative technology, such as AI, cloud and automation, across tech, industrials and utilities. It holds many stocks in small slices, with no company above about 1%, so no single name drives it.
TRIL: An actively managed fund aimed at assets valued at over a trillion dollars, which can include giant companies and other major assets. It may use options or swaps for indirect exposure, so it is a narrow bet on a small group of giants.
TRIO: An actively managed fund that uses options tied to ETFs holding US large company, small company and international stocks, aiming for a defined outcome that cushions part of the losses. Most of it is options on the S&P 500 through SPY.
TRND: A fund of other Pacer Trendpilot funds, split roughly evenly across US large caps, US mid caps, international stocks and US bonds. Each underlying fund uses a trend rule that can shift from stocks into Treasury bills when markets weaken, so the mix changes over time.
TROT: Moves between shorter and longer-term US Treasury bonds following an MSCI index rule that picks the maturity range. It aims to hold the part of the Treasury curve favored at the time, so its sensitivity to interest rates changes over time.
TRPA: An actively managed fund of AAA-rated collateralized loan obligations, bundles of corporate loans where the top-rated slice gets paid first. It holds many different CLOs, with none above about 3%, and its income floats with interest rates.
TRSY: Holds US Treasury bills and notes with one year or less left until they mature, tracking an index of those short-dated securities. Because the maturities are so short, the price barely moves, and the income closely follows short-term interest rates.
TRTY: An actively managed fund that mostly holds other Cambria ETFs, spread across global stocks, bonds and other assets, to give a mix of value-focused investments. Its fund-of-funds design means its holdings and risk depend on which underlying funds the manager chooses to hold.
TRUC: An actively managed fund of communication services companies, such as Alphabet, Meta and Netflix, a limited number of which dominate it. Alphabet and Meta alone make up around 40% of the fund.
TRUD: An actively managed fund of consumer discretionary companies, the businesses people buy when they choose to, like online retail, cars and home improvement. It is concentrated: Amazon and Tesla are about 32% of it, plus a large holding in another sector fund.
TRUF: An actively managed fund of US financial companies, about 60% of it held through the Financial Select Sector fund. The rest includes Berkshire Hathaway, JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard, so it is mostly big banks, insurers and payment firms.
TRUH: An actively managed fund of US health care companies. It is top heavy, with Eli Lilly, Johnson & Johnson, AbbVie, UnitedHealth and Merck together making up about half of it.
TRUI: An actively managed fund of industrial companies such as machinery, aerospace, defense and rail. Caterpillar is about 8% of it, with GE, GE Vernova and RTX next, so it leans on a handful of big names.
TRUM: An actively managed fund of US-focused materials companies, such as chemicals, gold and copper miners, paints and construction materials. Linde is about 18% of it, and a State Street materials sector ETF adds about 15% more.
TRUN: An actively managed fund of US energy companies, mainly oil and gas producers and refiners. It is concentrated at the top: ExxonMobil and Chevron are about 38% together, and a State Street energy sector ETF adds about another 23%.
TRUO: An actively managed fund of US consumer staples companies, which sell everyday necessities. About 40% is held through the Consumer Staples Select Sector fund, with Walmart, Costco, Procter & Gamble and Coca-Cola among the biggest holdings.
TRUR: An actively managed fund that invests mainly in real estate companies, such as real estate investment trusts that own and rent out properties. It aims to cover the US property sector, with the manager choosing which companies to hold.
TRUT: An actively managed technology fund that holds mostly big US tech stocks, with a large part held through a Technology Select Sector SPDR fund. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 35% of it, so it is very top-heavy.
TRUU: An actively managed fund of utility companies, the businesses that supply electricity, gas and water. NextEra Energy is about 13% of it, and the top eight holdings together are roughly half the fund.
TRXS: A fund that holds TRX, the cryptocurrency of the Tron network, and earns extra from staking, which means helping validate transactions in return for rewards. Its value follows the price of TRX, which can swing sharply.
TSCM: An actively managed fund of mid-sized US growth companies that the manager considers high quality, with steady earnings and solid finances. Technology is about a third of it, and the top holdings, including ServiceTitan, Samsara and Dynatrace, are each around 4%.
TSCV: An actively managed fund of smaller US companies that the managers think are undervalued. It leans toward regional banks and industrials, and the largest holdings, like UMB Financial and Valley National, are each only about 2% to 3%.
TSCZ: An actively managed bond fund that mostly holds securitized debt, meaning bonds backed by pools of loans such as home mortgages, commercial property loans and corporate loans bundled into CLOs. It aims to earn income by spreading across several kinds of these loan-backed bonds.
TSEC: An actively managed fund of securitized bonds, which are bonds backed by pools of loans such as mortgages, consumer loans and business receivables. It is spread out, with no single holding above about 3% of the fund.
TSEE: An actively managed fund of small US companies, defined as ones no bigger than the largest in the Russell 2000 index. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 2%, and leans toward health care, financials and industrials.
TSEL: An actively managed fund of about 30 large US growth companies from Sands Capital, bought with a long term view. It is top heavy, with NVIDIA at about 11% and Seagate, Micron and Alphabet each at roughly 6% to 8%.
TSEP: A defined outcome fund that holds options on an emerging markets stock ETF, aiming to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts each September. In exchange, gains are capped, so it works best when held for the full period.
TSES: US energy companies, including oil and gas producers and power-related firms, selected by an index built around American energy security. ExxonMobil and Chevron are each around 8% of the fund, and it also holds utilities and industrials.
TSIB: Aims to pay high income from Tesla by combining swaps and options on the stock, rather than just owning shares. Because it sells upside through options, it will not fully share in big Tesla gains.
TSIC: Tracks an index of leading US-listed companies seen as defining American life, such as Costco, Coca-Cola, Home Depot, Netflix and Walmart. It leans heavily toward consumer staples and consumer discretionary, and the top holdings are each only about 6% to 7%.
TSIE: A bond fund holding securitized debt, meaning loans such as mortgages and car loans that are bundled together and sold as bonds. It is a diversified mix of those bonds from a single manager, aimed at earning income.
TSII: An actively managed fund built around Tesla stock that uses options and other contracts to generate income while keeping exposure to Tesla's price. It is concentrated in a single company, so its ups and downs follow Tesla, and its Treasury bills are mainly collateral.
TSLP: An actively managed income fund tied to Tesla stock that uses options to pay out regularly. Selling options limits how much of Tesla's rise it can share in, and the Treasury bills listed are mostly collateral for the strategy.
TSLW: A fund tied to a single stock, Tesla, that aims to pay income weekly. It gets its exposure through derivatives backed mostly by Treasury bills, so it follows Tesla's moves but is not simply a holding of the shares.
TSLY: A fund built around one stock, Tesla, using options so it earns income, with the rest kept in Treasury bills. It pays high income, but it gives up much of Tesla's big gains while still sharing the losses, so it can be very risky.
TSME: Small and mid-sized US companies, with industrials and technology each about a quarter, then consumer businesses and health care. It's a growth-oriented way to add smaller companies to a portfolio, and it tends to swing more than large-company funds.
TSMY: An options income fund tied to Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM), the big chip maker. It uses options to collect income from the stock's moves, which limits how much of TSM's gains it can capture, and the Treasury bills it holds are mostly backing for those options.
TSNF: US-listed companies in areas like technology, health care and industrials that the Truth Social index considers part of America's next frontiers. It holds many stocks in small amounts, with none above about 1.5%, so it is spread out rather than top-heavy.
TSOL: A trust that holds Solana (SOL), a cryptocurrency, directly and tracks its price. Its value moves with the price of SOL, which can swing sharply, and it holds no stocks or bonds.
TSPA: Large US companies in a mix built to resemble the S&P 500, with technology about 40% and financials, communication and health care next. It's a core holding, but the managers' research-driven picks mean it can lead or lag the plain index.
TSPX: An actively managed fund that holds mostly a Vanguard S&P 500 index fund, about 78%, plus short-term bond funds, and adjusts the mix over time. It acts like a US large-company stock fund with a cushion of short-term bonds.
TSPY: Holds a large position in an S&P 500 index fund plus options trades meant to keep some of the market's growth while paying regular income. The options strategy limits some upside in strong markets, so it can trail the plain index.
TSRS: Holds real estate investment trusts, companies that own and rent out property, chosen by an index focused on companies tied to US states that lean Republican. Top holdings like Broadstone Net Lease, Four Corners, VICI and NNN REIT are about 7% each.
TSSD: A fund tracking an index of US-listed companies that earn much of their revenue supporting national security and defense, mixing cybersecurity and software firms with defense contractors. It is concentrated: Palantir, Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike are each roughly 10% of it.
TSUI: A fund that holds the SUI cryptocurrency directly and stakes it, meaning the coins are used to help run the network in exchange for extra rewards. Its value follows the price of SUI, which can swing a lot, and it holds no stocks or bonds.
TSYW: Aims to pay out weekly income tied to a Treasury bond ETF, using swaps (contracts that pay that ETF's returns) and shares of the ETF itself. Treasury bills listed in the holdings are mostly backing for those contracts, so the fund follows long-term Treasury bonds.
TSYX: A leveraged fund targeting about 120% to 140% of the daily price moves of TSPY, another TappAlpha fund. Because it resets every day, results over longer periods can drift away from that multiple, so it is meant for short term use.
TSYY: Aims to pay high income by selling options linked to Tesla stock, with most of the fund held in Treasury bills as backing. Its gains from Tesla are capped while big losses remain possible, and the payouts can change a lot.
TTEQ: Technology and tech-enabled companies, with technology nearly four fifths of the fund and communication next. It's a focused growth bet on the tech industry, and the managers choose the stocks, so it swings more than the broad market.
TTOP: Tracks an index of the ten largest cryptocurrencies by market value, holding them mostly through other crypto ETFs. Bitcoin is about 63% of it and Ethereum around 12%, so it is dominated by bitcoin and swings in price a lot.
TTTT: US Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, or TIPS, government bonds whose value adjusts with inflation, following a FTSE index. It is meant to hold its buying power when prices rise, though its price still moves with interest rates, and it is non-diversified.
TUA: Gets exposure to short-term US Treasury interest rates mainly through Treasury futures and options, with Treasury securities and cash-like holdings as backing. Because futures add borrowed-style exposure, its price can swing with interest rate moves more than the plain Treasuries it holds would suggest.
TUG: An actively managed fund that shifts between stocks tracking the Nasdaq-100, long-term Treasuries and other holdings depending on market signals. It is heavy in technology, with NVIDIA, Apple and Micron about 22% of the fund.
TUR: Tracks an MSCI index of large and mid sized Turkish companies, so it is a bet on one country's economy. Defense firm Aselsan and retailer BIM are about 22% of it, and returns also depend on the Turkish lira.
TURF: An actively managed fund buying companies that dig, drill or grow raw materials, such as oil producers, miners and fertilizer or crop firms. About half is materials and a third is energy, with Corteva, ExxonMobil and BHP among the biggest holdings.
TVAL: US stocks the manager sees as undervalued, led by technology and financials, with health care and consumer companies behind. It's a value-style core stock holding with a manager's judgment on top, and it can trail when growth stocks lead the market.
TWOX: Holds options linked to the iShares Core S&P 500 ETF that aim to give accelerated gains, a multiple of the index's rise up to a cap, over a set period. In exchange, it takes on the full risk of losses, so the outcome depends on when you buy.
TXBC: Exposure to the ten largest cryptocurrencies other than bitcoin, following a FTSE index, mostly through other crypto exchange-traded products. Ether is about 35% and XRP and Solana make up much of the rest, so it holds crypto rather than company stocks.
TXCA: California municipal bonds of intermediate length, whose interest is generally free of federal and California income taxes. It holds many bonds from local issuers across the state, so it depends on California's credit health.
TXNY: New York municipal bonds of intermediate length, whose interest is generally free of federal, New York State and New York City income taxes. It holds many bonds from local issuers in the state, so it depends on New York's credit health.
TXS: Mid-sized companies based in Texas, tracked by an index that is spread across industries and weighted by size. Its biggest holding, CrowdStrike, is about 8%, followed by McKesson, Digital Realty and Charles Schwab at around 4% to 5% each.
TXUE: Stocks of developed-market companies outside the US, led by industrials at about a quarter, then financials, technology and utilities. It's an actively managed way to add international diversification to a portfolio, with the manager choosing holdings rather than following an index.
TXUG: An actively managed fund of growth-minded companies outside the US, chosen for rising revenues and earnings and ranging from large to small. It is fairly top-heavy in chip-related names: ASML and Taiwan Semiconductor are about 14% of it, and technology is close to 40%.
TXXI: An actively managed portfolio of intermediate-term municipal and taxable bonds, picked to deliver good income after taxes. Municipal bonds are issued by state and local governments and are often free of federal income tax, so this mixes tax-free and taxable bonds.
TYA: An actively managed fund that uses Treasury futures, contracts on future bond prices, to aim to match or beat 20+ year Treasury returns over each calendar quarter. It uses leverage, so its exposure is larger than the money invested, and it holds a fund of other Simplify holdings.
TYLD: An actively managed bond fund that follows a model, shifting between bond types and ETFs depending on market signals. At the moment most of it sits in US Treasuries and cash, so it can look very different from a typical bond fund.
TYLG: Holds the technology stocks in the S&P 500 and sells call options on part of them to earn extra income. About half sits in the Technology Select Sector SPDR fund, and the options give up some gains when tech rises sharply.
TYYY: An income fund tied to Tesla stock that uses options and derivatives rather than just owning the shares, with most of its money parked in Treasury bills. It aims to pay frequent income, and in exchange it gives up part of Tesla's upside.
UAE: Companies listed in the United Arab Emirates, tracked through an MSCI index. It is a narrow, single country fund, with banks and property developers like First Abu Dhabi Bank and Emaar making up a large share of it.
UB: US Treasury bonds of intermediate length, following a FTSE index. It is a plain government bond fund, backed by the US government, whose price moves with interest rates, and it is non-diversified.
UBEW: A fund giving leveraged-style exposure to Uber stock, using swaps (contracts that pay the stock's returns) plus some shares, with Treasury bills as backing. It aims to pay income weekly, and the results depend on how Uber stock moves.
UBIQ: A fund that tracks an index of US-listed companies in the e-commerce ecosystem, such as online retailers, payments and delivery businesses. It holds the index's companies in about the same proportions as the index, so it is a focused theme.
UBND: A broad mix of bonds, mostly investment grade, from the US government, companies and mortgage lenders, with room for some riskier debt. It's meant as a core bond holding for income, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
UCBG: A mix of about nine tenths stocks and one tenth bonds, built to mimic the way a large university endowment invests. Technology is the biggest stock slice, and the goal is long-term growth with a bit of cushion from bonds, though it still falls in stock downturns.
