UCON: A flexible bond fund that mixes government, corporate and mortgage-backed bonds, along with a small slice of preferred stock. It aims for steady income with limited sensitivity to interest rates, and the managers shift between bond types freely rather than following a fixed list.
UCRD: US corporate bonds, mainly investment grade, picked by an index that is built to improve on a normal corporate bond index. It holds many bonds, and none is more than about 1%, from companies like AT&T and Bank of America.
UDI: An actively managed fund buying US companies that pay dividends and raise them over time, aiming for a high level of income first and growing income second. Johnson & Johnson and AbbVie are the biggest holdings at about 4% each.
UDIV: A US stock fund tracking an index built from the broad US market but tilted toward companies that pay higher dividends. It still looks like the overall market: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 18% of it, and technology is the largest sector.
UDN: A bet that the US dollar falls against a basket of six major currencies including the euro, yen and pound. It does this by holding short futures positions on the dollar index, with cash and Treasury-type holdings set aside as backing.
UEVM: Emerging market stocks picked for being cheap and having positive price momentum, following a VictoryShares index. It holds many companies, none above about 1%, and leans toward banks, which make up around 30% of it.
UFIV: Holds a single US Treasury note with about five years left until it matures, tracking an ICE BofA index of the current five-year Treasury. It swaps into a newly issued five-year note over time, so it stays at a roughly constant medium-term maturity.
UFO: Companies that earn at least half their revenue from space, mostly industrials such as satellite and aerospace makers, plus technology and communications firms. It's a focused bet on one theme, so it swings more than the broad market.
UFOD: An actively managed theme fund buying companies the manager thinks would benefit if governments disclosed information about UFOs. Holdings are mostly industrial and tech firms such as Amentum, Materion, SpaceX and Ouster, each around 3%, so it is a bet on a speculative idea.
UFOX: Technology companies behind satellites, space launches and the networks that connect devices, with technology about three quarters and industrials about an eighth. It's a focused bet on a young, fast-changing theme, so it swings far more than the broad market.
UGA: Holds gasoline futures contracts to follow the price of gasoline, backed by cash and short-term securities. It is a commodity fund, not a stock fund, so its price can move sharply with fuel markets and can drift from the actual gasoline price over time.
UITB: A diversified mix of US government, mortgage-backed and corporate bonds with medium-length maturities. A manager picks the bonds, aiming for steady income as a core holding that cushions stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
UIVM: Stocks from developed countries outside the US, chosen for being cheap compared with their size and for having recent price strength. It is spread thin, with no holding above about 1%, and leans toward banks and industrial companies.
ULTI: An actively managed fund that holds a changing group of US stocks, mostly technology and financials, and uses options to generate income. In exchange, the options limit how much the fund can gain when those stocks rise sharply, and the holdings can be quite volatile.
ULVM: About 200 large US companies picked for being cheap relative to their size and also having recent positive price momentum, a mix of two stock-picking styles. It is spread thin, with no holding above about 2%, and leans toward financials and health care.
UMI: Companies that run pipelines and storage for oil and natural gas, almost entirely in the energy sector. It's meant for high income from those businesses, which tend to pay generous payouts, but it's a focused bet that falls when energy prices or demand weaken.
UMMA: An actively managed fund of stocks from companies outside the US that meet Islamic (Shariah) investing rules. It leans heavily on technology, with Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK Hynix making up about 26% of it.
UNG: Natural gas futures contracts, with the rest held in cash and short term holdings, so its price follows natural gas rather than energy company stocks. It's a short term trading tool: the price swings widely and tends to lose value over time when futures cost more than current prices.
UNHW: An actively managed fund aiming for about 1.2 times the weekly return of UnitedHealth Group stock, using swaps and shares, and paying distributions every week. It is a leveraged, single-stock bet that resets weekly, so losses can be amplified too.
UNIY: A mix of US government, mortgage and corporate bonds, including some higher-risk ones, aiming for more income than a standard bond fund. It's a core bond holding that adds a little credit risk for extra yield, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
UNL: Holds natural gas futures contracts covering the next 12 months, rather than just the nearest one, which helps lessen the effect of price swings in any one month. It tracks natural gas prices, which can be volatile, and holds no company stocks.
UPGD: US mid and large companies whose analyst ratings have improved the most, according to Bloomberg analyst data, tracked by an index. The idea is to catch stocks that analysts are warming up to, and it is spread out, with the largest holdings at about 3% each.
UPGR: A passive fund tracking an index of companies that produce, generate or distribute green energy or support sustainable infrastructure. It spreads across industrials, materials and utilities, with names like FuelCell Energy, Bloom Energy and First Solar, and many holdings are smaller and volatile.
UPSD: A fund holding large US stocks, with Apple and NVIDIA each about 5% of it, alongside options meant to shape its returns. Options strategies like this change how much of the market's ups and downs it captures compared with a plain large-company index fund.
URA: Uranium miners and nuclear power businesses, with energy companies about 60% and industrials making up much of the rest. It's a focused bet on nuclear energy, so its price swings widely with uranium prices and energy policy, far more than the broad market.
URAN: Tracks an index of companies tied to uranium and nuclear power, including utilities that run nuclear plants and miners and builders. It is led by Constellation Energy at about 10%, and about a third of the fund sits in utilities.
URNJ: Smaller companies that mine, explore for or supply uranium, the fuel for nuclear power plants, tracked through a Sprott index. It is very concentrated: NexGen, Paladin, Denison and Energy Fuels together are about half of the fund.
URNM: Companies that mine uranium or own physical uranium, the fuel for nuclear power. It's a focused bet on one commodity and the nuclear energy theme, so it can swing wildly with uranium prices and energy policy.
URTH: Large and mid-sized companies from developed countries around the world, with technology about a third and financials, industrials and health care behind. It's a one-fund core holding for global stocks, though most of its money sits in US companies.
USAF: An actively managed fund mixing real estate stocks, bonds, inflation-protected Treasuries, gold and agriculture holdings. It spreads across several asset types, mostly through other ETFs, rather than focusing on one market.
USAI: North American energy infrastructure companies, mainly pipelines and liquefied natural gas operators, picked by a rules-based index. It is concentrated, with Cheniere, Energy Transfer, Enterprise Products and Enbridge together making up around 30% of it, and it aims to pay regular income.
USCA: Large US companies, with technology over two fifths, tilted toward firms with lower carbon emissions and better climate plans. It's a core stock holding with an environmental screen, so it looks much like the broad market but with fewer fossil fuel companies.
USCI: A basket of commodity futures (contracts to buy raw materials later) covering things like energy, metals and farm goods. The index picks commodities that are trending, so the mix changes over time, and the fund holds mainly futures plus cash and short-term securities.
USCL: Large US companies, with technology making up over two fifths and communication and health care next. It's a core stock holding that tilts toward firms with lower carbon emissions and better climate plans, so its mix differs a bit from the broad market.
USDU: A fund that aims to gain when the US dollar rises against a basket of major world currencies, using an index of the dollar against those currencies. It is actively managed and holds mostly short-term Treasury bills, so it is a bet on the dollar rather than on stocks or bonds.
USDX: An actively managed fund that holds mostly money market funds, which are very safe short-term cash-like holdings, and adds an ultra-short-term options strategy to earn extra income. The options part adds risk beyond a plain cash fund.
USE: An actively managed fund that trades oil, petroleum and natural gas futures, aiming to profit from the relationship between different contracts rather than simply betting on higher prices. Most of the money is held in Treasuries and cash as backing for the futures.
USEW: An actively managed fund aiming for roughly equal weighting of US stocks, mostly by holding other ETFs instead of individual stocks. Equal weighting gives smaller companies a bigger say than they have in a regular index, and no single underlying fund is more than about 6%.
USFE: An actively managed fund that mostly holds US stocks, aiming for long-term growth by picking companies the manager thinks are good value. It spreads across health care, technology and communication, with ONEOK, Alphabet and Becton Dickinson each around 5% of the fund.
USFI: An actively managed fund of US bonds, run by Brandywine Global, which can shift among government, corporate and other types of bonds. Because the manager picks the bonds rather than following an index, it can look different from a standard bond fund.
USFR: US Treasury bonds whose interest payments reset with short-term rates. It's a low-risk place to park cash for income, and because the rate adjusts, its price barely drops when rates rise, though income falls when rates fall.
USG: An actively managed fund that gets exposure to the price of gold through gold futures and warrants held in a subsidiary, and also aims to add income. The cash and futures positions shown are there to support the gold exposure, not a stock portfolio.
USHY: Bonds from US companies with lower credit ratings, often called junk bonds, spread across many issuers. It's meant for higher income than safer bonds, but the companies are likelier to default, so it tends to fall alongside stocks in a downturn.
USIG: US corporate bonds from financially solid companies, rated investment grade, with nearly everything in bonds. It's meant for steady interest income with a bit more yield than Treasuries, though its price drops when interest rates rise, and it can lose value if companies' finances weaken.
USIN: US Treasury bonds with about seven to ten years left until they mature, held in a ladder of roughly equal amounts spread across those maturities. Every holding is a US government bond, so credit risk is minimal, but prices still move when interest rates change.
USL: A fund that holds oil futures contracts, spread across the next 12 months of crude oil contracts rather than only the nearest one. Its price follows crude oil, not oil company stocks, and it doesn't hold barrels of oil.
USLN: Tracks an index of floating rate loans, loans to companies with below investment-grade credit, whose interest payments reset as short-term rates move. Because the payments adjust, it is less sensitive to rate changes than regular bonds, but it carries more credit risk.
USMC: The very largest US companies, with technology about 44% and financials, communication and health care behind it. It's a core holding focused on giants, so it moves with the overall US economy but leaves out smaller companies and leans heavily on tech.
USMD: An actively managed fund of US-listed companies the manager expects to benefit from strategic and emerging technology, like AI, chips and defense tech. It is mostly technology, and no single holding is above about 6%, with Palantir, AMD and Tesla near the top.
USMF: US mid-sized and larger companies picked for a blend of factors such as value, quality and momentum, then weighted to favor higher scores. Alphabet, Apple and NVIDIA are about 4% each, so it holds big tech but is far less top-heavy than a plain index fund.
USMV: Large US stocks picked and weighted to swing less than the overall market, with technology, health care and financials leading. It's built for a smoother ride, so it usually falls less in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
USNG: An actively managed fund of US companies tied to natural gas infrastructure, such as pipelines and power equipment. Around 80% is in energy stocks, with Williams, Kinder Morgan and Solaris Energy Infrastructure among the biggest, so it is a narrow bet on one industry.
USNZ: Large and mid-sized US companies chosen to meet a Paris-aligned, net zero climate screen, so it avoids or reduces companies that conflict with those goals. It still looks a lot like the broad market: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 25% of it.
USO: Futures contracts on crude oil, held alongside cash and short-term bonds that back them. It's a short-term way to bet on oil prices, but it can drift away from the oil price over time because it must keep swapping expiring contracts for new ones.
USOI: An exchange-traded note, which is a debt promise from UBS and not a fund that holds assets, that follows a covered call strategy on crude oil. It aims to pay income by giving up some oil price gains, and it carries UBS credit risk.
USOY: An actively managed fund that aims to pay income by selling options tied to the United States Oil Fund, which tracks crude oil prices. Selling those options caps how much it can gain if oil rises, and most of its assets sit in Treasury bills as backing.
USPX: The whole US stock market weighted by company size, with technology about two fifths, then financials, communication and health care. It's built to be a core holding that moves with the overall US economy, though it's top-heavy in a few giant tech firms.
USRT: US real estate investment trusts, companies that own properties like apartments, offices, shopping centers and storage and pass rental income to shareholders, excluding mortgage and infrastructure REITs. It's for income and real estate exposure, though it tends to fall when interest rates rise.
USSE: An actively managed fund of a limited number of US companies, chosen by managers looking for quality and growth. It is fairly concentrated: Alphabet, Palo Alto Networks, ATI and NVIDIA are about 27% of it.
USSG: Large and mid-sized US companies screened for strong environmental, social and governance records, so some industries such as tobacco and weapons are left out, with technology close to 40%. It's a core stock holding with an ethical filter.
USSH: US Treasury notes with one to three years left, spread evenly across a ladder of maturities. It is entirely government debt, so it carries little default risk and its price moves modestly when interest rates change.
USTB: Mostly short-term US bonds, with some cash and a bit of preferred stock. A manager picks mainly high-quality debt for steady income with modest price swings, which makes it a calmer cushion than longer-term bonds, though it can still dip when interest rates jump.
USVM: Small and mid-size US companies that look cheap and have recent price strength, led by financials, industrials and health care. It's a tilt for long-term growth that can swing more than the broad market, and it may lag when large companies lead.
USVN: A fund that tracks the most recently issued 7 year US Treasury note, so it holds essentially one government bond at a time. It sits in the middle of the yield curve, so its price moves more with interest rates than short-term Treasuries but less than long ones.
USXF: Large and mid-sized US companies with good environmental and social ratings, with fossil fuel companies removed. Technology is more than half of it, so it's a growth leaning core holding for values minded investors, and it moves with tech more than the broad market does.
UTEN: US Treasury notes with about ten years left to maturity, tracking a 10-year Treasury benchmark. It holds only government debt, so credit risk is minimal, but its price moves noticeably when interest rates change.
UTES: Electric, gas and water utilities and similar companies, all in the utility sector. It's meant for dividend income and a steadier ride, since people pay these bills in any economy, but it's a one-sector bet whose prices tend to drop when interest rates rise.
UTHY: Holds a single kind of asset: US Treasury bonds with about 30 years left until they mature, backed by the US government. Because the bonds are so long, their prices move a lot when interest rates change.
UTRE: A single Treasury note, the current 3-year US Treasury, followed through an ICE index. It holds basically one bond at a time and rolls to the new one, so it is a simple way to hold government debt with a few years' maturity.
UTWO: A single type of holding: the most recently issued 2-year US Treasury note. It's meant as a very safe place for money for a short while, earning steady interest, and because the maturity is short its price barely moves when interest rates change.
UTWY: US Treasury bonds with about 20 years left until maturity, held almost entirely in a small number of long government bonds. Because the bonds are so long, the price moves a lot when interest rates change, though credit risk is minimal.
UUP: Bets that the US dollar rises against a basket of major currencies, using futures on the US Dollar Index. It holds no foreign bonds or stocks, and the Treasury and cash holdings in its list are collateral backing the futures.
UUPP: Holds CLOs, which are pools of corporate loans packaged into bonds, and is actively managed by Principal. It is spread across many CLOs from managers like Ares and Apidos, each around 5%, and pays income that is higher than most bonds with more credit risk.
UX: A fund that gets its exposure to uranium through a mix of uranium mining company stocks, a physical uranium trust, and derivatives tied to uranium prices. Much of the portfolio is held in Treasury bills as backing, and the fund is non-diversified, so it is a narrow bet on one commodity theme.
UXAP: An actively managed fund using options on the SPDR S&P 500 fund over a one-year period starting in April. It aims to give extra gains if the market rises with no cap, but you are exposed to losses if it falls, since its protection is limited.
UXJA: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to try to deliver a multiple of the index's gains over a set one-year period that starts each January. It has no cap on those gains, but it also gives up some protection, so you can lose money if the market falls.
UXJL: A fund that uses options on an S&P 500 ETF to follow the US stock market over a one-year period, with some boosted exposure to gains and no cap on them. It also uses options to cushion a set amount of losses, and the outcomes only apply over the full period.
UXOC: Uses FLEX options, customizable exchange traded options, on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to seek boosted gains with no upper limit over a set period that starts each October. Results are designed for those who hold the full period, and losses are still possible.
VABS: A bond fund that mostly holds asset-backed securities and mortgage-backed securities, which are bundles of loans like car loans, mortgages and business debt that pay out as borrowers repay. It is actively managed and spread across many small positions, none above about 3%.
VAIC: Uses contracts that follow an NYSE index of 500 US stocks to pay regular income, with a payoff that can end early if the index reaches a set level (an autocallable). It does not hold the stocks directly, and losses are possible if the index falls.
VAIE: An actively managed income fund that gets its exposure through autocallable contracts tied to a US 500 stock index, which pay income and can end early if the index reaches set levels. It does not simply own the stocks, so it behaves differently from a plain index fund.
VALQ: US large and mid sized companies picked for looking cheaply priced while also showing quality and steady income. It is well spread across tech, health care and consumer firms, with no single holding above about 4%.
VAMO: An actively managed fund of US stocks picked for being cheap and having strong price momentum, with the option to hedge part of its holdings. A lot of the portfolio sits in cash, and energy refiners like PBF Energy and Valero show up among the larger holdings.
VAVX: A fund that directly holds AVAX, the token of the Avalanche blockchain, and tracks its price. It holds no stocks or bonds, and because crypto prices swing sharply, its value can change a lot in short periods.
VAW: US materials companies such as chemical makers, miners and producers of construction materials and packaging. It's a focused bet on one sector, so it tends to rise and fall with the economy and commodity prices, and it has almost no tech or health care.
VB: Small US companies spread across technology, industrials, health care and financials. It is used to add growth potential beyond large companies, but small firms are shakier, so it swings more than the broad market and can lag when investors favor big, stable names.
VBCA: A basket of investment grade US corporate bonds that all mature in 2027, tracking a Bloomberg index. As bonds mature, the fund winds down, so it behaves more like one bond with a set end date, and it is spread across hundreds of issuers.
VBCB: A basket of US investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2028, so the fund is designed to wind down around that date. It holds hundreds of bonds, with large banks and companies like CVS each under 1% of the fund.
VBCC: A basket of investment grade US corporate bonds that all mature in 2029, tracking a Bloomberg index. As bonds mature, the fund winds down, so it behaves more like one bond with a set end date, and it is spread across hundreds of issuers.
VBCD: Investment grade US corporate bonds that mature in 2030, held until the fund ends. It holds many bonds, with T-Mobile the biggest at about 1%, so it behaves more like one bond than a fund that keeps rolling.
VBCE: A basket of investment grade US corporate bonds that all mature in 2031, so the fund is designed to wind down around then. It is spread across many companies, such as Amazon, Goldman Sachs and Oracle, each around 1% of the fund.
VBCF: US investment grade corporate bonds that mature in 2032, tracked by an index. It is very spread out, with big banks like Bank of America and JPMorgan each only about 1% of the fund, and it winds down once the bonds mature.
VBCG: A basket of investment-grade US corporate bonds that all mature in 2033, tracking a target-maturity index. As the bonds near maturity, it winds down, so it pays interest and returns the bond principal around that year; large banks like Wells Fargo and Bank of America are among the issuers.
VBCH: A basket of US corporate bonds that all mature around 2034, tracking a Vanguard target maturity index. Because the bonds end near the same date, it behaves a bit like a single bond, with large banks like JPMorgan and Bank of America among the borrowers.
VBCI: A basket of US investment-grade corporate bonds that mature in 2035, from companies like Meta, Morgan Stanley and Broadcom. Each bond is a tiny slice of the fund, and it is designed to wind down around its target year rather than run forever.
VBCJ: Holds US investment-grade corporate bonds that mature around 2036, tracking a Bloomberg index of such bonds. The fund shuts down at that time and pays back its holders, and it is spread across many companies, none above about 2%.
VBIL: Very short US Treasury bills that mature within three months, backed by the federal government. It's a place to park cash for a short time while earning interest, and because the bills mature so fast, its price barely moves when rates change.
VBK: Small US companies expected to grow fast, led by technology at about 30 percent, with health care and industrials at roughly a fifth each. It's for long-term growth, but small companies swing more than large ones, so expect bigger ups and downs.
VBNB: A fund that holds BNB, the digital coin tied to the Binance crypto ecosystem, directly, rather than owning stocks or futures. Its price follows the market price of BNB, which can swing sharply, and it pays no income.
VBND: A flexible mix of US bonds, including government, corporate and mortgage-backed bonds, managed actively. It's meant for income with some growth potential as a core bond holding, and because the managers choose bonds themselves, results can differ from a standard bond index.
VBR: Small US value stocks, meaning smaller companies priced cheaply relative to their size, led by financials, industrials and consumer companies. It aims for higher long-run growth than large companies, but it swings more than the broad market and can lag for years.
VCEB: Investment-grade US corporate bonds, screened to favor companies with better environmental, social and governance records. It's meant for steady interest income with less risk than stocks, though bond prices drop when interest rates rise and it can slip when the economy weakens.
VCHY: Tracks an index of US dollar corporate bonds rated below investment grade, often called junk bonds, from many different companies. No single issuer is more than a fraction of a percent of the fund, so default risk is spread very thin.
VCIT: Bonds from investment-grade US companies that mature in five to ten years. It is meant for more income than government bonds, and it suits the bond part of a portfolio, but it can lose value if interest rates rise or the economy weakens.
VCLN: A fund of clean energy companies, such as solar, fuel cell and wind businesses, picked by the managers. It is concentrated, with First Solar, Bloom Energy and China Yangtze Power each making up about 7 to 8% of the fund.
VCLT: Investment-grade bonds from US corporations that mature in more than 10 years. It's meant for higher interest income than government bonds, but its price drops sharply when interest rates rise, and it can fall in a recession if companies struggle.
VCOB: An actively managed US bond fund holding government, corporate and mortgage-backed bonds, aiming for income plus some price growth. It is broadly spread across hundreds of bonds, with Treasuries the largest piece at under 10%.
VCR: Retailers, carmakers, restaurants, hotels, home builders and online shopping companies, all businesses that people buy more from when they feel flush. It's a focused bet on consumer spending, so it tends to do well in good economies and fall harder than the broad market in downturns.
VCRB: A broad mix of bonds, including US Treasuries, corporate bonds and mortgage-backed bonds, of various lengths and credit quality. It's meant as a core bond holding for steady income and a cushion for stocks, and an active manager can lean toward bonds that look attractive.
VCRM: Municipal bonds issued by US states, cities and local agencies, with interest free from federal income tax. It's meant for tax-free income and mostly appeals to people in higher tax brackets, though its price falls when interest rates rise.
VCSH: Investment-grade bonds from companies that mature in one to five years, spread across industrial, utility and financial borrowers. It aims for steady income with smaller price swings than longer bonds, though it pays a bit less than long-term corporate debt.
VDC: Companies that sell everyday necessities, such as food, drinks, household products and groceries, across the US. It's a focused bet on one industry, often used as a defensive holding because people keep buying these items in a downturn, though it can trail in strong rallies.
VDE: US oil, gas and fuel companies of all sizes, from producers to refiners and pipeline operators. It's a focused bet on the energy sector, so it rises and falls with oil prices and swings far more than the broad market.
VDG: Large and mid-sized growth companies in developed markets outside the US, tracked by a Vanguard-chosen index. It spans Europe, Japan, Canada and others, and SK Hynix, ASML and Samsung are the largest holdings at about 13% combined.
VDI: Dividend-paying stocks from outside the US, picked by a rules-based process aimed at income. Financials are over 40% of it, and holdings such as ASML, HSBC and Roche are each only around 2% to 3%.
VDIG: An actively managed fund of US companies that pay dividends and are expected to raise them over time, run by the Wellington team. It holds large companies in tech, finance and health care, with Broadcom, Eli Lilly and Microsoft together around 17% of the fund.
VDV: Tracks developed stock markets outside the US, but only the companies that look cheap compared to their size and earnings. It holds names like Samsung, Nestle, Shell and BHP, and leans toward financials, industrials and energy rather than growth stocks.
VEA: Companies in developed countries outside the US, such as in Europe and Japan, led by financials, industrials and technology. It is a way to add international stocks to a portfolio, and it leaves out emerging markets, so it is steadier than a fund that includes them.
VEEM: A fund of emerging-market stocks picked from the MSCI Emerging Markets Index for positive analyst sentiment, meaning analysts are leaning favorable on them. It is concentrated in chipmakers: Taiwan Semiconductor alone is about 17%, and technology is nearly half the fund.
VEFA: A fund of developed-market stocks outside the US and Canada, picked from the MSCI EAFE Index for positive analyst sentiment, meaning analysts are leaning favorable on them. It is fairly broad, with ASML the largest holding at about 5% and financials the biggest sector.
VEGA: An actively managed fund of other ETFs covering global stocks and bonds, which sells call options to earn extra income. Selling those options limits the upside in strong markets, and about 40% sits in one big US stock fund.
VEGI: Companies across the agriculture chain, such as tractor makers, seed and fertilizer firms and crop processors. It is top-heavy: Deere is about 26% of the fund, and Corteva and Archer Daniels Midland add around 17%.
VEGN: Follows an index built from about 500 of the largest US companies, screened to leave out businesses tied to animal products and fossil fuels. It leans heavily into technology, which is around two thirds of the fund, led by Micron, Apple, AMD and Broadcom.
VEGX: International companies outside the US selected by an index screening for vegan-friendly and climate-conscious practices. It ends up heavy in technology and industrials, with ASML, Shopify and Advantest among the largest holdings, each about 3% to 5%.
VEM: Dividend-paying companies from emerging markets such as Taiwan and South Korea, picked by an active manager. It is top-heavy in tech, with Taiwan Semiconductor alone about 16% and Samsung and SK Hynix adding roughly another 16%.
VEMY: An actively managed fund of high yield bonds, often called junk bonds, issued by governments and companies in emerging market countries. They pay higher interest because the issuers are riskier, and the fund is spread thinly, with each top holding only about 1% to 2%.
VETZ: Mostly holds mortgage-backed bonds guaranteed by US government agencies such as Ginnie Mae, which pool home loans and pass the payments on to bondholders. It is actively managed with a veteran-focused mission, and no single bond is more than about 6% of it.
VEU: Stocks from companies outside the US, in both developed and emerging countries, led by financials and technology with industrials next. It adds international diversification to a US-heavy portfolio, and it holds no US companies, so it moves differently from American markets.
VEXC: Large and mid-sized companies in emerging markets with China left out, tracking an index of about 1,000 stocks. It is top-heavy in one name: Taiwan Semiconductor is around 22% of the fund, with Taiwan, India and other markets making up most of the rest.
VFH: US financial companies of all sizes, including banks, insurers, asset managers and payment firms. It's a focused bet on one sector, so it swings more than the broad market and is sensitive to interest rates and the health of the economy.
VFLO: US mid-sized companies chosen for producing lots of spare cash after expenses, with technology, energy and health care the biggest groups. It's a value-style stock fund, and the tilt toward energy means it can behave differently from the broad market.
VFMF: US stocks screened for cheap prices, strong profits and recent momentum, spread across financials, technology, health care and consumer companies. It's a core stock holding with a factor tilt, so it can behave differently from the market and trail when growth stocks lead.
VFMO: US stocks that have recently been rising fastest, spread across technology, industrials, health care and energy. It's meant for growth beyond the broad market, but the mix shifts as winners change, and momentum can reverse quickly when the market turns.
VFMV: US stocks picked because they tend to swing less than the market, with technology about 30% and health care, communication and consumer staples each near a tenth. It aims for a smoother ride, so it usually falls less in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
VFQY: Mid-sized US companies with strong profits and healthy finances, spread across technology, financials, industrials and consumer companies. It's meant as growth-minded core stock exposure, and because it picks quality traits it may trail the market when low-quality stocks rally.
VFVA: US stocks that look cheap compared with their fundamentals, led by financials at about a quarter, then health care, consumer companies and technology. It's a value-style holding for stock investors, and it can trail the market for long stretches when growth companies are the ones leading.
VGHY: An actively managed fund of high yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, which pay higher interest because the companies borrowing are riskier. It holds many bonds, with none above about 1%, plus a small amount of Treasuries.
VGIT: US Treasury bonds that mature in three to ten years, backed by the federal government. It's meant as a cushion against stock market drops, with moderate price swings, though its price falls when interest rates rise.
VGK: Companies across Europe, led by financials and industrials, then health care. It adds European exposure to a US-heavy portfolio, and it has far less technology than US funds, while its results also depend on the euro and pound versus the dollar.
VGLT: US Treasury bonds that mature in more than ten years, all backed by the government. It's meant as a cushion when stocks fall, but its price swings a lot with interest rates, dropping sharply when they rise.
VGMS: An actively managed bond fund that spreads money across several bond sectors of varied credit quality, aiming for steady income. It holds a wide mix, including Treasuries, corporate and foreign bonds, and no single position is above about 2%.
VGRO: An actively managed fund of US companies with higher-than-average growth potential, all with at least $1 billion in market value. It is very top-heavy: NVIDIA and Alphabet are about 30% of it, and technology and communication make up about 70%.
VGSH: US Treasury bonds that come due in one to three years, backed by the federal government. It's a low-risk place for cash you may need soon, with small price swings, though it pays less than longer bonds.
VGSR: Real estate companies and real estate investment trusts around the world, all in the property sector. It's meant for income and diversification from property, with a screen for sustainability, and it tends to drop when interest rates rise.
VGT: US technology companies of all sizes, including software makers, chip companies and computer hardware. It is a focused bet on one sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and it leaves out most internet and social media companies, which are classed in other sectors.
VGTX: A fund holding technology company stocks and tech-focused ETFs, then selling options on them to earn extra income. Selling options brings in cash but caps some of the gains when tech rallies, so it trades part of the upside for income.
VGVT: An actively managed fund of bonds issued or backed by the US government and its agencies, including Treasuries and mortgage securities from Fannie Mae and similar groups. It can hold any maturity and aims for steady income with low credit risk.
VHT: US health care companies of all sizes, such as drugmakers, medical device makers, insurers and biotech firms. It's a focused bet on one sector, and it tends to hold up better than most in a downturn but can swing when drug pricing or regulation news hits.
VIDI: Stocks of companies outside the US, in both developed and emerging markets, chosen by a rules-based index rather than by company size. It holds many smaller positions, with the biggest around 2%, and leans toward industrials, financials and technology companies in places like South Korea and Taiwan.
VIG: Large US companies with a record of raising their dividends year after year, spread across technology, financials, health care and industrials. It aims for steady growth with modest income, and it leaves out the highest yielders, so it pays less than dedicated income funds.
VIGI: Large companies outside the US that have a record of growing their dividends, led by financials, industrials, technology and health care. It's meant for steady growth with some income, and it leaves out the highest-yielding stocks, so it may pay less than other dividend funds.
VIOG: Smaller US companies with faster growth, spread across technology, industrials, health care and financials. It's meant for growth in the small-company part of the market, so it swings more than large-company funds and can trail when investors favor big, stable names.
VIOO: Smaller US companies, spread across financials, technology, industrials and consumer businesses, screened to include only those that are profitable. It's a way to add growth potential from small companies to a portfolio, and the profit screen means it leaves out unprofitable firms, though it still swings more than large-company funds.
VIOV: Small US companies that look cheap compared to their size, with financials the largest group, followed by consumer, technology and industrial companies. It's a value tilt for long-term growth, and small companies can swing more than large ones.
VIS: US industrial companies of all sizes, such as aerospace and defense firms, machinery makers, airlines and railroads. It's a focused bet on one industry tied to economic growth, so it tends to do well when the economy is strong and drop when it weakens.
VLU: US stocks of all sizes, weighted toward companies that look cheaper, with technology, financials and health care leading. It's a value-tilted core holding, and it can trail growth-driven markets since it holds fewer of the priciest stocks than the usual index.
VLUE: US companies that look cheap compared with their earnings, sales and assets, though technology still makes up nearly half. It's built as a value-leaning core holding, and it can trail growth stocks in strong rallies while holding up better when expensive stocks fall.
VMAX: US large companies that look cheap compared to their size, picked by a rules-based value index, with a tilt toward banks and financials. It is widely spread, with the top holdings such as BNY Mellon, State Street and US Bancorp each only about 2%.
VMBS: Bonds backed by pools of home loans, guaranteed by US government agencies such as Ginnie Mae, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. It's meant for steady income with high credit quality, but homeowners paying off mortgages early when rates fall can cut the income, and prices drop when rates rise.
VMHY: Higher-yield municipal bonds, meaning loans to US state and local governments or related projects that pay more but carry more risk. Income is generally exempt from federal income tax, and it spreads across a large number of issuers.
VMSB: An actively managed bond fund that spreads money across several bond types, such as corporate, government-backed mortgage and other income-producing bonds, to earn high current income. Each holding is small, with the biggest positions around 1% to 2% of the fund.
VMSD: Short-term municipal bonds, which are loans to US states, cities and local governments, with income that is generally exempt from federal income tax. Short maturities mean its price moves less than longer-term bond funds when interest rates change.
VNAM: Vietnamese stocks from a broad MSCI Vietnam index. It is very top-heavy: Vingroup alone is about 24% of the fund, and real estate and financial companies make up around 60% of it.
VNIE: An actively managed fund of companies outside the US, picked by Vontobel for quality and growth in at least three countries. Its biggest positions include Taiwan Semiconductor, Tokyo Electron and ASML, each around 6% to 7%, and it is mixed across technology, industrials and financials.
VNLA: A mix of short-term, mostly investment-grade bonds that mature soon, plus a bit of cash. It's meant to earn more than cash while staying steady, and since the bonds are so short, its price barely moves when interest rates change.
VNM: Stocks of Vietnamese companies, with financials about a third, then real estate, consumer staples and industrials. It's a focused bet on a single small emerging economy, so it swings a lot and depends heavily on Vietnam's banks and property.
VNQ: Real estate companies, mostly trusts that own offices, apartments, warehouses, cell towers and shopping centers. It adds property exposure and income to a portfolio, but it drops when interest rates rise.
VNQI: Real estate companies from outside the US, such as property owners and developers in Europe, Asia and elsewhere, almost all in real estate. It's a way to add global property income, and its value moves with interest rates and with foreign currencies against the dollar.
VNSE: An actively managed fund holding a focused set of mostly large US and global companies picked by the manager rather than following an index. About 40% sits in technology, and NVIDIA, Taiwan Semiconductor, Eli Lilly and Alphabet are each roughly 7% to 8%.
VO: Mid-sized US companies, bigger than small firms but smaller than the giants, spread across industrials, technology, financials and health care. It offers more growth potential than large companies with less risk than small ones, and it has much less tech than a large-company fund.
VOE: Mid-sized US companies that look cheaply priced, spread across financials, energy, industrials and utilities. It leans to steady, older industries rather than tech, so it can do better when growth stocks stall but lag when they lead.
VOLT: Companies tied to electrification, mostly industrials such as electrical equipment, plus utilities, technology and energy firms. It's a themed growth bet on the shift to electric power, so it swings more than the broad market and has little in typical consumer stocks.
VONE: Nearly the whole US stock market's large companies in one fund, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and health care behind. It's a core holding that moves with the overall US economy, and includes more mid-sized names than a pure large-company fund.
VONG: Large US growth companies, with technology making up well over half and communication services about a sixth. It's built for growth investors who want big-company exposure, though with so much in tech it can swing more than the broad market.
VONV: Large US companies that look cheap relative to their earnings and assets, led by technology, financials and health care. It's a core value holding that can trail when fast-growing stocks drive the market and tends to hold up better when they falter.
VOO: Hundreds of the largest US companies, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and health care making up much of the rest. It is a simple core holding that moves with the big-company US market, and it is heavily weighted toward a handful of tech leaders.
VOOB: Aims to follow the S&P 500 while using options to protect against part of the losses. Because of that protection, it gives up some of the gains when stocks rise, and its holdings are mostly cash and option contracts rather than stocks.
VOOG: The faster-growing half of the S&P 500, with technology making up over half the fund, followed by communication, financials and consumer companies. It's built for growth, so it tends to rise more in strong markets and fall harder in downturns than the full index.
VOOV: The cheaper-priced half of the S&P 500's large companies, with technology the biggest slice, then financials, health care and industrials. It's a value tilt on a core US holding, and it can lag when expensive growth stocks lead.
VOOY: Holds the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF and adds an options strategy designed to produce extra monthly income. The options can limit gains when the stock market rises strongly, and it still falls when large US companies fall.
VOT: Mid-sized US companies expected to grow faster than average, led by technology and industrials, with consumer and health care firms behind. It's for long-term growth, and it swings more than a large company fund.
VOTE: US large companies in a mix resembling the S&P 500, with technology about 40% and financials, communication and health care behind it. It works as a core stock holding, and its manager votes shares on company issues to push for change, not just hold them.
VOX: Phone and cable companies, streaming services, social media and online search businesses, and media and entertainment firms, nearly all in the communication sector. It's a focused bet on one corner of the market, and a few giant internet companies dominate it, so it swings more than the broad market.
VOXP: A fund of mostly large US stocks, led by NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet, which together are about 20% of it. The managers pick holdings by their own approach, so it can differ from a plain index fund even though it looks much like one at the top.
VPC: Follows an index of US-listed closed-end funds and business development companies that make private loans to companies, so it is a private credit fund of funds. Oxford Lane, Eagle Point and Horizon Technology Finance are among its top holdings, and it aims for income.
VPFF: Preferred shares and similar hybrid securities, which pay fixed dividends and rank ahead of common stock but below bonds. It is actively managed, with no holding above roughly 2%, with a focus on income.
VPL: Companies from developed Pacific countries, mainly Japan, Australia, South Korea and Hong Kong, with technology at about 28% and financials a fifth. It's a way to add Asia-Pacific exposure to a portfolio, and it moves with those currencies and economies, not the US.
VPLS: A broad mix of bonds across US government, corporate, mortgage and some emerging market debt, all in US dollars. It's meant as a core bond holding for steady income and a cushion for stocks, with a bit of extra yield from riskier bonds, though prices drop when rates rise.
VPU: Electric, gas and water utility companies across the US, which sell essential services and tend to pay steady dividends. It's a focused bet on one industry, often used for income and stability, but its prices tend to drop when interest rates rise.
VPX: An actively managed US stock fund that shifts its mix of sectors depending on where it thinks we are in the economic cycle. About 20% sits in a broad US market fund, and the rest is in stocks such as Broadcom, NVIDIA and ExxonMobil.
VRAI: Stocks of companies tied to real assets such as energy, real estate, utilities, materials and agriculture, picked from an index built by Indxx. The idea is income from businesses that own physical things, and it is spread out, with no holding above about 2%.
VRIG: Investment-grade bonds whose interest payments reset as rates change, rather than staying fixed. It's meant as a low-risk place for income, and because payments adjust, its price barely drops when interest rates rise.
VRP: Preferred stocks and bonds from banks, insurers and utilities whose payouts adjust with interest rates. It's built for income, and because payouts float, its price holds up better than fixed-rate preferred funds when rates rise, but it can still drop in a credit scare.
VSDA: US companies with a record of raising dividends year after year, picked by the Nasdaq Victory Dividend Accelerator Index. It leans toward consumer staples and financials and holds firms like Franklin Resources, Kimberly-Clark and Altria, each near 4%.
VSDB: High quality short-term bonds, a blend of corporate debt, Treasuries and mortgage- or asset-backed bonds. It's meant for steady income and low risk, and since maturities are short, its price moves far less than regular bond funds when interest rates change.
VSDM: Short-term bonds from US states, cities and agencies whose interest is exempt from federal income tax. It's meant for tax-free income with a steadier price, since short maturities mean it moves far less than longer municipal bonds when interest rates change.
VSGX: Large companies in developed and emerging markets outside the US, with financials and technology each over a quarter, screened to leave out companies that fall short on environmental and social standards. It's a way to diversify abroad while following those values.
VSHY: An actively managed fund of high-yield bonds with shorter maturities, meaning bonds from weaker-credit companies that pay more interest. Shorter bonds usually swing less when rates change, and the fund is spread across many issuers, with none above about 1.5%.
VSLU: Large US companies chosen by a valuation formula that looks for cash-generating firms at fair prices, with technology around 40%. It's a core large-company holding with a value-minded twist, though it ends up heavy in tech like the broad market.
VSMV: A US stock fund tracking an index that picks stocks using several factors, then aims for lower price swings than the market. It is more concentrated than most, with Apple at about 10% and chip makers Lam Research and KLA near the top.
VSOL: A fund that holds the Solana cryptocurrency, SOL, directly instead of stocks or bonds. Its value follows the price of Solana as measured by a MarketVector benchmark, and like other crypto it can swing a lot.
VSS: Small and mid-sized companies from developed and emerging countries outside the US, with industrials about a fifth and technology, materials and financials following. It's a way to add smaller international companies to a portfolio, and it can swing more than funds of big foreign firms.
VT: Stocks from companies all over the world, both developed and emerging countries, with technology about a third and financials, industrials and health care next. It is a whole-world core holding in one fund, with roughly six tenths of it in the US.
VTC: Investment-grade bonds issued by US companies across many industries, held through a handful of Vanguard bond funds. It's meant for steady interest income that is higher than Treasuries, and its price drops when interest rates rise or when companies' credit worsens.
VTEB: Bonds issued by states, cities and local agencies, with interest that is exempt from federal income tax. It's meant for steady, tax-free income in a regular taxable account, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
VTEC: Municipal bonds issued by California governments and agencies, mostly investment grade with medium maturities. It's for income that is generally free of federal and California income taxes, so it suits high earners in the state, but it depends on one state's finances.
VTEI: Investment-grade US municipal bonds with maturities of up to 20 years, whose interest is free of federal income tax. It's meant for tax-efficient income for people in higher brackets, and it's a middle-ground choice whose price drops when interest rates rise.
VTEL: Long-term US municipal bonds, mostly from states, cities and public agencies, tracking an index of investment-grade muni bonds maturing in over ten years. The interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and longer maturities mean prices move more when interest rates change.
VTES: Short-term municipal bonds from state and local governments across the US, with a little cash, paying income that is generally free of federal tax. It's for a low-risk tax-friendly place to hold money, and because the bonds mature soon, its price moves very little.
VTG: A fund holding US Treasury bonds of all kinds, tracking a Bloomberg index of government debt, with middle-length maturities. Its holdings are spread across hundreds of Treasury issues, so no single bond is more than about 1%.
VTHR: Nearly the entire US stock market, from giants to small companies, with technology the largest slice at almost 40%. It's a one-fund core holding for US stocks, and it adds small companies that the S&P 500 leaves out.
VTI: Nearly every publicly traded US company, from giants to small firms, with technology around a third and financials and health care next. It works as a one-fund core holding for US stocks, and because it includes small companies it is slightly broader than an S&P 500 fund.
VTIP: US Treasury bonds that adjust their value with inflation and mature in under five years. It is meant to protect buying power while holding steady, and its price moves little, though its income falls when inflation cools.
VTP: US Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS) of all maturities, whose principal rises with inflation, tracking a broad Bloomberg TIPS index. It holds hundreds of government bonds, so credit risk is very low, but prices still move with interest rates.
VTV: Large US value stocks, meaning companies priced cheaply relative to their size, led by financials and health care with technology and industrials next. It leans toward established, steadier businesses, and it has far less tech than the broad market, so it often trails in growth-led rallies.
VTWG: Small US companies with faster expected growth, led by health care at about a third and technology at over a fifth. It's a growth bet on small companies, so it swings more than the broad market, and many of its holdings are biotech firms not yet profitable.
VTWO: Roughly 2,000 small US companies, with health care about a fifth, financials just under that, and technology and industrials making up much of the rest. It's a way to add growth potential to a portfolio, but small companies swing more than large ones and can fall harder in downturns.
VTWV: Small US companies priced cheaply compared to their earnings and assets, led by financials at about a quarter, then industrials, health care and real estate. It's a value tilt for diversifying beyond big names, and it tends to swing more than large company funds.
VUG: Large US growth companies, meaning firms expected to expand faster than average, with technology about 60 percent and communication and consumer companies next. It is built for long-term growth, but it is concentrated in tech and tends to fall harder than the broad market in downturns.
VUS: US stocks that pay dividends, chosen by a rules-based process that looks for dividend income. Despite the income focus it is heavy in big tech, with Apple, NVIDIA and Microsoft making up about 15% of the fund.
VUSE: Large US companies chosen by a rules-based score, with technology about 40 percent, then financials, health care and communication. It's a core stock holding with a tilt toward technology, so it can swing more than the broad market.
VUSG: An actively managed fund of large and mid-sized US companies that Wellington expects to grow earnings faster than average. It is very top-heavy and tech-driven: NVIDIA, Alphabet, Micron and Broadcom together are about 39% of the fund.
VUSV: An actively managed fund of US value stocks, meaning companies that look cheap relative to their earnings or assets, run by the Wellington team. It is spread widely, with Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft about 3% each, across financials, tech and health care.
VV: Large US companies making up the top share of the American market, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and health care next. It is a core holding for big-company US stocks, and a few tech leaders drive much of its movement.
VWO: Stocks from emerging markets such as China, India and Taiwan, with technology about a third and financials next. It offers growth from developing economies, but it swings more than developed market funds, and it includes mainland Chinese shares that can be affected by government policy.
VWOB: Bonds issued by the governments of emerging market countries, mostly priced in US dollars. It's for extra income beyond US bonds, and it carries more risk than safe bonds, since these countries can have weaker finances and prices fall when worries rise.
VXF: Small and mid-sized US companies, everything except the S&P 500, led by technology and industrials with health care and financials next. It is a way to add smaller companies beyond a big-company fund, and it swings more than the broad market.
VXUS: Stocks from companies outside the US, in both developed and emerging countries, led by financials and technology with industrials next. It adds international diversification to a US-heavy portfolio, and it has no US companies at all, so it moves differently from American markets.
VYM: Large US companies that pay above-average dividends, led by financials, technology, health care and industrials. It is built for dividend income with moderate growth, and it leaves out real estate trusts, so it often trails in growth-led rallies.
VYMI: Large companies outside the US that pay above-average dividends, with financials about 44 percent, then energy, consumer staples and materials. It's meant for income and international diversification, and it leans heavily on banks, which makes it sensitive to the financial sector.
WABF: An actively managed bond fund holding a broad mix of US government, corporate and other debt of different maturities. It can also hold some lower-rated and credit-linked bonds, so the managers have room to depart from a standard bond index.
WAGN: An actively managed, concentrated fund of small and mid-sized stocks from around the world, chosen using value investor Mohnish Pabrai's style of buying cheap companies. Warrior Met Coal and Transocean are about 10% each, and holdings range from energy to airports and retail.
WAMA: US large-company stocks that switch between full stock exposure and a defensive position depending on a moving-average trend signal, following a WisdomTree index. When the signal is positive it looks like a big-company index, with NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet about 21% of the fund.
WAR: An actively managed fund of companies tied to technology and national defense, such as drones, cybersecurity, semiconductors and aerospace, including many outside the US. It is fairly concentrated: Astera Labs, Axon and Micron are about 27% of it.
WARP: Companies tied to the space industry, such as rocket launchers, satellite operators and space communications firms, tracked by an index. It is concentrated and non-diversified: SpaceX and Rocket Lab together are about 35% of the fund.
WATS: An actively managed fund of companies that make or support battery energy storage, such as batteries and the systems that store power. Tesla is about 17% and Bloom Energy about 12%, so a couple of names drive much of the result.
WBEM: An actively managed fund of stocks from emerging markets, developing economies such as China, India and Brazil, picked by William Blair's managers. It does not follow an index, and being non-diversified it can place larger bets on fewer companies.
WBIE: An actively managed fund of stocks from companies outside the US, mostly large ones with strong growth prospects, picked by William Blair's managers. It invests mainly in common stocks and does not follow an index, so results depend on the manager's choices.
WBIF: An actively managed fund of value-priced stocks of all sizes, in the US and abroad, that can shift a large part of its money into cash when its model turns cautious. About a quarter is currently held back in cash, and individual stocks are each under 4%.
WBIG: A tactical fund that shifts between stocks, bonds and cash depending on market signals, focusing on dividend-paying US and foreign stocks. Holdings are spread widely, and a good part of it can sit in cash when the managers turn defensive.
WBIL: An actively managed fund that holds US and foreign stocks of all sizes, picked for quality, and can shift toward safer assets such as cash or Treasuries when the manager sees trouble. Technology is about 38% of it, with chip firms like Astera Labs and Marvell near the top.
WBIY: Holds about 50 higher-dividend US mid- and smaller-sized stocks picked by the Solactive index using a rules-based screen of yield and quality. No company dominates: Best Buy, HP, Altria and Campbell's are each about 5% of it.
WCAP: An actively managed stock fund that can invest in companies of any size, in any sector and anywhere, and does not follow an index. It holds mostly large US names plus a few ETFs, with Microsoft and Alphabet about 6% each.
WCBR: Global companies that make cybersecurity and security software, tracking a WisdomTree index of firms getting a meaningful share of revenue from it. It is a narrow technology theme, with CrowdStrike, Datadog and Palo Alto Networks about 21% of the fund.
WCEO: An actively managed fund of US companies that are led by women CEOs, leaning toward smaller and mid-sized firms. Holdings are spread thinly across many industries, with no single stock above about 2.5%, so it is not dominated by a few names.
WCLD: A fund of companies that sell software over the internet, known as cloud computing, tracked by an index that weights them about equally. Because no company dominates, with the top holdings each around 3%, it behaves more like a basket of many small tech bets.
WCME: Stocks of companies in developing countries, picked by an active manager looking for quality businesses. It leans on Asia: Taiwan Semiconductor is about 13% and Korean names like SK Hynix and Samsung add another 15% or so.
WCMG: An actively managed fund buying stocks of companies around the world, chosen by WCM using a focus on firms with strengthening competitive advantages. It is spread across health care, technology, communication and financials, and Nebius is the largest holding at about 7%.
WCMI: Companies outside the US, with technology, financials, industrials and health care making up most of it. Managers pick firms with strong competitive advantages, so it's a growth-focused way to own international stocks, though results can differ from the broad foreign market.
WCPB: An actively managed fund of bonds that mostly invests in investment-grade debt but can reach into lower-rated bonds for extra income, hence the 'core plus' name. Weitz picks holdings by hand rather than following an index, across government, corporate and mortgage bonds.
WDAF: Defense and aerospace companies in Asia, tracked through a WisdomTree index, with a big focus on India, South Korea and Japan. It is concentrated, with Hindustan Aeronautics, Bharat Electronics and Korea Aerospace each about 8%.
WDAI: Roughly 300 large companies from around the world picked by a rules-based S&P index that ranks firms using AI-driven scoring. Holdings are spread thinly, with no single company above about 1% of the fund.
WDE: Securitized debt, meaning loans like commercial mortgages, auto loans and equipment leases packaged into bonds. It uses futures and swaps to hedge and manage sensitivity to interest rates, and its holdings are spread out, with none above about 5%.
WDEF: European defense and aerospace companies, such as BAE Systems, Thales, Rheinmetall and Safran, picked to follow a WisdomTree index. It is a narrow theme: the top four holdings are about 34% of the fund, and nearly all of it is industrials.
WDGF: A fund of defense and aerospace companies from around the world, such as RTX, General Dynamics, BAE Systems, Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman. Each of those is about 5% of the fund, and nearly all of it is in industrials.
WDIG: A fund investing in companies that mine or process rare earths and strategic metals, such as Lynas, MP Materials and Materion, partly through futures contracts. It is a narrow bet on a small, volatile corner of the metals market.
WDIV: Dividend-paying companies from around the world, chosen from the S&P Global BMI for high yields and a record of managed dividend policies. It holds many positions, none above about 2%, and tilts toward financials, industrials, utilities and real estate.
WDNA: Global companies in biotech and genetic science, such as gene editing, DNA sequencing and new drug discovery. It holds a sample of the stocks in the WisdomTree BioRevolution index, with Twist Bioscience, Moderna and Eli Lilly among the largest at about 4% to 6%.
WDRN: Companies building physical AI such as humanoid robots, drones and the batteries and parts behind them, following a theme index. Tesla and NVIDIA lead at about 5% each, so it is a narrow, tech-heavy basket of fast-changing businesses.
WDTE: An actively managed fund that holds S&P 500 exposure through options and pays out income every week. Selling options caps how much it gains when the market rises, so it trades upside for income and still holds downside risk.
WEAT: A fund that tracks wheat prices by holding wheat futures contracts, which are agreements to buy wheat at a set price later, rather than real grain. Its returns follow wheat prices, which can swing a lot with weather and supply, and the cash-like holdings are just collateral.
WEED: An actively managed fund giving exposure to cannabis companies, including Curaleaf, using stocks and swaps, which are contracts that pay a stock's returns. The Treasury bills are collateral for the swaps, and the fund is concentrated in a small, volatile industry.
WEEI: An actively managed fund of energy companies that also sells options on some of its stocks to earn extra income. Oil giants dominate: ExxonMobil and Chevron together are about 39% of it, so the options income comes with limited upside on those stocks.
WEEK: Treasury bills maturing in three months or less, aiming to pay out income weekly. It works like a place to park cash that earns interest, and because the bills are so short, the price barely moves while the income follows short-term rates.
WEEL: An actively managed income fund that holds sector ETFs and some stocks, then sells options on them in a repeating strategy called the wheel. The option income can add yield, but it limits gains in rising markets and does not protect against falls.
WELD: An actively managed fund of mid-sized US companies that benefit from more manufacturing returning to America, such as makers of industrial parts and automation tools. It is concentrated in roughly 30 stocks, with the top four, including Cognex and Timken, each around 7%.
WEPN: An actively managed fund mixing defense and rare earth companies with other funds and options, aiming to produce income. Cybersecurity firms Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike are each about 10%, and part of it holds metals and steel funds.
WGMI: An actively managed fund of companies that mine bitcoin or supply the power and data center capacity around it. It is very concentrated, with its top four holdings around half the fund, and its fortunes tend to swing with bitcoin's price.
WIMA: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed countries outside the US, with a rules-based twist: it adjusts how much it holds in stocks versus cash-like assets depending on recent market trends. Top holdings such as ASML, HSBC and Novartis are each only a few percent.
WINC: An actively managed fund of bonds from emerging market countries, such as developing economies in Latin America, Asia and Africa, chosen by William Blair's managers. These bonds usually pay more interest than US ones but carry higher risk, and the fund may use derivatives to get exposure.
WINN: A small set of large US companies a manager expects to keep growing for years, with technology at about half and communication, consumer and health care businesses making up much of the rest. It's built for growth, so it tends to swing harder than the broad market.
WIP: Inflation protected government bonds from countries outside the US, whose payouts rise when prices rise. It's a hedge against inflation with some foreign currency exposure, so it can swing with exchange rates and falls when interest rates rise.
WISE: Holds companies tied to artificial intelligence, following a theme index and mostly picking technology firms. It is fairly concentrated, with Advanced Micro Devices at over 10% and a mix of big names like NVIDIA and smaller, lesser-known companies below that.
WLDR: A global stock fund tracking an index of roughly 150 to 250 companies in the US and at least three other countries. Right now it leans toward technology, with Dell, Micron and Seagate each making up about 5% to 7% of it.
WLTG: A fund of funds that holds other ETFs, mainly US stock funds, and shifts between asset classes and sectors based on market trends. It is actively managed and aims for long-term growth rather than tracking one index.
WMSB: An actively managed bond fund that spreads money across several types of bonds, such as corporate, government and securitized debt. The manager chooses the mix rather than following an index, so the holdings can shift over time.
WMTI: A fund built around Walmart stock that aims to pay income while keeping some exposure to Walmart's share price, using options and derivatives. It holds mostly Treasury bills as backing, so it follows a single company and does not match owning the stock.
WNDR: An actively managed fund of companies tied to travel and leisure, such as airlines, hotels, cruise lines, ride sharing and entertainment. Disney, American Express, Uber and Booking are among its biggest holdings, each around 4% to 7%.
WNTR: Pays income while giving inverse exposure to MicroStrategy stock, meaning it aims to gain when the stock falls, using options and swaps. Most of the fund sits in Treasury bills as backing, and it loses when the stock rises sharply.
WOMN: Holds large US companies picked for their record on women's leadership and gender equality, following an index built around that idea. Holdings look like a broad market mix, with Alphabet, Microsoft and NVIDIA each around 4 to 5%.
WOOD: Global companies tied to forests and timberland, such as landowners, paper and packaging makers and wood product producers, following the S&P Global Timber & Forestry Index. It is fairly spread out, but Weyerhaeuser, Smurfit Westrock and West Fraser are each about 7% to 9% of it.
WQTM: A fund tracking an index of companies working on quantum computing, a new kind of computer, including hardware makers, software firms and big tech. It is a narrow theme with some small, volatile names: Quantinuum, D-Wave and Rigetti together are about 18% of it.
WR: An actively managed basket of US companies that could benefit from geopolitical conflict, higher defense spending and US energy security. It leans heavily on energy, at roughly 60% of the fund, with defense and industrial firms and Palantir making up most of the rest.
WRND: Large companies around the world that spend heavily on research and development, picked by an index that treats that spending as a sign of innovation. It is top-heavy with big tech, as Alphabet, NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon together are about 30% of it.
WRTH: An actively managed income fund that sells options to collect premiums, run by a sub-adviser named Worth Charting Group. It keeps most of the money in Treasuries and cash as collateral for the options, which can limit gains when markets rise.
WSDB: An actively managed fund of short-term bonds, mostly US Treasuries and other government-backed debt. Because the bonds mature soon, its price tends to move less than longer-term bond funds when interest rates change.
WSGE: An actively managed fund that gets worldwide stock exposure mostly by holding other ETFs, covering companies of all sizes in the US, developed markets and emerging markets. The top holding, a global equity factor ETF, is about 17% of it.
WSLS: A mix of two US small-company stock approaches: one that buys some stocks and bets against others (long/short), and one that only buys. Because part of it bets against stocks, it can behave quite differently from a plain small-cap index fund.
WSMD: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US companies, selected by Wasatch's research team with an eye on growth. It invests at least 80% in these stocks, so it tends to be more volatile than funds of big companies.
WSML: Small companies from developed countries around the world, held in index-like proportions based on the MSCI World Small Cap Index. It is very spread out, with the largest holdings only about 2% or less, and the US makes up the biggest share.
WSPC: An actively managed fund of global companies in the space economy, such as launch firms, satellite makers and space services. SpaceX is about 16% of the fund, with Rocket Lab next at around 5%, so it leans heavily on a few names.
WTAI: Global companies tied to artificial intelligence, with technology about 80 percent, including memory and chip makers, and some communication and industrial firms. It's a focused growth bet on AI, so it swings far more than the broad market.
WTAL: An actively managed long-short fund that uses swaps and other derivatives to bet on some assets rising and others falling, aiming to profit whichever way markets move. Treasuries and cash are held as collateral for those contracts, not as the main investment.
WTBN: An actively managed bond fund that holds a mix of 5 to 20 other bond ETFs, following an index built by Bianco Research that weights them to hit target factors. It covers Treasuries, corporates and TIPS, so it works as a one stop mix of US bonds.
WTIB: An actively managed fund combining crude oil exposure and bitcoin exposure, mostly through futures contracts and another bitcoin fund, with a lot of cash held as backing. It mixes two very volatile markets, and its returns do not simply follow either one.
WTIP: An actively managed fund mostly holding US Treasury bonds, especially inflation-protected ones (TIPS) whose value adjusts with inflation. It also adds a small amount of other assets, including a bitcoin fund of about 5%, so it is not just plain Treasuries.
WTLS: An actively managed, model driven fund that combines a long/short US stock strategy, betting on some stocks rising and others falling, with a long only strategy. It gets much of its exposure through derivatives, backed by Treasury bills.
WTMF: An actively managed fund that uses futures and currency contracts to follow price trends across assets like stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities, and holds a small bitcoin fund. Most of what it holds is Treasury bills as collateral, not the point of the fund.
WTMU: A broad mix of US municipal bonds with intermediate maturities, spread out over different years in a ladder, where bonds come due steadily. The interest is generally free from federal income tax, and no single issuer is more than about 4% of the fund.
WTMY: A ladder of higher-yielding municipal bonds whose interest is generally exempt from US federal income tax. Many are riskier, lower-rated issuers, such as Puerto Rico and Chicago's school board, so it pays more income but with more credit risk than plain muni funds.
WTPI: A fund that sells put options on the S&P 500, collecting premiums as income, while holding short-term Treasuries as backing. It aims for monthly income with less ups and downs than stocks, but it can lose in sharp drops and trails in strong rallies.
WTRE: Follows an index of real estate companies tied to the digital economy, such as data centers, cell towers and warehouses, from around the world. Equinix, Prologis and Digital Realty are among the top holdings at around 5% each.
WTV: US companies chosen because their prices look low compared with their earnings, spread across financials, technology, health care and consumer staples. It's a value holding for the middle of the market, and it can lag when fast-growing stocks drive returns.
WUGI: An actively managed fund of companies tied to 5G and the digital economy, mostly chipmakers and equipment makers. It is heavy in technology, with Taiwan Semiconductor, Micron and Applied Materials about 21% of the fund.
WWJD: Large companies outside the US, including some from developing countries, screened to meet faith-based values, with industrials, financials, materials and utilities leading. It adds international stocks to a portfolio, and the screen leaves out businesses that conflict with those values.
WZRD: An actively managed fund that trades a mix of stocks, other ETFs and derivatives, with the manager shifting positions opportunistically. Its holdings lean toward technology and consumer companies, and its results depend on the manager's choices rather than an index.
XA: An actively managed fund of cybersecurity companies, firms that make software to defend computers and networks. It is concentrated, with Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike making up about 24% of it, and the whole fund is in technology.
XAGG: A wide mix of bonds, including corporate, mortgage-backed, asset-backed, emerging market and convertible bonds, with financials and real estate the biggest groups. It's meant for higher income than a regular bond fund, in exchange for more risk of losses in downturns.
XAIW: Invests in companies tied to the SpaceX and AI ecosystem, from SpaceX itself to chips and servers from NVIDIA, Dell, Super Micro and TSMC. It is concentrated, with SpaceX alone about 21% of the fund, and mostly technology and industrials.
XAIX: Global companies in artificial intelligence and big data, including chipmakers and software firms, tracking an index of developed and emerging markets. It is tech heavy, with memory makers Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix about 25% of the fund.
XAPR: A fund using options tied to the S&P 500 to give stock market gains up to a limit over a one year period starting in April. It aims to cushion a moderate amount of early losses, and the stated outcomes only apply if held for the whole period.
XAR: Aerospace and defense companies, from aircraft and engine makers to defense contractors and space businesses, all in industrials and held in roughly equal amounts. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it depends on government defense spending and air travel demand, and swings more than the broad market.
