XAUG: Uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to give extra upside, up to a limit, while cushioning part of the losses over a one-year period that resets each August. Gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the whole period.
XB: A basket of US dollar corporate bonds rated B, a middle tier of high yield (also called junk) debt that pays more interest but carries more risk of default. It is spread across hundreds of issuers, and no single bond is more than about 1% of the fund.
XBAP: Uses options tied to the S&P 500 to aim for a defined outcome over a one-year period starting in April. It is built to boost gains up to a cap while absorbing a set amount of losses, so what you get depends on when you buy within the period.
XBB: Corporate bonds from US companies with credit ratings just below investment grade, the top tier of high yield. It aims for higher income than safer bonds, but it can fall in recessions when companies struggle to repay.
XBCI: An income-focused fund tied to Bitcoin, using Bitcoin funds, a Cayman subsidiary and options-style strategies, with a large pile of Treasury bills alongside. Bitcoin prices drive its results, and the options income it aims for can limit gains when Bitcoin rallies.
XBFR: A fund using options on large US stocks to soften a set amount of losses over a one year period, in exchange for limiting how much it can gain. Its stock exposure is top heavy, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft making up about 20% of it.
XBI: Almost entirely biotechnology companies, spread fairly evenly across large and small drug developers rather than weighted toward the giants. It's a focused bet on the biotech industry, and because many holdings are small firms waiting on trial results, it swings much more than the broad market.
XBIL: Short-term US Treasury bills that mature in about six months, so the whole fund is government debt. It's a place to park cash for modest interest with very little price swing, though income drifts down when interest rates fall.
XBJA: Uses options on US large-company stocks to chase more than the market's gains up to a limit, while cushioning a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in January. Results depend on when you buy relative to that period.
XBJL: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF over a one-year period starting in July, aiming to absorb a set amount of losses and to speed up gains up to a cap. Protection only applies if held for the full period.
XBOC: Uses options tied to a US large company index to absorb losses, with a 9% buffer, over a one year period that starts in October. In return, it is able to capture a boosted share of gains up to a cap, so it works best when held for the full period.
XBTY: An options income fund built around Bitcoin, using derivatives on a Bitcoin ETF rather than owning coins directly. It aims to pay high income by selling options, which limits how much it gains if Bitcoin rises, and the Treasury bills it holds are mainly backing.
XC: Emerging market stocks, picked by an index that tries to reflect true emerging economies by leaving out state-owned companies. It is spread widely, with no holding above about 3%, and financials are around a third.
XCCC: US dollar corporate bonds rated CCC, the lowest tier of high-yield (junk) bonds, from companies with weaker finances. They pay higher interest than safer bonds, but there is more risk that borrowers fall behind on payments, and no single bond is above about 2%.
XCEM: Stocks from emerging markets like India, Taiwan and Brazil, with technology just over half and financials about a sixth. It's a growth holding for adding developing economies to a portfolio, and it leaves out China entirely, which sets it apart from most funds in this space.
XCHG: Large US companies chosen by an active manager, with technology the biggest slice at about 37%, followed by financials, communication and industrials. It's a core stock holding that aims to beat the market, though the manager's picks can also lag it.
XCNY: A fund following an S&P index of emerging-market stocks outside China, in places like Taiwan and South Korea. Taiwan Semiconductor alone is about 20% of the fund, and technology is around 40%.
XCOR: An actively managed fund that holds a changing mix of other ETFs, mostly US stock funds with growth, momentum and value styles. The managers rotate between them, and the top few holdings are each about 11% to 13% of the fund.
XCSH: A very short-term fund that uses box spreads, paired options trades that work like a short loan, with an average life under 90 days. It is meant to behave like a cash-like holding that earns interest, with little price movement.
XDAT: Companies that create, store, secure or analyze huge amounts of data, such as cloud, software and cybersecurity firms. It is concentrated, with Cloudflare and Alphabet each around 10% of the fund and technology plus communication stocks making up about 95%.
XDEC: A defined-outcome fund using options on an S&P 500 ETF over a set one-year period starting in December. It aims to cushion part of the losses while taking part of the gains, and results depend on buying at the start of the period.
XDEF: European companies that earn much of their revenue from defense, space and cybersecurity, tracked by a STOXX index with a passive, rules-based approach. It is concentrated in aerospace names: Airbus, Rolls-Royce, Safran and BAE Systems together are about a third of the fund.
XDIV: Gives exposure to the S&P 500 by holding an S&P 500 ETF, but is designed to avoid dividends, tilting returns toward price growth instead of income. Nearly all of it sits in the iShares Core S&P 500 ETF, so it looks like the index of large US companies.
XDQQ: Gives about two times the gains of the Nasdaq-100, through the Invesco QQQ fund, up to a set limit over a three-month period. Losses are not cushioned, so it can fall as much as the index when prices drop.
XDSQ: Gives about two times the gains of the S&P 500 up to a set limit over a three-month period, using options on an S&P 500 fund. In exchange, losses are not cushioned, so it can lose as much as the market if prices fall.
XDTE: A fund that gives exposure to the S&P 500 and sells short term call options on it, collecting that income and paying it out. Because those options are sold with very short lives, they cap gains on big up days while still leaving most of the losses.
XEMD: US-dollar bonds issued by governments and companies in emerging markets, with medium lives of one to ten years. It's meant for higher income than developed-market bonds, but these countries are riskier, so prices can fall when investors get nervous or interest rates rise.
XEML: Large, high-quality European companies picked by a rules-based index, rather than simply the biggest by size. It holds a mix of well-known names like ABB, Novo Nordisk, Richemont, ASML and L'Oreal, each around 5% of the fund.
XES: US companies that make equipment or provide services for oil and gas drilling, tracking an S&P index that weights them roughly equally. That makes it a fairly even mix of smaller firms, with each top holding about 4% to 5%.
XEY: A fund that uses options tied to Ether, the second largest cryptocurrency, to generate income. Selling options brings in cash but limits gains if Ether rises, and it does not simply hold Ether like a plain crypto fund.
XFEB: Uses customized options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to follow the large US companies of the S&P 500 while cushioning a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each February. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
XFIV: US Treasury bonds picked so the average duration, a measure of sensitivity to interest rates, is about five years. It is spread across many Treasuries, each only about 4% of it, so it sits in the middle between short and long.
XFLX: A fund of funds that mostly owns other bond ETFs, mixing corporate, high-yield, floating-rate and investment-grade bonds of different maturities. The manager shifts between them actively, and no single holding is more than about 11% of it.
XHB: US homebuilders and related companies like building materials and home improvement, with consumer discretionary about two thirds. It's a focused bet on housing, so it tends to fall when mortgage rates rise or the housing market cools, and it swings more than the broad market.
XHE: US makers of medical equipment such as devices and diagnostics, from the S&P Health Care Equipment Select Industry Index. It is equally weighted, so smaller companies count as much as bigger ones, and no stock is more than about 3% of the fund.
XHLF: Short US Treasury bills and notes averaging about six months to maturity. It's a very low-risk place to park cash and earn interest, and because the maturities are so short, its price barely moves when interest rates change.
XHS: Small and mid-sized US health care service companies such as clinics, labs and insurers, tracked with the S&P Health Care Services Select Industry Index. It holds many stocks in roughly equal amounts, so no company is above about 2%.
XIDE: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on a US stock ETF to absorb a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in December. It also aims to pay extra income by selling options, which limits how much it can gain.
XIDV: Tracks an index of stocks from developed countries outside the US, chosen to deliver a higher dividend yield without being much more volatile than the broader market. It leans toward financials and energy, with European banks and insurers among the biggest holdings.
XIGV: A fund that tracks an index of 100 large US tech companies with the software businesses left out. That leaves chips, hardware, internet and electric vehicle names, and its biggest positions each make up only about 5%.
XIJN: Uses options tied to a US stock ETF to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts in June, and also sells options to earn extra income. That mix of buffer and income means gains over the period are limited.
XIMR: Uses options tied to a US large company ETF, plus short-term Treasuries, to aim for protection from a set amount of losses over a one-year period that resets each March. It also seeks income from selling options, which limits how much of the market's gains it can capture.
XISE: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to cushion a set amount of losses over a one year period starting in September, and also aims to pay extra income. In return, upside is capped, and it holds some short term Treasuries alongside the options.
XITK: About 50 to 100 US-listed technology companies picked for being in innovative parts of the sector, held in roughly equal amounts. That makes it less top-heavy than most tech funds, with its top holdings each only around 3% to 5%.
XJAN: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to give a boosted share of gains up to a limit, while softening part of the losses over a one-year period starting in January. It holds options rather than stocks, so the outcome depends on when you buy.
XJH: About 400 US mid-sized companies from the S&P MidCap 400, with firms removed if they fail certain environmental, social or governance screens, such as those tied to controversial weapons or tobacco. It is widely spread, with no holding above about 1%.
XJR: Holds small US companies from the S&P SmallCap 600, leaving out those involved in controversial businesses or facing controversies. It is spread thinly across hundreds of stocks, with no holding above about 1%, and no one sector dominates.
XJUL: An options-based fund tied to the S&P 500 through a one-year outcome period starting in July, with a moderate buffer against losses and an enhanced cap on gains. The outcome only applies to those who hold for the full period.
XJUN: A fund that uses customized options on the S&P 500 to cushion part of the losses over a one-year period starting each June. In return, it limits how much of the market's gains you can capture, and the protection only works if held for the full period.
XLB: The materials slice of the S&P 500: chemical makers, mining firms, and packaging and construction materials companies. It's a focused bet on one sector tied to economic cycles, so it swings more than the broad market, and it doesn't hold tech or banks.
XLBI: Holds the Materials Select Sector SPDR fund, which covers chemicals, metals, mining and packaging companies from the S&P 500, and sells call options on it to earn extra income. That options income is meant to boost payouts, but it limits how much the fund gains when materials stocks rally.
XLC: The communication services slice of the S&P 500: social media, search, streaming, telecom and media companies. It's a focused bet on one sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and a couple of giant companies make up a big share of it.
XLCI: Holds the communication services stocks of the S&P 500 through a Select Sector SPDR fund, and adds an options strategy that generates extra income. The options bring in premium payments, but they can limit how much the fund gains when those stocks rally.
XLE: Entirely energy companies, mainly oil and gas producers, refiners and service firms. It's a focused bet on one sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and it rises and falls largely with oil and gas prices.
XLEI: The energy sector of the S&P 500, with an options strategy layered on top to produce extra monthly income. Selling call options caps some of the upside, so it can lag when energy stocks rally strongly.
XLEM: The energy companies of the S&P 500, such as oil and gas producers, refiners and pipeline firms. It tracks the sector slice of the index, so its results are tied closely to oil and gas prices and a few giant companies.
XLF: Nearly all financial companies, covering banks, insurers, and investment and payments firms. It's a focused bet on one sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and it tends to be sensitive to interest rates and the health of the economy.
XLFI: A fund that holds the Financial Select Sector SPDR, the financial companies of the S&P 500, and adds options to produce extra income. Nearly all of it is financials, and the income comes in exchange for limiting some of the upside.
XLG: Just the 50 largest US companies, with technology about half the fund and communication, financials and consumer companies behind. It's a core-style holding with heavy mega-cap concentration, so it leans harder on a few giants than the broad market does.
XLI: Nearly all industrial companies, including aerospace and defense, machinery, airlines, railroads and construction firms. It's a focused bet on one sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and it tends to follow the strength of the economy.
XLII: Holds the industrial companies of the S&P 500 through the Industrial Select Sector SPDR fund, and sells call options on them to earn extra income. That income can be paid out, but the options give up some gains when industrial stocks rally.
XLK: The technology slice of the S&P 500: software makers, chip companies, and computer and networking hardware. It's a focused bet on the tech sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and internet and social media companies are classed in other sectors, so they aren't in it.
XLKI: A fund that holds the Technology Select Sector SPDR (XLK) and sells options on it to generate extra monthly income. Selling those options limits how much it can gain if tech rallies, so it is built for income more than growth.
XLKM: The technology companies of the S&P 500, holding them in roughly the same proportions as the index. It tracks the tech slice of the market, so a handful of giant companies tend to make up a large share of it.
XLP: The consumer staples slice of the S&P 500: makers of food, drinks, household goods and personal care products, plus grocery and discount retailers. It's a defensive holding since people keep buying these items in downturns, though it can trail in strong rallies.
XLPM: The consumer staples companies of the S&P 500, makers and sellers of everyday goods like food, drinks and household products. It tracks the sector slice of the index, which is typically steadier than the overall market but concentrated in a few large companies.
XLRE: Real estate companies only, such as owners of apartments, offices, warehouses, cell towers and shopping centers, drawn from the S&P 500. It's a focused bet on property that pays solid dividends, and it tends to drop when interest rates rise.
XLRI: Holds the real estate stocks of the S&P 500 through a Select Sector SPDR fund, and adds an options strategy that generates extra income. The options bring in premium payments, but they can limit how much the fund gains when real estate stocks rally.
XLSI: Holds the Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR fund, covering makers and sellers of everyday goods like food, drinks and household products, and sells options on it to earn extra income. The options can limit gains when the sector rises, in exchange for that income.
XLSR: A fund of funds that shifts money among S&P 500 sector funds, favoring the sectors the manager expects to do best, now leaning toward technology at about 40%. It's a core stock holding with an active twist, so it can differ sharply from the plain S&P 500.
XLU: The utilities slice of the S&P 500: companies that supply electricity, gas and water. It's a focused sector holding known for steady dividends and steadier swings, but it's sensitive to interest rates and drops when rates rise.
XLUI: Holds the Utilities Select Sector SPDR, the utility companies of the S&P 500 such as electric and gas providers, and sells call options on it to earn extra income. The options give up some gains if utilities rally sharply, in exchange for that income.
XLV: Entirely health care companies, including drug makers, medical device firms, insurers and care providers. It's a focused bet on one sector, often viewed as steadier in downturns, though drug pricing news can move it sharply.
XLVI: Holds the Health Care Select Sector SPDR fund, which owns the health care companies of the S&P 500, and also sells call options to bring in extra income. The options cap some of the upside in strong markets, so it trades some growth for income.
XLY: The consumer discretionary slice of the S&P 500: retailers, carmakers, restaurants and travel companies selling things people want but don't strictly need. It's a focused bet on one sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and a few giants dominate it.
XLYI: Consumer discretionary stocks from the S&P 500, such as Amazon, Tesla and retailers, combined with options that bring in extra income. The income can be higher than regular dividends, but selling options can limit gains when the stocks rally.
XLYM: The consumer discretionary companies of the S&P 500, which sell things people buy when they have spare money, like cars, retail goods, hotels and restaurants. It tracks that slice of the index, so a few large companies carry much of the weight.
XMAG: Tracks an index of the 500 biggest US companies, with the Magnificent 7 tech giants removed. Without them it is more evenly spread, and its biggest holdings, like Broadcom, Micron and Eli Lilly, are each under 5%.
XMAR: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 over a set one-year period starting in March. It aims to gain with the market up to a cap, while cushioning a set amount of losses, and the options are held through a Cboe exchange.
XMAY: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to aim for about double the market's gains up to a set cap, while cushioning a set amount of losses. This only applies over a one-year period starting each May, so buying midway through the year gives a different result.
XME: Metals and mining companies such as steel, aluminum, copper and coal producers, with materials about 80% and energy about 14%. It's a focused bet on a cyclical corner of the market, so it swings more than the broad market and follows commodity prices.
XMHQ: US mid-sized companies chosen for high quality, meaning strong profits and sound finances, with industrials the biggest group at about 30% and technology, financials and health care behind it. It's a core mid-size holding that trades some breadth for sturdier businesses.
XMLV: Mid-sized US companies picked for the lowest price swings, heavy in financials, real estate and utilities, with little technology. It's meant to be a steadier way to own mid-size stocks, so it usually falls less in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
XMMO: Mid-sized US companies whose stock prices have been rising fastest lately, led by technology, industrials, health care and energy. It's a momentum bet on recent winners, and it can drop quickly when market leadership changes.
XMPT: Holds closed-end funds that themselves own municipal bonds, whose interest is generally free of federal income tax, so it is a fund of funds. Many of these funds trade at a discount or premium and use borrowing, which can make it bumpier than ordinary muni funds.
XMVM: Mid-sized US companies chosen for being cheaply priced and having recent price momentum, about 80 stocks. Financials are the biggest slice at over a third, then energy and consumer companies, so it's a value-style tilt and swings more than a broad market fund.
XNAV: A fund of other ETFs, chosen by the manager to lean into aggressive and sector-focused US stocks. Because it holds funds rather than individual companies, it is spread across many stocks, but more than half of it is in technology.
XNOV: A defined-outcome fund using options on the S&P 500 to cushion part of the losses over a one-year period starting in November. In exchange for boosted gains up to a cap, it limits how much of the upside it can keep.
XNTK: Large technology and tech-related companies, with about six sevenths in tech and small slices in communication and consumer firms. It's a concentrated growth bet on the tech sector, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
XOCT: An S&P 500 fund that uses options to cushion some losses over a one-year period starting in October while allowing gains up to a cap. It holds those options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF, so the protection only applies if held for the full year.
XOEF: The 400 or so large US companies in the S&P 500 that are not among the 100 biggest in the S&P 100. It is a way to hold the middle of the large-company market without the mega-cap giants, and no holding is above about 2%.
XOEX: A fund that holds the S&P 100 index with its 20 biggest companies taken out. That removes the mega-cap names, leaving large firms like AMD, Intel, Cisco and Caterpillar, none of which is above about 6%.
XOMO: Aims to earn income from Exxon Mobil stock using a synthetic covered call strategy, which uses options instead of owning the shares. It mostly holds Treasury bills as backing, pays out options income, and gives up some gains if Exxon rises sharply.
XONE: Short-term US Treasury bills and notes that average about one year until repayment, backed by the federal government. It's a place to park cash-like money for steady interest, and with such short maturities its price barely moves when interest rates change.
XOP: Oil and gas drillers and producers, almost all energy, with no big refiners or pipelines in the mix. It's a focused bet on energy prices, and since the companies are equal sized and many are small, it swings far more than the broad market.
XOVR: Growth-minded stocks led by technology, with communication companies and health care making up most of the rest. It also holds private companies through special investment vehicles, which makes it a more adventurous growth pick that can swing more than the broad market.
XPAY: Holds SPY FLEX options, tied to the S&P 500, to provide steady monthly income payouts at a target level. The structure limits how much it gains when the market rises, and its payouts are not the same as the dividends from the companies.
XPH: US drug companies, covering both large pharmaceutical makers and smaller ones. It's a focused bet on one health care industry, so it swings more than the broad market, and its equal-style weighting gives smaller companies a bigger role than usual.
XPND: A mix of large technology companies plus finance and communications companies that rely on technology, picked by an investment adviser and tracked by an index. It holds well-known names like Cisco, Broadcom, Lam Research and Alphabet, each around 5%.
XQBT: Holds a basket of about ten companies in quantum computing, from big names like Alphabet and Amazon to specialists like D-Wave and Rigetti. It is concentrated, with the top few holdings making up a large share, and a chunk is held in short-term government funds.
XQQI: An actively managed fund holding Nasdaq-100 stocks and selling options on them to generate extra income. That income can be large, but selling options limits how much it benefits when the market rises, and NVIDIA and Apple are about 14% of it.
XRLX: A fund of funds that mostly owns other ETFs, mixing stock funds such as growth and momentum with some balanced funds. The manager shifts the mix actively, and the largest holdings are Vanguard Growth at about 9% and an S&P 500 Top 50 fund at about 8%.
XRMI: Holds the stocks of the S&P 500 and sells call options on them (a covered-call collar) to generate monthly income. The options give up some gains in strong markets, and the fund is top-heavy, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft about 20% of it.
XRP: Holds the XRP digital token directly, so it has no companies, bonds or income behind it. It's a focused bet on a single cryptocurrency, and its price can swing wildly in a day.
XRPC: Holds XRP, a cryptocurrency, directly, with the coins stored by Gemini Trust Company and BitGo Trust Company. Its value follows the price of XRP, which can swing sharply, and it holds nothing else.
XRPI: A fund that aims to give exposure to the price of XRP, a digital currency that runs on the XRP Ledger. It holds XRP or contracts tied to it rather than stocks, so its value rises and falls with the crypto market.
XRPM: A fund giving exposure to the price of XRP, a cryptocurrency, while selling options on XRP ETFs to earn monthly income. The options cap some of the gains, and the fund holds a Canary XRP ETF and a short-term bond fund.
XRPR: A fund giving exposure to XRP, the cryptocurrency linked to the XRP Ledger, held partly directly and partly through other crypto products. About 59% is XRP itself, so it moves with the price of a single crypto asset and pays no regular income.
XRPZ: Holds XRP, the digital token linked to the XRP Ledger payments network, directly and passively. It does not use leverage or derivatives, so its price follows XRP, which can swing sharply, and it does not trade in or out to time the market.
XRT: Tracks the S&P Retail Select Industry Index, covering US retail companies such as clothing, home goods, online and grocery sellers. It holds each company in about equal amounts, so smaller retailers matter as much as the giants, and no single stock is more than about 2%.
XSD: Chip companies in the S&P Semiconductor index, which spreads money more evenly across large and small firms than most chip funds. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it swings far more than the broad market and rises and falls with chip demand.
XSEP: A defined outcome fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 (via the SPDR S&P 500 ETF) to aim for boosted gains up to a limit and a cushion against part of the losses. The outcome period runs about a year starting each September, and it only applies if you hold the whole period.
XSHD: Around 60 small US companies with high dividend yields and lower price swings, chosen by an S&P index. Real estate makes up about 40% of it, and it holds names like Innovative Industrial, Kinetik and Easterly Government Properties.
XSHP: An income fund built around SpaceX stock and contracts tied to its price, with a portfolio of bonds behind them. It uses options to generate income, which limits how much of SpaceX's gains it can capture, so it is a bet on a single company.
XSHQ: A fund that tracks the S&P SmallCap 600 Quality index, which picks the highest-quality small US companies based on profitability, earnings stability and low debt. It holds many stocks in small slices, none above about 3%, and leans toward financials, technology and industrials.
XSLV: The 100 least volatile stocks from the S&P SmallCap 600, with calmer stocks getting bigger weights. It leans heavily on real estate, utilities and financials, so it behaves differently from a typical small company fund.
XSMO: Small US companies chosen because their share prices have been climbing fastest lately, spread across technology, health care, financials and real estate. It's a growth-leaning way to own small companies, and momentum picks can reverse quickly, so it swings more than large-company funds.
XSOE: Emerging market stocks, with technology around two fifths and financials about a seventh. It's a growth holding for developing economies that screens out companies controlled by governments, which sets it apart from standard emerging market funds.
XSPC: Holds companies tied to space, satellites and artificial intelligence. It is concentrated: Space Exploration Technologies is about 16% and Palantir and NVIDIA add roughly 15% more, with industrials and tech making up almost all of it.
XSPI: An actively managed fund that holds the stocks of the S&P 500 and sells call options on the index to produce high monthly income. Selling those options limits how much it can gain in a strong market, and NVIDIA and Apple are about 14% of it.
XSVM: Small US companies that look cheap and have been rising lately, with financials such as banks making up almost half. It's a value-and-momentum play on smaller stocks, so it leans heavily on one industry and can swing more than the broad market.
XSVN: US Treasury bonds managed to keep an average sensitivity to interest rates of about seven years. It's meant as a medium-term, government-backed bond holding and a cushion for stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
XSW: Software and online services companies, with technology making up roughly 90% and a small slice of financials. It's a focused bet on one fast-moving corner of tech, with companies of all sizes weighted fairly evenly, so it swings more than the broad market.
XT: Companies building new technologies such as AI, robotics, genomics and cloud computing, with technology 45% and health care 26%. It's a growth bet on innovation spread across several themes, so it swings more than the broad market.
XTAP: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to aim for more than the market's gains up to a cap, while cushioning part of the losses. It only works as designed over a one-year period starting each April, and the fund also holds an S&P 500 fund directly.
XTEN: US Treasury notes and bonds picked so the fund's average sensitivity to interest rates matches that of a ten-year Treasury. It's a pure government bond holding for safety and income, and its price falls noticeably when interest rates rise.
XTJA: Uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to magnify gains, up to a limit, over a set period that starts each January. It can still lose money if the index falls, and results only line up with the design when held for the full period.
XTJL: A defined outcome fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 over a set one-year period starting in July. It aims to boost gains up to a limit by a multiple, but it takes on losses too, so the result depends on holding for the full period.
XTL: Telecom-related US companies, with technology firms such as communications equipment makers at nearly 60% and traditional communication services around a third. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it swings more than the broad market and is not mainly phone company stocks.
XTN: US transportation companies like airlines, trucking, railroads and shipping, held in roughly equal amounts using the S&P Transportation Select Industry Index. Airlines are a big part of it, with Allegiant, American, United, Alaska and JetBlue each near 3%.
XTOC: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to follow the S&P 500 over a set one-year period starting in October. It aims to magnify gains up to a cap while taking on the losses, and the outcome only applies if held for the full period.
XTR: The S&P 500 stocks plus put options, which pay off when the market drops, to soften big losses. The cost of those options can drag on returns in calm markets, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 20% of the fund.
XTRE: Holds US Treasury bonds chosen so that their average duration is about three years, which measures how sensitive prices are to interest rate changes. That puts it in between short-term bills and long bonds, with government backing on everything it holds.
XTWO: US Treasury bonds chosen so the portfolio's average duration is about two years, meaning its price moves moderately when interest rates change. It holds only government debt spread across many issues, so it is a short-to-medium term Treasury fund rather than a cash substitute.
XTWY: US Treasury bonds with an overall length of about 20 years, including Treasury STRIPS that pay nothing until maturity, tracking a Bloomberg index. Because the bonds are so long, its price swings a lot when interest rates move.
XUDV: Large US companies with high dividend yields, chosen from a large-cap index and weighted to boost income. Holdings like UPS, Pfizer, Altria and Kraft Heinz are each about 5%, so it leans toward mature dividend payers.
XUSM: A fund of stocks outside the US that have shown positive price momentum, meaning they have been rising over recent months. It is evenly spread, with no holding above about 2%, and it leans toward technology and electronics makers.
XUSP: An actively managed options fund that aims to deliver more than the S&P 500's price gain, within limits, over a set one year period, with no cap on upside. The extra boost applies only if held through the full period, and it can lose money when stocks fall.
XV: A fund that aims to pay out monthly income at an annual rate of 15% by combining interest from short-term holdings with an options spread strategy. That target is a goal, not a promise, and much of the fund sits in a Simplify money market fund.
XVAD: Holds AMD stock and sells options on it to generate income, so about half of the fund is in that single company. The options bring extra payouts but limit how much it can gain if the stock jumps, while still exposing it to losses.
XVAP: Holds Apple stock and sells options on it to generate income, so about half of the fund is in that single company. The options bring extra payouts but limit how much it can gain if the stock jumps, while still exposing it to losses.
XVAZ: A mix of Amazon stock and options on it, run to produce regular income. Amazon is about half of the fund, so it rides mostly on one company, and the options give up some upside in exchange for the income.
XVGL: A mix of Alphabet (Google) stock and options on it, run to produce regular income. Alphabet is about half of the fund, so it rides mostly on one company, and the options give up some upside in exchange for the income.
XVMS: Holds Microsoft stock and sells options on it to generate income, so about half of the fund is in that single company. The options bring extra payouts but limit how much it can gain if the stock jumps, while still exposing it to losses.
XVMT: A mix of Meta Platforms stock and options on it, run to produce regular income. Meta is about half of the fund, so it is tied closely to one company, and the options give up some upside in exchange for the income.
XVNV: Holds NVIDIA stock and sells options on it to generate income, so about half of the fund is in that single company. The options bring extra payouts but limit how much it can gain if the stock jumps, while still exposing it to losses.
XVPT: Holds Palantir stock and sells options on it to generate income, so about half of the fund is in that single company. The options bring extra payouts but limit how much it can gain if the stock jumps, while still exposing it to losses.
XVSP: Holds SpaceX stock and sells options on it to generate income, so about half of the fund is in that single company. The options bring extra payouts but limit how much it can gain if the stock jumps, while still exposing it to losses.
XVTS: A fund that holds Tesla stock and sells options on it to bring in extra income. Tesla is about three quarters of the fund, and the options limit how much it gains if the stock jumps.
XVV: Large US companies, with technology the biggest slice at nearly half, followed by financials and health care. It's a core stock holding that screens out firms with controversial businesses, so it can differ a bit from the plain S&P 500.
XWNG: An actively managed fund investing in about ten of the biggest space-related companies, such as satellite, aerospace and defense suppliers, including SpaceX. It is concentrated, and a large slice at the time was in short-term government money-market holdings.
XX: A defined outcome fund built from options on an S&P 500 ETF, shaped to behave like a call option with a 10,000 index target and a 2030 end date. It pays off if the market climbs toward that level by then, and it can lose value if not.
XXQQ: Companies from the Nasdaq-100, the index of 100 large non-financial Nasdaq stocks, minus a list of excluded companies the fund's sponsor chooses to avoid. It follows the growth-heavy tech tilt of that index but with those names removed, so it differs from a plain Nasdaq-100 fund.
XXSP: The companies in the S&P 500, the index of 500 large US stocks, minus a list of excluded companies the fund's sponsor chooses to avoid. It otherwise tracks the broad US market, so it is close to, but not the same as, a plain S&P 500 fund.
XXV: An actively managed income fund that mostly holds Treasury bills for interest and adds an options spread strategy to produce extra income. The aim is a regular payout, but the options part can limit gains or add losses, so it is more complex than a bond fund.
XXX: About three quarters of this fund is in the S&P 500, the 500 largest US companies, and about a quarter is in XRP, a cryptocurrency. It mixes a broad stock index with a risky crypto bet.
XYLD: Large US stocks, about 40 percent technology, paired with an options strategy that sells away much of the upside in exchange for regular income. It aims to pay out steady cash, but it trails in strong rallies and still drops when the market falls.
XYLG: Holds the stocks of the S&P 500 and sells call options on half of them, a covered call strategy, to collect extra income. That limits some upside when the market rallies, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft make up around 20% of it.
XYZY: Aims to pay income while tracking the share price of one stock, XYZ (Block), indirectly through options rather than owning the shares. Gains are limited if the stock soars, it does not protect against falls, and it is backed mostly by Treasury bills.
YALL: US stocks chosen to reflect a faith-and-America-first theme, with holdings spread across all eleven market sectors. It looks like a broad large-company fund, with Broadcom, NVIDIA and Tesla each making up around 7% of it, but its picks come from a custom method, not a standard index.
YBIT: An actively managed fund that gets indirect exposure to bitcoin through bitcoin ETPs and sells options on them to produce income. That options trade caps its gains if bitcoin jumps, and the fund mostly holds Treasury bills as backing.
YBST: A fund of other GraniteShares YieldBOOST ETFs, each one earning income from options on a single popular stock like Amazon, Meta, AMD and TSMC. It pays weekly income, spread evenly across many holdings, but options income caps the gains it can capture.
YBTC: Aims to pay monthly income by selling call options tied to Bitcoin ETFs, which caps some gains if Bitcoin rises. It does not hold Bitcoin directly, and the Treasury bills listed are collateral for the options.
YBTY: A fund of funds holding GraniteShares YieldBOOST ETFs, each of which uses options on a volatile stock to generate income, such as SMCI, Micron, Rigetti, D-Wave and Robinhood. It aims for weekly payouts, but those income strategies cap gains and can lose value.
YCLO: An actively managed fund that mostly holds collateralized loan obligations, which are bundles of company loans packaged together and sold in slices. Their payments usually float with short term interest rates, and the fund targets income.
YDEC: Uses options on the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, a basket of developed market stocks outside North America, to follow its price over a one-year period. It buffers a moderate amount of losses in return for a cap on gains, and the cycle resets each December.
YETH: Aims to pay monthly income using a covered call strategy tied to Ether, the second-largest cryptocurrency, mostly through options rather than owning it directly. Selling those options caps how much it gains when Ether rises, and its cash is held mainly in Treasury bills.
YFFI: An actively managed bond fund that mixes corporate bonds, Treasury securities, asset backed securities and preferred stocks, aiming for higher yield. Holdings are spread thin, with no single issuer above about 2%, and many are familiar US companies like Prudential, American Express and Disney.
YFYA: A fund of other ETFs, mostly ultrashort bond and income funds plus some preferred and high-yield bonds, aiming for steady income. It owns funds rather than individual securities, and a few of those holdings use options to boost income.
YGLD: Aims for gold exposure of up to about 150% of the fund's size using gold futures, while also earning income from an options strategy on other ETFs. Because of that extra exposure, it can move more than the price of gold itself.
YJUN: Gives exposure to developed markets outside the US and Canada, through options on the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, over a set one-year period starting in June. A set amount of losses is cushioned, but gains are capped, and the outcome only applies if you hold the full period.
YLD: Bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, which pay more interest to make up for the extra risk, with a bit of cash on the side. It's for higher income than safer bonds, and it tends to fall with stocks in downturns because defaults rise.
YLDE: Dividend-paying large US and global stocks, with call options sold on part of the portfolio to bring in extra income. That income comes at the cost of giving up some gains if stocks jump, and the fund is actively managed.
YLDW: An actively managed mix of dividend-paying stocks and some bonds, aimed at producing income. It also uses options to boost income, and about three-quarters of it is in stocks such as Gilead, Microsoft, Merck and NVIDIA.
YLDY: An actively managed fund of large US company stocks that also sells options on broad stock indexes to bring in income. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 20% of it, and the options can limit gains in strong markets.
YMAG: A fund of funds that holds YieldMax option income ETFs, each tied to one of the Magnificent Seven stocks like Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, NVIDIA and Apple. It aims to pay high income from options on those stocks, which limits gains when they rise and still leaves room for big losses.
YMAR: Uses options on the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, a basket of developed market stocks outside North America, to follow its price over a one-year period. It buffers a moderate amount of losses in exchange for a cap on gains, and it resets each March.
YMAX: A fund of funds that mostly holds other YieldMax ETFs, each of which sells options on a single stock to produce income. Those funds give up some gains when their stock rises, so this is a spread-out collection of option income funds.
YNOT: An actively managed fund of US and foreign companies tied to emerging technologies, mostly in tech. It is fairly top-heavy: NVIDIA, Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon together are about 27% of the fund, and the managers choose stocks rather than following an index.
YOKE: An actively managed fund that shifts between US and international stocks according to a tactical strategy that adjusts to market conditions. It holds a spread of stocks, with Alphabet, EMCOR, NVIDIA and Rolls-Royce among the biggest at about 4% each.
YOLO: An actively managed fund investing in companies tied to the cannabis industry, including growers and sellers such as Curaleaf, Trulieve and Village Farms. It is concentrated, with the top few holdings making up more than half of it, and cannabis stocks can swing sharply.
YQQQ: Aims to pay income while moving opposite to the Nasdaq-100, so it can gain when that index falls. Its upside is limited, and it mostly holds Treasury bills with options layered on top, which can mean losses when tech rallies.
YRAM: A fund focused on memory and storage chip companies such as Micron, SanDisk, Seagate and Western Digital, using options to earn extra income. The options limit gains if the stocks rally, and a large part of the fund sits in cash-like holdings.
YSAG: A fund that holds physical silver bars, so its price follows the price of silver. It does not pay income, and silver prices can swing quite a lot, so the value can rise or fall sharply.
YSAU: Physical gold bars held in a vault, so the fund's price follows the price of gold. It holds no stocks or bonds, and the gold is delivered to and from large trading firms when shares are created or redeemed.
YSEP: Uses options tied to developed markets outside the US, through the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, to aim for a defined outcome over a one-year period starting in September. It is built to cushion part of the losses in exchange for a cap on gains.
YSPC: Aims to give income and exposure to the price of SpaceX, a private rocket and satellite company, using options and other contracts rather than owning shares. The Treasury bills it holds are mostly backing for those contracts, so results depend on how its options strategy works.
YSPY: Aims to pay high income by selling options on a 3x leveraged S&P 500 fund, so it keeps some exposure to the market but caps how much it can gain. It holds mostly Treasury bills as backing, and it is complicated, with risk from leverage.
YUNG: An actively managed fund of US companies tied to longevity and consumer spending, such as health care, insurers, travel and senior housing. Eli Lilly alone is about 14% of the fund, and health care is the biggest sector at around 45%.
YXI: A bet against the 50 largest Hong Kong-listed Chinese companies, aiming to move opposite to the FTSE China 50 Index each day. It uses derivatives and resets daily, so over longer periods the results can drift away from simply the opposite of the index.
YYY: A fund of closed-end funds, holding other funds that mostly own bonds and stocks and pay high income. It's built for income, and the underlying funds use borrowing, so it can drop sharply in sell-offs.
YYYM: Follows an index of closed-end funds that hold municipal bonds, so it is a fund of funds. It aims for tax-advantaged income from higher yielding muni bonds, with each holding only about 4%, and the funds it owns can use borrowing, which adds risk.
ZALT: Large US stocks, with technology about 40 percent, held through options that absorb the first 10 percent of market losses over each three month period. It's for cautious investors who want stock exposure with a cushion, but gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
ZAP: US-listed companies involved in electrification, meaning utilities that generate and deliver power plus the firms that make electrical equipment and build grid infrastructure. About three quarters is utilities, with Dominion, Quanta, Eaton and AMETEK each at roughly 4% to 5% of the fund.
ZAPR: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to protect against a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each April. In return, gains are limited, and the protection only fully works if you hold from the start to the end.
ZAUG: Uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to follow the S&P 500 over a one-year period starting each August. It aims to protect against a set amount of losses in return for giving up part of the gains, and it resets every August.
ZCBA: Zero-coupon US Treasury bonds that mature in 2030, tracking an FTSE index. These bonds pay no interest along the way and are bought at a discount, so the fund's price is quite sensitive to interest rate changes until maturity.
ZCBB: Zero-coupon US Treasury bonds that mature in 2031, tracking an FTSE index. These bonds pay no interest along the way and are bought at a discount, so the fund's price is quite sensitive to interest rate changes until maturity.
ZCBC: Zero-coupon US Treasury bonds that mature in 2032, tracking an FTSE index. These bonds pay no interest along the way and are bought at a discount, so the fund's price is quite sensitive to interest rate changes until maturity.
ZCBE: Zero-coupon US Treasury bonds that mature in 2033, tracking an index of such bonds. These bonds pay no interest along the way and are bought at a discount, so the fund's price is quite sensitive to interest rate changes until maturity.
ZCBF: Zero coupon US Treasury bonds that mature in 2034, tracking the FTSE Zero Coupon U.S. Treasury STRIPS 2034 Maturity Index. These bonds pay no interest along the way and are bought at a discount, so the price swings more than normal bonds when interest rates move.
ZCBG: Zero coupon US Treasury bonds that mature in 2035, tracking the FTSE Zero Coupon U.S. Treasury STRIPS 2035 Maturity Index. These bonds pay no interest along the way and are bought at a discount, so the price swings more than normal bonds when interest rates move.
ZCSH: Holds Zcash, a cryptocurrency built around private transactions, rather than stocks or bonds. It gives brokerage account access to that single digital coin as a speculative bet, and its price can swing wildly from day to day, with no earnings or interest behind it.
ZDEK: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund over a one-year period starting each December to protect against a set amount of losses. In exchange, it limits how much of the market's gains you can capture, and the protection only works if held the full period.
ZDIS: An actively managed fund of fast growing US companies that are still relatively early in their growth. It is fairly concentrated, with Tesla, NVIDIA, Credo, Axon and Shopify each making up around 6% to 9% of it, and technology is about half.
ZECP: A portfolio of large US companies that have held up steadily through past recessions, chosen using a Zacks earnings-consistency screen. It is fairly top-heavy: Alphabet, Apple and Microsoft are about 23% of it, with industrial and financial names behind them.
ZFEB: A defined outcome fund using options on the S&P 500 over a set one-year period starting in February. It aims to protect against a set amount of losses at the end of the period, and in return gains are capped.
ZHDG: A fund that owns a large stock position in the S&P 500 and adds options and bonds to hedge, meaning to soften, market drops. The hedging gives up some gains, and it uses leverage-like exposure, so it holds more than 100% in stocks.
ZHOG: An actively managed bond fund that mixes corporate bonds, mortgage-backed securities, Treasuries and other bond funds to earn income. It can hold lower-rated debt as well as safer bonds, so it is a flexible blend rather than tracking one index.
ZIG: An actively managed fund holding about 30 US stocks that the manager thinks are undervalued but fundamentally strong, picked from the largest 25% of companies. It is a small, concentrated basket, with consumer discretionary and energy companies making up about two thirds of it.
ZINC: An actively managed fund of US stocks that its adviser considers good at producing income, mostly dividend payers. It leans toward financials, utilities, consumer staples and energy, with Altria, JPMorgan Chase, NorthWestern Energy and Chevron each making up roughly 3% to 5%.
ZINN: An actively managed fund of US growth companies that the manager believes are innovative and can expand quickly. It is fairly concentrated, with NVIDIA, AMD and Tesla each around 7% to 8% of the fund, and it leans toward tech and industrials.
ZJAN: Uses options tied to the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to follow the US stock market over a one-year period that starts each January. The options are designed to absorb a set amount of losses, so the fund gives up some upside in exchange for that protection.
ZJUL: Uses options on the S&P 500 to guard against losses over a one-year period that starts in July, with protection from a defined outcome strategy. It gives up some of the gains in exchange, and the protection only fully applies if held through the whole period.
ZJUN: A defined outcome fund using options on the S&P 500 over a set one-year period starting in June. It aims to protect against a set amount of losses at the end of the period, and in return gains are capped.
ZMAR: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund over a one-year period starting each March to protect against a set amount of losses. In exchange, it limits how much of the market's gains you can capture, and the protection only works if held for the full period.
ZMAY: A defined outcome fund that holds options on the S&P 500 over a one-year period starting in May, built to cushion a set amount of losses. In return, gains are limited, and the protection only applies to someone holding from the start of the period to its end.
ZNOV: Uses options tied to the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to follow the US stock market over a one-year period that starts each November. The options are designed to absorb a set amount of losses, so the fund gives up some upside in exchange for that protection.
ZOCT: Uses options tied to the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to follow the US stock market over a one-year period that starts each October. The options are designed to absorb a set amount of losses, so the fund gives up some upside in exchange for that protection.
ZROZ: Zero coupon US Treasury bonds that mature in about 25 years or more, which pay no interest until the end. They are very safe from default and can cushion a stock portfolio in a downturn, but prices swing sharply when interest rates move, especially upward.
ZSEP: A fund that uses options on an S&P 500 fund to protect against part of the losses over a one-year period starting each September. In return, there is a limit on how much it can gain, and the protection only applies if you hold the full year.
ZTAX: A fund of intermediate-term US municipal bonds, which are loans to state and local governments. The interest is exempt from federal and state income tax, and it is an actively managed bond fund holding mostly municipal debt.
ZTEN: Holds investment grade corporate bonds, meaning debt from companies considered likely to repay, with maturities around ten years. Because of that longer maturity, its price moves more when interest rates change than a short-term bond fund, and it is spread over many issuers.
ZTOP: Follows an index of high-yield bonds, meaning bonds from lower-rated companies that pay more interest, from the 100 largest issuers in the Bloomberg U.S. Corporate High Yield Index. Each issuer gets a similar weight of about 1%, so no one company dominates.
ZTRE: Investment grade US corporate bonds with roughly three years left until they come due, following a rules-based index. It is spread very thinly, with each of the top bonds only about 0.2% of the fund, so no single borrower matters much.
ZTWO: Investment-grade corporate bonds from US companies with about two years left to maturity, so it is a lower-risk way to earn corporate bond income. It holds a lot of bonds, with none above a fraction of a percent, and its price moves little.
ZVOL: An actively managed fund that tries to earn money from the way investors overpay for protection against market swings, using volatility-linked contracts. Its holdings are mostly derivatives, not ordinary stocks or bonds, so it behaves very differently from a plain stock fund.
